# Glossary

## Ü
The central province of Tibet surrounding Lhasa.

## Āśā
*nyer gnas*, Skt. *āśā*, One of the eight goddesses in the north, called upon to grant protection.

## Āṇā
*ANA*, Skt. *āṇā*, Unidentified; occurs in a mantra of enthrallment.

## Īṣāṇa
*yongs su tshol ba*, Skt. *īṣāṇa*, A land in the south of India.

## Śaśī
*zla ba’i lha mo*, Skt. *śaśī*, ‟Moon Goddess,” in the Bhūtaḍāmara maṇḍala she is one of the eight goddesses of offerings.

## a bodhisattva’s full maturity
*byang chub sems dpa’i skyon med pa*, Skt. *bodhi­sattva­nyāma*, See also “immaturity” and .

## a body that is beautiful in all respects
*kun nas mdzes pa*, Skt. *samanta­prāsādika*, Thirty-ninth of the eighty minor signs.

## a feeling of remorse
One of a common list of eleven positive mental states (kuśalacaittya) found in Buddhist abhidharma lists. Remorse is what one feels after having realized that one has done something wrong, and it serves as a mental state that hinders one from engaging in such wrong actions again. Often paired with hrī (ngo tsha shes pa).

## A Nga
The third Degé king, Pönchen A Nga (mid-fifteenth to early sixteenth century), was the head of the house of Degé in its thirty-third generation. He had two sons (though here it mentions seven), of whom the elder, Joden Namkha Lhunsang, took monastic vows and the younger, Yangyal Pal, took over the Degé kingdom. For more on his life see his entry at The Treasury of Lives.

## a person who makes things allowable
*rung ba byed pa*, Skt. *kalpikāra*, A layperson who makes things legally permissible in the context of Buddhist monastic law, doing tasks that are not allowed for monks.

## a practitioner without a dwelling
*gnas med par spyod pa*, Skt. *aniketacārī*, A meditative stability.

## a sense of shame
One of a common list of eleven positive mental states (kuśalacaittya) found in Buddhist abhidharma lists. Shame is what one feels after having realized that one has done something wrong, and it serves as a mental state that hinders one from engaging in such wrong actions again. Often paired with apatrāpya (khrel yod pa).

## A Thousand Houses
*khang bu stong*, Skt. *khang bu stong*, Refers to Encircled by a Thousand Houses in Ornament of the Mind.

## Aṃśa
*cha shas*, Skt. *aṃśa*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Aṭaṭa
*so thams thams*, Skt. *aṭaṭa*, One of the eight cold hells.

## Aṇḍabha
*sgo nga’i ’od*, Skt. *aṇḍabha*, A yakṣa general.

## Aṣṭabhaginīya
The name of a family lineage.

## Aṣṭaṃga
*nub*, Skt. *aṣṭaṃga*, A mountain in the west, called upon to grant wealth and protection.

## Aḍagavatī
The name of the capital city in the abode of Vajrapāṇi, as attested in the Sanskrit manuscript of this sūtra. The manuscript of the sūtra contains the variant spelling Abhagavatī, which could be a spelling error, though it occurs multiple times in the manuscript. The spelling of the name can vary in other texts, too, as the same term is attested for Alakāvatī, Aḍakavatī, and Aṭakāvatī in other sources. Its precise relationship to Alakāvatī, the capital of Vaiśravaṇa, as given in the Mahābhārata, is not entirely clear.

## Aṣṭa­grahāṣṭāviṃśati­nakṣatra­śrī
*gza’ brgyad dang rgyu skar nyi shu rtsa brgyad kyi dpal*, Skt. *aṣṭa­grahāṣṭāviṃśati­nakṣatra­śrī*, One of the names of Śrī Mahādevī.

## Ṣaḍaṅgula
*sor mo drug pa*, Skt. *ṣaḍaṅgula*, A nāga king.

## Aṭṭahāsa
*ha ha drag tu rgod pa*, Skt. *aṭṭahāsa*, The name of the great southeastern charnel ground.

## Aśaja
*yan lag skyes*, Skt. *aśaja*, One of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin.

## Aṣṭaka
*brgyad pa*, Skt. *aṣṭaka*, A ṛṣi in the past.

## Ṣaḍakṣarī
*yi ge drug pa*, Skt. *ṣaḍakṣarī*, The four armed goddess who is the embodiment of the six-syllable mantra. Though female in Sanskrit, it is translated into Tibetan as a male name.

## Aḍakavatī
*lcang lo can*, Skt. *aḍakavatī*, The main palace of the abode of the yakṣas on Mount Sumeru. It is ruled by the great king Vaiśravaṇa, also known as Kubera.

## Aṣṭamaka
*brgyad pa*, Skt. *aṣṭamaka*, A great ṛṣi.

## Aṣṭamaka level
*brgyad pa’i sa*, Skt. *aṣṭamakabhūmi*, Lit. “Eighth level,” sometimes rendered “Eighth Lowest.” The third of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the level of an ordinary person until reaching buddhahood. See “ten levels.”

## Aśanī
Skt. *aśanī*, A great rākṣasī.

## Aśani
*gnam lcags*, Skt. *aśani*, Lightning; also lightning personified.

## Aṭavī
*’brog*, Skt. *aṭavī*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Aṭavaka
*dz+ya Ta ba ka*, Skt. *aṭavaka*, A nāga king.

## Aḍavi
*brog gnas*, Skt. *aḍavi*, The name, possibly corrupt, of a country in ancient India.

## Aṭavika
*’brog gnas*, Skt. *aṭavika*, A certain yakṣa lord tamed by the Buddha.

## Aṭavika’s great city
*’brog gnas kyi grong khyer chen po*, The location where the Buddha taught The Dhāraṇī “The Mother of the Grahas.” Aṭavika is the name of a yakṣa lord.

## Aṭavīsaṃbhavā
*dgon pa na yod pa*, Skt. *aṭavīsaṃbhavā*, A lake in a wilderness. (Toh 556: ’brog khong khong na yod)

## Abala
*a ba la*, Skt. *abala*, The name of one of the eight nāga kings who obey the eight deities in Gaṇapati’s nine-section maṇḍala.

## Śabala
One of Yama’s two watchdogs.

## Abandoned Affliction

## abandoned the five branches
*yan lag lnga spangs pa*, [Buddha](#buddha)s have abandoned five branches or factors that perpetuate [saṃsāra](#saṃsāra): pursuing desires, ill will, lethargy and languor, regret and agitation, and [view](#view) and doubt.

## Abandoner of Anger
*tha spangs ma*, Skt. *tha spangs ma*, Mother of the buddha Merudhvaja.

## Abandoning Displeasure
*mi dga’ spong*, Skt. *mi dga’ spong*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Guṇagaṇa.

## Abandoning Doubt
*yid gnyis spong ba po*, Skt. *yid gnyis spong ba po*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Maṇiviśuddha (961 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Abandoning Doubts
*yid gnyis spong ba*, Skt. *yid gnyis spong ba*, Mother of the buddha Tīrthakara.

## Abandoning the Māras
*bdud spong*, Skt. *bdud spong*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Niyatabuddhi.

## Abandoning the Rivers
*chu bo spong*, Skt. *chu bo spong*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Anavanata.

## Abandonment
*spong ba*, Skt. *spong ba*, Abandonment (the act of giving up or forsaking), also the name of the father of the buddha Kṛtārtha.

## abandonment of all indolence
*le lo thams cad spangs pa*, Skt. *sarva­kausīdyāpagato*, The forty-fourth of the fifty-one meditative stabilities manifested to Sadāprarudita in chapter 73.

## abandonment of magical display
*sgyu ma rnam par spangs pa*, Skt. *māyāvivarjito*, The twelfth of the fifty-one meditative stabilities manifested to Sadāprarudita in chapter 73.

## Śabarī
*sha ba ri*, Skt. *śabarī*, A being in this sūtra.

## śabara
*ri khrod pa*, Skt. *śabara*, Both the name of specific group of people and a general reference to indigenous peoples living outside mainstream Indic society.

## Abbot
*mkhan po*, in general [means](#means) someone who gives monastic vows. This title is also given to a person who has attained a high degree of knowledge of the [Dharma](#dharma) and is in charge of teaching it. It can also simple be the title given to the eldest monk during a traditional summer retreat.

## Śabdavajrā
*sgra yi rdo rje ma*, Skt. *śabdavajrā*, One of the goddesses in the maṇḍala of Vajrasattva.

## abdhātvaparyanta
*chu’i khams mu med pa*, Skt. *abdhātvaparyanta*, Lit. “limitless water element.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## abdomen is not misshapen
*sku ma rnyongs pa*, Skt. *a­bhugna­kukṣi­tā*, Fifty-seventh of the eighty minor marks.

## abdomen is slender
*phyal phyang nge ba*, Skt. *kṣāmodara­tā*, Fifty-eighth of the eighty minor marks.

## abdomen that is not wrinkled
*phyal ma zhom pa*, Skt. *abhugnakukṣi*, Thirty-fifth of the eighty minor signs.

## abdomen that is unwrinkled
*sku la gnyer ma med pa*, Skt. *mṛṣṭa­kukṣi­tā*, Literally, “unwrinkled body;” fifty-ninth of the eighty minor marks.

## Abṛha
*mi che ba*, Skt. *abṛha*, The first of the “pure abodes;” also the name of the gods living there.

## Ṛṣabha
*khyu mchog*, Skt. *ṛṣabha*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK; a legendary king before the time of the Buddha.

## Abhava
*srid pa med pa*, Skt. *abhava*, A buddha realm.

## Abhayā
*mi ’jigs*, Skt. *abhayā*, One of the vidyārājñīs attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Abhaya
*’jigs med*, Skt. *abhaya*, The fifth of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin, who becomes the bodhisattva Gaganamudra and is prophesied to become the Buddha Padmottara.

## Abhayacitra
*mi ’jigs sna tshogs*, Skt. *abhayacitra*, A mountain king.

## Abhayadā
*mi ’jigs sbyin ma*, Skt. *abhayadā*, One of the great yakṣiṇīs.

## Abhayaṃkarā
*mi ’jigs pa byed pa*, Skt. *abhayaṃkarā*, A world realm in the distant past.

## Abhayakara
*’jigs pa dang bral ba*, Skt. **abhayakara*, Name of a tathāgata; lit. “without fear.”

## Abhayakīrti
*’jigs med grags pa*, Skt. *abhayakīrti*, A buddha. (Toh 555: bsnyengs pa mi mnga’ ba’i grags pa)

## Abhayapradā
*mi ’jigs sbyin*, Skt. *abhayapradā*, A great bodhisattva.

## Abhayākaragupta
Skt. *abhayākaragupta*, An influential scholar active at Vikramaśīla Monasery in the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries.

## Abhedyā
*mi phyed ma*, Skt. *abhedyā*, One of the subtle channels in the body.

## Abhedyabuddhi
*mi phyed blo mnga’*, Skt. *abhedyabuddhi*, The 899th buddha in the first list, 898th in the second list, and 889th in the third list.

## Ṛṣabhendrarāja
*khyu mchog gi dbang po’i rgyal po*, Skt. *ṛṣabhendrarāja*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## Abhibhava
*zil gyis gnon pa*, Skt. *abhibhava*, A world system.

## Abhi­bhūta­guṇa­sāgara­rāja
*yon tan rgya mtsho’i zil mnan rgyal po*, Skt. *abhi­bhūta­guṇa­sāgara­rāja*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## Abhibodhyaṅga­puṣpa
*byang chub kyi yan lag me tog*, Skt. *abhibodhyaṅga­puṣpa*, Name that the hundred billion trillion beings in this assembly will bear when they become buddhas.

## Abhidharma
*mngon pa*, one of the three [piṭakas](#piṭaka). The foundation of Buddhist psychology and logic. It describes the universe, the different kinds of beings, the steps on the [path](#path) to [enlightenment](#enlightenment), refutes mistaken beliefs, etc.

## Abhidharma Piṭaka
*chos mngon pa’i sde snod*, Skt. *abhidharmapiṭaka*, A collection of canonical texts with the purpose of presenting the Buddha’s teachings in a precise, systematic, and definitive way, using highly technical and impersonal descriptions and language. There are two traditional definitions of the word abhi-dharma depending on the sense of the prefix abhi-: (1) [teachings] pertaining to (abhi-) the Dharma, and (2) higher or superior (abhi-) Dharma. The second definition may point toward the fact that the mature Abhidharma is a body of Buddhist doctrine as well as a body of literature, not a mere reformulation and systematization of the Buddhist sūtras (see also the definition given in Abhidh-k-bh(P), 2, where Vasubandhu seems to employ both definitions in order to distinguish an ultimate and a conventional meaning of the word abhidharma). The word piṭaka means “basket” but is used in its derived or transferred sense “collection of canonical scriptures.” The piṭakas are usually Vinaya, Sūtra, and Abhidharma.

## Abhi­dharma­kośa
*chos mngon pa’i mdzod*, Skt. *abhi­dharma­kośa*, An important work written by Vasubandhu, probably in the fourth century, as a critical compendium of the Abhidharmic science.

## Abhigarjita
*mngon par sgrogs pa*, Skt. *abhigarjita*, A southern buddha realm that the Buddha Śākyamuni sees.

## Abhijā
*byi bzhin*, Skt. *abhijā*, The name of a nakṣatra. In one instance the name is given as Abhijit, which is the same as the name of one of the muhūrtas..

## Abhija
*bya bi bzhin*, Skt. *abhija*, One of the grahas.

## Abhijñaprāpta

## Abhijata
*byi bzhin gyi bu*, Skt. *abhijata*, One of the grahas.

## abhijñā­bala­vaiśāradya­prāpta
*mngon par shes pa dang / stobs dang / mi ’jigs pa thob pa*, Skt. *abhijñā­bala­vaiśāradya­prāpta*, Lit. “from which the clairvoyances, powers, and fearlessnesses are gained.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Abhijñāguṇarāja
*mngon shes yon tan rgyal po*, Skt. *abhi­jñāguṇa­rāja*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## Abhijit
“Victorious.” The asterism of the star Vega in the constellation Lyra.

## Abhijita
“Victorious.” The name of a muhūrta.

## Abhi­jñā­jñānābhi­bhū
*mngon shes ye shes zil gnon*, Skt. *abhi­jñā­jñānābhi­bhū*, A shorter form of the name of Buddha Mahābhijñā­jñānābhi­bhū.

## Abhijñāketu
*mngon shes tog*, Skt. *abhijñāketu*, The 551st buddha in the first list, 551st in the second list, and 544th in the third list.

## Abhimukhī
*mngon du gyur pa*, Skt. *abhimukhī*, Lit. “Directly Witnessed.” The sixth level of accomplishment pertaining to bodhisattvas. See “ten bodhisattva levels.”

## Abhiratī
*mngon par dga’ ba*, Skt. *abhiratī*, The realm of the Buddha Akṣobhya, beyond countless buddha realms in the eastern direction.

## Abhirati
*mngon par dga’ ba*, Skt. *abhirati*, The eastern realm where the ninth son of King Araṇemin has become the Buddha Akṣobhya, and after Akṣobhya’s nirvāṇa, where the tenth son will become the Buddha Suvarṇapuṣpa. It will be renamed Jayasoma when the eleventh son, Siṃha, becomes the Buddha Nāga­vinarditeśvara­ghoṣa there.

## Abhirāja
The name of a people in northern India.

## Abhirāmaśrī
*mngon par dga’ ba’i dpal*, Skt. *abhirāmaśrī*, The sixty-seventh buddha in a kalpa in the distant past.

## Abhirāma­śrīvakrā
*mngon par mdzes pa’i dpal*, Skt. *abhirāma­śrīvakrā*, A dancer’s daughter in the distant past.

## Abhirāmavartā
*yid du ’ong ba’i bzhin*, Skt. *abhirāmavartā*, An eminent daughter in Dhanyākara.

## Abhirūpa
*gzugs bzang*, Skt. *abhirūpa*, The name that the Buddha Ratnagarbha prophesies will be that of one of his eighty brothers (the forty-second) when he becomes a buddha.

## Abhisāra
The name of a country just to the southwest of the Kashmir valley.

## Abhiyaśa
The father of the future buddha Kāruṇika.

## Abhrakūṭa
*a bhra kU TA*, Skt. *abhrakūṭa*, A city in Godānīya.

## Abhrakrama Summit
*rtse mo lhang tsher*, Skt. *abhrakrama*, A mountain near the asura city Double Pleasure.

## Abhāskara
*nyi ma*, Skt. *abhāskara*, The ninth buddha in a kalpa in the distant past.

## Ṣaḍbhuja
*phyag drug pa*, Skt. *ṣaḍbhuja*, One of the vidyārājas dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Abhāva
*dngos po med pa las byung*, Skt. *abhāva*, A buddha countless eons in the past.

## Abhāva­samudgata­rāja
*dngos po med pa yang dag par ’phags pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *abhāva­samudgata­rāja*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Abhāva­svabhāva­rāśi
*dngos po med pa’i ngo bo’i phung po*, Skt. *abhāva­svabhāva­rāśi*, One of the uṣṇīṣa kings attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Abhāva­svabhāva­samudgata­rāja
*dngos po med pa’i ngo bo nyid yang dag par ’phags pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *abhāva­svabhāva­samudgata­rāja*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Abhāveśvara
*dngos med dbang phyug*, Skt. *abhāveśvara*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## abhāṣya
*gzhal du med pa*, Skt. *abhāṣya*, Lit. “cannot be measured.” An incredibly large number, higher than aparyanta.

## Abhyuccadeva
*shin tu mtho ba’i lha*, Skt. *abhyuccadeva*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Abhyuddhara
*shin tu mtho ’dzin pa*, Skt. *abhyuddhara*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Abhyudgata
*mngon ’phags ’od mnga’*, Skt. *abhyudgata*, The fifteenth buddha in a kalpa in the distant past, and also the seventy-fourth buddha in the same kalpa.

## Abhyudgatadhvaja
*mngon ’phags rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *abhyudgatadhvaja*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## Abhyudgata­karman
*phrin las ’phags pa*, Skt. *abhyudgata­karman*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Abhyudgatameru
*lhun po mngon ’phags*, Skt. *abhyudgatameru*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## Abhyudgata­parvata­rājālaṃ­kṛta
*mngon par ’phags pa’i ri rgyal ba rgyan pa*, Skt. *abhyudgata­parvata­rājālaṃ­kṛta*, A buddha.

## Abhyudgata­prabha­śrī
*mngon par ’phags ’od dpal*, Skt. *abhyudgata­prabha­śrī*, The fifty-third buddha in a kalpa in the distant past. BHS verse: Abhyudgata­prabha­śirī .

## Abhyudgataśrī
*shin tu ’phags dpal*, Skt. *abhyudgataśrī*, The 160th buddha in the first list, 159th in the second list, and 159th in the third list.

## Abhyudgatarāja
*mngon ’phags rgyal po*, Skt. *abhyudgatarāja*, An eon in the future.

## Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa

## Abhyupagatagāmin
A realized one whose name is attested in the Sanskrit manuscript of this sūtra.

## Abidance through Infinite Observations
*dmigs pa mtha’ yas pas gnas pa*, Skt. *dmigs pa mtha’ yas pas gnas pa*, A buddha.

## Abides in the Certainty of the Hero’s Steadfast Asceticism
*dpa’ brtan brtul zhugs nges pa la nye bar gnas pa*, Skt. *dpa’ brtan brtul zhugs nges pa la nye bar gnas pa*, A devaputra present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## abides in the sense field of infinite consciousness
*rnam shes mtha’ yas skye mched la gnas pa*, Skt. *vi­jñānānantyāyatanaṃ vi­harati*, Eighth of the eight sense fields of mastery. See also .

## abides in the sense field of infinite space
*nam mkha’ mtha’ yas skye mched la gnas pa*, Skt. *ākāśānantyāyatanaṃ vi­harati*, Seventh of the eight sense fields of mastery. See also .

## Abiding
*gnas pa*, Skt. *gnas pa*, Abiding (remaining or dwelling, enduring), also the name of an attendant of the buddha Sūryapriya.

## Abiding by Compassion
*snying rjes gnas*, Skt. *snying rjes gnas*, Mother of the buddha Akṣobhya.

## Abiding by Emptiness
*stong pa nyid la gnas pa*, Skt. *stong pa nyid la gnas pa*, Mother of the buddha Siṃharaśmi.

## Abiding by Freedom from Attachment
*chags dang bral bar gnas pa*, Skt. *chags dang bral bar gnas pa*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Vasuśreṣṭha.

## Abiding by Love

*gti mug med pa’i dbang phyug gnas*, Skt. *gti mug med pa’i dbang phyug gnas*, Attendant of the buddha Mayūra.

*rnam par gzigs gnas*, Skt. *rnam par gzigs gnas*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Abhaya (413 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Abiding by Supreme Discipline

## Abiding by the Training

## Abiding by Unshakable Power

## Abiding Free from Attachment
*chags pa med par gnas pa*, Skt. *chags pa med par gnas pa*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Vibhakta­jñā­svara.

## Abiding Free from Delusion
*’khrul med gnas*, Skt. *’khrul med gnas*, Attendant of the buddha Subhaga.

## Abiding Free from Dullness

## Abiding Free from Suffering

## Abiding in Equality

The fourth of the eight liberations.

## absence of afflicted mental states
*kun nas nyon mongs pa med pa*, Skt. *asaṃkliṣṭo*, The thirty-sixth of the fifty-one meditative stabilities manifested to Sadāprarudita in chapter 73.

## absence of aspiration
*smon pa med pa*, Skt. *apraṇihita*, The absence of any conceptual goal that one is focused upon achieving, knowing that all composite phenomena create suffering. One of the three doorways to liberation.

## absence of attributes
*mtshan ma med pa*, Skt. *animitta*, The absence of the conceptual identification of perceptions. Knowing that the true nature has no attributes, such as color, shape, etc. One of the three doorways to liberation.

## absence of conceptual elaborations

## absence of distinguishing counterparts
*ldog pa*, Skt. *vyāvṛtti*, In Buddhist logic, the term “distinguishing counterpart” (vyāvṛtti, ldog pa) denotes a given phenomenon that conceptually appears to be the opposite of a phenomenon of a dissimilar class but is not actually existent, such as the idea of a specific form that appears in conceptual thought.

## absence of distinguishing marks
*mtshan ma med pa*, Skt. *animitta*, One of the three gateways of liberation.

## Absence of Heat
*ma dros pa*, Skt. *ma dros pa*, A buddha realm located in the eastern direction during the time of the Buddha Śākyamuni. Also called Absence of Torment.

## absence of joy with respect to all happiness and suffering
*bde ba dang sdug bsngal thams cad la mngon par dga’ ba med pa*, Skt. *sarva­sukhaduḥkha­nirabhinandī*, The 99th meditative stability in chapters 6 and 8.

## absence of marks
*mtshan ma med pa*, Skt. *animitta*, The absence of the conceptual identification of perceptions, knowing that the true nature has no attributes, such as color or shape. One of the three gateways of liberation.

## absence of mentation in all phenomena
*chos thams cad sems pa med pa*, Skt. *sarva­dharmāmanana*, The fourth of twenty-four aspects of the perfection of wisdom taught by Dharmodgata, and realized as meditative stabilities by Sadāprarudita, in chapter 75.

## Absence of Objective Perception
*dmigs pa med pa*, Skt. *dmigs pa med pa*, A buddha realm.

## absence of self
*bdag med pa*, Skt. *anātmatā*, This describes actual reality, as finally there is no enduring person himself or thing itself, since persons and things exist only in the relative, conventional, or superficial sense, and not in any ultimate or absolute sense. To understand Buddhist teaching correctly, we must be clear about the two senses (conventional/ultimate, or relative/absolute), since mistaking denial of ultimate self as denial of conventional self leads to nihilism, and mistaking affirmation of conventional self as affirmation of ultimate self leads to absolutism. Nihilism and absolutism effectively prevent us from realizing our enlightenment, hence are to be avoided.

## absence of signs
*mtshan ma med pa*, Skt. *animitta*, See “signlessness.”

A clouded state of mind in which one is forgetful and unaware of one’s surroundings. One of the twenty secondary or minor afflicted mental states (Skt. upakleśa; Tib. nye ba’i nyon mongs).

## Absolute truth
*don dam bden pa*, Skt. *paramārtha satya*, actual truth perceived through [wisdom](#wisdom), without mental fabrications. Its characteristic is to be "beyond mind, unthinkable, inexpressible" ([Patrul Rinpoche](#patrul-rinpoche). See also [relative truth](#relative-truth).

## absorption
*snyoms par ’jug*, Skt. *samāpatti*, “Absorption” has been translated as “meditation,” “contemplation,” “attainment,” etc., and any of these words might serve. The problem is to establish one English word for each of the important Sanskrit words samāpatti, dhyāna, samādhi, bhāvanā, etc., so as to preserve a consistency with the original. Therefore, I have adopted for these terms, respectively, “absorption,” “contemplation,” “concentration” and “realization” or “cultivation,” reserving the word “meditation” for general use with any of the terms when they are used not in a specific sense but to indicate mind-practice in general.

## absorption in the state of cessation
*’gog pa la snyoms par zhugs pa*, Skt. *nirodhasamāpatti*, See Mvyut 1500 and 1988.

## absorption of neither discrimination nor non-discrimination
*’du shes min ’du shes med min gyi snyom ’jug*, Skt. *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā*, Fourth of the four types of formless meditative absorptions (caturārūpyasamāpatti, gzugs med snyoms ’jug bzhi) (Rigzin 369).

## absorption that tames arrogant beings

## absorptions
*snyoms par ’jug pa*, Skt. *samāpatti*, May refer to the “four formless absorptions” and/or the “nine serial absorptions.”

## absorptions into nine successive abodes
*mthar gyis gnas pa’i snyoms par ’jug pa dgu*, Skt. *navānupūrva­vihāra­samāpattayaḥ*, The four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions, and the absorption of cessation.

## abstinence
*bsnyen gnas*, Skt. *upavāsa*, As expressed in the Sanskrit and translated literally into Tibetan, the term means “to dwell near.” The term comes from the older Vedic traditions in which during full moon and new moon sacrifices, householders would practice abstinence in various forms such as fasting and refraining from sexual activity. These holy days were called upavasatha days because it was said that the gods that were the recipients of these sacrifices would “dwell” (√vas) “near” (upa) the practitioners of these sacrifices. While sacrificial practices were discarded by Buddhists, the framework of practicing fortnightly abstinence evolved into the poṣadha observance, and in fact the term poṣadha is etymologically related to the term upavasatha. See Dutt (1962), p. 73.

## acacia

## accept
*bzod pa*, Skt. *kṣam*, Monastics are asked to speak up if they cannot “accept” a motion or official act of the saṅgha.

## accept charge of
*gzung ba, nye [bar](#bar) gzhag pa*, To accept (e.g., a person) as a [novice](#novice).

## acceptance
*bzod pa*, Skt. *kṣānti*, A term also translated as “patience” and “forebearance” in this text, and in others sometimes as “receptivity”; here, often in the context of its association with dhāraṇī and samādhi, the term is probably to be understood as related to “forbearance that comes from realizing the birthlessness of phenomena” (q.v.).

## acceptance about phenomena
*chos kyi bzod pa*, Skt. *dharmakṣānti*, Sometimes an abbreviation of anutpattikadharmakṣānti, “acceptance of the nonorigination of phenomena,” this phrase describes a mode of realization acquired by bodhisattvas. Dharmakṣanti can also refer to a way one becomes “receptive” to key points of the Dharma.

## Acceptance of Certain Realization
*nges par rtogs bzod*, Skt. *nges par rtogs bzod*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Jñānakīrti (501 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Acceptance of Excellent Qualities
*yon tan bzhed*, Skt. *yon tan bzhed*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Prajñāna­vihāsa­svara (757 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Acceptance of Excellent Sight
*legs mthong bzod*, Skt. *legs mthong bzod*, Son of the buddha Mahāmitra.

## Acceptance of Merit
*bsod nams bzhed*, Skt. *bsod nams bzhed*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Praśāntagāmin (871 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Acceptance of phenomena concurring with reality
*rjes su ’thun pa’i chos la bzod pa*, Skt. *ānulomikadharmakṣānti*, A particular realization attained by a bodhisattva on the sixth bodhisattva level. This realization arises as a result of analysis of the essential nature of phenomena (dharmas).

## acceptance of phenomena that is consistent with reality
*rjes su ’thun pa’i chos kyi bzod pa*, Skt. *ānulomika­dharma­kṣānti*, A realization characteristic of the sixth ground of bodhisattvas, arising as a result of analysis of the essential nature of phenomena.

## acceptance of reality
*chos kyi bzod pa*, Skt. *dharmakṣānti*, Shorthand for anutpattika­dharma­kṣānti, “acceptance of the nonorigination of phenomena,” its realization being one of the qualities acquired by bodhisattvas. Dharmakṣanti can also refer to a way one becomes “receptive” to key points of the Dharma.

## acceptance of the fact that things do not arise
The third and final stage of the three levels of intellectual receptivity or acceptance (kṣānti) of the Dharma. Tantamount to an acceptance of the emptiness of all things, the fact that they do not arise or cease as substantial or essentially real phenomena. It follows from the second level of acceptance, which brings one into conformity with the Dharma (ānulomika­dharmakṣānti), which is in turn preceded by a first stage of acceptance in which one follows the voice (ghoṣānugā kṣānti) of the teacher of the Dharma. This is a distinctive but related use of the term kṣānti, which is also translated in this sūtra as “patience,” when it refers to the perfection (pāramitā) and virtue of patience more generally.

## Acceptance of the Hair
*dbu skra blangs pa*, Skt. *keśa­prati­grahaṇa*, A shrine built to commemorate the Buddha’s going forth.

## acceptance of the nonarising of phenomena
*mi skyes ba’i chos la bzod pa*, Skt. *anutpattika­dharma­kṣānti*, The stage of acceptance that is associated with the realization of an eighth bhūmi bodhisattva.

## Acceptance of the Saffron Robes
*ngur smrig blangs pa*, Skt. *kāṣāya­prati­grahaṇa*, A shrine built to commemorate the Buddha’s going forth.

## acceptance that brings one into conformity with the Dharma
The second of three levels of intellectual receptivity or acceptance (kṣānti), following from an earlier stage in which there is an acceptance that “follows the voice” (ghoṣānugā) of the teacher of the Dharma. At this second stage, there is a deeper acceptance that results in one’s thoughts and actions coming into accord with (literally, “going with the grain of”) the Dharma; that is, with the teachings and the nature of things. The third stage is the acceptance of the fact that things do not arise (anutpatti­kadharmakṣānti). This is a distinctive but related use of the term kṣānti, which is also translated in this sūtra as “patience,” when it refers to the perfection (pāramitā) and virtue of patience more generally.

## acceptance that concords with the truth
*rjes su ’thun pa’i bzod pa*, Skt. *ānulomikī kṣānti*, A particular realization attained by bodhisattvas that arises as a result of analysis of the essential nature of phenomena.

## acceptance that phenomena are nonarising
*mi skye ba’i chos la bzod pa*, Skt. *anutpattika­dharma­kṣānti*, Bodhisattvas’ realization that all phenomena are unproduced and empty. It sustains them on the difficult path of benefiting all beings so that they do not succumb to the goal of personal liberation. Different sources link this realization to the first or eighth bodhisattva ground (bhūmi).

## acceptance that phenomena are unborn
An attainment of effortless insight into emptiness—the realization that all phenomena are unborn (anutpāda) and empty of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). This acceptance supports bodhisattvas on the arduous path of returning through innumerable rounds of rebirth in order to benefit beings without being tempted by the goal of personal liberation. This attainment only occurs on the bodhisattva levels and is variously said to occur on the first and eighth bodhisattva levels.

## acceptance that phenomena are unproduced
*mi skye ba’i chos la bzod pa*, Skt. *anutpattika­dharma­kṣānti*, A bodhisattva’s realization that all phenomena are unproduced and empty. This attainment is variously said to occur on either the first or eighth bodhisattva level.

## acceptance that phenomena do not arise
*mi skye ba’i chos la bzod pa*, Skt. *anutpattikadharmakṣānti*, Bodhisattvas’ realization that all phenomena are unproduced and empty. It sustains them on the difficult path of benefitting all beings so that they do not succumb to the goal of personal liberation. Different sources link this realization to the first or eighth bodhisattva level (bhūmi).

## acquisition
*thob pa*, Skt. *prāpti*, A conditioned factor that according to Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma is responsible for the ripening of karmic actions subsequent to their having been performed. See also .

## acquisitive aggregates
*nye bar len pa’i phung po*, Skt. *upādānaskandha*, See “five acquisitive aggregates.”

## act
*las*, Skt. *karman*, Matters that govern the [saṅgha](#saṅgha) community’s daily life, regular observances (such as the rains retreat and the [restoration](#restoration)) and special events (like ordination) are ratified by a formal act of the [saṅgha](#saṅgha). There are one hundred and one such types of formal acts, all of which fall into one of three categories depending on the procedure needed for ratification. An [act of motion alone](#act-of-motion-alone) requires only a [motion](#motion); an [act whose second member is a motion](#act-whose-second-member-is-a-motion) require a [motion](#motion) and the statement of the act; while an [act whose fourth member is a motion](#act-whose-fourth-member-is-a-motion) require a [motion](#motion) and three statements of the act.

## act by motion alone
*gsol ba ’ba’ zhig gi las*, Skt. **muktikājñāptikarman*, A formal act of the saṅgha in which the motion suffices, with no need to formally state the act. Such an act is employed before a candidate for ordination is asked about confidential matters pertaining to his or her fitness for ordination.

## act by motion and resolution
*gsol ba dang gnyis kyi las*, Skt. *jñāpti­dvitīyakarman*, An official act of the saṅgha that requires an initial motion followed by the statement of the proposed act. I. B. Horner translates the Pāli correlate as “a vote following directly upon a motion.”

## act by motion and triple resolution
*gsol ba dang bzhi’i las*, Skt. *jñāpti­caturthakarman*, An official act of the saṅgha that requires an initial motion followed by the statement of the proposed act, repeated three times. Such an act is needed to fully ordain a person and to officially threaten an intransigent monk, for example. I. B. Horner translates the Pāli correlate as “a resolution at which the motion is put three times and then followed by the decision.”

## act of censure
*bsdigs pa'i las*, Skt. *tarjanīyakarman*, One of five types of [disciplinary act](#disciplinary-act)s meted out by the [saṅgha](#saṅgha). This was first imposed on the Pandulohitaka monks for their quarrelsomeness.

## act of chastening
*smad pa'i las*, Skt. *nirgarhaṇīyakarman*, One of five types of [disciplinary act](#disciplinary-act)s meted out by the [saṅgha](#saṅgha).

## act of expulsion
*bskrad pa'i las*, Skt. *pravāsanīyakarman*, One of five types of [disciplinary act](#disciplinary-act)s meted out by the [saṅgha](#saṅgha).

## act of motion alone
*gsol ba 'ba' zhig gi las*, Skt. *muktikājñāptikarman*, A formal [act](#act) of the [saṅgha](#saṅgha) in which the [motion](#motion) suffices, with no need to formally state the [act](#act). Such an [act](#act) is employed before a candidate for ordination is asked about private matters pertaining to his fitness for ordination.

## act of reconciliation
*phyir 'gyed pa'i las*, Skt. *pratisaṃharaṇīyakarman*, One of five types of [disciplinary act](#disciplinary-act)s meted out by the [saṅgha](#saṅgha).

## act of suspension
*gnas nas dbyung ba'i las*, Skt. *utkṣepaṇīyakarman*, One of five types of [disciplinary act](#disciplinary-act)s meted out by the [saṅgha](#saṅgha). A monk may be suspended on one of seven grounds: failing to acknowledge an offense; refusing to amend or rehabilitate one’s behavior; [deviant views](#deviant-views); being overly belligerent and quarrelsome; creating the circumstances for a quarrel; maintaining overly close relations with nuns, unruly people, and ne’er-do-wells; and refusing to let go of a [Dharma](#dharma) matter that has been peacefully resolved.

## (act of suspension for) refusing to acknowledge a fault
*mi snang bar gnas nas sbyung ba*, Skt. *adarśanāyotkṣepaṇīyaṃ karma*, Monks and nuns are expected to willingly confess (Tib. spro ba mthol bshags) or admit to any offenses they commit. If they fail to acknowledge wrongdoing when prompted by another monk or nun to do, the saṅgha may suspend them for their recalcitrance.

## (act of suspension for) refusing to amend one’s behavior
*phyir mi bchos pa gnas nas dbyung ba*, One of five types of disciplinary acts meted out by the saṅgha. A monk may be expelled on one of seven grounds: failing to acknowledge a fault; refusing to amend or rehabilitate one’s behavior; refusing to relinquish deviant views; being overly belligerent and quarrelsome; creating the circumstances for a quarrel; maintaining overly close relations with nuns, unruly people, or malingerers; and refusing to let go of a dharma matter that has been peacefully resolved.

## act of truth
*bden pa’i byin gyis brlabs*, Skt. *satyādhiṣṭhāna*, A blessing enacted by evoking the power of truth. See, for example, Toh 54, –.

## act whose fourth member is a motion
*gsol ba dang bzhi'i las*, Skt. *jñāpticaturthakarman*, A formal [act](#act) of the [saṅgha](#saṅgha) that requires an initial [motion](#motion) followed by the statement of the proposed [act](#act), repeated [three times](#three-times). Such an [act](#act) is required for several proceedings—among other occasions, to fully [ordain](#ordain) someone, or to officially threaten an intransigent monk.

## act whose second member is a motion
*gsol ba dang gnyis kyi las*, Skt. *jñāptidvitīyakarman*, A formal [act](#act) of the [saṅgha](#saṅgha) that requires an initial [motion](#motion) followed by the statement of the proposed [act](#act). Such an [act](#act) is needed to grant the vows of full ordination to a nun, among other occasions.

## action
*las*, Skt. *karman*, A single term is used in Sanskrit and Tibetan to denote both an “action” as a conditioning factor and the “karma” that it conditions. In translation it may be necessary to use one term or the other to clarify the meaning, but the source term is no different.

## Action Beyond Differences
*tha mi dad par spyod pa*, Skt. *tha mi dad par spyod pa*, A great bodhisattva.

## action devoid of forgetfulness
*brjed pa med par spyod pa*, Skt. *brjed pa med par spyod pa*, The name of an absorption.

## action family
The family to which women who dye cloth are said to belong in Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra.

## action mudrā

## actions that bring immediate retribution
*mtshams med kyi las*, Skt. *ānantaryakarman*, Matricide, parricide, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the monastic order, and drawing a buddha’s blood with malicious intention. These actions are said to result in immediate birth in the hells.

## activating syllable
*las kyi yi ge*, A phrase describing the mantra syllable hā in the “presentation of mantra” (Tib. sngags btu ba; Skt. mantroddhāra) in The Tantra of Great Gaṇapati.

## Active Intelligence
*spyod pa’i blo gros*, Skt. *spyod pa’i blo gros*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Sugandha.

## activity
*las*, Skt. *karman*, A ritual activity (such as pacifying, nourishing, etc.). This term is also translated in other instances as “rite,” “karma,” “karman,” or “karmic accumulation.” In the latter three cases the term refers to karmic accumulation, positive or negative, that will produce results in the future, unless it is purified.

## activity family
*las kyi rigs*, Skt. *karmakula*, One of the five buddha families.

## acts of attracting beings
*bsdu ba’i dngos po*, Skt. *saṃgrahavastu*, The means of winning over beings; traditionally there are four of them—generosity, kind talk, meaningful action, and impartiality.

## acts of immediate retribution
*mtshams med pa*, Skt. *ānantarya*, See “five acts of immediate retribution.”

## acts with immediate result on death
*mtshams med pa’i las*, Skt. *anantaryakarma*, The five actions that lead to going instantly to hell on death are killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, splitting the saṅgha, and wounding a buddha so that he bleeds.

## acts with immediate results
*mtshams ma mchis pa*, Skt. *ānantarya*, See “five acts with immediate results.”

## acts with immediate retribution
*mtshams med pa’i las*, Skt. *ānantaryakarman*, The five extremely negative actions that, once those who have committed them die, result in immediate rebirth in the hells without the experience of the intermediate state. They are killing an arhat, killing one’s mother, killing one’s father, creating a schism in the Saṅgha, and maliciously drawing blood from a tathāgata’s body.

## afflicted
*kun nas nyon mongs pa*, Skt. *saṃkleśika*, See “afflicted mental state.”

## afflicted mental state
*nyon mongs*, Skt. *kleśa*, The essentially pure nature of mind is obscured and afflicted by various psychological defilements known as the afflicted mental states, which destroy the mind’s peace and composure. Included among them are the primary afflictions of fundamental ignorance, attachment, aversion, pride, doubt, and twenty subsidiary afflictions.

## afflicted mind
Identified as the seventh consciousness in the Yogācāra system, this term refers to the aspect of mind that is responsible for maintaining a subtle sense of self and perpetuating the mental afflictions.

## affliction
*nyon mongs*, Skt. *kleśa*, In Buddhism, affliction (Skt. kleśa) refers to any destructive mental state that causes suffering and continued existence in saṃsāra. In this regard, the three basic kleśas are ignorance, attachment, and aversion (or hatred). In terms of etymology, the primary meaning is “defilement.” This is reflected in the middle-Indic kileśa and Pali kilesa which mean “to soil, stain, defile.” The meaning “affliction” is a secondary meaning that derives from a more general (non-Buddhist) classical understanding based on the verbal root kliś (“afflict, torment, cause pain”).

## afflictions
*nyon mongs*, Skt. *kleśa*, Mental and emotional traits that bind one to saṃsāra; the fundamental three are ignorance, desire, and anger. When the term refers to the fundamental three, it tends to be translated as “the afflictions.”

## afflictive emotion
*nyon mongs pa*, Skt. *kleśa*, Also called “delusions,” “afflictions,” or “addictive emotions,” these are mental states that produce turmoil and confusion and thus disturb mental peace and happiness (Rigzin 133).

In India, agarwood is primarily derived from the fifteen Aquilaria (Aquilaria malaccensis) and nine Gyrinops species of lign-aloe trees.

## age of perfection
*rdzogs ldan gyi dus*, Skt. *kṛtayuga*, The first of the four ages of human life in Jambudvīpa. Humans in this age enjoy good qualities such as long lifespans free from disease (see ). Over the course of the four ages humans will lose a quarter of these qualities between each age.

## age of strife
*rtsod ldan gyi dus*, Skt. *kaliyuga*, The last of the four ages of human life in Jambudvīpa. In this age humans are endowed with only one remaining quarter of the good qualities that they had during the age of perfection.

## age of threefold endowment
*gsum ldan gyi dus*, Skt. *tretayuga*, The second of the four ages of human life in Jambudvīpa. In this age humans are endowed with three quarters of the good qualities that they had during the age of perfection.

## age of twofold endowment
*gnyis ldan gyi dus*, Skt. *dvāparayuga*, The third of the four ages of human life in Jambudvīpa. In this age humans are endowed with two quarters, or half of the good qualities that they had during the age of perfection.

## Aggregate
*phung po*, Skt. *skandha*, This translation of skandha is fairly well established, although some prefer the monosyllabic “group.” It is important to bear in mind that the original skandha has the sense of “pile,” or “heap,” which has the connotation of utter lack of internal structure, of a randomly collocated pile of things; thus “group” may convey a false connotation of structure and ordered arrangement. The five “compulsive” (upādāna) aggregates are of great importance as a schema for introspective meditation in the Abhidharma, wherein each is defined with the greatest subtlety and precision. In fact, the five terms rūpa, vedanā, samjñā, saṃskāra, and vijñāna have such a particular technical sense that many translators have preferred to leave them untranslated. Nevertheless, in the sūtra context, where the five are meant rather more simply to represent the relative living being (in the realm of desire), it seems preferable to give a translation—in spite of the drawbacks of each possible term—in order to convey the same sense of a total categorization of the psychophysical complex. Thus, for rūpa, “matter” is preferred to “form” because it more concretely connotes the physical and gross; for vedanā, “sensation” is adopted, as limited to the aesthetic; for samjñā, “intellect” is useful in conveying the sense of verbal, conceptual intelligence. For samskāra, which covers a number of mental functions as well as inanimate forces, “motivation” gives a general idea. And “consciousness” is so well established for vijñāna (although what we normally think of as consciousness is more like samjñā, i.e., conceptual and notional, and vijñāna is rather the “pure awareness” prior to concepts) as to be left unchallenged.

## aggregates
*phung po*, Skt. *skandha*, Lit. a “heap” or “pile.” The five aggregates of form, feeling, perception, volitional factors, and consciousness. On the individual level the five aggregates refer to the basis upon which the mistaken idea of a self is projected. However, in this text, five pure or uncontaminated aggregates are also listed, namely: the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of meditative stabilization, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of knowledge and seeing of liberation.

## aggregates as the bases for clinging
*nye bar len pa’i phung po*, Skt. *upādānaskandha*, The five aggregates (skandha) of matter (rūpa), sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), karmic dispositions (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna). They are referred to as the “bases for clinging” (upādāna) insofar as all conceptual grasping arises on the basis of these aggregates.

## aggregates for appropriation
*nye bar len pa’i phung po*, Skt. *upādānaskandha*, Said of the aggregates individually, but more commonly in terms of all five as a collective, because they are “the basis of clinging to existence” (Edgerton).

## aggregates subject to clinging
*nye bar len pa’i phung po*, Skt. *upādānaskandha*, The five “heaps” that are clung to and thereby constitute individual existence in the desire realm: form (rūpa), feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), conditionings (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna).

## Aggressive rite
*drag po’i phrin las*, Skt. *raudrakarman*, Roughly synonymous with abhicāra (assaulting), this broad category of rites includes those ritual practices and magical acts that are used to curse, exorcise malevolent influences, deter, harm, and kill enemies, and otherwise engage in hostile activities directed towards human and nonhuman targets.

## Agnidatta (father of Śiṣyaka)

Not to be confused with Agnidatta (of Vārāṇasī), one of the magistrates of King Brahmadatta (past), nor with Agnidatta of the royal palace Śobhāvatī.

## Agnidatta (of Śobhāvatī)
*me sbyin*, Skt. *agnidatta*, A certain brahmin of the royal palace Śobhāvatī during the time of Buddha Krakucchanda. Not to be confused with Agnidatta of Vārāṇasī, nor with the Agnidatta (father of Śiṣyaka) prophesied to appear in the future, both of whose names are the slightly different Tib. mes sbyin.

## Agnidatta (of Vārāṇasī)
*mes sbyin*, Skt. *agnidatta*, One of King Brahmadatta’s magistrates, from Vārāṇasī. Father of Son of Fire and Tongue of Fire. Not to be confused with Agnidatta (father of Śiṣyaka) prophesied to appear in the future, nor with Agnidatta of the royal palace Śobhāvatī.

## Agnighaṭa
*me’i rdza ma*, Skt. *agnighaṭa*, This might be a variation on the name for the third of the eight hot hells, the “crushing hell,” (Tib. bsdus ’joms, Skt. saṃghāta) as the name occurs in no other sūtra than the Kāraṇḍavyūha.

*sor mo threng ba*, one of the [Buddha's](#buddha) [disciple](#disciple)s, who despite having killed nine hundred and ninety nine people, was able, by purifying his [negative action](#negative-action)s, to attain the level of [Arhat](#arhat). His name [means](#means) "Garland of Fingers."

## ṣaṇḍha

These flying palaces of the deities are well known in Indian mythology. Burnouf translates as “chariots”; Kern has “aerial cars.”

## Śakra
*brgya byin*, Skt. *śakra*, The Tibetan name used in this text corresponds to the Sanskrit “Śakra,” another name for the preeminent vajra-wielding Vedic deity Indra who is called “lord of the deities” and is associated with storms and righteous warfare. The Tibetan translation is based on an etymology that śakra is an abbreviation of śata-kratu, “one who has performed a hundred sacrifices.” In Buddhism, he is the god of the realm equivalent to the second heaven of the desire realm, the heaven of Thirty-Three Gods. In the Buddhist Avataṃsaka cosmology of innumerable (asaṃkhyeya) interpenetrating buddha realms, there are myriad Śakras (aka Indra), each presiding over his own world-system.

*srog ’joms byed*, Skt. *śakraghna*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

*yid kyi las thams cad ye shes sngon du ’gro zhing ye shes kyi rjes su ’brang ba*, Skt. *sarva­manaḥ­karma­jñāna­pūrva­gamaṃ jñānānu­pari­varti*, Fifteenth or eighteenth of the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas.

*thugs kyi phrin las thams cad ye shes sngon du ’gro ste/ ye shes kyi rjes su ’brang*, Skt. *sarva­manaḥkarma­jñāna­pūrvagamaṃ jñānānuparivarti*, Fifteenth of the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas.

*ngag gi las thams cad ye shes sngon du ’gro zhing ye shes kyi rjes su ’brang ba*, Skt. *sarva­vāk­karma­jñāna­pūrva­gamaṃ jñānānu­pari­varti*, Fourteenth of the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas.

*gsung gi phrin las thams cad ye shes sngon du ’gro ste/ ye shes kyi rjes su ’brang*, Skt. *sarva­vākkarma­jñāna­pūrvagamaṃ jñānānuparivarti*, Fourteenth of the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas.

## All victorious banner

## all-aspect omniscience
*rnam pa thams cad mkhyen pa nyid*, Skt. *sarvākārajñatā*, This key term in the Prajñā­pāramitā literature refers to the omniscience of a buddha, and is not to be confused with the “knowledge of the aspects of the path” of bodhisattvas, or with the knowledge of all the dharmas (thams cad shes pa, lit. “omniscience”) of śrāvakas. The “all-aspect” (sarvākāra) part of the term refers to the different aspects that it comprises, and is explained in two ways in The Long Explanation (Toh 3808, –). One way identifies the “aspects” as being qualities such as nonarising and unproduced, unceasing, primordially at peace, naturally in nirvāṇa, without intrinsic nature, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, etc. The other way identifies them as being the collections of the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral, and the collection of those destined for error and those of uncertain destiny. All-aspect omniscience is also the first of the eight progressive stages of clear realization.

## all-aspect omniscience in all its finest aspects
*rnam pa thams cad mkhyen pa’i ye shes rnam pa’i mchog thams cad dang ldan pa*, Skt. *rnam pa thams cad mkhyen pa’i ye shes rnam pa’i mchog thams cad dang ldan pa*, The “finest aspect(s)” are, according to the two explanations in the Long Explanation (Toh 3808 –, see “knowledge of all aspects”), either (in the first explanation) emptiness, as the root of all the other aspects, or (in the second explanation) the aspects that are included in the collections of the wholesome and those destined for what is right.

*kun tu snang ba’i zla ba*, Skt. *kun tu snang ba’i zla ba*, A bodhisattva.

*tshangs pa thams cad zil gyis gnon pa’i ’od*, Skt. *brahma­prabha­sarvābhibhavana­jyoti*, A bodhisattva.

## all-pervading meditation
*mkha’ khyab kyi bsam gtan*, Skt. *āsphānaka*, The Sanskrit name for a particular state of meditation the corresponding Pāli of which is appānaka or appāṇaka. An alternate Buddhist Sanskrit term is āspharaṇaka. This meditation is described most famously in the Mahāsaccaka Sūtta of the Majjhima Nikāya where it is explained as a type of meditation in which the breathing is fully stopped, which then prompts the Bodhisattva to experience a loud and unpleasant sound. He then abandons the meditation. Edgerton cites a different explanation found in the Lalitavistara in which the meditation involves pervading everything while not agitating or disturbing the space element at all.

## ḍamaru
An implement held by several forms of Mahākāla and a number of forms of the goddesses in Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra. The ḍamaru is typically a hand-held, double-sided drum with two strikers. Each side of the drum can be made out of various substances, but in many tantric Buddhist traditions the two halves of this drum are made out of human skulls.

## Amitāyus (of the past)
*tshe dpag med*, Skt. *amitāyus*, A past buddha. His name (meaning “infinite life”) can refer more generally to the buddha associated with longevity and life energy who dwells in the western realm of Sukhāvatī and who is also known as Amitābha (“infinite light”). However, it is uncertain in this text whether this is referring to the same buddha; see . Elsewhere, this name refers to the buddha who is 283 among the buddhas of the Good Eon; see “Amitāyus (of the Good Eon).”

## amogha
*don yod pa*, Skt. *amogha*, The quality of being unfailing, and also the unfailing quality of Avalokiteśvara and the deities related to him, such as Amoghapāśa; in the latter sense, the term can appear before nouns in much the same way as “vajra,” when used adjectivally or adverbially.

*don yod mthong*, Skt. *amoghadarśana*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

*a mo g+ha k+ShA na ti*, Skt. *amoghakṣānti*, Amoghakṣānti (“Unfailing Forbearance”) seems to be here another epithet of Amoghapāśa.

## Amoghakrodha
*a mo g+ha kro d+ha*, Skt. *amoghakrodha*, Another paraphrase of the name Amogha­krodha­rāja, usually referred to simply as Krodharāja.

## Amogha­krodha­rāja
*don yod khro bo’i rgyal po*, Skt. *amogha­krodha­rāja*, Another name for the wrathful aspect of Amoghapāśa, usually referred to simply as Krodharāja.

## Amogha­krodhāṅkuśa
*don yod pa’i khro bo lcags kyu*, Skt. *amogha­krodhāṅkuśa*, Seems to be an elaboration of the name Krodhāṅkuśa.

## Amoghaśīla
*a mo g+ha shI la*, Skt. *amoghaśīla*, Amoghaśīla (“Unfailing Morality”) seems to be a context-specific epithet of Amoghapāśa.

## Amogha­maṇi­padma­pāśa
*don yod pa’i nor bu’i pad+ma zhags pa*, Skt. *amogha­maṇi­padma­pāśa*, The name of a dhāraṇī, referring to the deity Amoghapāśa. When amogha and pāśa are separated by maṇipadma, the phrase evokes the image of Avalokiteśvara holding a jeweled rosary and a lotus.

## Amogha-Ocean-Like Immaculate Splendor with the Gaze of the Great Holder of the Jewel and the Lotus
*don yod pa’i rgya mtsho’i nor bu chen po pad+ma la rnam par blta ba’i dpal dri ma med pa*, Skt. *amogha­sāgara­mahā­maṇi­padma­vilokita­śrī­vimala*, The name of a lotus king.

## Amoghapāśa
*don yod zhags pa*, Skt. *amoghapāśa*, “Unfailing Noose,” a prominent emanation of Avalokiteśvara in esoteric literature. The Amoghapāśakalparāja, a Kriyātantra, is dedicated to his rites.

## Amogha­pada­vikrāmin
*don yod gom pas rnam par gnon pa*, Skt. *amogha­pada­vikrāmin*, A great bodhisattva.

## Amoghapadmā
*don yod pa’i pad+ma*, Skt. *amoghapadmā*, One of the goddesses associated with Amoghapāśa.

## Amoghapadma
*a mo g+ha pad+ma*, Skt. *amoghapadma*, This seems to be another name for Amoghapāśa. However, it is often impossible to determine whether amoghapadma should be taken as a proper name or in its literal meaning of “amogha lotus.”

## Amogha­padma­hastā
*don yod pa’i phyag*, Skt. *amogha­padma­hastā*, One of the goddesses associated with Amoghapāśa.

## Amoghapadminī
*a mo g+ha pad+mi ni*, Skt. *amoghapadminī*, This seems to be another name of Amoghatārā.

## Amogha­padmoṣṇīṣa
*don yod pa pad+ma’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *amogha­padmoṣṇīṣa*, “Unfailing Lotus Uṣṇīṣa,” this seems to be a highly esoteric emanation of Amoghapāśa. Here he is also called Padmoṣṇīṣa.

## Amogha­padmoṣṇīṣa­pāśa
*don yod pad+ma gtsug tor gyi zhags pa*, Skt. *amogha­padmoṣṇīṣa­pāśa*, Amogha­padmoṣṇīṣa­pāśa seems to be another variant of the name Amoghapāśa-Padmoṣṇīṣa.

## Amogha­pāśa­krodha
*khro bo don yod pa’i zhags pa*, Skt. *amogha­pāśa­krodha*, Amogha­pāśa­krodha is another paraphrase of the name of Krodharāja as the wrathful form of Amoghapāśa (Amogha­pāśa-Krodha­rāja). When the name refers specifically to the deity’s mantra, it has been translated as “Wrathful Amoghapāśa.”

## Amogha­pāśāṅkuśa
*don yod pa’i zhags pa’i lcags kyu*, Skt. *amogha­pāśāṅkuśa*, The longer version of the name Amoghāṅkuśa.

## Amogha­pāśoṣṇīṣa
*don yod zhags pa’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *amogha­pāśoṣṇīṣa*, Possibly refers to Amoghapāśa-Padmoṣṇisa.

## Amogharaśmi
*’od zer don yod*, Skt. *amogharaśmi*, The 406th buddha in the first list, 405th in the second list, and 399th in the third list.

## Amogharāja
*don yod pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *amogharāja*, “Unfailing King” is used as an epithet of Amoghapāśa and any of his forms and is also used for some of his mantras. Arguably, it can also refer to the text of the Amogha­pāśa­kalpa­rāja as a whole, especially in the opening paragraphs where this text is introduced.

## Amogha­rāja­krodha
*khro bo don yod pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *amogha­rāja­krodha*, Another paraphrase of the name Amogha­krodha­rāja, usually referred to simply as Krodharāja.

## Amoghasiddhi
*don yod grub pa*, lit. he who accomplishes that which is meaningful. The [Buddha](#buddha) of the Action Family. See [five families](#five-families)

## Amoghatārā
*don yod par sgrol ba*, Skt. *amoghatārā*, “Unfailing Savioress” seems to be the name of the female counterpart of Amoghapāśa and of her vidyā mantra.

## Amoghavajra
*amoghavajra*, Skt. *amoghavajra*, 705–74. A famous and prolific translator, he is particularly renowned for his Chinese translations of Indian Buddhist esoteric works. He is known to have sailed from South India to China via Sri Lanka between 741 and 746. Not to be confused with the eleventh century paṇḍita of the same name who translated texts into Tibetan. Disciple of the translator and missionary Vajrabodhi.

## Amoghavikramin
*don yod rnam par gnon pa*, Skt. *amoghavikramin*, The 183rd buddha in the first list, 182nd in the second list, and 182nd in the third list.

## Amoghavilokita
*don yod pa rnam par lta ba*, Skt. *amoghavilokita*, “Unfailing Gaze” seems to be a short form of Amoghavilokita­pāśa.

## Amoghavilokita­pāśa
*don yod pa rnam par lta ba’i zhags pa*, Skt. *amoghavilokita­pāśa*, A paraphrase of the name Amoghāvalokita­pāśa. It is also the name of a mantra. The name translates literally as “Unfailing-Gaze-Noose,” a phrase too vague to venture a definitive interpretation.

## Amoghavipula
*a mo g+ha bi pu la*, Skt. *amoghavipula*, “Unfailing Vastness.” Seems to be here an epithet of Avalokiteśvara/Amoghapāśa.

## Amoghinī
*a mo g+ha ni*, Skt. *amoghinī*, A goddess associated with Amoghapāśa; a goddess with the same name is also found in the Śaiva Western Kaula tradition, associated with the goddess Kubjikā.

## Amoghāṅkuśī
*don yod pa’i lcags kyu*, Skt. *amoghāṅkuśī*, A goddess associated with Amoghapāśa.

## Amoghāṅkuśa
*don yod lcags kyu*, Skt. *amoghāṅkuśa*, The name of one of the emanations (“Unfailing Goad”) of Avalokiteśvara. Also, the name of a dhāraṇī mantra that is referred to in the text as “the heart dhāraṇī of precious amogha offerings.”

## Amoghāṅkuśa­krodha­rāja
*khro bo’i rgyal po don yod lcags kyu*, Skt. *amoghāṅkuśa­krodha­rāja*, Seems to be an elaboration of the name Krodhāṅkuśa.

## Amoghoṣṇīṣa
*don yod pa’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *amoghoṣṇīṣa*, Amoghoṣṇīṣa must be a short form of Amoghapāśa-Padmoṣṇīṣa.

## Amoghāvalokita­pāśa
*don yod par rnam par lta ba’i zhags pa’i snying po*, Skt. *amoghāvalokita­pāśa*, Another name of Amoghapāśa, associated with a particular mantra, whose meaning implies that it is his gaze that constitutes the “unfailing” noose.

## Amohavihārin
*gti mug med par gnas pa*, Skt. *amohavihārin*, The 821st buddha in the first list, 820th in the second list, and 810th in the third list.

## amply curved and elegant shoulders
*phrag pa’i lhun mdzes par grub pa*, Skt. *susaṃvṛta­skandhatā*, Nineteenth of the thirty-two major marks.

## amply curved shoulders
*dpung mgo shin tu zlum po*, Skt. *su­saṃ­vṛta­skandha­tā*, Sixteenth of the thirty-two major marks.

## Amra
*a mra*, Skt. *amra*, A yakṣa.

## Amradhara
*a mra ’chang*, Skt. *amradhara*, A yakṣa. (Toh 555: a mra thogs pa)

## amrita
The nectar of immortality possessed by the gods (deva). It is frequently used as a metaphor for the teachings that brings liberation.

## Amṛtā
*bdud rtsi ma*, Skt. *amṛtā*, One of eight children, a daughter, of King Siṃhahanu of Kapilavastu.

## amṛta
*bdud rtsi*, Skt. *amṛta*, The ambrosia that prevents death or spiritual death (hence the Tibetan term meaning “crushes spiritual death”). The Sanskrit term literally means “immortality.” It is often used metaphorically to mean the Dharma.

## Amṛtabhavana Monastery
*bdud rtsi ’byung gnas kyi gtsug lag khang*, Skt. *bdud rtsi ’byung gnas kyi gtsug lag khang*, A Buddhist monastery in Kashmir that is reported in Chinese sources to have existed as early as ca. 750 ce.

## Amṛtabindu
*bdud rtsi*, Skt. *amṛtabindu*, A pore on Avalokiteśvara’s body.

## Amṛtaṃdhara
*bdud rtsi ’dzin*, Skt. *amṛtaṃdhara*, A great bodhisattva.

## Amṛtadhāra
*bdud rtsi rgyun*, Skt. *amṛtadhāra*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Amṛtadhārin
*bdud rtsi ’chang*, Skt. *amṛtadhārin*, The 145th buddha in the first list, 145th in the second list, and 145th in the third list.

## Amṛtaghoṣa
*bdud rtsi’i dbyangs*, Skt. *amṛtaghoṣa*, A great bodhisattva.

## Amṛtaguṇatejarāja
*yon tan bdud rtsi gzi brjid rgyal po*, Skt. *amṛtaguṇatejarāja*, One of ten names of a thousand buddhas prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha, with presumably a hundred buddhas having this name.

## Amṛtakānikāṭippanī
Skt. *amṛtakānikāṭippanī*, Raviśrījñāna’s commentary on the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti.

## Amṛtakīrti
*bdud rtsi grags pa*, Skt. *amṛtakīrti*, A buddha.

## Amṛtakuṇḍalī
*bdud rtsi ’khyil ldan*, Skt. *amṛtakuṇḍalī*, A deity, one of the five kings of vidyās ( vidyārāja ).

## Amṛtakuṇḍalin
*bdud rtsi thab sbyor can*, Skt. *amṛtakuṇḍalin*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Amṛtamati
*bdud rtsi blo gros*, Skt. *amṛtamati*, Lit. “Nectar Intelligence.”

## Amṛta­parvata­prabhā­tejas
*bdud rtsi’i ri bo’i gzi brjid*, Skt. *amṛta­parvata­prabhā­tejas*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Amṛtaprabha
*bdud rtsi’i ’od*, Skt. *amṛtaprabha*, The 709th buddha in the first list, 708th in the second list, and 698th in the third list.

## Amṛtaprasanna
*bdud rtsi gsal ba*, Skt. *amṛtaprasanna*, The 785th buddha in the first list, 784th in the second list, and 774th in the third list.

## Amṛtasāra
*bdud rtsi’i snying po*, Skt. *amṛtasāra*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Amṛtaśuddha
Skt. *amṛtaśuddha*, The name of King Araṇemin in the latter half of The White Lotus of Compassion Sūtra.

## Amṛtavilokinī
*a mra ta bi lo ki ni*, Skt. *amṛtavilokinī*, In the Sampuṭodbhava, this deity is invoked to help obtain a son.

## Amṛtādhipa
*bdud rtsi bdag po*, Skt. *amṛtādhipa*, The 882nd buddha in the first list, 881st in the second list, and 872nd in the third list.

## Amṛtodana
*bdud rtsi zas*, Skt. *amṛtodana*, One of eight children, a son, of King Siṃhahanu of Kapilavastu.

## amugala
An unidentified ritual ingredient.

## amuha
An unidentified medicinal and ritual substance.

## Ṣaṇmukhā
*gdong drug ma*, Skt. *ṣaṇmukhā*, One of the dhāraṇī goddesses present at the delivery of the MMK.

## Amśurāja
*snang ba’i rgyal po*, Skt. *amśurāja*, The name of a bodhisattva meaning “King of Illumination.”

## Amṛṣya
*bzod par dka’ ba*, Skt. *amṛṣya*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## śamyāprāsa
The Vedic ritual in which offerings are made at intervals of a “wedge throw” (śamyāprāsa).

## An Adornment for the Precious Path to Liberation
*dam chos yid bzhin nor bu thar pa rin po che’i rgyan*, Skt. *dam chos yid bzhin nor bu thar pa rin po che’i rgyan*, A celebrated text on the graduated path by Gampopa, also known as the Dakpo Thargyen (dwags po thar rgyan).

## An Shigao
*安世高*, An Shigao (安世高, fl. c. 148–180 ce) was an early Central Asian Buddhist missionary to China, and the earliest known translator of Indian Buddhist texts into Chinese. He was active in the Chinese imperial capital of Luoyang (洛陽) in the latter half of the 2nd century ce.

## Anabhibhūta
*zil mi non pa*, Skt. *anabhibhūta*, A buddha field in the eastern direction.

## Anabhibhūta­mukuṭa
*zil gyis non pa myed pa’i cod pan*, Skt. *anabhibhūta­mukuṭa*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## anabhilakṣita
*mngon par ma dmigs pa*, Skt. *anabhilakṣita*, Lit. “not distinguished.” Name of a meditative stabilization

## anabhilāpya
*brjod du med pa*, Skt. *anabhilāpya*, Lit. “inexpressible.” An incredibly large number, higher than abhāṣya.

## anabhilāpyānabhilāpya
*brjod du med pa’i yang brjod du med pa*, Skt. *anabhilāpyānabhilāpya*, Lit. “inexpressibly inexpressible.” An incredibly large number, higher than anabhilāpya.

## anabhilāpyānabhilāpya­parivarta
*brjod du med pa’i yang brjod du med pa la bsgres*, Skt. *anabhilāpyānabhilāpya­parivarta*, The term for the largest number given in this sūtra.

## Anabhilāpyodgata
*brjod du med par ’phags pa*, Skt. *anabhilāpyodgata*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Anabhrakā
*sprin med*, Skt. *anabhrakā*, Lit. “Cloudless.” The tenth of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and pure abodes‍‍, or Śuddhāvāsa, it is listed as the first of the three heavens that correspond to the fourth of the four concentrations.

## Anabhraka
*sprin med*, Skt. *anabhraka*, Literally meaning “Cloudless,” the more usual name for what is, in the Prajñāpāramitā literature, the fourteenth of the sixteen levels of the god realm of form that correspond to the four meditative concentrations, and in this text and in the Hundred Thousand is instead rendered Parīttabṛhat (q.v.). Anabhraka is used in the later Sanskrit manuscripts that correspond more closely to the eight-chapter Tengyur version of this text. In other genres, it is the tenth of twelve levels corresponding to the four meditative concentrations.

## An­abhraka
*sprin med*, Skt. *an­abhraka*, Tenth god realm of form, meaning “cloudless.”

## Anaṅgaṇa
*nyon mongs med*, Skt. *anaṅgaṇa*, The fourth of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin. He becomes the bodhisattva Vajraccheda­prajñā­vabhāsaśrī and is prophesied to become the Buddha Samantabhadra.

## Anaṅgana
*nyon mongs med*, Skt. *anaṅgana*, The head of a guild who was Jyotiṣka in a former life.

## Anagha
*sdig med*, Skt. *anagha*, The ninth son of King Araṇemin, who becomes the bodhisattva Akṣobhya and is prophesied to become buddha Akṣobhya.

## Śanaiścara
“The Slow-Going One.” The planet Saturn.

## Śanairgāmin
*dal bzhud*, Skt. *śanairgāmin*, The 454th buddha in the first list, 453rd in the second list, and 447th in the third list.

## Analā
*me*, Skt. *analā*, A great rākṣasī.

## anal fistula
*bkres ngab*, Skt. *aṭakkara*, Symptom that may be evidence of an illness considered an impediment to ordination.

## Anala
*me*, Skt. *anala*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## analysis
*dpyod pa*, Skt. *vicāra*, A mental factor understood either as “the subtlety of the mind” or as the cause for such subtlety. More elaborate definitions explain it as a type of “mental murmur” (manojalpa) that is searching (paryeṣaka) and can be either based on intention (cetanā) or on wisdom (prajñā). See also “deliberation” (vitarka).

## analytical ability
May refer to the four analytical abilities, listed here as analytical ability in relation to objects, analytical ability in relation to phenomena, analytical ability in relation to language, and analytical ability in relation to eloquence.

## analytical knowledge
*so sor yang dag par rig pa*, Skt. *pratisaṃvid*, See Har Dayal 2004, p. 260ff.

## analyze
*so sor rtog par byed*, Skt. *pratyavekṣaṇa*, The term so sor rtog pa has two meanings in our text: (1) analysis (pratyavekṣa) and (2) comprehension, realization, awakening (pratibodha).

## Anantā
*mtha’ yas ma*, Skt. *anantā*, One of the female śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Ananta
*mtha’ yas*, Skt. *ananta*, One of the principal nāga kings. Also known as Śeṣa or Anataśeṣa. Considered the source of Patañjali grammar in Buddhism. In Vaiśnavism he is the serpent that Viṣṇu rests upon in between the creations of worlds.

## Anantaṭī
*’gro ba mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantaṭī*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## A­nanta
*mtha’ yas*, Skt. *a­nanta*, A king of the nāgas.

## Ananta­bala­vighuṣṭa­nirnādita­śrī­saṃbhava­mati
*stobs mtha’ yas grags par brjod pa’i dpal yang dag par ’byung ba’i blo gros*, Skt. *ananta­bala­vighuṣṭa­nirnādita­śrī­saṃbhava­mati*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Anantabhūta
Skt. *anantabhūta*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Anantabuddhi
A bodhisattva whose name is attested in the Sanskrit manuscript of this sūtra, which says he will become the last of the one thousand buddhas in this fortunate eon.

## Anantacāritra
*spyod pa mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantacāritra*, One of the four principal bodhisattvas who emerged from the ground at the time of the teaching of the Lotus Sūtra.

## Anantadruma
*ljon pa mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantadruma*, One of the kinnara kings.

## Anantagati
*mtha’ yas ’gros*, Skt. *anantagati*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Anantaghoṣa
*mtha’ yas dbyangs*, Skt. *anantaghoṣa*, The name of two separate buddhas from whom Śākyamuni received the Samādhirāja in previous lifetimes.

## Anantagrīva
*mgrin pa mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantagrīva*, One of the vidyārājas dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Anantaguṇa­kīrti
A realized one whose name is attested in the Sanskrit manuscript of this sūtra.

## Anantaguṇaratnavyūha
A world visited by the Buddha, as narrated by Vajrapāṇi in this sūtra.

## Ananta­guṇa­ratna­vyūha
*yon tan rin chen mtha’ yas bkod pa*, Skt. *ananta­guṇa­ratna­vyūha*, Lit. “infinite array of jewel-qualities.” A universe of Buddha Ratnavyūha, also mentioned in the Lalita­vistara­sūtra.

## Ananta­guṇa­sāgarajñānottara
*yon tan rgya mtsho’i mtha’ yas ye shes bla ma*, Skt. *ananta­guṇa­sāgarajñānottara*, One of ten names of a thousand buddhas prophesied by Buddha Ratnagarbha, with presumably a hundred buddhas having this name.

## Ananta­guṇa­tejorāśi
*yon tan mtha’ yas gzi brjid phung po*, Skt. *ananta­guṇa­tejorāśi*, The 953rd buddha in the first list, 952nd in the second list, and 943rd in the third list.

## Anantaśiras
*mgo mtha’ yas pa*, Skt. *anantaśiras*, One of the kings of the rākṣasas.

## Anantajñānavicita
*ye shes mtha’ yas rnam par bsags pa*, Skt. *ye shes mtha’ yas rnam par bsags pa*, A buddha (“He in Whom Infinite Wisdom Is Amassed”).

## Anantaketu
*mtha’ yas tog ma*, Skt. *anantaketu*, One of the dhāraṇī goddesses present at the delivery of the MMK.

## Anantakrama
*gom stabs mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantakrama*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Anantakīrti
*grags pa mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantakīrti*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Anantakuṇḍalin
*mtha’ yas thab sbyor can*, Skt. *anantakuṇḍalin*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Anantamati
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra, whose name is attested in the Saddharma­puṇḍarīka.

## Ananta­mati­pratipatti
*blo mtha’ yas sgrub pa*, Skt. *ananta­mati­pratipatti*, The name of a bodhisattva. “Accomplished Limitless Intellect.”

## Anantamukhī
*a nan+ta mu khi*, Skt. *anantamukhī*, “One with the Face of Ananta.” One of the eight nāga queens.

## Anantamukhasādhakā
The name of a dhāraṇī goddess.

## Anantanemi
*mu khyud mtha' yas*, Skt. *anantanemi*, King of [Ujjayinī](#ujjayinī) and father of [Pradyota](#pradyota).

## Ananta­parikara­sāgara­megha­vyūha­tejo­maṇḍala­chartākāra­rāja
*rgya mtsho’i sprin bkod pa’i gzi brjid kyi dkyil ’khor gdugs lta bu’i rgyal po*, Skt. *ananta­parikara­sāgara­megha­vyūha­tejo­maṇḍala­chartākāra­rāja*, Lord of the nāgas in the trichiliocosm.

## Anantapatra
*’dab ma mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantapatra*, One of the uṣṇīṣa kings attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Anantaphala
*mtha’ yas ’bras bu*, Skt. *anantaphala*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Anantapāṇi
*mtha’ yas phyag*, Skt. *anantapāṇi*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Anantapīlu
*pI lu mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantapīlu*, One of the kings of the piśācas.

## anantaprabha
*’od mtha’ yas pa*, Skt. *anantaprabha*, Lit. “endless light.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Ananta­prabhāsamati
*mtha’ yas snang ba’i blo gros*, Skt. *ananta­prabhāsamati*, The name of a bodhisattva. “Infinite Radiant Intellect.”

## Anantapratibhāna
*spobs pa mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantapratibhāna*, Name of a bodhisattva.

## ananta­pratibhāna
*spobs pa mtha’ yas pa*, Skt. *ananta­pratibhāna*, Lit. “endless confidence.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Ananta­prati­bhāna
*spobs pa mtha’ yas*, Skt. *ananta­prati­bhāna*, A bodhisattva present during the delivery of the King of the Array of all Dharma Qualities.

## Ananta­pratibhāna­ketu
*spobs pa mtha’ yas tog*, Skt. *ananta­pratibhāna­ketu*, The 933rd buddha in the first list, 932nd in the second list, and 923rd in the third list.

## Ananta­pratibhāna­ketu­dhvaja­vikurvita­ghoṣa
*spobs pa mtha’ yas pa’i tog gi rgyal mtshan rnam par sprul pa’i dbyangs*, Skt. *ananta­pratibhāna­ketu­dhvaja­vikurvita­ghoṣa*, A bodhisattva mahāsattva present in the Buddha’s assembly. His name means, “Magical Voice like a Victory Banner of Infinite Eloquence.”

## Ananta­pratibhāna­raśmi
*spobs pa mtha’ yas ’od zer*, Skt. *ananta­pratibhāna­raśmi*, The 943rd buddha in the first list, 942nd in the second list, and 933rd in the third list.

## Anantaśrī
Skt. *anantaśrī*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Anantaraśmi
*’od zer mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantaraśmi*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## Ananta­raśmi­dharma­dhātu­samalaṃkṛta­dharma­rāja
*chos kyi dbyings ’od gzer mtha’ yas pas yongs su brgyan pa’i chos kyi rgyal po*, Skt. *ananta­raśmi­dharma­dhātu­samalaṃkṛta­dharma­rāja*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Anantaraśmin
*’od zer mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantaraśmin*, A buddha.

## Ananta­rati­kīrti
*dga’ ba mtha’ yas grags*, Skt. *ananta­rati­kīrti*, The 964th buddha in the first list, 963rd in the second list, and 954th in the third list.

## Anantaśriyā
*mtha’ yas dpal*, Skt. *anantaśriyā*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Anantarāśmin
*’od zer mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantarāśmin*, A buddha.

## Anantarūpa
*mtha’ yas gzugs*, Skt. *anantarūpa*, The 178th buddha in the first list, 177th in the second list, and 177th in the third list.

## Anantasvara
*mtha’ yas pa’i sgra*, Skt. *anantasvara*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Anantatejas
*gzi brjid mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantatejas*, The 237th buddha in the first list, 236th in the second list, and 236th in the third list.

## Anantatreya
*mtha’ yas rgyun shes kyi bu*, Skt. *anantatreya*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Anantaujas
*gzi brjid mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantaujas*, A tathāgata mentioned here as one of the thirty-five buddhas of confession.

## Anantavikrama
*mtha’ yas rnam par gnon pa*, Skt. *anantavikrama*, A buddha.

## Anantavikrāmiṇ
*mtha’ yas gnon*, Skt. *anantavikrāmiṇ*, A bodhisattva present at the sūtra’s teaching.

## Anantavikrāmin
*mthu rtsal mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantavikrāmin*, The 215th buddha in the first list, 214th in the second list, and 214th in the third list.

## Anantavinaya
*mtha’ yas ’dul ba*, Skt. *anantavinaya*, A buddha.

## Anantavīrya
*brtson ’grus mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantavīrya*, A bodhisattva great being present in the audience of this sūtra.

## Anantavyūha
*bkod pa mtha’ yas pa*, Skt. *anantavyūha*, Name of a bodhisattva, the main recipient and interlocutor of the Ananta­mukhapariśo­dhana­nirdeśa Sūtra.

## Anantayaśas
*grags pa mtha’ yas*, Skt. *anantayaśas*, The 405th buddha in the first list, 404th in the second list, and 398th in the third list.

## Anantābha
*mtha’ yas ’od*, Skt. *anantābha*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Anantānta

Skt. *pitṛvana*, A haunt of the ancestor spirits and a place where rites can be performed to them. A cemetery or charnel ground.

## ancient linguistic usage
*brda rnying*, Translational terminology used before the revisions and codification of the ninth century.

## Ancient Tradition
*rnying ma pa*, the followers of the first teachings of [Secret Mantra](#secret-mantrayāna) propagated in Tibet by the great master [Padmasambhava](#padmasambhava-of-oḍḍiyāna) in the 8th century. [Patrul Rinpoche](#patrul-rinpoche) belonged to this school. See also [Nyingmapa](#nyingmapa) and [Ancient Translations](#ancient-translations).

## Ancient Translations
*snga 'gyur*, name given to the first teachings translated from Sanskrit and propagated in Tibet, those of the Ancient, or [Nyingmapa](#nyingmapa) Tradition, as opposed to the teachings that were translated and propagated from the 10th century onwards and which gave birth to the [New Tradition](#new-tradition) of Tibetan Buddhism.

## Andhaka

## Andhra
The name of a region along the southeast coast of the Indian subcontinent, roughly corresponding to the present-day state of Andhra Pradesh.

## aneṣa
*tshol ba med pa*, Skt. *aneṣa*, Lit. “not seeking.” Name of a meditative stabilization. Edgerton says the correct form is aneṣa. Animiṣa usually means “unblinking,” but here it is a different form of aneṣa.

## anger
*zhe sdang*, Skt. *dveṣa*, Aversion in all its forms. One of the three poisons (Tib. dug gsum, Skt. triviṣa) that, along with desire and delusion, perpetuate the sufferings of cyclic existence. In its subtle manifestation as aversion, it obstructs the correct perception of forms, and in its extreme manifestations as anger and fear, it is characteristic of the hells.

## anguished spirit
*yi dags*, Skt. *preta*, Also called a “hungry ghost,” an inhabitant of one of the three lower realms who suffers constantly from insatiable hunger and thirst, the karmic fruition of past miserliness. See “five destinies.”

*gnas dang bral ba*, Skt. *aniketa*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.
