*dul ba’i bshes gnyen*, Skt. *dul ba’i bshes gnyen*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Raśmi.

## Friend of Wandering Beings
*’gro ba’i bshes gnyen*, Skt. *’gro ba’i bshes gnyen*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Suviniścitārtha.

## Frightening Form
*skrag byed gzugs can*, Skt. *skrag byed gzugs can*, A rākṣasa king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Frightful Direct Teacher
*’jigs pa mngon du ston pa*, Skt. *mahābhīmadarśana*, A yakṣa.

## Frolicking
*rab tu rtse bar byed pa*, Skt. *rab tu rtse bar byed pa*, Frolicking (playing or moving about cheerfully), also the name of a pond on Equal Peaks.

## frontier tribesmen
*mtha’ ’khob kyi mi rnams*, Skt. *pratyanta­jana­pada*, I.e., those living beyond the pale of civilization, out of reach of the sacred doctrine.

## fruit
*’bras bu*, Skt. *phala*, Effect, result, fruit.

## Fruit empowerment
*'bras bu'i dbang*, the [empowerment](#empowerment) that takes place at the moment of attaining full [enlightenment](#enlightenment).

## fruit of being destined for only one more rebirth
*lan gcig phyir ’ong ba’i ’bras bu*, Skt. *sakṛdāgāmī­phala*, Second of the four fruits attainable by śrāvakas.

## fruit of being tied to one more rebirth
*lan cig phyir ’ong ba’i ’bras bu*, Skt. *sakṛd­āgāmī­phala*, Second of the four fruits attainable by śrāvakas.

## fruit of entering the stream
*rgyun tu zhugs pa’i ’bras bu*, Skt. *śrotaāpanna­phala*, First of the four fruits attainable by śrāvakas, that of the first stage in which one has entered the “stream” of practice that leads to nirvāṇa. See also “entering the stream.”

## fruit of no longer being subject to rebirth
*phyir mi ’ong ba’i ’bras bu*, Skt. *āgāmīphala*, Third of the four fruits attainable by śrāvakas.

## fruit of non-returner
*phyir mi ’ong ba’i ’bras bu*, Skt. *āgāmīphala*, Third of the four fruits attainable by śrāvakas. See “non-returner.”

## fruit of once-returner
*lan gcig phyir ’ong ba’i ’bras bu*, Skt. *sakṛdāgāmī­phala*, Second of the four fruits attainable by śrāvakas. See “once-returner.”

## fruit of stream-entry
*rgyun du zhugs pa’i ’bras bu*, Skt. *srotāpatti­phala*, The first of the four spiritual achievements, which is considered to be entering “the stream” of the noble ones that flows inexorably toward awakening.

## Fruitful Conduct
*gdon mi za ba’i spyod pa*, Skt. *gdon mi za ba’i spyod pa*, A thus-gone one of the past.

## fruition of actions
*las kyi rnam par smin pa*, Skt. *karmavipāka*, See “ripening of karma.”

## fruitional buddha body of reality
*’bras bu chos sku*, Skt. *dharma­kāya*, Eighth of the eight progressive sections of clear realization.

## Fruits of Constant Beauty
*’bras bu rtag tu mdzas*, Skt. *’bras bu rtag tu mdzas*, A forest of the asuras.

## Fulfillment of Wishes
*bsams ’gro*, Skt. *bsams ’gro*, (1) A lake near Sudharma (bsams ’gro). (2) A lotus pool in Lateral (yid bzhin sna tshogs).

## Fulfilment of Excellent Aspirations
*legs par bsams pa’i smon lam yongs su grub pa*, Skt. *legs par bsams pa’i smon lam yongs su grub pa*, A buddha.

## Fulfilment of Wishes
*bsam pa ji lta ba bzhin ’byung ba*, Skt. *bsam pa ji lta ba bzhin ’byung ba*, Birthplace of the buddha Siddhārtha.

## Full
*gang po*, Skt. *gang po*, Full (holding as much as possible; complete), also the name of an attendant of the buddha Vairocana.

## Full Array
The name of a buddha domain of the past where there lived a buddha named King Arrangement of Manifold Precious Jewels of Virtues Without End.

## Full Ears
*rna ba gang po*, Skt. *rna ba gang po*, A householder in this sūtra.

## Full effect
*rnam smin gyi 'bras bu*, Skt. *vipākaphala*, the point at which an action has its maximum effect, for instance a rebirth in [hell](#hell).

## full moon
A type of worm (srin bu) that lives in and feeds on the body.

## Full of Hundreds of Birds
*bya brgya phrag gis kun tu gang ba*, Skt. *bya brgya phrag gis kun tu gang ba*, A lake on Equal Peaks.

## Full of Lotuses
*pad mas khyab par gyur pa*, Skt. *pad mas khyab par gyur pa*, A lotus pond on the fifth minor mountain on Lofty Summit.

## full ordination
*bsnyen pa rdzogs pa*, Skt. *upasampadā*, The ceremony of full or higher ordination by which a novice (śrāmaṇera) or a female postulant (śikṣamāṇā) is confirmed as a fully ordained member of the order of nuns or monks (see Buswell and Lopez 2014, s.v. “upasaṃpadā”).

## full probation
*yongs su spo ba*, A full probation is imposed when a monk who has incurred a [saṅgha](#saṅgha) stigmata offense nurses for a full night his intention to conceal that offense (Viśeṣamitra, folio 135.b).

## Full Realization through Joy
*dga’ bas rgyas pa yang dag par rtogs pa*, Skt. *dga’ bas rgyas pa yang dag par rtogs pa*, Birthplace of the buddha Yaśas.

## full set of forty even teeth
*tshems mnyam zhing bzhi tshang ba*, Skt. *sama­catvāriśaddantatā*, Thirtieth of the thirty-two major marks.

## Fully Absorbing
*mngon par sdud pa*, Skt. *mngon par sdud pa*, A daughter of Māra present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## fully accomplished buddha
An epithet of a buddha.

## Fully Adorned with Jewels
*rin po che thams cad kyis spras pa*, Skt. *rin po che thams cad kyis spras pa*, A buddhafield in the northern direction of the Tathāgata Countless Qualities Precious Courage.

## Fully Arrayed
*kun tu bkod pa*, Skt. *kun tu bkod pa*, Name of the world system of the thus-gone one Jewel Foundation.

## fully awakened
*mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas*, Skt. *abhisaṃbuddha*, A person who has manifested the complete enlightenment of a buddha of the Greater Vehicle.

## Fully Blooming
*kun tu rgyas pa*, Skt. *kun tu rgyas pa*, Birthplace of the buddha Ṛṣideva.

## Fully Cleansed
*rnam par sbyong ba*, Skt. *rnam par sbyong ba*, A realm that will appear in the eon Universal Illumination, one hundred incalculable eons from now.

## Fully Endowed with Qualities
*kun tu yon tan can*, Skt. *kun tu yon tan can*, Birthplace of the buddha Ratnaprabhāsa.

## Fully Hanging
*rab tu ’phyang ma*, Skt. *rab tu ’phyang ma*, One of the eight great yakṣīs.

## Fully Illuminated Oceanic King of Many Hundreds of Virtues
*kun nas ’od zer yon tan rtag tu mang ba brgya mtsho’i rgyal po*, Skt. *kun nas ’od zer yon tan rtag tu mang ba brgya mtsho’i rgyal po*, A buddha who lives in the east in a buddha realm called Elevated by Abiding in Aspiration.

## Fully Illuminating
*rnam par snang byed*, Skt. *rnam par snang byed*, The realm of the Buddha Candrasūrya.

## Fully Joyous
*kun tu dga’ ba dang ldan pa*, Skt. *kun tu dga’ ba dang ldan pa*, Name of the world system of the thus-gone one Immeasurable Light.

## fully ordained
*rdzogs par bsnyen pa*, Skt. *upasampanna*, Someone fully ordained.

## fully ordained monk
*dge slong*, Skt. *bhikṣu*, A fully ordained male practitioner observing 253 Vinaya vows.

## fully ordained nun
*dge slong ma*, Skt. *bhikṣuṇī*, A fully ordained female practitioner observing 364 Vinaya vows.

## Fully-adorned Sky
*nam mkha’ yongs su brgyan pa*, Skt. *nam mkha’ yongs su brgyan pa*, Name of the world system of the thus-gone one Lamp of the Sky of Dharma. Likely the same as the world system Palmyra Trees Reaching the Sky.

## Fumes of Incense
*spos kyi ngad ldang*, Skt. *spos kyi ngad ldang*, A buddha realm.

## fundamental ignorance
*ma rig pa*, Skt. *a­vidyā*, First of the twelve links of dependent origination; first of the four torrents; third of the fetters associated with the higher realms.

## fundamental precepts
*bslab pa’i gzhi rnams*, Skt. *śikṣāvastu*, (1) Not killing (srog gcod spong ba), (2) not stealing (ma byin par len pa spong ba), (3) not indulging in sexual conduct (ma tshangs spyod spong ba), (4) not lying (brdzun du smra ba spong ba), (5) not taking intoxicants (myos ’gyur btung ba spong ba), (6) not using cosmetics, ornaments and garlands, etc. (spos dang kha dog byug pa spong ba), (7) not using high and luxurious seats or beds (khri stan che mtho spong ba), and (8) not taking untimely food/not eating after noon (dus min zas spong ba).

## fundamental transgression
*phas pham pa*, Skt. *pārājika*, The four downfalls for monastics resulting in the forfeit of the monastic vows: sexual intercourse, theft, murder, and claiming greater realization than one has.

## furlong
*dpag tshad*, Skt. *yojana*, An ancient Indian measure of distance. Variously defined, a “furlong” is often said to be the distance cattle can plow without a rest and to be four or eight times as long as an “earshot.”

## Furnace
*me thab*, Skt. *agnikuṇḍa*, Furnace (an enclosed chamber for intense heat or fire), also the name of one of sixteen realms that surround the Crushing Hell.

## further probation
*yang gzhi nas bslang ste mgu [bar](#bar) bya ba, yang gzhi nas bslang ste spo ba*, Skt. *mūlāpakarṣamānāpya, mūlāpakarṣamānātva, mūlāpakarṣaparivāsa*, Imposed on a monk who incurs a third [saṅgha remnant](#saṅgha-remnant) offense while serving his [probation](#probation).

## Future Hearers
*nyan thos ma ’ongs pa*, Skt. *nyan thos ma ’ongs pa*, Name of the world system of the thus-gone one Stūpa That Overwhelms with Jewel Light.

## Gö Chödrup
*’gos chos grub*, A prolific translator active in Dunhuang during the early ninth century (c. 755–849) who translated this sūtra from Chinese to Tibetan.

## Gö Khukpa Lhetse
A Tibetan translator active in the eleventh century.

## Gö Lhetsé
*’gos lhas btsas*, Skt. *’gos lhas btsas*, Eleventh century translator and teacher of Guhya­samāja­tantra.

## Ṛg Veda
*nges brjod kyi rig byed*, Skt. *ṛgveda*, Along with the Yajur Veda, Sāma Veda, and Atharva Veda, one of the four Vedas, the most ancient Sanskrit religious literature of India.

## Ga
The people of the Mutsa Ga clan are said to have originated from Azha (’a zha), also known as Tuyuhun. According to The Treasure of the Ancestral Clans of Tibet, they are known for being studious and hence erudite in matters of learning. Their element is wood, and their spirit animal (bla zog) is the goat.

## gaṇḍī
A percussion instrument made from a wooden beam drawn from specific trees to particular proportions. It has been widely used in Buddhist monasteries to signal timed events like the assembling of monastics.

## Śṛṅga
*rtse mo*, Skt. *śṛṅga*, An ancient city corresponding to the modern Śṛṅgeri in Karnataka, in southwestern India.

## gaṇḍī beam
*gaN D+'i, gaN+D+'i*, Skt. *gaṇḍī*, An elongated, shoulder-held wooden [bar](#bar) (or beam) struck with a wooden striker to call the [saṅgha](#saṅgha) community to assembly.

## Öga Pünsum
A place in Tibet.

## gaṇa
*tshogs pa*, Skt. *gaṇa*, The name for the troops or classes of lower deities and beings, particularly those considered attendants of the god Śiva over whom Ganeśa (lit. “Lord of the Gaṇas”) has control.

## Gaṇaśaṅkara
*grong byed bde byed*, Skt. *gaṇaśaṅkara*, Probably another name of Śaṅkara, a contemporary of Mahendra.

## gaṇacakra feast
*tshogs kyi dkyil ’khor*, Skt. *gaṇacakra*, A ritual feast offered to the deities and all beings in the three realms.

## Gaṇapati
*tshogs bdag*, Skt. *gaṇapati*, Gaṇapati, or Ganeśa, is the lord of the gaṇas, a class of demigods usually associated with the god Śiva. In the Purāṇic traditions Gaṇapati is portrayed as the elephant-headed son of Śiva and Pārvatī.

## Gaṇḍa­vyūha­sūtra
*sdong pos brgyan pa’i le’u*, Skt. *gaṇḍa­vyūha­sūtra*, The Gaṇḍavyūha­sūtra (Toh 44-45) is an important Sanskrit ­sūtra that traces the journey of the young pilgrim Sudhana toward awakening. It was later incorporated into the large scriptural omnibus Buddhāvataṃsaka­sūtra as its forty-fifth chapter.

## Gada
*sgra*, Skt. *gada*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Gadgadasvara
*sang sang po’i dbyangs*, Skt. *gadgadasvara*, A bodhisattva in a distant realm.

## Gaṇendra
*tshogs dbang*, Skt. *gaṇendra*, The 736th buddha in the first list, 735th in the second list, and 725th in the third list.

## Gaṇendrarāja
*tshogs kyi dbang po’i rgyal po*, Skt. *gaṇendrarāja*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## Gaṇeśvara
*tshogs kyi dbang phyug*, Skt. *gaṇeśvara*, A name that appears twice in the list of buddhas from whom Śākyamuni in previous lifetimes received the Samādhirāja, and who is described in particular in chapter 38.

## Gaṅgā
*gang gA*, Skt. *gaṅgā*, The most important holy river in India, more commonly known in English as the Ganges.

## Gaṅgā River
*gang gA’i klung*, Skt. *gaṅgā*, The sacred river of India.

## Gagaṇagañja
*nam mkha’ mdzod*, Skt. *gagaṇagañja*, A bodhisattva who resided in the Varagaṇā world of the Thus-Gone One Gaṇendra’s buddha realm, and proceeded to Bodhgayā to venerate the Buddha.

## Gagaṇapāṇi
*nam mkha’i phyag*, Skt. *gagaṇapāṇi*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Gaṅgadevī
*gang gA’i lha mo*, Skt. *gaṅgadevī*, The name of a nun who commits to the practice of the six perfections and worships the Buddha with golden-colored flowers. The Buddha predicts her future awakening as the buddha Suvarṇapuṣpa, during the eon called Tārakopama.

## Gagana
*nam mkha’*, Skt. *gagana*, The 766th buddha in the first list, 765th in the second list, and 755th in the third list.

## Gagana­buddhi
*nam mkha’i blo*, Skt. *gagana­buddhi*, A bodhisattva present with the Buddha at Śrāvastī, and also the name of a buddha in the distant past.

## Gagana­citta
*nam mkha’i thugs*, Skt. *gagana­citta*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Gaganagañja
*nam mkha’ mdzod*, Skt. *gaganagañja*, In the Kāraṇḍavyūha it is the name of both a bodhisattva and a samādhi. In this sūtra the bodhisattva is a pupil of Buddha Viśvabhū, but he is also portrayed in other sūtras receiving teaching from Śākyamuni, and is one of the sixteen bodhisattvas in the Vairocana maṇḍala.

## Gagana­garbha
*nam mkha’i snying po*, Skt. *gagana­garbha*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## Gagana­ghoṣa
*nam mkha’i dbyangs*, Skt. *gagana­ghoṣa*, The eighth buddha in a kalpa in the distant past, and also the name of the sixty-second buddha in another kalpa. The Tibetan has dbyings in error for dbyangs for the sixty-second buddha.

## gaganakalpa
*nam mkha’ dang mtshungs pa*, Skt. *gaganakalpa*, Lit. “sky-like.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Gaganaketu
*nam mkha’i tog*, Skt. *gaganaketu*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Gagana­kānta­rāja
*nam mkha’ mdzes pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *gagana­kānta­rāja*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Gagana­kośā­nāvaraṇa­jñāna­garbha
*nam mkha’i mdzod ye shes bsgribs pa med pa’i snying po*, Skt. *gagana­kośā­nāvaraṇa­jñāna­garbha*, A bodhisattva mahāsattva.

## Gagana­megha­śrī
*nam mkha’i sprin gyi dpal*, Skt. *gagana­megha­śrī*, The forty-third buddha in a kalpa in the distant past. BHS verse: Gagana­megha­śirī.

## Gaganamudra
*nam mkha’i phyag rgya*, Skt. *gaganamudra*, The bodhisattva who was Abhaya, the fifth son of King Araṇemin. As prophesied, he became a pupil of the Buddha Candrottara. After Candrottara’s passing, he became the Buddha Padmottara in the southeastern buddha realm, Padmā, and he is present there during Śākyamuni’s lifetime.

## Gagana­netra
*nam mkha’i myig*, Skt. *gagana­netra*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## Gagana­nirghoṣa­svara
*nam mkha’i dbyangs kyi sgra*, Skt. *gagana­nirghoṣa­svara*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## Gagana­pradīpa
*nam mkha’i sgron ma*, Skt. *gagana­pradīpa*, The sixty-sixth buddha in a kalpa in the distant past.

## Gagana­pradīpābhirāma­śrī
*nam mkha’i sgron ma’i ’od bzang dpal*, Skt. *gagana­pradīpābhirāma­śrī*, A tathāgata.

## Gagana­prajña
*nam mkha’i shes rab po*, Skt. *gagana­prajña*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Gagana­śrī
*nam mkha’i dpal*, Skt. *gagana­śrī*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## Gaganasvara
*nam mkha’i dbyangs*, Skt. *gaganasvara*, The 968th buddha in the first list, 967th in the second list, and 958th in the third list.

## Gaganāḍhya
Skt. *gaganāḍhya*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## gaganākalpa
*nam mkha’ rtog pa med pa*, Skt. *gaganākalpa*, Lit. “inconceivable sky.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Gaganālaya
*nam mkha’i gzhi*, Skt. *gaganālaya*, The eleventh buddha in a kalpa in the distant past.

## gaganāparyata
*nam mkha’ mu med pa*, Skt. *gaganāparyata*, Lit. “limitless sky.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Gaṅgottarā
The laywoman who features prominently in this sūtra, as well as the name of one thousand laywoman of the past who attained nirvāṇa, according to the Buddha in this sūtra.

## Gaṅgāpāla
*gang gA skyong*, Skt. *gaṅgāpāla*, A rich man who was Upālin in a former life.

## Gaṅgāsarva­tīrthamukha­maṅgala­śrī
*gang gA’i mu stegs kyi sgo thams cad kyi bkra bshis kyi dpal*, Skt. *gaṅgāsarvatīrtha­mukha­maṅgala­śrī*, A tathāgata.

## Gaṇimukha
*tshogs can gtso bo*, Skt. *gaṇimukha*, The 233rd buddha in the first list, 232nd in the second list, and 232nd in the third list.

## Gaṇimuktirāja
*tshogs can grol rgyal*, Skt. *gaṇimuktirāja*, The 902nd buddha in the first list, 901st in the second list, and 892nd in the third list.

## Gaṇin
*tshogs ldan*, Skt. *gaṇin*, The 41st buddha in the first list, 41st in the second list, and 42nd in the third list.

## Gaṇiprabha
*tshogs can ’od*, Skt. *gaṇiprabha*, The 115th buddha in the first list, 115th in the second list, and 116th in the third list.

## Gaṇiprabhāsa
*tshogs can gsal ba*, Skt. *gaṇiprabhāsa*, The 404th buddha in the first list, 403rd in the second list, and 397th in the third list.

## gait is that of a lion
*seng ge’i stabs su gshegs pa*, Skt. *siṃha­vikrānta­gāmi­tā*, Forty-second of the eighty minor marks.

## gait is that of a mighty elephant
*glang po che’i dbang po’i stabs su gshegs pa*, Skt. *nāga­vikrānta­gāmi­tā*, Forty-third of the eighty minor marks.

## gait is that of a swan
*ngang pa’i stabs su gshegs pa*, Skt. *haṃsa­vikrānta­gāmi­tā*, Forty-fourth of the eighty minor marks.

## gait of a leading bull
*khyu mchog gi stabs su bzhud pa*, Skt. *vṛṣabha­vikrānta­gāmin*, Fourteenth of the eighty minor signs.

## gait of a lion
*seng ge’i stabs su ’gro ba*, Skt. *siṃha­vikrānta­gāmin*, Having the “gait of a lion” is included in the list of the eighty excellent signs (asītyānuvyañjana), a subset of the 112 physical characteristics of both buddhas and cakravartins.

## gait of a swan
*ngang pa’i stabs su bzhud pa*, Skt. *haṃsa­vikrānta­gāmin*, Thirteenth of the eighty minor signs.

## gait of an elephant
*glang po’i ’gros su bzhud pa*, Skt. *nāga­vikrānta­gāmin*, Twelfth of the eighty minor signs.

## gait turning to the right‍
*g.yas phyogs su bzhud pa*, Skt. *pradakṣiṇāvarta­gāmin*, Fifteenth of the eighty minor signs.

## Gajagandha
*glang po’i spos*, Skt. *gajagandha*, One of the celestial bodhisattvas.

## Gajagandhahastin
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra, whose name is attested in the Vimalakīrti­nirdeśa.

## gajapippalī
*glang chen pi pi ling*, Skt. *gajapippalī*, Scindapsis officinalis.

## Gajaśīrṣa
*ba lang mgo*, Skt. *gajaśīrṣa*, A nāga king.

## Gajasāhvaya
*glang chen brjod pa*, Skt. *gajasāhvaya*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Gajendreśvara
*glang po che’i dbang po’i dbang phyug*, Skt. *gajendreśvara*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## gañjira
Roof ornaments.

## Gajānana
*glang po’i gdong*, Skt. *gajānana*, A virtuous nāga king.

## śṛṅgāṭaka
*shing sring ga ta ga*, Skt. *śṛṅgāṭaka*, The name of several types of tree.

## Gaṅkara
*gang ka ra*, Skt. *gaṅkara*, A city in Godānīya.

## galarṭa
An unidentified ritual ingredient.

## gales of wind
*rnam par ’thor ba’i rlung*, Skt. *vairambhavātā*, A kind of powerful, gusty wind (the Tibetan translation means “scattering wind” referred to in a wide range of Buddhist literature. The Pali forms are veramba or verambha. The term Vairambha is also found in Buddhist literature as the name of a city and as the name of a sea, famed for its powerful winds. For a detailed discussion, see Skilling 2021, pp. 304–8.

## Āgama
*lung*, Skt. *āgama*, The Mūlasarvāstivādin tradition grouped the [Buddha](#buddha)’s early [sūtra](#sūtra) discourses into four divisions, or āgama (Tib. mdo sde’i lung sde bzhi): the Dīrghāgama (Tib. lung ring po), the Madhyamāgama (Tib. lung [bar](#bar) ma), the Ekottarikāgama (Tib. lung gcig las ’phros pa), and the Saṃyuktāgama (Tib. lung dag ldan/yang dar par ldan pa’i lung). They are more familiar to many English-speaking Buddhists through the translations of their Pali correlates: the Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Samyutta Nikāya, for which see the [Wisdom](#wisdom) Publications titles: The Long Discourses of the [Buddha](#buddha), The Middle-Length Discourses of the [Buddha](#buddha), The Numerical Discourses of the [Buddha](#buddha), and The Connected Discourses of the [Buddha](#buddha), respectively.

## Gambhīra­dharma­guṇa­rāja­śrī
*zab chos ’od kyi rgyal po dpal*, Skt. *gambhīra­dharma­guṇa­rāja­śrī*, The fifty-sixth buddha in a kalpa in the distant past. BHS verse: Gambhīra­dharma­guṇa­rāja­śirī.

## gambhīra­dharma­prabhā­kara
*chos zab mo’i ’od byed pa*, Skt. *gambhīra­dharma­prabhā­kara*, Lit. “illuminator of the deep dharmas.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Gambhīra­dharma­prabhā­rāja­śrī
*zab mo’i chos kyi ’od kyi rgyal po’i dpal*, Skt. *gambhīra­dharma­prabhā­rāja­śrī*, A tathāgata.

*spobs pa zab pa*, Skt. *gambhīra­pratibhāna*, A great bodhisattva.

*dbyangs zab mo*, Skt. *gambhīreśvara*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

*don zab dgongs pa nges par ’grel*, Skt. *gam­bhīrārtha­saṃdhi­nirmo­cana*, A bodhisattva mahāsattva.

*sgam po pa*, see [Dagpo Rinpoche](#dago-rinpoche).

## Gandhā
*dri chab ma*, Skt. *gandhā*, A goddess of perfume invoked in a mantra.

## Gandha

## Gandhadhvajā
*spos kyi rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *gandhadhvajā*, A royal city in the distant past.

## Gandhahastī
*spos kyi glang po che*, Skt. *gandhahastī*, A great bodhisattva.

## Gandhahasti
*spos kyi glang po che*, Skt. *gandhahasti*, A principal bodhisattva in the Mahāyāna sūtras. He is described in this sūtra as coming from Akṣobhya’s realm.

## Gandhahastin
*spos kyi glang po che*, Skt. *gandhahastin*, A bodhisattva residing in a buddha realm in the southern direction at the time of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Gandhahastiprabhāvarāja
*rgyal po spos kyi glang po che’i byin gyi mthu dang ldan pa*, Skt. *gandhahastiprabhāvarāja*, A garuḍa king.

## Gandhakūṭa
*spos rtsegs*, Skt. *gandhakūṭa*, A buddha.

## Gandhamādana
*spos kyi ngad ldang ba*, Skt. *gandhamādana*, A mountain north of the Himalayas, said to be fifty yojanas from Mount Kailash. In other sūtras, it is translated as spos ngad can, spos ngad ldang, or spos nad ldan. Mount Gandhamardan in Orissa, India, was at one time a center for Buddhist study and practice. (In other sūtras, this is translated as spos ngad can; spos ngad ldang; or spos nad ldan)

## gandha­mādana
*ri spos kyi ngad ldang ba*, Skt. *gandha­mādana*, One of ten “kings of mountains” according to Abhidharma cosomology.

## Gandha­megha­vyūha­dhvajā
*spos kyi sprin gyis brgyan pa’i rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *gandha­megha­vyūha­dhvajā*, A buddha realm in the southeastern direction.

## Gandhapadma
*spos kyi pad ma*, Skt. *gandhapadma*, A buddha in a previous eon when the Sahā realm was called Arajamerujugupsita.

## Gandha­padma­vijitakīrti­rāja
*spos kyi pad ma rnam rgyal grags pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *gandha­padma­vijitakīrti­rāja*, One of ten names of a thousand buddhas prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha, with presumably a hundred buddhas having this name.

## Gandha­padmottaravega
*spos kyi pad ma dam pa’i shugs*, Skt. *gandha­padmottaravega*, One of ten names of a thousand buddhas prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha, with presumably a hundred buddhas having this name.

## Gandhapāṇi
*lag na spos*, Skt. *gandhapāṇi*, A great bodhisattva.

## Gandhaprabha
*spos kyi ’od*, Skt. *gandhaprabha*, The thirty-sixth buddha in a kalpa in the distant past.

## Gandhaprabhāsa
Lit. “Incense-Light.” The world system of the Buddha Incense-Emitting Light during the time of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Gandhapradīpa
*spos kyi mar me*, Skt. *gandhapradīpa*, A buddha in a southeastern buddha realm.

## Gandha­pradīpa­megha­śrī
*spos sgron sprin gyi dpal*, Skt. *gandha­pradīpa­megha­śrī*, A buddha realm in the distant past. BHS verse: Gandha­pradīpa­megha­śiri.

## Gandha­pradīpa­śrī
*spos kyi sgron ma’i dpal*, Skt. *gandha­pradīpa­śrī*, A tathāgata.

## Gandhaśrī
*spos dpal*, Skt. *gandhaśrī*, A great bodhisattva.

## Gandhara
*sa ’dzin*, Skt. *gāndhāra*, The present-day Gandhara region was located in northwest Pakistan and northeast Afghanistan. This region was historically important for the development of Buddhism. In this chapter, Gandhara is identified as the region in which the dwelling place of bodhisattvas called Cave of Provisions is located.

*dri’i rgyal po*, Skt. *gandharāja*, A buddha.

## Gandharva
*dri za*, Skt. *gandharva*, lit. smell eaters. Spirit feeding on smells. Also used for beings in the [intermediate state](#intermediate-state).

*mthong na dga’ ba dri za’i rgyal po*, Skt. *mthong na dga’ ba dri za’i rgyal po*, A devaputra present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni

*dri za mo*, Skt. *dri za mo*, One of the eight nāga ladies.

## Gandharva Melody

## Gandharva Mind
*dri za’i blo*, Skt. *dri za’i blo*, Attendant of the buddha Sūryaprabha.

*dri za’i grong khyer*, Skt. *gandharva­nagara*, See “gandharva.”

## Gandharva­kāya­prabha­rāja
*dri za lus ’od rgyal po*, Skt. *gandharva­kāya­prabha­rāja*, The thirty-eighth buddha in a kalpa in the distant past.

## Gandharva­rāja
*dri za’i rgyal*, Skt. *gandharva­rāja*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Gandhatejas
*spos gzi*, Skt. *gandhatejas*, The 650th buddha in the first list, 649th in the second list, and 641st in the third list.

## Gandhavatī
*spos ldan*, Skt. *gandhavatī*, Lit. “Fragrant.” The city in which the bodhisattva great being Dharmodgata resides.

## Gandhavati
*spos can*, Skt. *gandhavati*, The city where Dharmodgata resides and teaches.

## Gandha­vyūhāhāra
*spos bkod pa’i zas*, Skt. *gandha­vyūhāhāra*, Deities who attend on the Buddha Sugandhakūta in the universe Sarva­gandha­sugandhā.

*spos ’od*, Skt. *gandhābha*, The 870th buddha in the first list, 869th in the second list, and 859th in the third list.

## Gandheśvara
*spos kyi dbang phyug*, Skt. *gandheśvara*, The name that the Buddha Ratnagarbha prophesies will be that of one of his eighty brothers (the seventy-sixth) when he becomes a buddha.

## Gandheśvara­rāja
*spos kyi dbang phyug rgyal po*, Skt. *gandheśvara­rāja*, The name of a bodhisattva. “Fragrant Sovereign King.”

*spos kyi myu gu’i rtse mo las ’od kyi sprin ’byung ba*, Skt. *gandhāṅkura­prabha­megha*, A park in another world in the distant past.

## Gandhālaṃkāra­rucira­śubha­garbhā
*spos kyi rgyan yid du ’ong ba’i dge ba’i snying po*, Skt. *gandhālaṃkāra­rucira­śubha­garbhā*, A world realm in the northwest.

*spos mchog*, Skt. *gandhottama*, Name of a tathāgata.

## Gandhottama­kūṭa
*spos mchog brtsegs pa*, Skt. *gandhottama­kūṭa*, Buddha of the universe Sarva­gandha­sugandhā, from whom Vimalakīrti’s emanation-bodhisattva obtains the vessel of ambrosial food that magically feeds the entire assembly without diminishing in the slightest.

## Gandhottamarāja
*spos mchog rgyal po*, Skt. *gandhottama­rāja*, A buddha.

## Gandhārī
Skt. *gandhārī*, A great rākṣasī.

## Gandhāra
*sa ’dzin*, Skt. *gandhāra*, An ancient kingdom once located in northwestern India in what is now Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan. It lasted from around the sixth century bce to the eleventh century ce and attained its height in the first to fifth centuries under the Buddhist Kushan kings.

## Gandhārci­megha­śrī­rāja
*spos ’od ’phro ba’i sprin phun sum tshogs pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *gandhārci­megha­śrī­rāja*, One of countless buddhas in a past kalpa.

*spos kyi ’od ’phro ba rab tu snang ba’i rgyal po*, Skt. *gandhārciravabhāsa­rāja*, One of countless buddhas in a past kalpa.

## Ganeśa
*tshogs bdag*, Skt. *ganeśa*, The elephant-headed deity, more popularly known as Ganesh and associated with overcoming obstacles. The son of Śiva.

*gang gA’i klung*, Skt. *gaṅgā*, The sacred river of North India.

## Ganges Offering

*gang gAs skyong*, Skt. *gang gAs skyong*, A Licchavi youth present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Ganges River
*gang gA’i klung*, Skt. *gaṅgā*, The sacred river of North India.

## Ganges Water Cloud
*gang gA’i chu sprin*, Skt. *gang gA’i chu sprin*, A tathāgata.

## Gar
The Gar is a Tibetan clan of ancient provenance, the origin of which traces back to the ministers of Newo Trana, one of the twelve kingdoms of preimperial Tibet. According to the Catalog, it's one of the eighteen tribes of Nguchen Gyalmo, belonging to the divine lineage of Go.

## Gar Dampa Chödingpa
According to the Catalog, an ancestral figure of the Degé royal family who went to central Tibet and studied tantra with Jikten Gönpo at Drigung. He later moved to Powo where he established Phulung Rinchen Ling monastery. Other sources indicate he spent time at the court of the Tangut empire (Tib. mi nyag, Ch. xi xia)

## Gar Sherab Jungne
The Tibetan translator credited with translating this Dhāraṇī along with the female Indian master Vajrasattvī.

## gara
*dug*, Skt. *gara*, This word can mean “poison,” and it can also refer to a class of spirits associated with poisons.

## Garab Dorje
*dga' rab rdo rje*, better known by his Tibetan name than by his Sanskrit names, Pramudavajra, Prahevajra, Surativajra or Prajñabhava. The first human teacher in the lineage of the [Great Perfection](#great-perfection).

## garbage collector
*g.yung po’i khyim*, Skt. *puṣkasa­kula*, Also translated here as “refuse scavenger.”

## Garbhagaṇa
*snying po’i tshogs*, Skt. *garbhagaṇa*, A buddha.

## Garbha­kīrti­rāja
*snying po grags pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *garbhakīrti­rāja*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## Garbhāhāriṇī
*mngal za ma*, Skt. *garbhāhāriṇī*, A great rākṣasī.

## Garchen Yeshé Sangpo
One of Gar Dampa Chodingpa’s three brothers.

## Gardabha
“Donkey.” The name of a muhūrta.

## Gardabhaka

## garden of Prince Jeta
*rgyal bu rgyal byed kyi tshal*, Skt. *jetavana*, The grove in Śrāvastī offered to the Buddha by Anāthapiṇḍada, who had purchased it at great expense from its namesake, Prince Jeta.

## garden of the householder Ghoṣila
*gdangs las rig gi kun dga’ ra ba*, Skt. *ghoṣilārāma*, A garden in Kauśāmbī that the householder Ghoṣila donated to the Buddhist saṅgha. This Tibetan rendering of Ghoṣilārāma only appears in The Hundred Deeds, and the precise correlation between the Tib. las rig and the standard Sanskrit for this location remains unclear.

## gardenia
*par shi ka*, Skt. *vārṣika*, Gardenia gummifera. A white fragrant flower that blooms in the rainy season. In other texts transliterated as bar sha ka or par sha ka.

## Gardhava
A rākṣasa king.

## Gargā
*gar gA*, Skt. *gargā*, A famous Puranic rishi of India, who features particularly in the Vaishnavite literature.

## Garga
*gar ga*, Skt. *garga*, An alternate spelling of Bharga, a country during the time of Buddha Śākyamuni that had its capital at Mount Śiśumāri.

## Gargā’s Pond
A place in the city of Campā.

## Garjanī
*’brug sgrogs*, Skt. *garjanī*, A great rākṣasī.

*’brug sgrogs*, Skt. *garjana*, A nāga king.

## Garjasphoṭaka
*’brug sgrogs*, Skt. *garjasphoṭaka*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

*rgya mtsho chos kyi sprin sgra sgrogs pa’i dbyangs*, Skt. *garjita­dharma­sāgara­nirghoṣa*, A buddha in the distant past.

*sgra sgrogs dbang phyug*, Skt. *garjiteśvara*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Garland

## Garland Abode

*pad ma’i rdzing bu’i phreng ba*, Skt. *pad ma’i rdzing bu’i phreng ba*, Ponds in the Forest of Amusements.

## garlands of the buddhas
*sangs rgyas phal po che*, Skt. *buddhāvataṃsaka*, Here, the name of a particular state of concentration (but also the title of a composite Mahāyāna sūtra or “family” of sūtras, Toh 44).

## Garmuka
The name of a king.

## garuḍī
A female garuḍa.

## Garuḍa
*khyung*, a mythical bird of very large size which is able to fly as soon as it is hatched, symbolizing [primal wisdom](#primal-wisdom). The five colors in which it is sometimes represented symbolize the [five wisdoms](#five-wisdoms). It is the enemy of the [nāgas](#nāga), and is depicted with a snake in its beak, symbolizing consuming the [negative emotions](#negative-emotions).

## Garuḍa He
A deity whose vidyāmantra is employed in the rituals described in this text.

## Garuḍa-Winged Revatī
A grahī. This seems to be another name for the grahī otherwise called Great Revatī the Garuda-Winged Ḍākinī (nam gru chen mo mkha’ ’gro khyung gshog ma).

## Garutman
Skt. *garutman*, The celestial garuḍa, often serving as the mount of Viṣṇu.

## Āgata
*a ga ta*, Skt. *āgata*, A god who is the king of lightning in the eastern direction.

## Gate of Auspiciousness
*bkra shis kyi sgo*, Skt. *maṅgaladvāra*, The gate of King Śuddhodana’s palace, in Kapilavastu, through which Prince Siddhārtha leaves, both for one of his trips outside and when he finally forsakes palace life.

## Gate of Warm Water
*chu dron can gyi sgo*, Skt. *tapodadvāra*, One of the gates in the city of Rājagṛha.

## gates of liberation
*rnam par thar pa’i sgo*, Skt. *vimokṣamukha*, There are three, namely emptiness as a gateway to liberation, signlessness as a gateway to liberation, and wishlessness as a gateway to liberation. Among them, emptiness is characterized as the absence of inherent existence, signlessness as the absence of mental images, and wishlessness as the absence of hopes and fears.

## gateway entering into all phenomena
*chos thams cad la ’jug pa’i sgo*, Skt. *sarva­dharma­praveśa­mukha*, A meditative stability.

## gateway to liberation
*rnam par thar pa’i sgo*, Skt. *vimokṣa­mukha*, There are three, namely emptiness as a gateway to liberation, signlessness as a gateway to liberation, and aspirationlessness as a gateway to liberation. Among them, emptiness is characterized as the absence of inherent existence, signlessness as the absence of mental images, and aspirationlessness as the absence of hopes and fears.

## gateways of liberation
*rnam par thar pa’i sgo*, Skt. *vimokṣamukha*, See “three gateways of liberation.”

## gateways to liberation
*rnam par thar pa’i sgo*, Skt. *vimokṣa­mukha*, There are three, namely emptiness as a gateway to liberation, signlessness as a gateway to liberation, and aspirationlessness as a gateway to liberation. Among them, emptiness is characterized as the absence of inherent existence, signlessness as the absence of mental images, and aspirationlessness as the absence of hopes and fears.

## gateways to the letters
*yi ge’i sgo*, Skt. *akṣaramukha*, One aspect of a set of forty-four syllables listed at as dhāraṇī gateways. See also “introduction to the letters.”

## gather at the site
*gnas bsdu ba*, To “gather at the site” in order to do the restoration rite and so on together. If one of the monks on site does not come to the site where an official act of the saṅgha is to be done (or send his consent for the act through a proxy), the saṅgha will not have a quorum, and the act will not be established. See (Toh 4113, F.313.b).

## Gathered
*tshogs pa*, Skt. *tshogs pa*, Gathered (brought or come together), also the name of an area in Kuru.

## Gathered Flowers
*me tog bsags*, Skt. *me tog bsags*, Mother of the buddha Jyeṣṭha.

## Gatherer
*tshogs can*, Skt. *tshogs can*, Gatherer (one who collects or brings together), also the name of an attendant of the buddha Candrārka.

## Gatherer of Myriad Creations

## Gathering of Awakening
*byang chub tshogs*, Skt. *byang chub tshogs*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Buddhimati.

## Gathering of Fame
*grags pa bsdus*, Skt. *grags pa bsdus*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Puṃgava (548 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Gathering of Flowers

## Gaurī
“The Fair One.” The name of a vidyādevī, a goddess invoked in sorcery.

## Gautama
*gau ta ma*, Skt. *gautama*, The family name of Prince Siddhārtha. Gautama means “descendant of Gotama,” while his clan name, Gotama, means “Excellent Cow.” When the Buddha is addressed as Gautama in the sūtras, it typically implies that the speaker does not share the respect of his disciples, who would rather refer to him as the “Blessed One” (Bhagavān) or another such epithet.

## Gautamīya
The name of a family lineage.

## Gauṇāyana
One of the sublineages connected with the Kautsa lineage of the brahmanical tradition.

*ba lang gi bdag po*, Skt. *gavampati*, A great bodhisattva.

*bal glang mgo*, Skt. *gavayaśīrṣa*, A nāga king.

## Gaveśīrṣa

## Gavāmpati
*ba lang bdag*, Skt. *gavāmpati*, One of the first to join the [Buddha](#buddha)’s order of monks. He followed his friend [Yaśas](#yaśas) into the Buddhist order.

## Gavāṃpati
*ba lang bdag*, Skt. *gavāṃpati*, One of the group of five friends who were the second group to become students of the Buddha, and he was one of the ten students of the Buddha who were the first to become arhats.

## Gayā
*ga yA*, Skt. *gayā*, One of the sacred towns of ancient India, south of the Ganges in present-day Bihar. In the Buddha’s lifetime, this was in the kingdom of Magadha. Uruvilvā, the area including Bodhgayā where the Buddha attained enlightenment, is nearby to the south, upriver from Gayā.

## Gayādhara
Gayādhara, c. 994–1043; Indian (possibly Bengali) paṇḍita who visited Tibet three times; teacher of Drokmi Śākya Yeshé; a complex personality and a key figure in the transmission to Tibet of the Hevajra materials later incorporated in the Lamdré (lam ’bras) tradition.

## Gayā-Kāśyapa
*ga yA ’od srung*, Skt. *gayā-kāśyapa*, A monk (bhikṣu) and disciple of the Buddha.

## Gayākāśyapa
*ga ya ’od srung*, Skt. *gayākāśyapa*, The brother of Nadīkāśyapa and Uruvilvākāśyapa. A practitioner of fire offering at Uruvilvā (Bodhgaya), he and his two hundred pupils were converted to the Dharma, becoming bhikṣus (monks) under the Buddha. He and his brothers and their pupils were the third group to become followers of the Buddha Śākyamuni after his awakening. Also known as Mahāgayākāśyapa.

## Gayāśīrṣa
*ga yA mgo*, Skt. *gayāśīrṣa*, Site of a [stūpa](#stūpa) where the [Buddha](#buddha) instructed the thousand monks from [Uruvilvā](#uruvilvā) by displaying three miracles, thereby freeing them from the wilds of [saṃsāra](#saṃsāra) and establishing them in the utterly final state of perfection and the unsurpassably blissful state of [nirvāṇa](#nirvāṇa).

## Gayā­śīrṣa Hill
*ga yA mgo’i ri*, Skt. *gayā­śīrṣa*, A sacred hill immediately to the south of the city of Gayā. Its name means “Gayā head,” and may derive from pre-Buddhist legends of a buried, reclining giant—in one version, a demon king called Gayāsura who was immoblised by Viṣṇu, and in another a saintly prince called Gaya; this hill marks the position of his head, with other features of the landscape in the region associated with other parts of his body.

## Gayāśīrṣa Hill
*ga yA mgo’i ri*, Skt. *gayāśīrṣa*, A hill near Bodhgayā where the present sūtra takes place.

*thugs rje chen pos sems can thams cad la gzigs pa*, Skt. *thugs rje chen pos sems can thams cad la gzigs pa*, A tathāgata in the southwestern buddhafield Virtuous Eye.

## Gṛdhrakūṭa
*bya rgod kyi phung po*, Skt. *gṛdhrakūṭa*, A mountain in Magadha where the Buddha preached many times.

## Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain
*rgod kyi phung po’i ri*, Skt. *gṛdhrakūṭa*, Also known as “Vulture Peak,” a hill located in modern-day Bihar, India, and in the vicinity of the ancient city of Rājagṛha. A location where many sūtras were taught and which continues to be a sacred pilgrimage site for Buddhists to this day.

*byang chub kyi sems bskyed*, Skt. *bodhicittotpāda*, The altruistic resolve to achieve complete and perfect buddhahood for the sake of oneself and all sentient beings.

## Generation phase
*bskyed rim*, Skt. *utpattikramā* "meditation [yoga](#yoga) through which one purifies oneself of one's habitual [clinging](#clinging)s to the four kinds of birth and in which one meditates on forms, sounds and [thought](#thought)s as having the nature of deities, [mantra](#mantra)s and [wisdom](#wisdom)" DICT.

## generation stage
One of the two primary categories for the practice of union (yoga) in Vajrayāna Buddhism. These two stages include a variety of practices. Generally speaking, the generation stage consists of practices for attaining spontaneous union as the deity maṇḍala, while the completion stage consists of practices to test, demonstrate, or perfect this union.

Also translated here as “completely perfect buddha.”

## Given by the Frightful One
The son of Ajātaśatru according to the Tibetan translation of this sūtra. Unfortunately, the corresponding Sanskrit of this portion of the text is not extant. In Pāli Buddhist literature, Ajātaśatru’s son is named Udāyibhadda, which does not seem to correspond well to this Tibetan translation. In the Lalitavistara, ’jigs byed is attested for the name Bhayaṃkara, but there it refers to one of attendants of Māra. It is also attested as a translation for Bhairava in some Buddhist texts. It is common for sbyin to translate the form datta, which is a common ending in names. Taken together here this gives us Bhairavadatta or Bhayaṃkaradatta. The former is an attested name in India, but it is too tenuous to use it here.

## global summary
*spyi’i sdom*, Skt. *piṇḍoddāna*, The content of The Chapters on Monastic Discipline is condensed into metered lists called “summaries” (Tib. sdom; Skt. uddāna) or “verse summaries” (Tib. sdom gyi tshigs su bcad pa; Skt. uddānagāthā). Each chapter has a “global summary,” composed of several topics, which form the basis of subsequent “summaries.” Very occasionally, specific elements of a chapter will be recapitulated in “intervening summaries” (Tib. bar sdom; Skt. antaroddāna).

## glory, renown, and good reputation
*grags pa dang sgra dang tshigs su bcad pa*, Skt. *yaśo-śabda-śloka*, A stock phrase in (Buddhist) Sanskrit texts, each word of which carries a specialized meaning. There are other variants of this phrase in The Exposition of Karma, e.g., “glory, praise, renown, and good reputation” (grags pa dang brjod pa dang sgra dang tshigs su bcad pa).

## gnosis
*ye shes*, Skt. *jñāna*, This term denotes the modality of buddha mind. Although all sentient beings possess the potential for actualizing gnosis within their mental continuum, the psychological confusions and deluded tendencies which defile the mind obstruct the natural expression of these inherent potentials, making them appear instead as aspects of mundane consciousness.

## Gönpo Sung
The son of Gendün Gyaltsen.

## Go
The people of the Go Lharik clan are said to be the native inhabitants of Dokham (mdo khams) or eastern Tibet. They are said to be a “divine” lineage in that they descended from the skies on a miraculous rope. Their element is fire, and their spirit animal (bla zog) is the goat.

## Go forth
*rab tu 'byung ba*, Skt. *pravrajati*, To leave the life of a householder and embrace the life of a wandering, [renunciant](#renunciant) follower of the [Buddha](#buddha).

## goat poison
*ra dug*, Skt. *śṛṅgaka*, Possibly a poisonous plant of the Ranunculaceae family, known more commonly by names such as wolfsbane and monkshood.

## goat-swallowing snake
*Literally “goat devourer,” ajagara*, Skt. *ajagara*, Literally “goat devourer,” ajagara is alternately the name of a mythical snake or the Sanskrit term for a boa constrictor.

## god
*lha*, Skt. *deva*, One of the five or six classes of living beings, specifically engendered and dominated by exaltation, indulgence, and pride. Like human beings and asuras, they are all within the higher realms (svarga, mtho ris) of rebirth, but nonetheless remain trapped within cyclic existence. The gods are said to exist in realms higher than that of the human realm, their realms and abodes set out in their own hierarchy. The god realms altogether comprise (1) six god realms within the realm of desire (kāmadhātu), commencing with Caturmahā­rāja­kāyika and Trayastriṃśa, and concluding with Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarata, and Para­nirmita­vaśa­vartin; (2) twenty-one realms in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), including (a) the sixteen Brahmā realms, extending from Brahmakāyika through Brahmapurohita, Brahma­pariṣadya, Mahābrahmā, Ābha, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Śubha, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhat, Parīttabṛhat, and Apramāṇabṛhat to Bṛhatphala, which are attained corresponding to lesser, middling, and higher degrees of the four meditative concentrations; (b) the five Pure Abodes at the pinnacle of the realm of form, extending from Avṛha, through Atapa, Sudṛśa, and Sudarśana to Akaniṣṭha; and (3) the four formless realms at the summit of existence. See and similar passages. Note that the list in this text differs from those in other texts in including four realms (instead of three) for each of the four groups of Brahmā realms, i.e., in listing sixteen Brahmā realms instead of twelve, and therefore twenty-one realms of form in all.

The name is the same for both the location and the inhabitant deities. These gods enjoy the creations of others, as opposed to the Nirmāṇarati gods who enjoy their own creations.

The name is the same for both the location and the inhabitant deities. These gods create their own pleasing enjoyments.

*’og min gyi lha*, Skt. *akaniṣṭhānāṃ devānām*, See “Highest Heaven.”

The name is the same for both the location and the inhabitant deities. Tuṣita is of note for being the abode of Maitreya until his eventual birth on Earth (and indeed all buddhas in their penultimate birth before their final birth).

## Gośṛṇga
*ba lang gi mgo bo*, Skt. *gośṛṇga*, A hill in the Central Asian oasis city-state of Khotan. According to The Prophecy on Mount Gośṛṅga (Toh 357), it is here that the Buddha prophesied that this area would one day become a great Buddhist kingdom. Gośṛṅga means “cow horn” in Sanskrit, and the hill is said to have received this name due to having two pointed peaks. Note that in The Prophecy on Mount Gośṛṅga this place name is rendered ri glang ru.

## Gonakī
*go na kI*, Skt. *gonakī*, A location in Jambudvīpa renowned for soft cotton.

*mthu chen gnas su phyin*, Skt. *mthu chen gnas su phyin*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Dharmakośa (534 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

*thogs med gshegs pa po*, Skt. *thogs med gshegs pa po*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Siṃharaśmi (343 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## gongpo
A type of Tibetan spirit.

## Good Cave
*phug bzang po*, Skt. *phug bzang po*, Dwelling place of bodhisattvas located in the great ocean.

## Good Compassion
*snying rje bzang po*, Skt. *snying rje bzang po*, Son of the Vaiśālī army chief Siṃha at the time of the Buddha’s stay there, he was sentenced to death for the murder of a prostitute. The Buddha secured his release, ordained him, and he attained arhatship.

## good conduct
*tshul khrims*, Skt. *śīla*, The second of the six perfections. Morally virtuous or disciplined conduct and the abandonment of morally undisciplined conduct of body, speech, and mind. Also commonly called discipline and ethical conduct.

## good Dharma
Literally “white dharma,” epithet of the teachings of the Buddha.

## Good Eon
*skal pa bzang po*, Skt. *bhadrakalpa*, Our present eon in which over a thousand buddhas will appear. The meaning is “good” because of the number of buddhas that will appear. In the sūtra, it is usually called bhadraka.

## Good Kalpa
*bskal pa bzang po*, Skt. *bhadrakalpa*, the present [kalpa](#kalpa), called good because it is a [kalpa](#kalpa) in which one thousand [Buddhas](#buddha) appear.

## Good Moon
*zla legs*, Skt. *zla legs*, Attendant of the buddha Nakṣatrarāja.

## Good Profit
*legs par rnyed pa*, Skt. *legs par rnyed pa*, Name of Buddha Śākyamuni in a past life, when he was a merchant practicing bodhisattva conduct.

## good reputation
*tshigs su bcad pa*, Skt. *śloka*, Part of the Tibetan translation of a Skt. stock phrase for the expression of esteem. See glory, renown.

## gooseberry
*skyu ru ra*, Skt. *āmalaka*, The Indian gooseberry, or emblic myrobalan. The simile of an āmalakī in the palm of one’s hand is used to illustrate yogic perception (yogipratyakṣa) where the clarity aspect (compared to a crystal) is emphasized. See, e.g., Dharmottara’s Nyāyabindhuṭīkā 1.11. It is also used to illustrate omniscience, or seeing all aspects of things, probably on the analogy of being able to see through the semi-transparent skin of the berry into its interior structure.

## Gopā
*sa ’tsho ma*, Skt. *gopā*, Wife of Prince Siddhārtha prior to his leaving the kingdom and attaining awakening as the Buddha. She was the daughter of the Śākya nobleman Daṇḍapāṇi.

## Gopa
*glang rdzi*, Skt. *gopa*, Identified as Goparāja, early sixth century, of the imperial Gupta dynasty.

## Gopagiri
*ba lang srung*, Skt. *gopagiri*, A mountain king.

## Gopendra
*ba lang srung dbang*, Skt. *gopendra*, A south Indian king contemporary with Mahendra.

## gopi
*phyugs rdzi*, Skt. *gopī*, Female cow herders or milk maids, the gopis are well known from their role in the mythology of Kṛṣṇa, in particular, Rādhā, who became his lover. (Toh 555: rdzi’i bu mo)

## Gopāla
*ba lang skyong*, Skt. *gopāla*, A yakṣa general and a yakṣa who is a “Dharma brother” of Vaiśravaṇa.

## Gopālaka
*sa srung*, Skt. *gopālaka*, More often called Gopāla, the ruler of Bengal around the middle of the eighth century.

## gośīrṣa
*tsan dan sa mchog pa*, Skt. *gośīrṣa*, A type of sandalwood that is reddish in color and has medicinal properties. It is said to have the finest fragrance of all sandalwood. In the Mahāvyutpatti it is translated as sa mchog, which means “supreme earth.” Later translations translate gośirṣa literally as “ox-head,” which is said to refer to the shape or name of the mountain where it grows. Appears to be red sandalwood, though that appears separately in the list of incenses.

## gośīrṣa sandalwood
*ba lang gi spos kyi tsan dan*, Skt. *gośīrṣacandana*, A particular kind of sandalwood, known as “ox-head,” that grows in southern India. It is reddish in color and has medicinal properties. It is said to have the finest fragrance of all sandalwood. The Sanskrit word go means “ox,” and śīrṣa means “head;” candana means “sandalwood.” The name of this sandalwood is said to derive from either the shape of or the name of a mountain upon which it grew. The Tibetan translated gośīrṣa as ba lang gi spos or “ox incense.”

## gośīrṣacandana
*tsan dan sa mchog*, Skt. *gośīrṣacandana*, A kind of sandalwood.

## Gośīrṣaka
*go shiR+Sha pa*, Skt. *gośīrṣaka*, A minor mountain on Lofty Peak.

## gorakṣataṇḍula
A plant identified in Āyurvedic sources with snake mallow (nāgabalā).

## Gorgeous
*mdzes ldan*, Skt. *mdzes ldan*, Gorgeous (strikingly beautiful), also the name of the father of the buddha Mahābala.

*rtse mo yid ’ong gser*, Skt. *rtse mo yid ’ong gser*, A mountain near the asura city Double Pleasure.

## Gorgeous Heaven
*shin tu mthong*, Skt. *sudarśana*, The sixteenth of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and the pure realms, it is listed as the fourth of the five pure realms.

## Gorgeous Mount
*ri mdzes pa*, Skt. *ri mdzes pa*, A part of Mountainous Garland.

## Gotsangpa (Gonpo Dorje)
*rgod tshang pa mgon po rdo rje* (1189 - 1258), [Kagyupa](#kagyupa) master, [disciple](#disciple) of Tsangpa Gyare, founder of a branch of the Drukpa Kagyu school and of many monasteries.

## grace

## grahī
A type of female spirit understood to cause illness through possession.

## graha
Grahas are understood to be both evil spirits and evil influences that are contained within or connected with a particular spirit or deity. They are also closely associated with the planets and other astronomical bodies. Grahas can inflict great harm on the human body and mind. For more information, see: Gail Hinich Sutherland, The Disguises of the Demon: The Development of the Yakṣa in Hinduism and Buddhism, (Albany: State University of New York Press, 1992), pp. 166–167.

## Āgraha
*kun ’dzin*, Skt. *āgraha*, A householder in this sūtra.

## Graha Lords
A set of grahas (a type of harmful spirit) that rule or lead (nāyaka) other categories of grahas. This list likely varies, but one attested version includes the deities that govern the directions: Aindra, Āgneya, Yama, Nairṛita, Varuṇa, Maruta/Vāyu, Kubera, and Aiśāna. This set also includes two additional figures, Grahaka and Paiśācika, who are not associated with the directions.

*gzas byin*, Skt. *grahadatta*, Name of a bodhisattva.

*gzas byin*, Skt. *graha­datta*, Name of a bodhisattva.

## grain of barley
A measure of length defined as being equal to seven lice.

## grammar
The third of the five major fields of learning.

## granary
*sbyang*, Skt. *koṣṭhāgāra*, De Jong points out that “the word sbyaṅ is recorded in Sumatiratna’s Tibetan-Mongolian Dictionary, II, (Ulanbator, 1959), p. 357: rtsva daṅ ‘bru-la sogs-pa ’jog-pa’i gnas-te sgo daṅ skar-khuṅ med-pa/yaṅ baṅ-ba ’am rdzaṅ yaṅ źes-pa sbyaṅ “a place without doors and windows where herbs and grains are stored; also a store-room or a box” (De Jong 1975, p. 117). (We thank James Gentry for pointing out the sense of “granary.”) The term sbyang, if it may indeed be understood as something akin to a “box,” could rather match the term mutoḍī (see Edgerton 1993, p. 436), reported by Samtani as the reading of ANe Comy (the manuscript of the Nibandhana commentary), and also appearing (as mūtoḍī) in the relevant Śikṣāsamuccaya parallel (see Samtani 1971, p. 24, n. 2), rather than the term koṣṭhāgāra in the printed edition. The term mutoḍī matches the Pāli putoỊī/mūtoỊī/mutoli found in Pāli passages parallel to this and explained as follows: “A putoḷi is a circular container made by tying together clothes and so forth in the shape of a sack” (vatthādīhi pasibbakākārena bandhitvā kataṃ āvāṭanaṃ putoḷi, ṭīkā on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta, Mahāvagga, Dīghanikāya; vatthādīhi pasibbakākārena bandhitvā kataṃ āvaṭanaṃ putoḷi, ṭīka on the Mahāsatipaṭṭānasutta, Mūlapaṇṇāsa, Majjhima­nikāya; here we take it that āvāṭanam/āvaṭanam = āvaṭṭanam).

## grand monk Tingézin
Myangben Tingdzin Sangpo (myang ban ting ’dzin bzang po, eighth–ninth century) served as a guardian of the young emperor Senalek and also as a minister of state in the emperor’s court. He was very influential in the courts of both Senalek and Ralpachen.

## grand monk Yönten
Also known as Drenka Palkyi Yönten (bran ka dpal gyi yon tan, ninth century), he was the first to hold the position of grand monk (ban de chen po), a title given to the highest-ranking monks in the imperial court.

In equivalent passages in other versions of the sūtra, the metaphorical part of the term is rendered literally in the Tibetan. See also .

In equivalent passages in other versions of the sūtra, the metaphorical part of the term is rendered literally in the Tibetan. See also .

*rgyal rigs che zhing mtho ba’i rigs*, Skt. *kṣatriya­mahā­śāla­kula*, Note that the metaphor within the Sanskrit term (“a great sal tree”) is here interpreted in the Tibetan term. ## Great Assembly

*sems dpa’ chen po*, Skt. *mahāsattva*, An epithet of advanced bodhisattvas, often defined as having attained at least the seventh bhūmi and the path of vision. These bodhisattvas have several special qualities that bodhisattvas on the lower bhūmis do not have.

*dmyal ba chen po thig nag*, Skt. *kāla­sūtra­mahānaraka*, One of the eight hot hells, the name refers to the black thread that is used to make lines on the bodies of those reborn there so that they can be cut into pieces.

## Great Brahmā
*tshangs chen*, Skt. *mahābrahma*, The third of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and the pure realms, it is listed as the third of the three heavens that correspond to the first of the four concentration.

## Great Brahmā gods
*tshangs chen*, Skt. *mahābrahman*, The gods in the abode of Mahābrahmā, the fourth of the four classes of gods of the form realm in the first dhyāna. The name is the same for both the location and the inhabitant deities.

## Great Brahmā, sovereign of this Sahā world
The brahmā deity who is sometimes called Sahāṃpati, “sovereign of this Sahā world.” This is the name given to the great brahmā deity described in this sūtra as the lord (īśvara) of the cosmos of a billion worlds. The name attested in the Sanskrit manuscript. Also called Great Brahmā (mahābrahmā) or even simply Brahmā in this sūtra and elsewhere, as well as vaśavartin, the “powerful one.” In this sūtra, he also seems to be identified with Brahmā Śikhin, but at the same time Brahmā should be distinguished from the class of brahmā deities who dwell in the Brahmā heavens over which Great Brahmā is also lord.

## great brahmas
A term used to refer to gods in the Great Brahma Realm.

## great brahmās
One of the form realms, listed here between the previous brahmā realms and the Heaven of Lesser Light, the first of the realms of the second dhyāna in the form realm.

## great compassion
*snying rje chen po*, Skt. *mahākaruṇā*, This refers to one of the two central qualities of buddhas or high bodhisattvas: their feeling born of the wish for all living beings to be free of suffering and to attain the supreme happiness. It is important to note that this great compassion has nothing to do with any sentimental emotion such as that stimulated by such a reflection as “Oh, the poor creatures! How they are suffering!” On the contrary, great compassion is accompanied by the clear awareness that ultimately there are no such things as living beings, suffering, etc., in reality. Thus it is a sensitivity that does not entertain any dualistic notion of subject and object; indeed, such an unlimited sensitivity might best be termed “empathy.”

## Great Compilation
*’dus pa chen po*, Skt. *mahāsannipāta*, An anthology of Great Vehicle Sūtras. A collection of seventeen sūtras under this title is available in Chinese translation, but The Questions of Sāgaramati is not included among them. It is thus likely that there were more than one anthology using this title.

## great element
*’byung ba chen po*, Skt. *mahābhūta*, The four great elements of earth, water, heat, and wind do not refer to the coarse entities by the same name, but rather to minimal entities characterized by specific features (such as “hardness” for the earth element) and specific functions (such as “supporting” for the earth element). These elements are usually believed to be in principle invisible; all primary rūpa (“form/materiality”) is in principle invisible, while visibility is a type of secondary rūpa, which depends on the four great elements but is not to be confused with them.

## great elements
*’byung ba chen po*, Skt. *mahābhūta*, The four great elements are earth, water, fire, and wind. They are called “great” because they are found in the external world as well as inside the bodies of beings.

## great eon
*bskal pa chen po*, Skt. *mahākalpa*, Definitions regarding the duration of one “great eon” vary, but are normally given in billions of (human) years. One great eon is divided into eighty intermediate eons, or, according to a different system, into four. Both systems of division are reconciled by grouping the eighty intermediate eons into four units of twenty.

*tshogs kyi bdag po chen po*, Skt. *mahāgaṇapati*, An epithet of the elephant headed deity Gaṇapati.

## Great Gathering
*phung po chen po*, Skt. *phung po chen po*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Dharmacandra (953 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Great Glorious Expanse
A deity whose vidyāmantra is employed in the rituals described in this text. This may be the same deity referred to as Expanse of Wrath (dbyings kyi khro bo).

## Great Glorious One
A deity whose vidyāmantra is mentioned in this text. This epithet is often applied to Hayagrīva or other wrathful deities.

## Great Glory
*dpal chen*, Skt. *dpal chen*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Vigata­mohārtha­cintin (715 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

*nor lha chen po*, An epithet of the elephant headed deity Gaṇapati.

An epithet for the goddess who acts as the primary interlocutor in Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra.

## Great Golden Radiance Ornament
*gser gyi ’od rgyan chen po*, Skt. *mahā­suvarṇa­prabha­vyūha*, A bodhisattva.

## Great Golden Radiant Array
*gser ’od chen pos bkod pa*, A bodhisattva. (Toh 555: gser gyi ’od rgyan chen po)

## Great Guhyaka
*gsang ba pa chen po*, Skt. *mahāguhyaka*, Name of a yakṣa.

## Great Heat
*rab tu tsha ba*, Skt. *pratāpana*, One of the eight hot hells.

## great hell
*dmyal ba chen po*, Skt. *mahānaraka*, The great hells are also often called hot hells in secondary literature because beings there suffer from heat and being burned. They are Wailing, Loud Wailing, Black Thread, Crushing, Revival, Heat, Intense Heat, and Incessant Torture. Within in the Kangyur, one elaborate description of the eight hells is found in The Application of Mindfulness of the Sacred Dharma (Toh 287), 2.294–2.1280.

## Great Hell of Unceasing Torture
*dmyal ba chen po mnar med pa*, Skt. *avīci­mahānaraka*, The lowest of the eight hot hells, it is characterized as endless not only in terms of the torment undergone there, but also because of the ceaseless chain of actions and effects experienced, the long lifespan of its denizens, and their being so densely crowded together that there is no physical space between them.

## great hells
*sems can dmyal ba chen po*, Skt. *mahānaraka*, Also called the hot hells because beings born there suffer from heat and burning.

## Great Hollow
*phrag chen*, An asura lord.

## Great Howling Hell
*ngu ’bod chen po*, Skt. *mahāraurava*, The fifth of the eight hot hells in the Buddhist classification.

## Great Illumination
*snang ba che*, Skt. *mahāprabhāsa*, The name of the eon in the future in which Siṃha and his attendants are prophesied to become buddhas by the Buddha Śākyamuni. This name varies significantly in the Chinese versions of Siṃha’s Questions (see ).

## Great Illusion
*sgyu ’phrul chen mo*, Skt. *mahāmāyā*, The female central deity of the Mahā­māyā Tantra who appears in the form of the male Heruka. She was also a popular form of the Brahmanical great goddess (Mahādevī), to whom the Buddhist figure is intimately related. Also rendered here as “Mahāmāyā.”

## Great Indra
Skt. *mahendra*, An epithet of Indra, the chief god of the realm of Thirty-Three.

## Great Insight
*shes rab chen po*, Skt. *shes rab chen po*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Prajñādatta.

## Great Intelligence
*blo gros chen mo*, Skt. *blo gros chen mo*, Mother of the buddha Sumati.

## Great Intention
*dgongs pa chen po*, Skt. *dgongs pa chen po*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Buddhimati (739 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Great Jewel
*rin chen chen mo*, Skt. *rin chen chen mo*, Mother of the buddha Dharmaprabhāsa.

## Great Jewel Crest
*rin po che chen po’i tog*, Skt. *mahāratnaketu*, A buddha.

## Great Joy
In The Dharma Council, the world system in which the bodhisattva Nirārambha is prophesied to become the Buddha Great Light.

## great kalpa
*bskal pa chen po*, Skt. *mahākalpa*, The name of a certain kind of kalpa. The number of years in this kalpa differs in the various sūtras that give it a number, although it is said to equal four asaṃkhyeya (“incalculable”) kalpas.

## Great King
*rgyal po chen po*, Skt. *mahā­rājā*, A king ruling over a particularly large territory, often including the territories of other petty rulers; a class of divine beings assigned to the cardinal directions who guard the earth, Buddhist practitioners, and Buddhist institutions against demonic forces.

*rgyal po chen po*, Skt. *mahārāja*, See “Four Great Kings.”

*shAkya chen po*, Skt. *shAkya chen po*, The identity of this person is unknown.

## great śāla tree
*shing sA la chen po*, Skt. *mahāśāla*, An adjectival phrase typically linked to a brahmin, kṣatriya, or other upper-caste family, it denotes that the person in question has a large and prosperous household, family, or clan.

*’od chen*, Skt. *’od chen*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Brahmadatta (103 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

*mchu mchog*, Skt. *mchu mchog*, One of the four parasites that are said to be inside the birth canals of women.

*dbang phyug chen po*, Skt. *dbang phyug chen po*, Father of the buddha Bhīṣaṇa.

## Great Lord of the Feast
*tshogs kyi dbang po chen po*, Skt. *tshogs kyi dbang po chen po*, A bodhisattva.

## Great Lord of Wrath
*khro bo’i rgyal po chen po*, Skt. *mahākrodharāja*, An epithet of Yamāntaka; also the namesake mantra. The name is also written in this translation as “Lord of Great Wrath.”

*pad mo chen po*, Skt. *mahāpadma*, Name of a meditative absorption.

## Great Lotus Hell
*pad ma ltar gas pa chen po*, Skt. *mahā­padma*, See “Splitting Open Like a Great Lotus Hell.”

## great love
*byams pa chen po*, Skt. *mahāmaitrī*, In an effort to maintain distinctions between Buddhism and Christianity, translators have used all sorts of euphemisms for this basic term. Granted, it is not the everyday “love” that means “to like”; it is still the altruistic love that is the finest inspiration of Christ’s teaching, as well as of the Mahāyāna.

## great loving kindness
*byams pa chen po*, Skt. *mahāmaitrī*, Not defined as such in this text, but in the Ten Thousand (2.7) great loving kindness is described as “action in which the tathāgatas engage on behalf of all beings, treating enemies and friends identically.”

*’od zer gyi phung po chen po*, A buddha in the distant past.

*dbang chen*, Skt. *dbang chen*, Father of the buddha Sucīrṇabuddhi.

*tshangs pa’i gzer bu chen po*, Skt. *mahā­brahmā­śaṅku*, Or “Great Spike of Purity,” the name of a bodhisattva. Possibly śaṅku is a misreading or misspelling of sanatku, which would be “the bodhisattva Sanatkumāra” (Pali: Sanaṅkumāra), who was a being of the class of Mahābrahmās—in Vedic legend, one of the four or seven “mind-born” sons of Brahmā—and who appears in various suttas in the Pali canon.

*klu chen*, Skt. *klu chen*, Attendant of the buddha Balanandin.

## great nirvāṇa
*mya ngan las ’das pa chen po*, Skt. *mahānirvāṇa*, The full awakening of a buddha. A synonym of parinirvāṇa

*don chen*, Skt. *don chen*, Son of the buddha Satyabhāṇin.

*rgya mtsho chen po*, Skt. *mahāsamudrā*, In Buddhist cosmology, the four oceans in between the four continents that are at the cardinal points of the flat disc of the world, with the gigantic Mount Sumeru in its center.

## Great Outer Oceans
*phyi'i rgya mtsho chen po*, the great oceans which surround [Mount Meru](#meru-mount) and the four continents in the ancient Indian cosmology.

## great parinirvāṇa
*yongs su mya ngan las ’das pa chen po*, Skt. *mahā­parinirvāṇa*, Synonymous with parinirvāṇa, the final or complete nirvāṇa, which occurs when a buddha passes away. It implies the non-residual nirvāṇa where the aggregates have also been consumed within emptiness.

## Great Perfection
*dzogs pa chen po*, other name of [Atiyoga](#atiyoga), the summit of the nine [vehicle](#vehicle)s. *Perfection* [means](#means) that the mind, in its nature, naturally contains all the qualities of the three bodies: its nature is [emptiness](#emptiness), the [dharmakāya](#dharmakāya); its natural expression is [clarity](#clarity-experience), the [saṃbhogakāya](#saṃbhogakāya), and its compassion is all-encompassing, the [nirmāṇakāya](#nirmāṇakāya). *Great* [means](#means) that this perfection is the natural condition of all things. AT: great completeness. The teachings of the Great Perfection are classified in three [section](#section)s: the mind [section](#section) (*sems sde), the space [section](#section) (*klong sde*), and the pith-instruction [section](#section) (*man ngag gi sde*). See also the [Translators' Introduction](https://wordsof.guru/#introduction).

## Great Renown

*dge sbyong chen po*, Skt. *mahāśramaṇa*, Epithet of the Buddha.

The name of one of the eighteen primary emanations of the goddess described in this text.

The name of one of the eighteen primary emanations of the goddess described in this text.

## great trichiliocosm
*stong gsum gyi stong chen po’i ’jig rten gyi khams*, Skt. *trisāhasra­mahā­sāhasra­loka­dhātu*, The largest universe spoken of in Abhidharma cosmology. Each great trichiliocosm is composed of one thousand worlds, each of which contains one thousand worlds, each of which contains one thousand worlds, therefore totaling one billion worlds.

## guardians (of the world)
*skyong ba*, Skt. *pāla*, In this case, “guardians” seems to refer to the Four Great Kings of the cardinal directions, namely, Vaiśravaṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, and Virūpākṣa, who pledged to protect the Dharma and practitioners.

## guardians of the world
*’jig rten skyong ba*, Skt. *lokapāla*, Literally “world protectors.” They are the same as the four Mahārājas, the Four Great Kings of the quarters (Tib. rgyal chen bzhi), namely, Vaiśravaṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, and Virūpākṣa, whose mission is to report on the activities of humankind to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven (Heaven of the Thirty-Three) and who have pledged to protect the practitioners of the Dharma. Each universe has its own set of four.

## guhyaka
A class of nonhuman beings, similar to yakṣas and perhaps synonymous with them in some contexts. They are closely associated with Kubera or Vaiśravaṇa, the lokapāla and god of wealth who is one of the Four Great Kings, but they also have a strong association with Vajrapāṇi, especially in this sūtra. Guhyakas are sometimes considered the guardians of Vaiśravaṇa’s treasure, or even hidden treasures in general, such as veins of gold and other lodes of precious substances concealed or hidden (guhya) beneath the ground. In this way, the terms guhyaka (“divine guardian of hidden treasure”), and guhya (“secret” or “hidden treasure”), play off each other throughout this sūtra.

## guilty conscience
*ngo tsha*, Skt. *hrī*, One of the eleven virtuous mental factors (Tib. sems byung dge ba; Skt. kuśalacaitta), a subgroup of the mental states or factors associated with the mind (Skt. caitasika; caitta), according to the Abhidharma. According to Vasubandhu (in his Pañcaskandhaka), ngo tsha (“scruples,” “conscience”) is different from khrel (“embarrassment” or “shame”) in that it is independent from others’ judgment of one’s behavior, and solely internal, in that it contradicts one’s internalized values and one’s inner moral compass. See “embarrassment.”

A title given to Thogme Zangpo (1295 - 1369), a great master of the [Nyingma](#nyingmapa) and [Śākya](#sakyapa) traditions and author of the *Thirty Seven Elements of a [Bodhisattva](#bodhisattva)'s Practice (rgyal sras lag len)*.

## Gyaltsen Bum
The second Degé king, Gyaltsen Bum (fifteenth century) was the head of the house of Degé in its thirty-second generation. He had four sons, of whom Pönchen A Nga became the third Degé king and the other three became monks. For more on his life see his entry at The Treasury of Lives.

## Habitat of Kalandaka
*bya ka lan da ka gnas pa*, Skt. *kalandakanivāsa*, A woodland within the Bamboo Grove; in the Pali tradition the compound is usually interpreted as “squirrels’ feeding place,” but according to Tibetan sources kalandaka refers to a kind of bird. markup link to knowledgebase article--> The exact referent of the word kalandaka is contested, and its etymology is unclear (see Mayrhofer 1956, s.v.). While in the Pali Buddhist tradition the word is generally believed to refer to a kind of squirrel (see Dhammika 2015, 61 and 110), the Tibetan tradition understood ka lan da ka to be a species of bird that nested in the Bamboo Grove. In the Pali tradition, kalandakanivāpa is the name of a locality in or near the Veṇuvana, the Bamboo Grove north of the ancient town of Rājagṛha, in which a certain king had placed food (nivāpa) for the squirrels. According to legend, a tree spirit in the form of a squirrel had warned the intoxicated, sleeping, and unattended king that a venomous snake was approaching to bite him. Out of gratitude, the king ordered that the squirrels be fed regularly. According to Tibetan sources, King Bimbisāra of Magadha confiscated the park that was later to become the Bamboo Grove from a local landowner. The landowner, angry about the expropriation, took rebirth as a venomous snake in that park. One day, when Bimbisāra and his attendants had fallen asleep after a picnic in the park, the snake approached to bite the king. Some kalandaka birds, however, saw the snake and seized it. Their cries awoke one of the king’s wives, who then killed the snake, thus saving the king’s life. As a sign of his gratitude, Bimbisāra planted bamboo that the birds especially liked (cf. Rockhill 1884, 43–44, for a translation of the Kangyur passage relating this story). According to some Chinese sources kalandaka is the name of the person who donated the Bamboo Grove to the Buddha (for references, see Vinītā 2010, 415 and 417, footnote b). We have followed the Tibetan interpretation in our translation.

## hall
*khyams*, Skt. *prāsāda*, The Tib. khyams (Skt. prāsāda) is one of many related terms for an assembly “hall” that appears in the Kangyur and Tengyur, such as (1) “meditation hut/hall” (Tib. spong khang; Skt. prahāṇaśālā), (2) “multistoried structure” (Tib. khang pa rtseg ma’i khyams; Skt. kūṭāgāraśālā), (3) “temple” (Tib. khang bzangs; Skt. prāsāda), (4) “steps” (Tib. bang rim; Skt. pariṣaṇḍa), and (5) “courtyard” (Tib. ’khor gyi khyams; Skt. maṇḍalavāṭa).

## hall steps
*khyams*, Skt. *pariṣanḍā*, Kalyāṇamitra describes the “hall steps” as the vihara entrance’s middle level (F.316.a).

## hall with an upper chamber
A distinctive Indian assembly hall or temple with one ground-floor room and a high ornamental roof, sometimes a barrel shape with apses but more usually a tapering roof, tower, or spire. It contains at least one additional upper room within the structure. The term kūṭāgāra literally means “upper chamber” and is short for kūṭāgāraśālā (“hall with an upper chamber”).

## hammer

## hand mudrā
*phyag rgya*, Skt. *mudrā*, An array of symbolic hand gestures, which range from the gesture of touching the earth displayed by the Buddha upon attaining awakening to the numerous gestures used in tantric rituals to symbolize offerings, consecrations, etc. Iconographically, mudrās are used as a way of communicating an action performed by the deity or a specific aspect a deity or buddha is displaying, in which case the same figure can be depicted using different hand gestures to signify that they are either meditating, teaching, granting freedom from fear, and so forth.
