## hatred
*zhe sdang*, Skt. *dveśa*, Second of the five fetters associated with the lower realms; one of the three poisons (dug gsum) that, along with desire and delusion, perpetuate the sufferings of cyclic existence. In its subtle manifestation as aversion, it obstructs the correct perception of forms, and in its extreme manifestation as hatred and fear, it is characteristic of the hells.

## Hatred Vajrī
*zhe sdang rdo rje ma*, Skt. *dveṣavajrī*, Consort of Black ‌Acala.

## Hṛṣṭavadanā
*rangs ma’i gdong*, Skt. *hṛṣṭavadanā*, One of the subtle channels in the body.

## have circular faces
This term describes a race of people.

## have entered nirvāṇa
*mya ngan ’das pa*, Skt. *parinirvṛta*, Literally “those who have been fully extinguished.” In Sanskrit, the term nirvāṇa literally means “extinguishment” and the Tibetan mya ngan las ’das pa literally means “gone beyond sorrow.” As a general term, it refers to the cessation of all suffering, afflicted mental states (kleśa), and causal processes (karma) that lead to rebirth and suffering in cyclic existence, as well as to the state in which all such rebirth and suffering has permanently ceased.

## have hands and feet adorned with the glorious śrīvatsa motif, the auspicious svāstika motif, and the nandyāvarta motif
*phyag dang zhabs dpal gyi be’u dang / bkra shis dang dga’ ba ’khyil pas brgyan pa*, Skt. *śrī­vatsa­svastika­nandyāvarta­lalita­pāṇi­pāda*, Eightieth of the eighty minor signs.

## having a palate
*rkan ldan*, Skt. *rkan ldan*, A type of worm (srin bu) that lives in and feeds on the body.

## Having a Retinue of Clouds
*sprin gyi ’khor ldan*, Skt. *sprin gyi ’khor ldan*, A goddess.

## Having a Shaved Head and Water Jar
*mgo reg dang ril ba spyi blugs can*, Skt. *mgo reg dang ril ba spyi blugs can*, A ṛṣi. See also

## having iron
*lcags can*, Skt. *lcags can*, A type of worm (srin bu) that lives in and feeds on the body.

## Having Light Hues
*’od kyi kha dog can*, Skt. *’od kyi kha dog can*, Mother of the buddha Pratibhāna­varṇa.

## having near-iron
*nye ba’i lcags can*, Skt. *nye ba’i lcags can*, A type of worm (srin bu) that lives in and feeds on the body.

## having no basis
*gzhi med pa*, Skt. *gzhi med pa*, Also translated here as “groundlessness.”

## having primacy
*sngon du ’gro*, Skt. *pūrvaṃ­gamā bhavati*, Also translated here as “precede.”

## having stored
*mkhos su phab ste*, Skt. *pratiśāmayya*, Kalyāṇamitra explains that monks stored their robes and bowls in specified or individual spots in the dwelling. See F.223.b: lhung bzed dang chos gos mkhos su phab nas zhes bya ba ni so sor des pa’i gnas su rnam par bzhag nas so and F.268.b: mkhos su dbab pa zhes bya ba ni gnas khang du ’jug tu gzhug pa’o.

## Hayagrīva
An important wrathful deity of the lotus (padma) family and thus closely associated with Avalokiteśvara. Hayagrīva is also a deity in the Brahmanical pantheon.

## Hayāsyā
*rta yi gzugs*, Skt. *hayāsyā*, One of the goddesses in the retinue of Heruka.

## Hūṁchen
A wrathful deity whose dagger is employed in the rituals described in this text.

## Hṛīdeva
*khrel yod pa’i lha*, Skt. *hṛīdeva*, A god who comes to Prince Siddhārtha’s palace to serve and venerate him.

## He Who Acts as Supreme
*mchog mdzad*, Skt. *mchog mdzad*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Triumphant.

## He Who Gave a Chariot
*shing rta sbyin*, Skt. *shing rta sbyin*, A future solitary buddha.

## He Who Gives Freedom from Fear
*mi ’jigs pa sbyin pa*, Skt. *abhayaṃdada*, An epithet for Avalokiteśvara.

## He Who Has Thought Well
A bodhisattva in the audience, whose name is not attested in Sanskrit.

## He Who Is Proclaimed King of the Pile of Śrīgarbha Jewels
*dpal gyi snying po brtsegs pa rnam par bsgrags pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *śrīgarbhakūṭavinarditarāja*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Pile of Śrīgarbha Jewels.

## He Who Outshines All
*zil gyis gnon pa*, Skt. *zil gyis gnon pa*, A buddha in the distant past.

## He Who Possesses a Beautiful Form
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra.

## He Who Possesses a Body Adorned, Exalted by All Jewels
*rin chen kun gyis ’phags pa ste rab tu brgyan pa’i gzugs ’dzin pa*, Skt. *rin chen kun gyis ’phags pa ste rab tu brgyan pa’i gzugs ’dzin pa*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Family of Jewels. Likely the same as the thus-gone one He Who Possesses a Body Adorned with All Jewels and the thus-gone one Victory Banner at the Pinnacle of Dharma.

## He Who Possesses a Body Adorned with All Jewels
*rin po che thams cad kyis brgyan pa’i gzugs ’dzin pa*, Skt. *rin po che thams cad kyis brgyan pa’i gzugs ’dzin pa*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Family of Jewels.

## He Who Possesses a Refined and Immaculate Splendor
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra, whose name is not attested in Sanskrit but could be something like Sucalitavimalatejodhara or -tejasvin.

## He Who Proclaims the Dharma with Inexhaustible Melodious Voice
*sgra dbyangs mi zad pa sgrogs pa*, name of a [Buddha](#buddha).

## He Who Resounds Throughout the Quarters
*phyogs rab sgrogs*, Skt. *phyogs rab sgrogs*, A buddha.

## He Who Turned the Wheel of Dharma Immediately upon Developing the Mind of Awakening
*sems bskyed ma thag tu chos kyi ’khor los sgyur ba*, One of twenty-five bodhisattvas in Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta’s retinue at the outset of this sūtra.

## He Whose Body Hairs Never Rise in Fear
*spu zing zhes byed pa’i ’jigs bral*, Skt. *spu zing zhes byed pa’i ’jigs bral*, A buddha.

## He Whose Great Intelligence Is Strong as a Vajra
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra. The Sanskrit could be something like Vajramahāmati.

## He Whose Intelligence Is His Treasure
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra whose name is not attested in the Sanskrit, but Dhanamati is a good guess, since Dhanapati is attested.

## He Whose Intelligence Rests on What Is Certain
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra, whose name in Sanskrit is not attested but could be something like Viniścitamati.

## He Whose Mind Dispels All Darkness
The name of a bodhisattva.

## He Whose Power Is Great
A bodhisattva in the audience for this sūtra, and in other texts attested as an alternative translation for the name Nārāyaṇa.

## Head
*mgo*, Skt. *mgo*, Head (the top part of the body; a leader), also the name of one of the hearers in the world known as Torch.

## head is [large], similar to a parasol
*dbu gdugs ’dra ba*, Skt. *pūrṇottama­māṅga­tā*, Forty-fifth of the eighty minor marks.

## Head of Indra
*dbang po’i mgo*, Skt. *dbang po’i mgo*, A certain master archer in Vaiśālī.

## head of the gods
*lha’i dbang po*, Skt. *devānām indriya*, A common epithet of Śatakratu, also known as Indra.

## head that is very broad‍
*dbu shin tu rgyas pa*, Skt. *supari­pūrṇottamāṅga*, Seventy-third of the eighty minor signs.

## Healer
*sman pa*, Skt. *sman pa*, Healer (one who cures or heals), also the name of the father of the buddha Mahendra.

## Healer of Men
*mi’i sman*, Skt. *mi’i sman*, Name of Buddha Śākyamuni in a past life, when he was a prince practicing bodhisattva conduct.

## health problem
*nyes pa*, Skt. *doṣa*, Literally a “fault,” this term signifies a wide range of health problems that might be brought on by an imbalance of the humors (doṣa) or some extraneous cause that has affected an individual because of some kind of behavioral or physical fault or defect (doṣa).

## Heap
*phung po*, Skt. *phung po*, Heap (a pile or mass of things), also the name of a son of the buddha Ketuprabha.

## Heap in the Stream
*klung na brtsegs pa*, Skt. *klung na brtsegs pa*, A mountain in Living on the Peak.

## Heap of Diligence
*brtson ’grus phung po*, Skt. *brtson ’grus phung po*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Ojaṅgama.

## Heap of Excellence
*phung po bzang*, Skt. *phung po bzang*, Father of the buddha Bhadradatta.

## Heap of Flowers
*me tog phung po*, Skt. *me tog phung po*, Birthplace of the buddha Kusumaprabha.

## Heap of Glory
*dpal gyi phung po*, Skt. *dpal gyi phung po*, Dwelling place of the bodhisattva Dharmamati.

## Heap of Incense
*spos kyi phung po*, Skt. *spos kyi phung po*, Dwelling place of the bodhisattva Gandhahastin.

## Heap of Iron
*lcags kyi phung po*, Skt. *lcags kyi phung po*, A mountain off Videha.

## Heap of Jewels
*dkon mchog brtsegs pa*, Skt. *ratnakūṭa*, Forty-nine selected sūtras on a range of themes, compiled as a separate collection.

## Heap of Live Coals of Iron-dust
*lcags kyi phye ma me mdag gi ra ba*, Skt. *ayaś­cūrṇāṅgāra­nikara*, One of sixteen realms that surround the Crushing Hell. Alternatively referred to as Metallic Fire (lcags kyi me).

## Heap of Lotuses
*pad ma’i phung po*, Skt. *pad ma’i phung po*, Birthplace of the buddha Padmakośa.

## Heap of Merit
*bsod nams phung po*, Skt. *bsod nams phung po*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Nala.

## Heap of Qualities
*yon tan phung po*, Skt. *yon tan phung po*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Ratnottama (494 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Heap of Splendid Light
*gzi brjid phung po’i ’od*, Skt. *gzi brjid phung po’i ’od*, Mother of the buddha Pradīparāja.

## Heaped Up
*spungs pa can*, Skt. *spungs pa can*, A city or village.

## Heaps of Eloquence
*spobs pa brtsegs pa*, Skt. *spobs pa brtsegs pa*, A bodhisattva present in the circle around Śākyamuni.

## Heaps of Fresh Butter
*mar sar gyi gong bu*, Skt. *mar sar gyi gong bu*, A lake on the mountain called “Excellence of Exquisite Intelligence.”

## Heaps of Insight
*shes rab brtsegs pa*, Skt. *shes rab brtsegs pa*, A bodhisattva present in the circle around Śākyamuni.

## hearer
*nyan thos*, Skt. *śrāvaka*, The term is most simply interpreted as “those who hear” the Buddha’s teaching, i.e., his disciples, but the additional element that they then “make it heard” to others is often present in canonical glosses. In a Mahāyāna context it refers to those disciples of the Buddha who aspire to attain the state of a worthy one (arhat), and not to embarking on the path of a bodhisattva (with buddhahood as its ultimate goal).

## Hearer Vehicle
*nyan thos kyi theg pa*, Skt. *śrāvakayāna*, The vehicle comprising the teachings of the “hearers” (śrāvaka), those disciples of the Buddha who aspire to attain the state of a “worthy one” (arhat) by seeking self-liberation. The hearers are typically defined as “those who hear the teaching from the Buddha and make it heard by others.”

## Hearing lineage of ordinary beings
*gang zag snyan brgyud*, lineage of transmission in which it is necessary for the teacher to use words and the [disciple](#disciple) to hear them, rather than transmitting the teachings mind-to-mind or using symbols.

## heart essence
*snying po*, Skt. *hṛdaya*, Literally “heart,” this term means the heart essence or the essence of the deity and can refer to its mantra, mudrā, or maṇḍala.

## heart is excellently adorned with the śrīvatsa motif
*thugs kar dpal gyi be’us legs par brgyan pa*, Skt. *śrī­vatsa­vibhuṣitoraska­tā*, Seventy-sixth of the eighty minor marks.

## heart mantra
*snying po*, Skt. *hṛdaya*, A term for the most important and often (but not always) the most simplified spell associated with a particular buddha, bodhisattva, or other being.

## Heart of Great Merit
*bsod nams dpal gyi snying po*, A householder in this sūtra.

## Heart of Joy
*dga’ ba’i snying po*, Skt. *dga’ ba’i snying po*, The realm of the Buddha Ratnaśrī.

## Heart of Power
*mthu rtsal snying po*, Skt. *mthu rtsal snying po*, Birthplace of the buddha Sāgara.

## Heart of the Doctrine
*bstan pa’i snying po*, Skt. *bstan pa’i snying po*, A buddha.

## Heart of the Glorious Lotus
*pad ma dpal gyi snying po*, One of the main characters in this sūtra.

## Heart of the Jewel
*nor bu’i snying po*, Skt. *nor bu’i snying po*, A buddha field in the future where the bodhisattva Discriminating Intellect attains buddhahood.

## Heartbreaking Cries
*snying rje rje skad sgra ’byin pa*, Skt. *karuṇānināda*, A realm that neighbors the Hell of Intense Heat.

## Heat
*tsha ba*, Skt. *tapana*, Heat (the quality of being hot; high temperature), also the name of one of the great hells (Skt. mahānaraka). Inhabitants of this hell are boiled in cauldrons, roasted in pans, beaten with hammers, and skewered with spears as their bodies burst into flame. See Guenther 1986, 58; Konchog Gyaltsen 1998, 99, for descriptions of this hell.

## heaven
*mtho ris*, Skt. *svarga*, The blissful realms of devas according to Buddhist cosmology.

## Heaven Born from Merit
*bsod nams skyes*, Skt. *puṇyaprasava*, The eleventh of the heavens of the form realm. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing the third or, according to the Mvy, fourth meditative absorption. See also .

## Heaven Free from Conflict
*’thab bral*, Skt. *yāma*, One of the six heavens of the desire realm.

## Heaven Free from Strife
*’thab bral*, Skt. *yāma*, The third of the six heavens of the realm of desire; also the name of the gods living there. The Tibetan translation ’thab bral, “free from strife or combat,” derives from the idea that these devas, because they live in an aerial abode above Sumeru, do not have to engage in combat with the asuras who dwell on the slopes of the mountain.

## Heaven Fully Free from Strife
*’thab bral rab*, Skt. *suyāmā*, A heavenly realm and the class of gods who inhabit it.

## Heaven of Boundless Radiance
*tshad med ’od*, Skt. *apramāṇābha*, The fifth of the heavens of the form realm. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing the second meditative absorption.

## Heaven of Boundless Virtue
*tshad med dge ba*, Skt. *apramāṇaśubha*, The eighth of the heavens of the form realm. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing the third meditative absorption. See also .

## Heaven of Brahmā’s Assembly
The first heaven of the form realm, counting from lowest to highest. Associated with the first state of meditation (dhyāna).

## Heaven of Brahmā’s Ministers
*tshangs pa’i mdun na ’don*, Skt. *brahmapurohita*, The second of the heavens of the form realm and of the three Brahmā heavens. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing the first meditative absorption.

## Heaven of Brahmā’s Priests
The second heaven of the form realm, counting from lowest to highest. Associated with the first state of meditation (dhyāna).

## Heaven of Brahmā’s Retinue
*tshangs ris*, Skt. *brahmakāyika*, The lowest of the heavens of the form realm and of the first of the three Brahmā heavens. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing the first meditative absorption. See also .

## Heaven of Brilliance
Sixth god realm of form, it is the highest of the three heavens that make up the second meditative state.

## Heaven of Concept-Free Beings
*sems can ’du shes med pa*, Skt. *asaṃjñisattva*, A heavenly realm listed in this text between the twelfth heaven of the form realm, the Heaven of Great Fruition, and the five pure realms of the form realm.

## Heaven of Controlling Others’ Emanations
The highest of the six heavens of the desire realm, its inhabitants enjoy objects created by others.

## Heaven of Controlling the Emanations of Others
*gzhan ’phrul dbang byed*, Skt. *para­nirmitavaśavartin*, The name for the highest heavenly realm in the desire realm, which is considered higher than the Nirmāṇarati gods who generate their own pleasing magical emanations.

## Heaven of Delighting in Emanations
*’phrul dga’*, Skt. *nirmāṇarati*, One of the heavens of Buddhist cosmology, counted among the six heavens of the desire realm. Its inhabitants magically create the objects of their own enjoyment, and also dispose of them themselves.

## Heaven of Excellent Appearance
The third of the pure abodes and the fifteenth heaven of the form realm.

## Heaven of Exceptional Sight
The fourth of the pure abodes and the sixteenth heaven of the form realm.

## Heaven of Good Emanation
*rab ’phrul*, Skt. *nirmāṇarati*, A heaven in the desire realm.

## Heaven of Great Brahmā
*tshangs chen*, Skt. *mahābrahmā*, The third of the heavens of the form realm and the third of the three Brahmā heavens. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing the first meditative absorption.

## Heaven of Great Fruition
*’bras bu che*, Skt. *bṛhatphala*, The twelfth of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and the pure realms, it is listed as the third of the three heavens that correspond to the fourth of the four concentrations.

## Heaven of Great Results
The twelfth heaven of the form realm, counting from lowest to highest. Associated with the fourth state of meditation (dhyāna).

## Heaven of Great Reward
*’bras bu che ba*, Skt. *vṛhatphala*, The twelfth of the heavens of the form realm. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing an ordinary form of the fourth meditative absorption. See also .

## Heaven of Great Vision
*shin tu mthong ba*, Skt. *sudarśana*, The third highest of the Pure Abodes in the form realm; non-returners and those who have mastered the fourth meditative absorption are reborn there. See also .

## Heaven of Immeasurable Light
Fifth of the god realms of form, it is the second of three heavens that make up the second meditative state.

## Heaven of Immeasurable Splendor
The eighth heaven of the form realm, counting from lowest to highest. Associated with the third state of meditation (dhyāna).

## Heaven of Increased Merit
*bsod nams skyes*, Skt. *puṇyaprasava*, The eleventh of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and the pure realms, it is listed as the second of the three heavens that correspond to the fourth of the four concentrations.

## Heaven of Joy
*dga’ ldan*, Skt. *tuṣita*, The fourth of the six heavens of the desire realm; also the name of the gods living there. It is the paradise in which the Buddha Śākyamuni lived as the tenth-level bodhisattva and regent Śvetaketu, prior to his birth in this world, and is also where all future buddhas dwell prior to their awakening. At present the regent of the Heaven of Joy is the bodhisattva Maitreya, the future buddha.

## Heaven of Lesser Light
Fourth god realm of form, meaning “Lesser Light,” it is the lowest of the three heavens that make up the second meditative state in the form realm.

## Heaven of Limited Radiance
*’od chung*, Skt. *parīttābha*, The fourth of the heavens of the form realm. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing the second meditative absorption.

## Heaven of Limited Splendor
The seventh heaven of the form realm, counting from lowest to highest. Associated with the third state of meditation (dhyāna).

## Heaven of Limited Virtue
*dge chung*, Skt. *parīttaśubha*, The seventh of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and the pure realms, it is listed as the first of the three heavens that correspond to the third of the four concentrations.

## Heaven of Limitless Virtue
*tshad med dge*, Skt. *apramāṇaśubha*, The eighth of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and the pure realms, it is listed as the second of the three heavens that correspond to the third of the four concentrations.

## Heaven of Luminous Radiance
*’od gsal*, Skt. *ābhāsvara*, The sixth of the heavens of the form realm. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing the second meditative absorption. See also .

## Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations
*gzhan ’phrul dbang byed*, Skt. *nirmāṇa­vaśavartin*, The Heaven of Controlling Others’ Emanations is the highest (or sixth) of the six heavens of the desire realm.

## Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Emanations
*gzhan ’phrul dbang byed pa*, Skt. *paranirmitavaśavartin*, One of the heavens of Buddhist cosmology, highest of the six heavens of the desire realm. The inhabitants enjoy objects created by others, then dispose of them themselves.

## Heaven of Mastery over Others’ Emanations
*gzhan ’phrul dbang byed*, Skt. *paranirmitavaśavartin*, The heaven of the highest class of gods of the world of sensuous desire (kāmadhātu); the gods here possess the ability to control the magical creations of others.

## Heaven of Neither Perception nor Nonperception
The fourth of the four formless realms.

## Heaven of No Distress
The second of the pure abodes and the fourteenth heaven of the form realm.

## Heaven of No Hardship
*mi gdung ba*, Skt. *atapa*, The fourteenth of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and the pure realms, it is listed as the second of the five pure realms.

## Heaven of Nonperception
A heavenly realm listed in this text between the twelfth heaven of the form realm, the Heaven of Great Results, and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Nonperception, the fourth of the four formless realms.

## Heaven of Nothing Greater
The first of the pure abodes and the thirteenth heaven of the form realm.

## Heaven of Perception
A heavenly realm listed in this text between the twelfth heaven of the form realm, the Heaven of Great Results, and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Nonperception, the fourth of the four formless realms.

## Heaven of Perfect Virtue
*dge rgyas*, Skt. *śubhakṛtsna*, The ninth of the heavens of the form realm. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing the third meditative absorption. See also .

## Heaven of Perfected Virtue
*dge rgyas*, Skt. *śubhakṛtsna*, The ninth of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and the pure realms, it is listed as the third of the three heavens that correspond to the third of the four concentrations.

## Heaven of Pure Abode
*gnas gtsang ma*, Skt. *śuddhāvāsa*, The name given to the five highest levels of existence within the form realm.

## Heaven of Radiance
One of the form realms, listed here between the brahmā realms and the Heaven of Lesser Light, the first of the realms of the second dhyāna in the form realm.

## Heaven of Sublime Vision
*gya nom snang*, Skt. *sudṛśa*, One of the heavens of Buddhist cosmology belonging to the form realm. The fourth-highest heaven of the Pure Abodes. Non-returners and those who have mastered the fourth meditative absorption are reborn there. See also .

## Heaven of the Beautiful Ones
The fifteenth heaven of the form realm, counting from lowest to highest. Associated with the fourth state of meditation (dhyāna).

## Heaven of the Clear-Sighted Ones
The sixteenth heaven of the form realm, counting from lowest to highest. Associated with the fourth state of meditation (dhyāna).

## Heaven of the Contented
The fourth heaven of the desire realm, counting from lowest to highest.

## Heaven of the Cool
The fourteenth heaven of the form realm, counting from lowest to highest. Associated with the fourth state of meditation (dhyāna).

## Heaven of the Four Great Kings
*rgyal bo bzhi’i lha yul*, Skt. *caturmahārājika*, One of the heavens of Buddhist cosmology, lowest of the six heavens of the desire realm. It is located on the slopes of Mount Meru and ruled by the Four Great Kings.

## Heaven of the High Priests of Brahmā
*tshangs pa’i mdun na ’don*, Skt. *brahmapurohita*, The second of the seventeen heavens of the form realm.

## Heaven of the Joy of Creation
The fifth of the six heavens of the desire realm; also the name of the gods living there. Its inhabitants magically create the objects of their own enjoyment.

## Heaven of the Masters of Others’ Creations
*gzhan ’phrul dbang byed*, Skt. *paranirmitavaśavartin*, One of the heavens of Buddhist cosmology, highest of the six heavens of the desire realm. The inhabitants enjoy objects created by others, then dispose of them themselves.

## Heaven of the Power over Others’ Creations
The highest of the six heavens of the desire realm, its inhabitants enjoy objects created by others.

## Heaven of the Thirty-Three
Skt. *trāyastriṃśa*, According to Buddhist cosmology, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three is the second lowest of the six heavens of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), just above the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (Caturmahārāja­kāyika) and below the Yāma Heaven. It is situated on the flat summit of Mount Sumeru and has thirty-three regions each presided over by one of thirty-three chief gods, the overall chief being Śakra. The presiding gods are divided into four groups named in the Abhidharma­kośa­ṭīkā (Toh 4092): the eight gods of wealth, two Aśvin youths, eleven fierce ones, and twelve suns. The thirty-three regions themselves are enumerated and described in The Application of Mindfulness of the Sacred Dharma, Toh 287, et seq.).

## Heaven of Those Who Possess the Power to Transform Others’ Delight into Their Own
The highest of the six heavens of the desire realm. Also rendered poetically in this sūtra as The Heaven of Transforming Others’ Delight.

## Heaven of Those Whose Delight Comes from Magical Creations
The second highest of the six heavens of the desire realm. Also rendered poetically in this sūtra as The Heaven of Delighting in Magical Creations.

## Heaven of Total Splendor
The ninth heaven of the form realm, counting from lowest to highest. Associated with the third state of meditation (dhyāna).

## Heaven of Vast Virtue
The ninth heaven of the form realm, it is the third of the three heavens that correspond to the third dhyāna.

## Heaven without Conflict
*’thab bral*, Skt. *yāma*, A heaven in the desire realm.

## Heaven Without Strife
*’thab bral*, Skt. *yāma*, The third of the six heavens of the desire realm.

## Heavenly
*bde ’gro ma*, Skt. *bde ’gro ma*, Heavenly (of or relating to heaven; divine), also the name of the mother of the buddha Praśāntagāmin.

## heavens
*mtho ris*, Skt. *svarga*, The realms of gods according to Buddhism; in Vedism the blissful afterlife presided over by Yama.

## heedfulness
*bag yod pa*, Skt. *apramāda*, One of the main aspects of mindfulness as broadly construed, heedfulness indicates stable introspective awareness and guarding the mind against negative thoughts and emotions while fostering positive or virtuous states of mind. As explained in The Questions of the Nāga King Anavatapta, its more fundamental meaning is retaining an abiding awareness of the true nature of all phenomena through the correct understanding of dependent origination.

## heir of the victorious ones
An epithet for bodhisattvas.

## heirs of victors
*rgyal sras*, Skt. *jinaputra*, A synonym for bodhisattvas.

## Held by the Victorious One
*rgyal bas ’dzin*, Skt. *rgyal bas ’dzin*, Father of the buddha Nāgadatta.

## Hell
*dmyal ba*, Skt. *naraka*, one of the [six realms](#six-realms-of-existence), in which one experiences intense suffering. In the hell [realm](#realm) one generally experiences the [effects of actions](#effects-of-actions) rather than creating new causes.

## hell being
*dmyal ba pa*, Skt. *nāraka*, One of the five or six classes of sentient beings, considered to be the karmic fruition of past anger and harmful actions. According to Buddhist tradtion there are eighteen different hells, namely eight hot hells, eight cold hells, neighbouring and ephemeral hells, all of them tormented by increasing levels of unimaginable suffering.

## hell beings
*sems can dmyal ba*, Skt. *naraka*, One of the six classes of sentient beings engendered by anger and powerful negative actions. They are dominated by great suffering and said to dwell in different hells with specific characteristics.

## Hell of Burning Coals
One of the neighboring hells.

## Hell of Ceaseless Agony
*mnar med pa*, Skt. *avīci*, Eighth (and heaviest) of the eight hot hells of Buddhist cosmology. Only their miserable cries distinguish beings in this hell from the flames that engulf them.

## Hell of Ceaseless Torment
*mnar med*, Skt. *avīci*, Eighth (and lowest) of the eight hot hells of Buddhist cosmology. The beings reborn in this hell experience being ceaselessly consumed by flames.

## Hell of Chattering Teeth
*so thams thams*, Skt. *aṭaṭa*, Third of the eight cold hells of Buddhist cosmology. It is named for the sounds its inhabitants make while enduring unthinkable cold.

## Hell of Crushing
*bsdus gzhom*, Skt. *saṅghāta*, One of the eight hot hells.

## hell of Destructive Wood Fire
*shing skam ltar ’jigs par ’tshed*, Skt. *shing skam ltar ’jigs par ’tshed*, A realm that neighbors the Hell of Intense Heat.

## Hell of Endless Torment
*mtshams med*, Skt. *avīci*, The most severe among the eight hot hell realms. It is characterized as endless not only in terms of the torment undergone there, but also because of the ceaseless chain of actions and effects experienced, the long lifespan of its denizens, and their being so intensely crowded together that there is no physical space between them.

## Hell of Extreme Heat
*rab tu tsha ba*, Skt. *pratāpana*, Seventh of the eight hot hells of Buddhist cosmology. Inhabitants of this hell undergo all the sufferings of the Hot Hell, as well as being seared, beaten, and skewered.

## Hell of Heat
*tsha ba*, Skt. *tapa­namahānaraka*, One of the eight hot hells. Inhabitants of this hell are boiled in cauldrons, roasted in pans, beaten with hammers, and skewered with spears as their bodies burn.

## Hell of Incessant Torture
The lowest and worst of the major hot hells according to Buddhist cosmology. In The Benefits of the Five Precepts, rebirth in this hell is the full karmic result of speaking falsehood.

## Hell of Intense Heat
*rab tu tsha ba*, Skt. *pratāpana­mahānaraka*, One of the eight hot hells. Inhabitants of this hell undergo all the sufferings of the Hell of Heat, as well as being seared, beaten, and skewered.

## Hell of Intense Wailing
*ngu ’bod chen po*, Skt. *mahāraurava*, One of the eight hot hells.

## Hell of Iron-Thorn Trees
Skt. *śalmali*, One of the neighboring hells. Named after the trees Bombax ceiba, also known as silk-cotton trees or kapok trees. They are covered by large woody thorns. Inhabitants of this hell are made to climb the thorny trees.

## Hell of Lamentation
*kyi hud zer ba*, Skt. *hahava*, Fourth of the eight cold hells of Buddhist cosmology. It is named for the sounds its inhabitants make while enduring unthinkable cold.

## Hell of Loud Screams
*ngu ’bod*, Skt. *raurava*, Fourth of the eight hot hells of Buddhist cosmology. Named for the cries of its inhabitants, who are engulfed in a tremendous blaze.

## Hell of Razor Blades
One of the neighboring hells.

## Hell of Revival
*yang sos*, Skt. *sañjīva*, One of the eight hot hells.

## Hell of the Lump
*bsdus pa*, Skt. *piṇḍonaraka*, One of sixteen realms that surround the Crushing Hell. ’khums pa in Tibetan.-->

## Hell of Ultimate Torment
*mnar med*, Skt. *avīci*, The lowest hell; the eighth of the eight hot hells.

## Hell of Unceasing Torment
*mnar med pa*, Skt. *avīci*, One of the eight hot hells.

## Hell of Uninterrupted Torment
*mnar med*, Skt. *avīci*, The lowest hell; the eighth of the eight hot hells.

## Hell of Wailing
*ngu ’bod*, Skt. *raurava*, One of the eight hot hells.

## hell realms
*sems can dmyal ba*, Skt. *naraka*, A set of subterranean prisons whose denizens undergo various tortures as retribution for their misdeeds. Also, a denizen of those realms, one of the six classes of beings.

## heroism
*brtson ’grus*, Skt. *vīrya*, The term vīrya is related to, and often derived from, vīra, which is related to the Latin vir, from which both “virility” and “virtue” are derived. Vīrya brings to mind heroism, valor, virility, courage, and strength. Although vīrya is often translated as “diligence,” we have here chosen to render it “heroism.”

## Heruka
*he ru ka*, Skt. *heruka*, A type of bloodthirsty, charnel ground-dwelling being considered threatening to people and practitioners. In the higher classes of Buddhist tantra, the central deity of many maṇḍalas takes the form of a heruka. His practice is taught in The Tantra of Black Yamāri.

## Heshang Moheyan
Ca. eighth century. A Chinese master of the Chan tradition who tradition holds lost a debate with Kamalaśīla regarding sudden versus gradual paths to awakening. He upheld the view of the sudden path.

## high resolve
*lhag pa’i bsam pa*, Skt. *adhyāśaya*, This is a stage in the conception or initiation of the spirit‌ of enlightenment‌. It follows upon the positive thought, or aspiration to attain it, wherein the bodhisattva becomes filled with a lofty determination that he himself should attain enlightenment, that it is the only thing to do to solve his own problems as well as those of all living beings. This high resolve reaches its most intense purity when the bodhisattva simultaneously attains the Path of Insight and the first bodhisattva-stage, the Stage of Joy. The translation follows Lamotte’s happy coinage “haute résolution.”

## higher cognition
*mngon par shes pa*, Skt. *abhijñā*, The higher cognitions are listed as either five or six. The first five are: clairvoyance (divine sight), divine hearing, knowing how to manifest miracles, remembering previous lives, knowing what is in the minds of others. A sixth, knowing that all defects have been eliminated, is often added. The first five are attained through dhyāna, and are sometimes described as worldly, as they can be attained to some extent by non-Buddhist yogis; while the sixth is supramundane and attained only by realization—by bodhisattvas, or according to some accounts only by buddhas.

## higher cognitions
*mngon par shes pa*, Skt. *abhijñā*, The higher cognitions are listed as either five or six. The first five are divine sight, divine hearing, knowing how to manifest miracles, remembering previous lives, and knowing what is in the minds of others. A sixth, knowing that all defects have been eliminated, is often added. The first five are attained through concentration (Skt. dhyāna), and are sometimes described as worldly, as they can be attained to some extent by non-Buddhist yogis, while the sixth is supramundane and attained only by realization.

## higher insight
*lhag mthong*, Skt. *vipaśyanā*, An important form of Buddhist meditation focusing on developing insight into the nature of phenomena. Often presented as part of a pair of meditation techniques, the other being “stilling.”

## higher knowledge
*mngon par shes pa*, Skt. *abhijñā*, A category of extrasensory perception gained through spiritual practice, in the Buddhist presentation consisting of five types: miraculous abilities, divine eye, divine ear, knowledge of others’ minds, and recollection of past lives. A sixth, knowing that all defilements have been eliminated, is often added.

## higher knowledges
*mngon par shes pa*, Skt. *abhijñā*, Special abilities or modes of cognition that arise from meditative realization. They are traditionally listed as five: divine sight, divine hearing, the ability to know past and future lives, the ability to know the minds of others, and the ability to produce miracles.

## higher perception
*mngon par shes pa*, Skt. *abhijñā*, The higher perceptions are listed as either five or six. The first five are divine sight, divine hearing, knowing how to manifest miracles, remembering previous lives, and knowing the minds of others. A sixth, knowing that all defilements have been eliminated, is often added. The first five are attained through concentration (Skt. dhyāna), and are sometimes described as worldly, as they can be attained to some extent by non-Buddhist yogis, while the sixth is supramundane and attained only by realization‍—by bodhisattvas, or according to some accounts, only by buddhas.

## higher perceptions
The higher perceptions are listed as either five or six. The first five are clairvoyance (divine sight), divine hearing, knowing how to manifest miracles, remembering previous lives, and knowing what is in the minds of others. A sixth, knowing that all defects have been eliminated, is often added. The first five are attained through meditative concentration (Skt. dhyāna), and are sometimes described as worldly, since they can be attained to some extent by non-Buddhist yogis, while the sixth is supramundane and attained only through the realization of bodhisattvas, or, according to some accounts, only by buddhas.

## higher realms
Here the Tibetan term “higher realms” (mtho ris) translates the Sanskrit svarga, meaning “heaven” or “heavenly realms.”

## Hīnayāna
This is a collective term used by proponents of the Mahāyāna to refer to the Śrāvakayāna and the Pratyekabuddhayāna. The name stems from their goal‍—nirvāṇa and personal liberation‍—being seen as small or lesser than the goal of the Mahāyāna—buddhahood and the liberation of all sentient beings.

## homa
*sbyin sreg*, Skt. *homa*, The casting of a prescribed offering into a ritual fire. The practice of homa is first attested in pre-Buddhist Vedic literature, and serves as a core, pervasive ritual paradigm in exoteric and esoteric rites in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist traditions into modern times. In Buddhist esoteric rites, the ritual offerings are made repeatedly, with each offering accompanied by a single repetition of the respective mantra.

## hosts of grahas
*gdon la ’jebs*, Skt. *gdon la ’jebs*, The translation of this term remains tentative but is read here as a potential translation of the Sanskrit compound *grahaprācurya in which the Tibetan has employed an incorrect grammatical particle. An alternate translation that favors the meaning that the term ’jebs pa bears in Tibetan and the Tibetan reading of the compound indicates that this could be either a collective noun or a proper name that translates as “Pleasing to the Grahas.”

## Hot and Fiercely Hot hells
*tsha dang rab tsha ba*, Skt. *tapanapratapana*, Two of the eight hot hells: the hell of scorching heat, while being pierced by spears; and the hell of fiercely scorching heat, while being pierced by tridents.

## Hot Hell
*tsha ba*, Skt. *tapana*, Sixth of the eight hot hells of Buddhist cosmology. Inhabitants of this hell are boiled in cauldrons, roasted in pans, beaten with hammers, and skewered with spears as their bodies burst into flame.

## hot springs
*ta po ta*, Skt. *tapodā*, ta po ta (or ta la po ta?) is the Tibetan transliteration of the Pali and Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit word tapodā (or tapoda), which, in the Pali texts, designates a hot spring outside of ancient Rājagṛha. This site, together with its surrounding area, the tapodārāma (Hot Springs Park), was favored as a bathing place by the early Buddhist saṅgha. The hot springs are in operation, even today, near the Veṇuvana site in Rajgir.

## hundred sextillion
Skt. *koṭīniyutaśatashasra*, A number calculated by multiplying a koṭi (bye ba), or ten million, by a niyuta (khrag khrig), or a hundred billion according to the Abhidharma system (although it is only one million in Classical Sanskrit), and by a śatasahasra (brgya stong), or one hundred thousand, all of which together equals ten to the twenty third power or a hundred sextillion. This term is often used as to express a number so large as to be inconceivable.

This term is often used as to express a number so large as to be inconceivable.

*yi dags*, Skt. *preta*, Literally “the departed,” and analogous to the ancestral spirits of the Vedic tradition, the pitṛs, who starve without the offerings of descendants. They live in the realm of Yama, the Lord of Death. In Buddhism they are said to suffer intensely, particularly from hunger and thirst.

## Hyecho
Ca. 701–780. A Buddhist monk and translator originally from the Silla kingdom (modern-day Korea), he is famous for his pilgrimage to India. He was a disciple of Amoghavajra, with whom he collaborated in the translation of tantric texts into Chinese.

*gang yang bdag gis lam ’phags pa’i ’byung ba rtogs par ’gyur ba de byed pa’i sdug bsngal yang dag par zad par ’gyur bar bstan pa de dag la nan tan byas na/ sdug bsngal yang dag par zad par ’gyur bar myi ’byung ngo*, Skt. *pratipadākhyātāryā­nairyāṇikī­niryāti­karasya samyagduḥkha­kṣayāya*, Fourth of the Buddha’s four fearlessnesses.

He was a previous incarnation of the Buddha who as a bodhisattva bargained his own flesh and blood away to Śakra (appearing in the guise of a cannibal demon) in return for hearing the verse that appears as the first in the Udānavarga collection.

## identity
*rang bzhin*, Skt. *svabhāva*, Svabhāva is usually rendered as “self-nature,” sometimes as “own-being,” both of which have a certain literal validity. However, neither artificial term has any evocative power for the reader who has no familiarity with the original, and a term must be found that the reader can immediately relate to his own world to fulfill the function the original word had in its world. In our world of identities (national, racial, religious, personal, sexual, etc.), “identity” is a part of our makeup; thus, when we are taught the ultimate absence of identity of all persons and things, it is easy to “identify” what is supposedly absent and hence to try to understand what that entails.

## ignorant of the Dharma
*ngan pa*, Skt. *ngan pa*, Lacking knowledge of or being ignorant [of the Dharma]. J. S. Negi (Negi 935, s.v. ngan pa) cites a few instances where Tibetan ngan pa represents the Sanskrit semantic field “lack of understanding,” e.g., Bodhi­caryāvatāra (Tib. ngan pa; Skt. ajñaḥ “not knowing,” “devoid of knowledge,” “stupid,” “foolish,” etc.); Jātakamālā (Tib. ngan pa; Skt. jaḍā matiḥ “dull,” “stupid,” “irrational”); Avadāna­kalpalatā (Tib. ngan pa; Skt. mūrkhāḥ “stupid, dull-headed; a fool”). Context suggests that this is one sense of ngan pa in Transformation of Karma when it talks about the Dharma and knowledge thereof. Also translated here as “bad deed.” See also .

## Śikṣāsamuccaya

The quotations he included from the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa were the only extant remnants of the original Sanskrit of the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa until the discovery of a Sanskrit text in the Potala Palace in 2002.

## Ikṣvāku
*bu ram shing*, Skt. *ikṣvāku*, This is a family lineage that many royal families claimed adherence to. It is the name of an early royal dynasty in India, which is said to be a solar dynasty. Though there are many versions of how the dynasty received its name, they all relate it to the sugar cane (ikṣu). In Buddhism he was said to have been miraculously born from the rishi Gautama’s semen and blood when it was heated by the sun, and subsequently hid among sugar cane. Buddha Śākyamuni was also considered to be in this family line.

## illusion
A magical illusion created by a conjurer or illusionist, or the power to create such an illusion. In the context of Buddhist literature, this is not considered to be a sleight of hand or visual trick but the actual appearance of something, such as an elephant or palace, created by magical means. Although this sort of magical illusion appears, it is unreal in the sense that there is no substantial basis for it beyond its magical appearance. In the Mahāyāna in particular, this sort of illusion (māyā created by magical means) is given as one example of how phenomena are empty and yet vividly appear; it is included in several lists of analogies for phenomena’s illusory nature.The Prophecy for Bhadra the Illusionist uniquely describes the Buddha’s miraculous powers in comparison to the powers of Bhadra the illusionist, also describing the Buddha’s power with the term māyā; however, it is declared () that the Buddha’s māyā is superior to Bhadra’s, which is limited and incomplete.Also translated as “power of illusion.”

## illusionist
A conjurer, sorcerer, or magician who has the ability to create illusions. See Introduction .

*rdul dang bral ba’i rgyal mtshan*, A world realm in the distant future.

## Immaculate Center of the Sky
*nam mkha’i dkyil dri ma med pa rnam par sems pa*, Skt. *nam mkha’i dkyil dri ma med pa rnam par sems pa*, The tathāgata of the northeastern buddhafield Pure Immaculate Dwelling.

## Immaculate Consecration
*dri med dban bskur*, Skt. *dri med dban bskur*, A king and sage; a former incarnation of the Buddha.

## Immaculate Fragrant Star of Bright Splendor
*rdul med spos snang skar ma’i dpal*, Skt. *rdul med spos snang skar ma’i dpal*, The name of the buddha that the sage Jyotīrasa will become, according to a prophecy by the Buddha.

## Immaculate Hand
*phyag dri ma med pa*, Skt. *phyag dri ma med pa*, A buddha.

## Immaculate Heart
*dri ma med pa’i snying po*, Skt. *dri ma med pa’i snying po*, The world where the twelve thousand nāgas will reach buddhahood.

## Immaculate Intelligence
*blo gros rnyog med*, Skt. *blo gros rnyog med*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Hutārci (490 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## immaculate light
*’od dri ma med pa*, Skt. *vimalaprabhā*, The 40th meditative stability in chapters 6 and 8.

## Immaculate Limitless Intelligence
*blo mtha’ yas dri med*, Skt. *blo mtha’ yas dri med*, A bodhisattva in the northeastern buddhafield Pure Immaculate Dwelling.

## immaculate moon
*zla ba dri ma med pa*, Skt. *candravimala*, The 50th meditative stability in chapters 6 and 8.

## Immaculate One
*dri ma med pa dang ldan pa*, Skt. *dri ma med pa dang ldan pa*, Name of the world system of the thus-gone one Radiant Light.

## Immaculate Pure Precious Light, Sovereign of the Uninterrupted Luminous Display of Dharma Endowed with the Factors of Awakening
*dri med rnam dag rin chen ’od byang chub kyi yan lag dang ldan pa’ chos rgyun mi ’chad pa’i ’od zer bkod pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *dri med rnam dag rin chen ’od byang chub kyi yan lag dang ldan pa’ chos rgyun mi ’chad pa’i ’od zer bkod pa’i rgyal po*, A tathāgata in the eastern buddhafield Endowed with the Vast Display of the Precious Merits of Endless Qualities.

## Immaculate Victory Banner
*rdul bral rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *rdul bral rgyal mtshan*, A bodhisattva.

## Immaculate Visage
*dri ma med pa’i zhal*, Skt. *dri ma med pa’i zhal*, A buddha.

## Immaculately Moved by Beings
*sems can la g.yo zhing rdul dang bral ba*, Skt. *sems can la g.yo zhing rdul dang bral ba*, A bodhisattva who seeks a prophecy from Śākyamuni.

## Immaterial
*rdul bral*, Skt. *rdul bral*, Immaterial (not consisting of matter; incorporeal), also the name of the mother of the buddha Jñānin.

## immature elder
*gnas brtan byis pa*, A monk who has been ordained for at least ten years yet still cannot recite the Prātimokṣasūtra or its supplements and is thus not entitled to grant entry into the order, grant ordination, [accept charge of](#accept-charge-of) [novice](#novice)s, give [refuge](#refuge), or [live independently](#live-independently).

## immaturity
*skyon*, Skt. *āma*, With respect to bodhisattva great beings, “immaturity” (āma, skyon) suggests rawness—something that is uncooked, unrefined, and flawed—while “maturity” (niyāma, skyon med) implies certitude, refinement, cooking, softening, and flawlessness.

## immeasurable
*gzhal du med pa*, Skt. *gzhal du med pa*, In the context of sentient beings being “immeasurable.” One of the ten topics to be expounded to the bodhisattva who has perfected application.

## Immeasurable Array
*bkod pa dpag med*, Skt. *bkod pa dpag med*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Dyutimat (409 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## immeasurable aspiration
*tshad med*, Skt. *aprameya*, See “four immeasurable aspirations.”

## immeasurable attitudes
*tshad med*, Skt. *apramāṇa*, See “four immeasurable attitudes.”

## immeasurable contemplations
*tshad med pa*, Skt. *apramāṇa*, See “four abodes of Brahmā.”

## Immeasurable Eye
*dpag med mig*, Skt. *dpag med mig*, Mother of the buddha Sūryaprabha.

## Immeasurable Fame
*grags pa dpag med*, Skt. *grags pa dpag med*, Son of the buddha Suviniścitārtha.

## Immeasurable Insight
*shes rab dpag tu med pa*, Skt. *shes rab dpag tu med pa*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Muniprasanna.

## Immeasurable Light
*tshad med ’od*, Skt. *apramāṇābha*, Second of three heavens of gods on the second concentration level.

## Immeasurable Melody
*dbyangs dpag med*, Skt. *dbyangs dpag med*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Flowered.

## Immeasurable Movement
*dpag med ’gro*, Skt. *dpag med ’gro*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Vimalaprabha.

## Immeasurable Splendor
*gzi brjid dpag med*, Skt. *gzi brjid dpag med*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Gaṇimukha (390 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## immeasurable states
*tshad med pa*, Skt. *apramāṇa*, The four immeasurable states are immeasurable love, immeasurable compassion, immeasurable joy, and immeasurable equanimity.

## immeasurable states of mind
*sems kyi tshad med*, Skt. *apramāṇa*, This refers to the four meditations on love (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā), as well as the states of mind and qualities of being that result from their cultivation.

## Immeasurable Virtue
*tshad med dge*, Skt. *apramāṇaśubha*, One of the heavens of Buddhist cosmology, second of three levels of the third dhyāna realm.

## immeasurables
*tshad med pa*, Skt. *catvāryapramāṇāni*, The four immeasurables: loving-kindness (Tib. byams pa, Skt. maitrī); compassion (Tib. snying rje, Skt. karuṇā); joy (Tib. dga’ ba, Skt. muditā); and equanimity (Tib. btang snyoms, Skt. upekṣā).

## Immediacy
Immediacy (the quality of being immediate or without delay), also the sixth of the bodhisattva grounds, understood as ten in number.

## immediate retribution
*mtshams med*, Refers to the five acts of immediate retribution (pañcānantarya), for which one will be reborn in hell immediately after death, without any intervening stages: killing an arhat, killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, causing a schism in the monastic community, and maliciously drawing blood from a tathāgata.

## Immense Vista
*shin tu mthong ba*, Skt. *shin tu mthong ba*, A royal palace.

## Immersed in Joy
*dga’ ba spyod pa*, A householder who was the householder called Bhadradeva in the past, under the Buddha Dīpaṅkara.

## Immortal One
*mi ’chi*, Skt. *mi ’chi*, A previous ruler of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

## immortality
*bdud rtsi*, Skt. *amṛta*, The ambrosia that prevents death or spiritual death (hence the Tibetan term means “crushes spiritual death”). The Sanskrit term literally means immortality. It is often used metaphorically to mean the Dharma.

## Immovable
*mi g.yo ba*, Skt. *acalā*, Immovable (not able to be moved; fixed), also the eighth bodhisattva level; see also Acala (the masculine form), another name of the deity Caṇḍa­mahā­roṣaṇa.

## Immovable Subjugator
*mi g.yo rnam par gnon pa*, Skt. *mi g.yo rnam par gnon pa*, A great bodhisattva.

## Immutable
*mi ’khrugs pa*, Skt. *mi ’khrugs pa*, Immutable (unchanging; unable to be changed), also the name of the father of the buddha Priyaprasanna.

## Immutable Abiding
*gnas pa mi ’khrugs pa*, Skt. *gnas pa mi ’khrugs pa*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Priyaprasanna.

## Immutable Array
*bkod pa mi ’khrugs pa*, Skt. *bkod pa mi ’khrugs pa*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Sukhita.

## Immutable Beauty
*mdzes pa mi g.yo ba*, Skt. *mdzes pa mi g.yo ba*, Birthplace of the buddha Sārodgata.

## Immutable Intelligence
*mi g.yo blo gros*, Skt. *mi g.yo blo gros*, Mother of the buddha Dharmakīrti.

## Immutable Mind
*mi g.yo’i blo*, Skt. *mi g.yo’i blo*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Susthita (88 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## immutable nature of phenomena
*chos mi ’gyur ba nyid*, A synonym for emptiness and the realm of phenomena.

## Immutable One
*mi ’gyur*, Skt. *mi ’gyur*, A previous ruler of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

## Immutable One Endowed with the Original Generation of the Mind
*sems dang po bskyed pa ldan pa’i mi ’khrugs pa*, Skt. *sems dang po bskyed pa ldan pa’i mi ’khrugs pa*, A buddha.

## Immutable Splendor
*gzi brjid mi g.yo ba*, Skt. *gzi brjid mi g.yo ba*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Vyūharāja.

## Immutable Strength
*mthu rtsal mi g.yo ba*, Skt. *mthu rtsal mi g.yo ba*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Gandhābha.

## Impartial Gaze
*mnyam par lta*, Skt. *samadṛṣṭi*, A bodhisattva.

## impeccable
*smad du med pa*, Skt. *na jugupsanīya*, Literally, “cannot be disliked.”

## Impeccable Limbs
*yan lag ma smad pa*, Skt. *yan lag ma smad pa*, Attendant of the buddha Abhedyabuddhi.

## impediments
*bar chad kyi chos*, Skt. *antarāyikadharma*, Personal qualities or circumstances that impede the start of or success in a person's monastic career.

## impelling mantra
*sbad pa’i gsang sngags*, A mantra that can be used to impel or incite beings to perform a particular action.

## Impenetrable
*tshugs pa med pa*, Skt. *tshugs pa med pa*, Impenetrable (impossible to pass through or enter), also the name of the birthplace of the buddha Śūra.

## Impenetrable Dwelling Place
*gzings pa’i ’dug gnas*, Skt. *gzings pa’i ’dug gnas*, May, or may not, correspond to the Giñjakāvasatha of other texts. See .

## imperceptible form
*rnam par rig byed ma yin pa*, Skt. *avijñaptirūpa*, Entities, such as vows, that are categorized as form composed of the physical elements yet remain imperceptible.

## imperishable
*’jig pa med pa*, Skt. *[vivṛta]*, The 48th meditative stability in chapter 8. The translation here follows the Tibetan; in the Sanskrit texts, this meditative stability is vivṛta, “uncovered.”

## imperturbability of all phenomena
*chos thams cad mi non pa*, Skt. *sarva­dharmāstambhita*, The fifth of twenty-four aspects of the perfection of wisdom taught by Dharmodgata, and realized as meditative stabilities by Sadāprarudita, in chapter 75.

## Imperturbable Intelligence
*mi khrugs pa’i blo gros*, Skt. *mi khrugs pa’i blo gros*, A sage.

## Impervious
*gdul dka’*, Skt. *gdul dka’*, Impervious (not allowing passage through; unaffected), also the name of the world system of the thus-gone one Highly Renowned.

## Impervious practitioner
*chos dred*, let. [Dharma](#dharma) bear. "Someone who has not been tamed by the [Dharma](#dharma), who knows the [Dharma](#dharma) but does not practice it, so that his mind has become stiff..." DICT. someone who only has an intellectual understanding, without any real experience, but considers that he or she knows all about the [Dharma](#dharma).

## ḍimphika
*byis pa*, Skt. *ḍimphika*, A class of malevolent spirits.

## impinge upon (to)
*glags*, Skt. *avatāra*, (in the expressions ava­tāra na labhate, glags mi rnyed, “no opportunity for … to impinge upon …”).

## implore
*rbad*, A term for the imperative commands that appear in a mantra.

## impossible
*gnas ma yin*, Skt. *asthāna*, This terms refers to all that is unreasonable and cannot be expected to occur. Among the ten powers of a Buddha, the first is knowing what is tenable and untenable (Skt. sthānāsthāna, Tib. gnas dang gnas ma yin), i.e., the natural laws that govern the world in which we live.

## Impossible to Die
*gsod med*, Skt. *nirmarmara*, One of sixteen realms that surround the Howling Hell. Also known as No Death.

## impostor
*rku thabs su gnas pa*, Skt. *steyasaṃvāsika*, Someone who pretends to have been ordained though they have not. One class of person barred from joining the renunciate order.

## Improving Intellect
*phel ba’i blo gros*, Skt. *phel ba’i blo gros*, A bodhisattva.

## impure conduct
*mi tshangs par spyod pa*, Skt. *abrahmacarya*, This term is the opposite of brahmacarya, “pure conduct” or “holy life,” which denotes the chaste life of those who have renounced the world. The term abrahmacarya therefore refers to sexual conduct, which is regarded as a root downfall for monastics on the śrāvaka path.

## imputation
*sgro ’dogs pa*, Skt. *samāropa*, A term that refers to the activity of superimposition or imputing characteristics to things that they do not possess. A paradigm case in Buddhism is the imputation of a singular, self-existent, enduring self to the transient bundle of skandhas that make up a person.

## imputed
*kun tu brtags pa*, Skt. *parikalpita*, Conceptual cognition; an alternative translation is “the imaginary.” One of the three natures that are a central philosophy of the Yogācāra tradition.

## in an apprehending manner
*dmigs pa’i tshul du*, Skt. *upa­lambha­yogena*, The expression “in an apprehending manner” implies that ordinary persons perceive phenomena as inherently exisiting, whereas bodhisattvas are said to act and teach “without apprehending anything.” On the latter term, see respective glossary entry.

## in brief, as mentioned before
*de bzhin du sbyar te*, Skt. *peyālaṃ*, “Et cetera,” “in short,” “in brief”; a résumé of a preceding series of stanzas. Cf. Mahāvyupatti §5435; Edgerton 1953, p. 354a.

## in charge of providing clean drinking water
*skom gyi gtsang sbyor*, Skt. *pānakavārika*, One of several official administrative or managerial positions at a monastery.

## In Tune with All Pleasures
*’dod pa thams cad rjes su ’thun pa*, Skt. *’dod pa thams cad rjes su ’thun pa*, A forest in Shining in Manifold Ways.

## In Two Minds
*yid gnyis can*, Skt. *yid gnyis can*, A buddha realm.

## inaction
*bya ba ma yin*, Skt. *akriyā*, Inaction here implies the mistaken view that, owing to emptiness, engagement in virtuous acts is to be avoided.

## inactivity of all phenomena
*chos thams cad spyod pa med pa*, Skt. *sarva­dharma­niśceṣṭa*, The twenty-third of twenty-four aspects of the perfection of wisdom taught by Dharmodgata, and realized as meditative stabilities by Sadāprarudita, in chapter 75.

## inadmissible act
*kha na ma tho ba*, Skt. *avadya*, Unwholesome actions that result in suffering.

## in-between worlds
*’jig rten gyi bar*, Skt. *lokāntarika*, Permanently dark places in between the four continents.

## incalculable eon
*skal pa grangs med pa*, Skt. *asaṃkhyeyakalpa*, The number of years in this eon differs in various sūtras that give a number. Also, twenty intermediate eons are said to be one incalculable eon, and four incalculable eons are one great eon. In that case, those four incalculable eons represent the eons of the creation, presence, destruction, and absence of a world. In this sūtra, buddhas are often described as appearing in a second “incalculable eon.”

## incant
*mngon par bsngags*, Skt. *abhimantr*, To imbue something with power by reciting the mantra over it.

## incantation
*gzungs*, Skt. *dhāraṇī*, The incantations, or spells, are mnemonic formulas, possessed by advanced bodhisattvas, that contain a quintessence of their attainments, not simply magical charms—although the latter are included. The same term in Sanskrit and Tibetan also refers to a highly developed power present in bodhisattvas that is a process of memory and recall of detailed teachings, best translated “retention” in certain contexts.

## incarnation
*sprul pa*, Skt. *nirmāṇa*, See “emanated incarnation.”

## incarnation-body
*sprul pa’i sku*, Skt. *nirmāṇakāya*, See “emanated incarnation.”

## Incense Array
*spos bkod pa*, Skt. *spos bkod pa*, A buddha realm.

## incense censer
A vessel used to offer incense.

## Incense Elephant
*glang chen spos kyi bal glang*, Skt. *glang chen spos kyi bal glang*, A bodhisattva in the retinue of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Incense Flower
*spos kyi me tog*, Skt. *spos kyi me tog*, A buddha.

## Incense Glory
*spos kyi dpal*, Skt. *spos kyi dpal*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Pradīpa (963 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Incense King of the Infinite Mountain
*mtha’ yas pa’i lhun po spos kyi rgyal po*, Skt. *mtha’ yas pa’i lhun po spos kyi rgyal po*, A buddha.

## Incense Leader
*spos kyi khyu mchog*, Skt. *spos kyi khyu mchog*, A buddha.

## Incense Light
*spos snang*, Skt. *spos snang*, A buddha realm.

## Incense Mansion
*spos kyi khang pa*, Skt. *spos kyi khang pa*, A buddha.

## Incense Master
*spos kyi dbang phyug*, Skt. *spos kyi dbang phyug*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Amoghagāmin (643 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Incense Mountain
*spos kyi lhun po*, Skt. *spos kyi lhun po*, A buddha.

## Incense of Joy
*dga’ ba’i spos*, Skt. *dga’ ba’i spos*, A buddha realm.

## Incense of Wisdom
*ye shes spos*, Skt. *ye shes spos*, A buddha realm.

## Incense Ornament
*spos kyis brgyan*, Skt. *spos kyis brgyan*, Birthplace of the buddha Surabhigandha.

## Incense River
*spos chu*, Skt. *spos chu*, A river in the realm of the Four Great Kings.

## Incense Sender
*spos rab btang*, Skt. *spos rab btang*, A great bodhisattva.

## Incense Splendor
*spos kyi dpal*, Skt. *spos kyi dpal*, A great bodhisattva.

## Incense Stūpa
*spos kyi mchod rten*, Skt. *spos kyi mchod rten*, Mother of the buddha Sugandha.

## Incense Voice
*spos kyi dbyangs*, Skt. *spos kyi dbyangs*, Third of the five great kings.

## Incense-Emitting Light
The buddha of the world system called Gandhaprabhāsa during the time of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Incessant
*mnar med pa*, Skt. *avīci*, Incessant (never ceasing; continuous), also the name of one of the eight hot hells.

## Incessant Hell
The lowest hell, the eighth of the eight hot hells.

## Incessant Pain
*mnar med*, Skt. *avīci*, One among the eight hot hells.

## Incessant Torture
*mnar med*, Skt. *avīci*, The lowest and worst of the major hot hells according to Buddhist cosmology; see also .

## Incessantly Intense Pain
*tshor ba rtag tu ’dus pa*, Skt. *samāhṛta­vedana*, A realm that neigbors the Black Line Hell. (The term Samāhṛtavedana is reading, on the authority of the Tib., samāhūta˚ as samāhṛta˚)

## incinerating all afflicted mental states
*nyon mongs pa thams cad sreg pa*, A meditative stability.

## incineration of all afflicted mental states
*nyon mongs pa thams cad ma lus par sreg pa*, Skt. *sarva­kleśa­nirdahana*, A meditative stability.

## incineration of all afflictions
*nyon mongs pa thams cad ma lus par sreg pa*, Skt. *sarva­kleśa­nirdahana*, A meditative stability.

## inclination
*mos pa*, Skt. *adhimukti*, In vernacular Tibetan usage, the term mos pa carries meanings of “respect,” “devotion,” and “faith.” In a sūtra context, it tends to mean “inclination” or “propensity”—the level of interest and aptitude, as well as confidence, of the Buddha’s disciples. It has also been translated here, depending on the context, as “belief” and “aptitude.” See also .

## Incomparable
*mtshungs pa med*, Skt. *mtshungs pa med*, Incomparable (beyond comparison; matchless), also the name of the buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Guṇaprabha (30 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Incomparable Buddha Who Is a Splendorous Source of Flowers
*sangs rgyas dpe med me tog ’byung ba’i dpal*, Skt. *sangs rgyas dpe med me tog ’byung ba’i dpal*, A buddha.

## Incomparable Ground
The eighth of the twelve buddha grounds.

## Incomparable Harm
*gnod pa dpe med pa*, Skt. *pīḍānupama*, One of sixteen realms that surround the Great Howling Hell.

## Incomparable Mind
*mnyam pa dang mi mnyam pa’i blo*, Skt. *mnyam pa dang mi mnyam pa’i blo*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Vardhana.

## Incomparable Strength
*shugs mthungs pa med pa*, Skt. *shugs mthungs pa med pa*, A bodhisattva; former incarnation of the Buddha.

## incomprehensibility
*mi dmigs pa*, Skt. *anupalambha*, This refers to the ultimate nature of things, which cannot be comprehended, grasped, etc., by the ordinary, conditioned, subjective mind. Hence it is significant that the realization of this nature is not couched in terms of understanding, or conviction, but in terms of tolerance (kṣānti), as the grasping mind cannot grasp its ultimate inability to grasp; it can only cultivate its tolerance of that inability.

## inconceivability
*bsam gyis mi khyab pa*, Skt. *acintyatā*, Lit. “unthinkability,” (on the part of a mind whose thinking is conditioned and bound by conceptual terms). This is essentially synonymous with “incomprehensibility” (see entry).

## inconceivability of all phenomena
*chos thams cad bsam gyis mi khyab pa*, Skt. *sarva­dharmācintya*, The twenty-fourth of twenty-four aspects of the perfection of wisdom taught by Dharmodgata, and realized as meditative stabilities by Sadāprarudita, in chapter 75.

## inconceivable
A term that refers not only to something that cannot be imagined or conceived, generally speaking, but also to something of inconceivably great quantity or quality.

## Inconceivable Array
*bkod pa bsam gyis mi khyab pa*, Skt. *bkod pa bsam gyis mi khyab pa*, Father of the buddha Vyūharāja.

## inconceivable liberation
*rnam par thar pa bsam gyis mi khyab pa*, Skt. *acintyavimokṣa*, Inconceivable liberation of the bodhisattvas, a name of the Avataṃsaka, and a subtitle of the Vimala­kīrti­nirdeśa.

## Inconceivable Light
*bsam gyis mi khyab ’od*, Skt. *bsam gyis mi khyab ’od*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Vāsanottīrṇa­gati (888 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Inconceivable Radiance
*snang ba bsam gyis mi khyab pa*, Skt. *acintya­prabhāsa*, A bodhisattva in, and principle protagonist of, The Teaching by the Child Inconceivable Radiance. This is also the name he will have as a buddha in the future, as prophesied by the Buddha.

## inconceivable realm
*bsam gyis mi khyab pa’i dbyings*, Skt. *acintyadhātu*, A synonym of ultimate reality.

## Inconceivable Support
*bsam gyis mi khyab stegs*, Skt. *bsam gyis mi khyab stegs*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Vasuśreṣṭha (951 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## inconspicuous ankle bones
*zhabs long mo’i tshigs mi mngon pa*, Skt. *ucchaṅka­pāda­tā*, Seventh of the thirty-two major marks.

## inconspicuous ankles
*long bu mi mngon pa*, Skt. *gūḍhagulpha*, Ninth of the eighty minor signs.

## inconspicuous blood vessels and nerves
*rtsa mi mngon pa*, Skt. *gūḍhaśira*, Seventh of the eighty minor signs.

## incorrect mental engagement
*tshul bzhin ma yin pa’i yid la byed pa*, Skt. *ayoniśomanas­kara*, Identifications and discernments that run counter to the actual nature of things.

## incorrect view
*log par lta ba*, One of the ten nonvirtuous actions.

## Increaser
*'phel byed*, Increaser (one who or that which increases something), also the name of a householder in this sūtra.

## increasing
*rgyas pa*, Skt. *pauṣṭika*, A common class of ritual activity (Skt. karman; Tib. las).

## Increasing Joy
*dga’ ba ’phel ba*, Skt. *dga’ ba ’phel ba*, The region in which the dwelling place of bodhisattvas called Sthavira Cave is located.

## Increasing Majesty
*dpal ’phel*, Skt. *dpal ’phel*, The name of a king in the southern region in the distant future.

## Increasing Merit
*bsod nams skyes*, Skt. *punyaprasava*, One of the heavens of Buddhist cosmology, second of three levels of the fourth dhyāna realm.

## Increasing Purity and Truth
*gtsang zhing bden pa’i mtshams ’phel bar mdzad pa*, Skt. *gtsang zhing bden pa’i mtshams ’phel bar mdzad pa*, The name of a tathāgata in a future eon in the world system Refined Purity.

## Increasing Qualities
*yon tan ’phel*, Skt. *yon tan ’phel*, Attendant of the buddha Ratnagarbha.

## Increasing Wealth
*nor ’phel*, Skt. *nor ’phel*, A great bodhisattva.

## Increasing Wisdom
*ye shes ’phel*, Skt. *ye shes ’phel*, Father of the buddha Jñānaprāpta.

## Indala

## Indra Kauśika
“Indra who belongs to the Kuśika lineage.” An epithet of the god Śakra, also known as Indra, the king of the gods in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. In the Ṛgveda, Indra is addressed by the epithet Kauśika, with the implication that he is associated with the descendants of the Kuśika lineage as their supporting deity. In later epic and Purāṇic texts, we find the story that Indra took birth as Gādhi Kauśika, the son of Kuśika and one of the Vedic poet-seers, after the Puru king Kuśika had performed austerities for one thousand years to obtain a son equal to Indra who could not be killed by others.

## inherent existence
*rang bzhin*, Skt. *sva­bhāva*, This term denotes the ontological status of phenomena, according to which they are attributed with existence in their own right, inherently, in and of themselves, objectively, and independent of any other phenomena such as our conception and labelling. The absence of such an ontological reality is defined as the true nature of reality, emptiness.

## inherent nature
*rang bzhin*, Skt. *prakṛti*, rang bzhin (also rendered here as “inherent existence”) literally means “own-being” and can be used in an ordinary sense to denote the most fundamental or characteristic quality, property, or nature of things. In Mahāyāna literature it is also used in several different ways in the examination of the ontological status of phenomena, most frequently in statements denying that phenomena may ultimately possess any such existence or nature, objectively in their own right, apart from ignorantly attributed concepts and designations. However, in the Yogācāra system and later literature the incompleteness of an ontological status is described in three or more successive levels or aspects that also use modulations of the same term.--> The Tibetan term rang bzhin (also rendered here as “inherent existence”) literally means “own-being” and can be used in an ordinary sense to denote the most fundamental or characteristic quality, property, or nature of things. In Mahāyāna literature it is also used in several different ways in the examination of the ontological status of phenomena, most frequently in statements denying that phenomena may ultimately possess any such existence or nature, objectively in their own right, apart from ignorantly attributed concepts and designations. ## initiation
*dbang*, Skt. *abhiṣeka*, A ritual initiation into the maṇḍala and practice system of a specific tantric deity. The term means “to anoint,” as it evokes Indic rites of royal coronation that involve sprinkling consecrated water.

## innate joy
*lhan cig skyes pa’i dga’ ba*, Skt. *sahajānanda*, Although referred to as the “fourth” in the fourfold division of the joys, the innate joy does not fit into a sequential order in quite the same way as the other three joys. It is first discerned when the supreme joy gives way to the joy of cessation, and is gradually extended through practice until it becomes ever present.

## Innate (wisdom, joy, etc.)
*lhan skyes*, Skt. *sāhaja*, lit. born together, meaning that [wisdom](#wisdom), joy, and [nirvāṇa](#nirvāṇa) in general are latently present even as we experience ignorance, suffering and [saṃsāra](#saṃsāra). The two aspects of one and the same nature are "born together", but perceived as opposites by unenlightened minds.

The three cycles of twenty years that occur within the larger sixty-year cycles.

## inopportune states
*mi khom pa*, Skt. *akṣaṇa*, The Sanskrit literally means “without leisure”; this refers to being born in a state in which one will not have the opportunity to meet with a buddha or their teachings. Eight situations are typically listed: (1) being born in a hell realm, (2) as an animal, (3) as a hungry ghost, (4) as a long-life god, (5) in a borderland or non-Buddhist country, (6) having wrong views, (7) as someone with impaired faculties who is unable to understand the teachings, or (8) in a time or place where no buddha has come.

## Insentient Beings
*’du shes med pa’i sems can*, Skt. *asaṃjñāsatva*, A class of beings in the form realm, and the thirteenth heaven of the form realm on a level just below the devas of the Pure Abodes. The Insentient Beings are characterized by having a body but no conscious experience at all; this state is the karmic result of an ordinary or worldly form of the fourth meditative absorption called the attainment of the meditative state without consciousness. See also .

## insight
As the sixth of the six perfections, it refers to the profound understanding of the emptiness of all phenomena, the realization of ultimate reality‍. In other translations it is sometimes rendered as “wisdom”; however, we have reserved this latter term for the translation of jñāna. In other contexts it refers to the mental factor responsible for ascertaining the specific qualities of a given object, or whether it should be taken up or rejected.

## insight consort
A term for the consort—whether actual, imagined, or spontaneously realized—with which an initiated practitioner engages in sexual yoga in Buddhist tantric literature. This particular term invokes the general principle that the female half of the tantric couple is the perfect embodiment of insight or prajñā.

## inspired eloquence
The trait of being able to speak readily and fluently and with inspiration and confidence about the Dharma and, indeed, in any teaching situation. Connected with the Sanskrit term pratibhā, which can have the sense of coming into view, appearing to the mind, becoming clear, and thus it has the sense of brilliance and clarity of thought expressed in speech.

## inspired speech
The quality of intelligence, inspiration, and confident knowledge that allows one to teach and talk in the most appropriate way, even for very long stretches of time.

## inspired to speak
*spobs*, See “eloquence.”

## inspired utterance
A genre of Buddhist literature, included in the list of both nine or twelve types. There is a specific text in the Pali canon that compiles a number of such stories, which give a short prose narrative concluding with the Buddha giving an inspired utterance in verse. The Udāna in Chinese does not include the frame story, but only the verses.

## instructor

The [Buddha](#buddha) specified five types of instructor: instructors of [novice](#novice)s, [privy advisor](#privy-advisor)s, [officiant](#officiant)s, [givers of instruction](#givers-of-instruction), and [recitation instructor](#recitation-instructor)s.

While both these meanings can be derived from the Sanskrit viramānanda, the Tibetan dga’ bral dga’ ba seems to reflect only the joy of cessation.

*’dun pa*, Skt. *chanda*, One of the four bases of miraculous power.
