## interdependence
*rten ’brel*, Skt. *pratītyasamut­pāda*, A mode of describing the relative nature of phenomena, in which each phenomenon arises in dependence upon causes and conditions. In many contexts, the term refers specifically to the twelve links of interdependent origination that describe the process of being bound in cyclic existence: ignorance, formation, consciousness, name and form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, appropriation, becoming, birth, and old age and death.

## intermediate eon
*bar gyi bskal pa*, Skt. *antarakalpa*, This eon is one cycle of the increase and decrease of the life span of beings. It is also called “a small eon.” It consists of four ages, or yugas, and the last is the kaliyuga.

## intermediate kalpa
*bskal pa bar ma*, Skt. *antarakalpa*, This kalpa is one cycle of the increase and decrease of the lifespan of beings. It is also called a “small kalpa.” It consists of four ages, or yugas.

## Intermediate state
*bar do*, Skt.*antarābhava*, term used for the various stages of experience between death and the next, with a wider interpretation that includes the various states of consciousness in life. Four intermediate states are distinguished: 1) the natural intermediate state of this life (*rang bzhin skyes gnas [bar](#bar) do*), 2) the intermediate state of the moment of death (*'chi kha'i [bar](#bar) do*), 3) the [intermediate state of absolute reality](#intermediate-state-of-absolute-reality) (*chos nyid [bar](#bar) do*), and 4) the [intermediate state of becoming](#intermediate-state-of-becoming) (*srid pa'i [bar](#bar) do*); or, to make six intermediate states, two more particular states, within the first, can be added: 5) the intermediate state of dream (*rmi lam [bar](#bar) do*) and 6) the intermediate state of meditative [concentration](#concentration) (*bsam gtan [bar](#bar) do*).

## intermediate state between death and rebirth
*bar ma do*, Skt. *antarābhava*, A transitional, discarnate state of a sentient being between death and rebirth, classically said to last up 49 days; its existence was and is not accepted by all Buddhist schools (not, e.g., by the Theravādins).

## Intermediate state of absolute reality
*chos nyid [bar](#bar) do*, [intermediate state](#intermediate-state) during which absolute reality manifests as pure forms of peaceful or wrathful aspect, according to one's own individual [tendencies](#tendencies).

## Intermediate state of becoming
*srid pa'i [bar](#bar) do*, the [intermediate state](#intermediate-state) during which the force of [karma](#karma) propels one towards one's next rebirth in [saṃsāra](#saṃsāra). AT: [intermediate state](#intermediate-state) of possibilities, [intermediate state](#intermediate-state) of existence.

## internal differentiation
*nang rab tu ’byed pa*, Skt. *nang rab tu ’byed pa*, The name of a karmic wind involved in the formation of an embryo in its fourth week.

## interpretable meaning
*drang don*, Skt. *neyārtha*, See “definitive meaning.”

## interrupting the rains
*dbyar ral*, Skt. *chinnavarṣā*, If a monk does not fulfill his pledge to remain at a site for the duration of the earlier or later rains, his rains retreat has been “interrupted.” Such “interruptions” in the rain retreat violate the pledge to stay in one place.

## intersex person
*skyes nas ma ning*, Skt. *jātipaṇḍaka*, Someone born with both male and female sexual organs. One of the five types of [person labeled a paṇḍaka](#person-labeled-a-paṇḍaka), all of whom are barred from joining the renunciate order.

## intervening summary
*bar sdom*, Skt. *antaroddāna*, A summary or synopsis in verse form comprising a list of topics or keywords. One of several types of summary (uddāna) characteristic of the vinaya and abhidharma literature and also found in longer sūtras of the Dīrghāgama and (less often) Madhyamāgama. An intervening summary, found less often than the other types, typically summarizes the subject matter of a topical subsection of which it may also mark the end. See also Uddāna-->.

## intoxicant
*bcos pa’i chang*, Drink made from any source which has the power to intoxicate.

## intoxicated
One who is still under the influence of the “intoxicants” (āsrava), of which there are sometimes said to be four: “lust” (kāma), “becoming” (bhava), “ignorance” (avidyā), and “views” (dṛṣṭi)

## Intoxicating Abode
*myos gnas*, Skt. *myos gnas*, A forest in Distinguished in Many Colorful Ways.

## intrinsic nature
*rang bzhin*, Skt. *svabhāva*, This term (also rendered here as “inherent existence” and “inherent nature”) literally means “own-being” and can be used in an ordinary sense to denote the most fundamental or characteristic quality, property, or nature of things. In Mahāyāna literature it is also used in several different ways in the examination of the ontological status of phenomena, most frequently in statements denying that phenomena may ultimately possess any such existence or nature, objectively in their own right, apart from ignorantly attributed concepts and designations. However, in the Yogācāra system and later literature the incompleteness of an ontological status is described in three or more successive levels or aspects that also use modulations of the same term; see “three natures.”

## introduction
*gleng gzhi*, Skt. *nidāna*, The introductory section of a sūtra or other Buddhist scripture that establishes the time and setting of the discourse.

## introduction to the letters
*yi ge la ’jug pa*, Skt. *akṣarapraveśa*, One aspect of a set of forty-four syllables listed at as dhāraṇī gateways. See also “gateways to the letters.”

## introductions
*gleng gzhi*, Skt. *nidāna*, Sixth of the twelve branches of the scriptures.

*sdom pa phyin ci log pa*, Skt. *viparīta­saṃvara*, Refers to unconventional practices of a tantric yogin.

## investigation
*dpyod pa*, Skt. *vicāra*, In our text, the specific quality of vicāra is to remain mindful of nimitta in the sense of “mentally watching” or noting them without engaging in a more discursive way.

*thub pa med pa’i ’od*, Skt. *thub pa med pa’i ’od*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Cakradhara.

## Invisible
*mi mthong ba*, Skt. *mi mthong ba*, Invisible (unable to be seen), also the name of a river on Eye Garland.

## invisible crown
*spyi gtsug bltar mi mthong ba*, Skt. *anavalokitamūrdhata*, One of the features of a tathāgata, sometimes included as an additional characteristic of the uṣṇīṣa (q.v.) and sometimes as a separate sign, either within the major and minor marks or in addition to them. Although sometimes explained with the sense almost of a prohibition against looking down on a tathāgata from above, it is more usually linked to the idea that the uṣṇīṣa extends upwards so far that its top is literally out of sight. Its mention in this text relates to the overall stature of a tathāgata, presumably in more than one sense.

## Invisible Summit
*rtse rtse mi snang*, Skt. *rtse rtse mi snang*, A mountain near the asura city Double Pleasure.

## Invisible Wrists
*tshigs mi mngon*, Skt. *tshigs mi mngon*, A nāga king.

## iron aperture
*lcags kyi sgo*, Skt. *lcags kyi sgo*, The name of a karmic wind involved in the formation of an embryo in its thirtieth week.

A reference to, or epithet of, the garuḍas, on account of their sharp beaks.

## iron bolt
*dbang po’i phur pa*, Skt. *indrakīla*, More literally rendered as “Indra’s stake,” the term indrakīla is used in Indic architectural treatises to refer to any pin, nail, or bolt used to firmly bind other architectural features together. The term can also be used to refer generically to a mountain, likely due to its similar firm and unwavering nature.

## ironwood flowers
*nA ga ge sar*, Skt. *nāgakeśara*, Mesua ferrea. Evergreen tree up to 100 feet tall. Known as Assam ironwood, Ceylon ironwood, Indian rose chestnut, Cobra’s saffron, and nāgakesara. The flowers are large and fragrant, with four white petals and a yellow center.

## irreversibility
*phyir mi ldog pa*, A stage on the bodhisattva path at which the practitioner will never turn back, or be turned back, from progress toward the full awakening of a buddha.

## irreversible
*phyir mi ldog pa*, Skt. *avaivartika*, The term avaivartika should not be confused with anāgamin. While the first is a Mahāyāna term referring to someone “not turning back,” i.e., irreversibly established on the path to full awakening, the other is a term referring to one who will not return to this world again after death but will attain arhatship in one of the highest heavens.

## irreversible eyes
*phyir mi ldog pa’i mig*, Skt. *avivartya­cakṣur*, The thirtieth of the fifty-one meditative stabilities manifested to Sadāprarudita in chapter 73.

## Irreversible Wheel
*phyir mi ldog pa’i ’khor lo*, Skt. *phyir mi ldog pa’i ’khor lo*, A great bodhisattva.

## irreversible wheel of the Dharma
*phyir mi ldog pa’i chos kyi ’khor lo*, Skt. *avaivartika­dharma­cakra*, The fact that the Dharma is not a single dogma, law, or fixed system, but instead an adaptable body of techniques available for any living being to aid in his development and liberation is emphasized by this metaphor. This wheel is said to turn by the current of energy from the needs and wishes of living beings, and its turning automatically converts negative energies (e.g., desire, hatred, and ignorance) to positive ones (e.g., detachment, love, and wisdom).

## irreversibly established on the path to buddhahood
*phyir mi ldog pa*, Skt. *avaivartika*, The term avaivartika should not be confused with anāgamin. While the first is a Mahāyāna term referring to someone “not turning back,” i.e., irreversibly established on the path to full awakening, the other is a Hīnayāna term referring to an arhat of the third level who will not return to this world again.

## Island of Begburchepa
*gling begs bur chad pa*, Skt. *gling begs bur chad pa*, An island in or near the kingdom of Kaliṅga. “Begburchepa” is a phonetic rendering of the Tibetan, which has no known Skt. equivalent and is unclear in meaning.

## Isle of Jewels
*rin po che’i gling*, Skt. *rin po che’i gling*, A mountain in the sea far beyond Jambudvīpa

## Isolated Highlands
*’brog tu rnam par chad pa*, Skt. *’brog tu rnam par chad pa*, A city in Videha.

## isolation
*dben pa*, Skt. *viveka*, This may refer to either literal, bodily isolation, i.e., seclusion, or to the isolation of the mind from certain (usually undesirable) mental factors. The two senses are related, and as the relationship between the two senses is both implicitly and explicitly thematized in Buddhist texts, a single translation for both the more “outer” and the more “inner” forms of isolation is here meant to respect a clearly intended suggestion found throughout Buddhist literature. The term can also refer to conceptual isolation, i.e., discernment.

## itivṛttaka
*’di lta bu ’das pa*, Skt. *itivṛttaka*, As one of the twelve aspects of the Dharma, it means accounts of the lives of past buddhas and bodhisattvas. See also “twelve wheels of the Dharma.”

## Śiśu
*byis pa*, Skt. *śiśu*, Could be one of Vākāṭaka kings.

*mda’ thogs*, Skt. *iṣudhara*, The son of Daṇḍadhara (more commonly Daṇḍapāṇi) and brother of Yaśodharā and Venerable Aniruddha. His name in Tibetan, mda’ thogs, is rendered here with the potential back-translation Iṣudhara .

*shi shu mA ra*, Skt. *śiśumāra*, A sea monster; lit. “the child-killer,” the Gangetic porpoise or dolphin (Monier-Williams).

## Śiva
One the primary brahmanical gods. Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra notes that the deity Śiva, presumably in his form as Mahākāla, acts as a protector of the Buddhist teachings.

## Śiva Mahādeva
*grong khyer sum brtsegs dgra bo*, Skt. *tripurāri*, A Hindu deity.

*zhi ba bzang po*, Skt. *śivabhadra*, A yakṣa general.

## Ṛṣivadana
A place in the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva) outside Vārāṇasī where the Buddha Śākyamuni first turned the wheel of Dharma. The name, meaning “speech of ṛṣis (sages or seers),” may refer to a story that in this same place during the time of the previous buddha, Kāśyapa, five hundred seers (in some versions pratyekabuddhas) uttered prophecies and attained nirvāṇa on hearing that the Buddha Śākyamuni was to come. Also known as Ṛṣipatana.

## Śivadūtī
*pho nya mo zhi ba*, Skt. *śivadūtī*, One of the kṛtī (or kṛti) spirits.

## śivaliṅga
*rtags*, Skt. *śivaliṅga*, A physical representation of god Śiva in the form of his penis planted in a circular base representing the vagina.

## Śivapurādhāna
*zhi ba’i grong len*, Skt. *śivapurādhāna*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Śivarāgra
*zhi ’dzin mchog*, Skt. *śivarāgra*, A brahmin, the kalyāṇamitra of chapter 52.

## Śivasudaṃṣṭra
*zhi ba dang mche bzang*, Skt. *śivasudaṃṣṭra*, This could be an extended name of Sudaṃṣṭra, the son of Kṛṣṇa.

## ivory tree
*cang skyer*, Skt. *kuṭaja*, Holarrhena pubescens.

## Jé
A clan or tribe in Tibet. According to the Catalog, one of the eighteen tribes of Nguchen Gyalmo, belonging to the divine lineage of Go.

## Jaṭā
*ral pa ma*, Skt. *jaṭā*, One of the female śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Jaṃbu Forest
*’jam bu’i tshal*, Skt. *’jam bu’i tshal*, A peak on Sumeru.

## Jackal
*wa*, Skt. *wa*, Jackal (a wild dog-like animal), also the nickname of the child of wealthy householders in Śrāvasti, so called because of his penchant for eating excrement and drinking urine. After taking instruction from the philosophical extremist Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who admired his ostenisible austerities, he heard the Dharma from the Buddha, went forth, and manifested arhatship.

## jackfruit
Artocarpus heterophyllus. The jackfruit tree.

*dza gad+dA la*, Skt. *jagaddala*, An important Buddhist monastery located in Bengal (modern day Bangladesh), founded by King Rāmapāla (ruled 1077–1120 ce).

## Jagadmati

## Jagadraśmi

## Jagadīśvara
*’gro ba’i dbang phyug*, Skt. *jagadīśvara*, The 928th buddha in the first list, 927th in the second list, and 918th in the third list.

*’gro ba ma*, Skt. *jaṅgamā*, A great rākṣasī.

## Jaga­mantra­sāgara
*’gro skad rgya mtsho*, Skt. *jaga­mantra­sāgara*, The hundred-and-third buddha in a kalpa in the distant past.

*gro ba ’dzin*, Skt. *jagatīdhara*, A kṣatriya.

## Jagatīṃdhara
*’gro ba ’dzin*, Skt. *jagatīṃdhara*, Name of a bodhisattva.

## Jagatindhara
*’gro ba ’dzin*, Skt. *jagatindhara*, A bodhisattva layman of Vaiśālī, who is saved by Vimalakīrti from being fooled by Māra posing as Indra. This bodhisattva is mentioned in Mvy, No. 728, and in the Rāṣṭra­pāla­paripṛccha (Toh 62, in the Ratnakūṭa; see Lamotte, p. 204, n. 120 and Vienna Buddhist Studies Translation Group, trans., The Questions of Rāṣṭrapāla, ).

## Jagatīndhara
*’gro ba ’dzin*, Skt. *jagatīndhara*, Literally “Bearer of the World.” A great bodhisattva present at this discourse.

## Jagatpūjita
*gros mchod*, Skt. *jagatpūjita*, The 640th buddha in the first list, 639th in the second list, and not listed in the third list.

## Jagatpālinī
*’gro ba bskyong ma*, Skt. *jagatpālinī*, ‟Protectress of the World,” one of the eight great bhūtinīs.

## Jagattoṣaṇa
*skye bo dga’ mdzad*, Skt. *jagattoṣaṇa*, The 830th buddha in the first list, 829th in the second list, and 819th in the third list.

## jaggery
*bur mar*, Skt. *guḍa*, The “lump” (guḍa) of solidified molasses that is made with the juice of sugar cane.

## Jaṅghā
*byin pa can*, Skt. *jaṅghā*, A short form of Jaṅghākāśyapa, a disciple of the Buddha.

## Jaṅghā Kāśyapa
*byin pa ’od srung*, Skt. *jaṅghā kāśyapa*, Close Śravaka disciple of the Buddha.

## Jaṅghākāśyapa
*’dzang ga ka shas*, Skt. *jaṅghākāśyapa*, The identity of this person is unknown. In Benares he offered a meal to a pratyekabuddha, but only after the appropriate mealtime had passed; due to that, when he became a noble person himself, he arrived too late to obtain any food during the morning alms round.

## Jahnu
*rgyal byed*, Skt. *jahnu*, A rishi of ancient India, who was said to have swallowed the Ganges when it first appeared, and then on being supplicated allowed it to come out of his ear.

## Jaṭiṃdhara
*ral pa ’dzin*, Skt. *jaṭiṃdhara*, A head merchant and physician in the distant past. (Toh 555: Jaladhara; chu ’dzin)

## Jaimini
*’dza’ man*, Skt. *jaimini*, A rishi who was a pupil of Vyāsa, the first master of the Sāmaveda and the source of the Mīmāṃsā tradition.

## Jain
*gcer bu pa*, Skt. *nirgrantha*, In Buddhist texts, a term often used to refer to the community around the Jain teacher Jñātiputra, but can refer to the Jain tradition generally. Their practices, as presented in Buddhist literature, focused on intense asceticism as a means to mitigate the consequences of past actions and on nonaction as a means to prevent future ramifications.

## Jakra
Jakra is a location near present day Degé, Kham, associated with Jakra monastery, which was converted from the Drigung school to the Sakya school in the thirteenth century. Formerly a residence of the kings of Ling, it became the summer palace of the Degé royalty some generations prior to the time of Tenpa Tsering.

## Jalabhuja
*chu la spyod*, Skt. *jalabhuja*, The third of the five young brahmin attendants of the brahmin Samudrareṇu. The Buddha Ratnagarbha prophesies that he will be the Buddha Sārthavādi, the 1,002nd of the 1,005 buddhas in the Bhadraka eon.

## Jalacara
*chu na spyod pa*, Skt. *jalacara*, Name of a yakṣa.

## jalacaraḍivva
An unidentified ritual ingredient.

## Jaladhara
*chu ’dzin*, Skt. *jaladhara*, A head merchant and physician in the distant past.

## Jalaṃdhara
*chu ’dzin*, Skt. *jalaṃdhara*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Jala­dhara­garjita­ghoṣa­susvarana­kṣatra­rāja­saṃkusumitābhi­jña­
*’brug sgra sbyangs snyan skar ma’i rgyal po me tog kun tu rgyas pa*, Skt. *jala­dhara­garjita­ghoṣa­susvarana­kṣatra­rāja­saṃkusumitābhi­jña­*, A buddha in the distant past. Also the name of a prince in the distant past.

## Jalagarbha
*chu’i snying po*, Skt. *jalagarbha*, The younger son of Jalavāhana and Jalāmbuja­garbhā.

## Jalandhar
*chu ’dzin*, Skt. *jaladhara*, An ancient city in northern India, possibly the present-day Jalandhar in the Punjab region. Here it is identified as the region in which the dwelling place of bodhisattvas called Teaching with Hands Folded་is located.

## Jalataraṅga
*chu rlabs*, Skt. *jalataraṅga*, A future buddha.

## Jalavāhana
*chu ’bebs*, Skt. *jalavāhana*, A learned physician in the distant past and son of Jaṭiṃdhara who, as a result of performing Dharma recitations while standing in a lake, ensured the rebirth of ten thousand fish into the paradise of Trāyastriṃśa. He was the Buddha in a previous life.

## Jalendrā
*chu dbang*, Skt. *jalendrā*, A deity in Ekajaṭā’s maṇḍala.

## Jalendra
*chu dbang*, Skt. *jalendra*, This seems to be another name for Jambhala.

## Jalāgamā
*chu skyes*, Skt. *jalāgamā*, The name of the river in this story, which means “Arriving Water.”

## Jalūkā
*srin bu pad pa*, Skt. *jalūkā*, A forest.

## Jalāmbara
*chu’i gos*, Skt. *jalāmbara*, The elder son of Jalavāhana and Jalāmbuja­garbhā.

## Jalāmbujagarbhā
*chu’i pad ma’i mdzod*, Skt. *jalāmbujagarbhā*, The wife of Jalavāhana.

## Jalāmbuja­garbhā
*chu’i pad ma’i snying po*, Skt. *jalāmbujagarbhā*, The wife of Jalavāhana.

## Jalānantaścara
*chu nang spyod*, Skt. *jalānantaścara*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## jalu root
The exact identity of this plant remains unclear, but it is possible that this is a shortened form for lajjālu, or the sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica), also known as touch-me-not.

## Jamadagni
*’dza’ mag ni*, Skt. *jamadagni*, One of the seven great rishis of ancient India. Also known as the father of Paraśurāma, the sixth incarnation of Viṣṇu.

## Jambū
*’dzam bu*, Skt. *jambū*, Legendary river carrying the golden fruit fallen from the legendary jambu (“rose apple”) tree.

## Jambū River
*’dzam bu’i chu klung*, Skt. *jambūnada*, The rivers that flow down from the immense lake at the foot of the legendary Jambu tree, including the Ganges. The fruits of that tree are made of gold and are carried down by the rivers through Jambudvīpa. Such gold is considered the best kind.

## Jambū river gold
*’dzam bu’i gser*, Skt. *jāmbū­nada­suvarṇa*, A particularly fine type of gold deposited in the Jambū river, sometimes said to be remains of the fruits from the rose-apple trees growing there which fall into the river and are consumed.

## Jambūcchāya
*’dzam bu’i grib ma*, Skt. *jambūcchāya*, The name that the Buddha Ratnagarbha prophesies will be that of one of his eighty brothers (the eighth) when he becomes a buddha.

## Jambūdvīpa
*’dzam bu gling*, Skt. *jambūdvīpa*, The continent (dvīpa) on which we live which, according to ancient South-Asian cosmology, is shaped like a jambū fruit (probably Syzygium cumini, the jambolan, Malabar plum, or Java plum; or possibly S. amarangense, the Java apple, rose-apple, or wax jambu).

## Jambha
*’dzam bha*, Skt. *jambha*, An asura.

## Jambhaka
*rmugs byed*, Skt. *jambhaka*, A name of a spirit or class of spirits; variously identified as a type of demon that lives in magical weapons or that causes illness.

## Jambhalā
*dzam+b+ha la*, Skt. *jambhalā*, A deity in Ekajaṭā’s maṇḍala.

## Jambhala
*gnod ’dzin*, Skt. *jambhala*, A yakṣa king associated with wealth and often identified with Kubera/Vaiśravaṇa.

## Jambhala, the Lord of Waters
*dzam bha la chu dbang*, Skt. *jambhalajalendra*, This seems to be another name of Jambhala.

## Jambhanī
*dzam+b+ha ni*, Skt. *jambhanī*, A goddess invoked to crush wayward beings.

## Jambūnada
*’dzam bu’i chu klung*, Skt. *jambūnada*, The name of an eastern buddha realm.

## Jambūprabha
*’dzam bu’i ’od*, Skt. *jambūprabha*, A southern buddha realm that the Buddha Śākyamuni sees.

## Jambu
*’dzam bu*, Skt. *jambu*, Legendary river carrying the golden fruit fallen from the legendary jambu (“rose apple”) tree. This term is used as an adjective for the gold found in rivers.

## Jambu continent
*’dzam bu’i gling*, Skt. *jambudvīpa*, The southern continent according to Buddhist cosmology, where humans live.

## Jambu Golden Victory Banner Golden Appearance
*’dzam bu gser gyi rgyal mtshan gser du snang ba*, Skt. *Jambu­suvarṇa­dhvaja­kanaka­prabha*, A tathāgata. (Toh 555: gser tog ’od)

## Jambu Golden Victory Banner That is Golden in Appearance
*’dzam bu gser gyi rgyal mtshan gser du snang ba*, A tathāgata. (Toh 555: Suvarṇaketuprabha; gser tog ’od)

## Jambu Movement
*’dzam bu ’gro*, Skt. *’dzam bu ’gro*, Son of the buddha Gandheśvara.

## Jambu River
*’dzam bu chu klung*, Skt. *jāmbūnada*, The Sanskrit here literally means “from the Jambu River,” and in this text it describes the gold (Skt. suvarṇa, Tib. gser) of this mythical river. The river was said to carry the golden fruit fallen from the legendary jambu tree after which the southern continent is named.

## Jambu river gold
*’dzam bu chu bo’i gser*, Skt. *jāmbu­nada­suvarṇa*, The remains of the golden fruit fallen from the legendary jambu tree and carried away by this divine river. It is considered to be a particularly fine type of gold.

## Jambudhvaja
*’dzam bu rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *jambudhvaja*, An alternative name for Jambudvīpa (“Rose-Apple Continent”), which means “Rose-Apple Banner.”

## Jambudvīpa
*'dzam bu gling*, the southern continent, one of the four main "continents" in ancient Indian cosmology, the one in which we live. In some contexts this name refers to South Asia, and in others to the world in a general sense.

## Jambu­dvīpa
*’dzam bu gling*, Skt. *jambu­dvīpa*, The name of the southern continent in Buddhist cosmology, signifying either the known human world, or sometimes more specifically the Indian subcontinent. The name comes from the jambu (“rose apple” or “black plum”) tree said to grow near Lake Anavatapta in the continent’s northern mountains, considered to be the source of the four great rivers of India.

## Jambudvīpa Garland
*’dzam bu’i gling gi phreng ba*, Skt. *’dzam bu’i gling gi phreng ba*, An island to the north of Jambudvīpa.

## Jambudvīpa years
*’dzam bu’i gling gi tshe lo’i grangs*, Skt. *’dzam bu’i gling gi tshe lo’i grangs*, The length of a year as experienced by a sentient being born on Jambudvīpa in the desire realm.

## jambul tree
*’dzam bu’i shing*, Skt. *jambāvṛkṣa*, Syzygium cumini. At present mainly called the jambul tree, it is the Indian version among the various species of rose apple trees.

## Jambūvana
*’dzam bu’i tshal*, Skt. *jambūvana*, “Rose-Apple Tree Park.” The name of the park in which the Buddha Ratnagarbha teaches King Araṇemin and his family and subjects.

## Jamgak Pakṣi
Also known as Chim Jampaiyang (mchims ’jam pa’i dbyangs). A student of Chomden Rikpai Raldri who served as preceptor at the court of the Yuan emperor Buyantu Khan (known in Chinese as Renzong, r. 1311–20). He provided material assistance for the compilation of the Old Narthang manuscript Kangyur.

## Jamgön Kongtrul Lodrö Thayé
1813–1899. A well-known and prolific Tibetan master who promoted a non-sectarian (ris med) approach to Buddhist study and practice.

## Jamgön Kongtrul (the Great), Lodrö Thayé
*jam mgon kong sprul blo gros mtha' yas* (1813 - 1899) was a great teacher of the non-sectarian movement and was responsible, with Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo, for compiling several great collections of teachings and practices from all traditions, including the *Treasury of Rediscovered Teachings* (*rin chen gter mdzod*).

## Jampa Phuntsok
Jampa Phuntsok (late sixteenth century) was one of the sons of the sixth Degé king. He greatly expanded the Degé kingdom’s territory by incorporating neighboring regions and is credited with founding Lhundrup Teng.

## Jampaiyang
A monk who compiled the catalog that would come to be known as the Narthang Kangyur

## jamun
Eugenia jambolana, also known as Java plum, black plum, and jambolan.

## Jamyang Gawai Lodrö
The secretary to the Degé king, Tenpa Tsering.

## Jamyang Loter Wangpo
1847-1914. A master of the Sakya tradition.

## Janaka
*skyed pa po*, Skt. *janaka*, A virtuous nāga king who was a bodhisattva.

## Jana­pada­kalyāṇī
*yul gyi bzang mo*, Skt. *jana­pada­kalyāṇī*, Name of a princess in a story the Buddha tells.

## Janasthāna
The name of a region in central India, situated in the basin of the Godāvarī River in the present-day state of Mahārāṣṭra.

## Janendra
*skye dbang*, Skt. *janendra*, The 311th buddha in the first list, 310th in the second list, and 305th in the third list.

## Janendrarāja
*skye dbang rgyal po*, Skt. *janendrarāja*, The 975th buddha in the first list, 974th in the second list, and 965th in the third list.

## Jang
A historical kingdom in the southeast of Tibet, in the present-day Chinese province of Yunnan. Also known as Jang Satham (’jang sa tham), Naxi, or Lijiang.

## Jangchub O
*byang chub ’od*, Skt. *(not in the skt. source of the mmk)*, The nephew of Lha Lama Yeshe O, a king of the Yarlung imperial Tibetan line who ruled in the Western Tibetan kingdom of Gugé. Jangchub O is famously remembered for inviting the Indian teacher Atiśa to come to Tibet on his uncle’s orders. He was likely born in the early 11th century.

## Jangsho
*jang sho*, Skt. *jang sho*, A senior minister at the court of the Chinese king Cayang.

## Janmacitra
*skye ba sna tshogs pa*, Skt. *janmacitra*, A nāga.

## Janārdana
*skye bo ’tshe*, Skt. *janārdana*, A nāga king.

## jantupiśācī
The juice or sap (rasa) of this substance appears as an ingredient in the preparation of a collyrium for attaining invisibility in Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra. The precise identity of this substance is not clear.

## Jaṭāpura
*ral pa can grong*, Skt. *jaṭāpura*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## jar
*gdos bu*, Skt. *ghaṭikā*, The Sanskrit term ghaṭikā, has two meanings, “water-jar, bucket” and “small stick.” For full details see .

## Jarjaramukhī
*rgan mo gdong*, Skt. *jarjaramukhī*, ‟One with an Aged Face,” one of the eight demonesses who inhabit the eight great charnel grounds.

## Jarāyana
*rga ba ’byung*, Skt. *jarāyana*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Jasmine
*sna ma’i me tog*, Skt. *sumanā*, Jasmine (a fragrant white flowering plant), also a child of householders in Śrāvastī, eventually ordained. At the time of his entrance into the womb and again upon his birth a rain of jasmine flowers fell. He went on to attain arhatship and various spiritual qualities from the cause of having scattered loose jasmine petals over, and having made offerings and prayers to reliquary stūpas in a previous life.

*sna ma’i me tog*, Skt. *sna ma’i me tog*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Viṣāṇin.

*mkhris nad*, Skt. *pittadoṣa*, Symptom that may be evidence of an illness considered an impediment to ordination.

*shugs kyi mu khyud*, Skt. *javanemin*, One of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin.

## Jayā

The twenty-eighth in the sixty-year cycle of Vedic astrology. The name literally translates as “victory.”

## Jayadatta

*rgyal ba’i blo gros*, Skt. *jaya­mati*, A great bodhisattva.

*ka ta ya na rgyal ba’i bzhin can ma*, Skt. *jaya­mukha­kātyāyanī*, ‟Kātyāyanī Face of Victory,” one of the eight kātyāyanī spirits.

*rgyal bas dgyes*, Skt. *jayanandin*, The 348th buddha in the first list, 347th in the second list, and 342nd in the third list.

*rgyal*, Skt. *jayantī*, One of the eight goddesses in the east, called upon to grant protection.

## Jayaprabhā
*rgyal ba’i ’od*, Skt. *jayaprabhā*, King Śrīsena’s wife.

## Jayaprabha
*rgyal ba’i ’od*, Skt. *jayaprabha*, Presumably a member of the royal dynasty in Kaliṅgavana. He is said to have donated the parkland that Bhikṣuṇī Siṃha­vijṛmbhitā dwells in. Also the name of a king in another world realm in the distant past.

## Jayaprabhurāja
*rgyal ba’i rje dpon*, Skt. *jayaprabhu*, A king; the context suggests that he is a king of the nāgas or the asuras.

An unidentified ingredient used in ritual and alchemical applications

Eighth- to ninth-century Tibetan translator.

## Jayasaṃkhya
*rgyal ba’i grangs*, Skt. *jayasaṃkhya*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

*rgyal ba’i sde*, Skt. *jayasena*, Name of a past king, a former incarnation of the Buddha while he was a practicing bodhisattva.

*mtshon mgar rgyal sde*, Skt. *mtshon mgar rgyal sde*, Name of a former incarnation of the Buddha while he was a practicing bodhisattva.

## Jayavaiśraya
*rgyal ba’i gnas rab*, Skt. *jayavaiśraya*, The name of an eastern buddha realm.

## Jayavatī
*rgyal ldan ma*, Skt. *jayavatī*, One of the female śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Jayendra
*rgyal ba’i dbang po*, Skt. *jayendra*, Lit. “Victorious Indra.” A buddha in a world system called Jayā, in the northern direction.

## Jayoṣṇīṣa
*rgyal ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *jayoṣṇīṣa*, One of the eight uṣṇīṣa kings.

*rgyal ba’i drod kyi skye mched*, Skt. *jayoṣmāyatana*, A brahmin, the kalyāṇamitra of chapter 12.

## Jayottama
*rgyal ba dam pa*, Skt. *jayottama*, A head merchant who is the kalyāṇamitra of chapter 26.

## Jayāvatī
*rgyal ba can*, Skt. *jayāvatī*, A realm to the west of the Buddha Ratnagarbha’s realm in which resides the Buddha Jitendriya­viśāla­netra.

## jealousy
*phrag dog*, Skt. *īrṣyā*, The mental state of jealousy, īrṣyā is sometimes translated as “envy.” It is classified as one of the twenty subsidiary afflictions (upakleśa).

## Jeṣṭhā
*snron*, Skt. *jeṣṭhā*, A constellation in the west, personified as a semidivine being. Here called upon for protection.

## Jeta
*dze ta*, Skt. *jeta*, A short form of Jetavana, a park in Śrāvastī, the capital of Kosala, which had been owned by Prince Jeta. Anāthapiṇḍada bought it from him at a high price in order to offer it to the Buddha as a place to house the monks during the monsoon period, thus creating the first Buddhist monastery. See also “Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.”

## Jeta Grove
*rgyal bu rgyal byed kyi tshal*, Skt. *jetavana*, A name of one of the first Buddhist monasteries, which is located outside of Śrāvastī. The monastery is also known as Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Anāthapiṇḍada, a merchant and benefator of the Buddha, bought the land from Prince Jeta and donated it to the saṅgha. It is said that both names are mentioned to acknowledge their mutual efforts in building the monastery. It was there that the Buddha spent several rainy seasons and gave discourses there that were later recorded as sūtras.

## Jetadhvaja
*dze ta’i rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *jetadhvaja*, An alternative name for Jetavana Park in Śrāvastī, the capital of Kosala, which had been owned by Prince Jeta. Anāthapiṇḍada bought it from him at a high price in order to offer it to the Buddha as a place to house the monks during the monsoon period, thus creating the first Buddhist monastery. See also “Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.”

## Jeta’s Grove
*rgyal byed kyi tshal*, Skt. *jetavana*, See “Prince Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.”

## Jetavana
*rgyal byed kyi tshal*, Skt. *jetavana*, See "[Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park](#jetavana-anāthapiṇḍadas-park)."

## Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park
*rgyal rgyal byed kyi tshal mgon med zas sbyin gyi kun dga' ra ba*, Skt. *jetavanam anāthapiṇḍadasyārāmaḥ*, One of the first Buddhist monasteries, located in a [park](#park) outside [Śrāvastī](#śrāvastī), the capital of the ancient kingdom of Kośala in northern India. This [park](#park) was originally owned by Prince Jeta, hence the name [Jetavana](#jetavana), meaning Jeta's grove. The wealthy merchant Anāthapiṇḍada, wishing to offer it to the [Buddha](#buddha), sought to buy it from him, but the prince, not wishing to sell, said he would only do so if Anāthapiṇḍada covered the entire property with gold [coin](#coin)s. Anāthapiṇḍada agreed, and managed to cover all of the [park](#park) except the entrance, hence the name Anāthapiṇḍadasyārāmaḥ, meaning Anāthapiṇḍada's [park](#park). The place is usually referred to in the [sūtra](#sūtra)s as "Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada's park," and according to the Saṃghabhedavastu the [Buddha](#buddha) used Prince Jeta's name in first place because that was Prince Jeta's own unspoken wish while Anāthapiṇḍada was offering the [park](#park). Inspired by the occasion and the [Buddha](#buddha)'s use of his name, Prince Jeta then offered the rest of the property and had an entrance gate built. The [Buddha](#buddha) specifically instructed those who recite the [sūtra](#sūtra)s to use Prince Jeta's name in first place to commemorate the mutual effort of both benefactors. Anāthapiṇḍada built residences for the monks, to house them during the monsoon season, thus creating the first Buddhist monastery. It was one of the [Buddha](#buddha)'s main residences, where he spent around nineteen rainy season retreats, and it was therefore the setting for many of the [Buddha](#buddha)'s discourses and events. According to the travel accounts of Chinese monks, it was still in use as a Buddhist monastery in the early fifth century ᴄᴇ, but by the sixth century it had been reduced to ruins.

## Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park
*rgyal rgyal byed kyi tshal mgon med zas sbyin gyi kun dga’ ra ba*, Skt. *jetavanam anāthapiṇḍadasyārāmaḥ*, Known also as Jetavana, this was an important early site for the Buddha’s growing community. Anāthapiṇḍada, a wealthy patron of the Buddha, purchased the park, located outside Śrāvasti, at great cost, purportedly covering the ground with gold, and donated it to the saṅgha. It was there that the Buddha spent several rainy seasons and gave discourses there that were later recorded as sūtras. It was also the site for one of the first Buddhist monasteries.

## Jetsun Mila
*rje brtsun mi la* (1040 - 1123), Tibet's great yogī and poet, whose biography and spiritual songs are among the best loved works in Tibetan Buddhism. One of the foremost [disciple](#disciple)s of [Mārpa](#mārpa), he is among the great masters at the origin of the [Kagyupa](#kagyupa) school.

## Jigme Lingpa
*'jigs med gling pa* (1729 - 1798), the master who discovered the Longchen Nyingtik (*klong chen snying thig*), the Heart-essence of the Vast Expanse, the [spiritual treasure](#spiritual-treasure) whose preliminary practices *The Words of My Perfect Teacher* explains. A prodigy who became immensely learned with almost no [study](#study), he aroused his [wisdom](#wisdom) mind in a series of long meditation retreats and received the Heart-essence of the Vast Expanse in a series of visions of [Longchenpa](#longchenpa), the great fourteenth-century [lama](#lama) who was in fact his principal teacher. Having first mastered the teachings himself, he passed them to a few close [disciple](#disciple)s capable of [becoming](#becoming) pure holders of the doctrine, among them [Patrul Rinpoche](#patrul-rinpoche)'s own teacher, Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu. He is considered to be a combined [emanation](#emanation) of [Vimalamitra](#vimalamitra), [King Trisong Detsen](#trisong-detsen) and Gyalse Lharje. [Patrul Rinpoche](#patrul-rinpoche) is often considered to be the [emanation](#emanation) of Jigme Lingpa's speech.

## Jigten Sumgon
"Jigten Sumgon and the Drikung lineage are best known for the set of teachings known as The Five Profound [Path](#path)s of [Mahāmudrā](#mahāmudrā). Some of Jigten Sumgon's sayings were collected by Sherab Jungne into what is known as the Gongchig (Wylie transliteration: dgongs gcig, "the single intention") a profound philosophical compendium that further developed in commentary works written in following generations. Some of Jigten Sumgon's teachings were collected by another [disciple](#disciple) into what is known as The Heart of the [Great Vehicle](#great-vehicle)'s Teachings (theg chen bstan pa'i snying po)." [src](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jigten_Sumg%C3%B6n)

## Jinamitra
*dzi na mi tra*, Skt. *jinamitra*, Jinamitra was invited to Tibet during the reign of King Trisong Detsen (khri srong lde btsan, r. 742–98 ce) and was involved with the translation of nearly two hundred texts, continuing into the reign of King Ralpachen (ral pa can, r. 815–38 ce). He was one of the small group of paṇḍitas responsible for the Mahāvyutpatti Sanskrit–Tibetan dictionary and also author of the Nyāya­bindu­piṇḍārtha (Toh 4233), which is contained in the Tengyur (bstan ’gyur) collection.

## Joden Namkha Lhunsang
Son of the third Degé king, A Nga, and elder brother to the fourth Degé king, Yagyal Pal.

## joint progression
The joint progression of an asterism with the moon, meaning that the moon neither trails behind the asterism nor precedes it.

## joints are elegant
*tshigs mdzes pa*, Skt. *śubha­sandhi­tā*, Sixtieth of the eighty minor marks.

## joints are extended
*tshigs ring ba*, Skt. *dīrgha­sandhi­tā*, Sixty-first of the eighty minor marks.

## joints of their bodies are well articulated
*sku’i tshigs legs par ’brel pa*, Skt. *su­saṃ­baddha­gātra­tā*, Seventieth of the eighty minor marks.

## Jonang Lotsāwa Lodrö Pal
*jo nang lo tsA ba blo gros dpal*, Skt. *jo nang lo tsA ba blo gros dpal*, A great fourteenth century (1299–1354) Jonangpa scholar of Sanskrit and translator, student of Dolpopa, who had earlier studied at Sangphu and Sakya. He is best known for his revised translations, made with Sabzang Mati Paṇchen, of the Kālacakra­tantra and Vimala­prabhā.

## Jowo
*jo bo*, lit. lord. A title often used by Tibetans for the Indian [paṇḍita](#paṇḍita) [Atīśa](#atīśa).

## Jowo and Śākya
*jo shag rnam gnyis*, [Jowo](#jowo) Mikyö Dorje and [Jowo](#jowo) [Śākyamuni](#śākyamuni), two statues of the [Buddha](#buddha) brought to Tibet respectively by the Nepalese and Chinese princesses whom [King Songtsen Gampo](#songtsen-gampo) married in the 7th century.

## Jowo Rinpoche
*jo wo rin po che*, a statue representing [Buddha](#buddha) [Śākyamuni](#śākyamuni) at the age of 12, in the Jokhang [temple](#temple) in Lhasa.

## joy
*dga’ ba*, Skt. *prema*, One of the four practices of spiritual practitioners and one of the four immeasurables (the other three being: loving-kindness or love, compassion, and equanimity.

*dga’ dang grags*, Skt. *dga’ dang grags*, Son of the buddha Vāsanottīrṇa­gati.

*dga’ ’dzin*, Skt. *dga’ ’dzin*, Son of the buddha Arthakīrti.

*thar dga’*, Skt. *thar dga’*, Son of the buddha Ananta­pratibhāna­raśmi.

## Joy of Wisdom
*ye shes dga’*, Skt. *ye shes dga’*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Pūjya.

Joyful (full of joy), also the name of the first of the bodhisattva grounds, here understood as ten in number.

*bde gnas blo gros*, Skt. *bde gnas blo gros*, A king.

## Joyful Garland

## Joyful Gods

*dga’ bas mtho ba’i rgyal po*, A bodhisattva. (Toh 555: ’phags par dga’ ba)

## Joyful King

## Joyful Light

*dga’ ldan ma*, Skt. *dga’ ldan ma*, One of King Inexhaustible Merit’s queens.

## joyous effort
*brtson ’grus*, Skt. *vīrya*, In this sūtra, the tenth of the ten factors that lead to awakening. Often translated as “diligence” or “perseverance,” it involves taking delight in virtue and enthusiasm for engaging in virtuous deeds. It is listed among the five faculties (indriya), eleven virtuous mental factors, and as the fourth of the six perfections of a bodhisattva.

## joyweed
Monier-Williams identifies this as Achyranthes triandra, which is synonymous with sessile joyweed or Alternanthera sessilis.

## jātaka
*skyes pa’i rabs*, Skt. *jātaka*, As one of the twelve aspects of the Dharma, it means accounts of the Buddha’s previous lifetimes. See also “twelve wheels of the Dharma.”

## jātaka tale
One of the genres of Buddhist literature, included as one of both the nine or twelve types. Jātakas are like avadānas and pūrvayogas in that they tell about past lives, but they are sometimes distinguished from the other types of past-life stories in that they typically tell stories about the past lives of the Buddha.

## Ājñātakauṇḍinya
*kun shes kauN+Di n+ya*, Skt. *ājñātakauṇḍinya*, A court priest in the Buddha’s father’s kingdom who predicted the Buddha’s enlightenment, he later became one of the Buddha’s five companions in asceticism. These five renounced the Buddha (then Siddhartha) when he abandoned asceticism, but after his enlightenment they became his disciples. Kauṇḍinya famously was the first to comprehend the Buddha’s teaching, and in that way became the first (after the Buddha) to gain the status of an arhat.

## Ājñāta­kauṇḍinya
*kun shes kau N+Di nya*, Skt. *ājñāta­kauṇḍinya*, One of the monks attending this teaching in Śrāvastī, at Jeta’s Grove. He was one of the five companions who joined Prince Siddhārtha while practicing austerities and attended his first turning of the wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park, after the Buddha’s awakening. As he was the first to understand the teachings on the four truths, he received the name Ājñāta­kauṇḍinya, meaning “Kauṇḍinya who understood.” Also known simply as Kauṇḍinya.

## Jātavedas
*me*, Skt. *jātavedas*, Another name for Agni, the god of fire.

## Jñātiputra

## Jñātiputra, the Nirgrantha
*gnyen gyi bu gcer bu*, Skt. *nirgrantha jñātiputra*, One of the six [tīrthika](#tīrthika) teachers contemporaneous with [Śākyamuni](#śākyamuni). According to some, one and the same with Mahāvira, the last Tīrthaṅkara of the Jains.

The name of a family lineage.

## Jātukarṇa
One of the lineages within the Yajurveda branch of the brahmanical tradition.

## Jātukarṇya

## Ju Mipham Gyatso
*’ju mi pham rgya mtsho*, Skt. *’ju mi pham rgya mtsho*, A famous polymath of the Tibetan Ancient (rnying ma) tradition (1846-1912) whose collected writings fill thirty-three volumes.

*ngan to re*, Skt. *jujjuka*, A brahmin. See also .

## jujube
Ziziphus jujuba or Ziziphus mauritiana. A small deciduous tree or shrub with edible fruits. The leaf of jujube is from three to seven centimeters long and from one to three centimeters wide.

## Jungpo
*'byung po*, a class of malignant spirits.

## junior exemplar

Skt. *bṛhaspati*, See “Bṛhaspati.”

## Jīvaka
A highly skilled healer and personal physician of the Buddha Śākyamuni and King Bimbisāra, he figures into many stories of the Buddha and his disciples and is often, as here, referred to as the “king of physicians” or “king of medicine.”

## Jyotis
A future realized one whose name is attested in the Sanskrit manuscript of this sūtra.

## Jyotiḥsaumya­gandhāvabhāsa­śrī
*skar ’od zhi ba’i spos snang dpal*, Skt. *jyotiḥsaumya­gandhāvabhāsa­śrī*, A tathāgata.

## Jyotis­saumya­gandhāvabhāsa­śrī
*’od kyi zla ba dri snang ba’i dpal*, Skt. *jyotis­saumya­gandhāvabhāsa­śrī*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Jyotivaruṇā
*’od zer chu’i lha*, Skt. *jyotivaruṇā*, The guardian deity of the gate at the Buddha’s monastery near Rājagṛha.

## Jyotīrasa
*skar ma la dga’ ba*, Skt. *jyotīrasa*, A buddha who in accord with his prayers became a buddha in a kaliyuga at the time of the Buddha Ratnagarbha. He is only seven thumbs in size in the realm Aṅguṣṭhā where the beings are the height of a thumb.

## Jyotīrāma
*skar ma la ni dgyes*, Skt. *jyotīrāma*, The 757th buddha in the first list, 756th in the second list, and 746th in the third list.

## Jyotsnā
*zla ’od ma*, Skt. *jyotsnā*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Jyotsna
*zla ba’i ’od*, Skt. *jyotsna*, One of the rāśis.

## Jyotīśvara
*snang ba’i dbang phyug*, Skt. *jyotīśvara*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## Ké
A clan or tribe in Tibet. According to the Catalog, it's one of the eighteen tribes of Nguchen Gyalmo, belonging to the divine lineage of Go.

## Kāśī
*ka shi*, Skt. *kāśī*, The old name for [Vārāṇasī](#vārāṇasī).

## Kāṇā
Skt. *kāṇā*, One of the great yakṣiṇīs.

## Śākī
*rig ldan*, Skt. *śākī*, A brahmin woman who briefly hosts Prince Siddhārtha after he leaves his home.

## Kṛṣṇā Draupadī
*gnag dang stabs myur srid*, Skt. *kṛṣṇā draupadī*, One of the eight goddesses in the west, called upon to grant protection.

## Kṛṣṇa
*nag po*, Skt. *kṛṣṇa*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Ākāśa
*nam mkha’*, Skt. *ākāśa*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Ḍāka
*mkha 'gro*, lit. moving through space, or *dpa' bo*, hero. [Tantric](#tantric) equivalent of [Bodhisattva](#bodhisattva). Male equivalent of [ḍākinī](#ḍākinī).

## Ṛkṣa
*’byor pa*, Skt. *ṛkṣa*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK; one of the grahas.

## kṣaṇa
A measure of time defined as consisting of one hundred twenty tatkṣaṇas. Sixty kṣaṇas make one lava (defined as a thirtieth part of a muhūrta), which means that the duration of one kṣaṇa is 1.6 seconds. In the Abhidharmakośa (III 88), Vasubandhu defines the terms kṣaṇa and tatkṣaṇa inversely, stating that one hundred twenty kṣaṇas make one tatkṣaṇa.

## Kaḍaṅgara
*lhag par brtson*, Skt. *kaḍaṅgara*, A lay brother living in Nādikā.

## Kaṇṭaka
*tsher ma*, Skt. *kaṇṭaka*, One of [Upananda](#upananda)'s two [novice](#novice)s whose homoerotic play led the [Buddha](#buddha) to forbid allowing two [novice](#novice)s to live together.

## kaṭaka
*ka ta ka*, Skt. *kaṭaka*, Strychnos potatorum; clearing nut.

## Kaṭaṅkaṭa
Skt. *kaṭaṅkaṭa*, A yakṣa general.

## kaṭaṅkaṭamālinī
*ka Tang ka Ta’i tshogs can*, Skt. *kaṭaṅkaṭamālinī*, A class of supernatural beings

## kaṇṭakamālinī
*tsher ma ’don pa*, Skt. *kaṇṭakamālinī*, A class of supernatural beings.

## kaṭakamālinī
*re lde ’don pa*, Skt. *kaṭakamālinī*, A class of supernatural beings. Please see concerning the relationship between the Sanskrit and Tibetan terms.

## Kaṇṭakasthala Forest
*gnas tsher ma can gyi nags*, Skt. *kaṇṭakasthala­mṛga­dāva*, A forest in Sunrise in Kosala. See also

## kaṭaḍākinī
*lus mkha’ ’gro ma*, Skt. *kaṭaḍākinī*, A class of supernatural beings.

## Kaṭamorakatiṣya
*ka ta mo ra ka ti sha*, Skt. *kaṭamorakatiṣya*, One of the members of a group of four monks described in the Vinaya as followers of Devadatta that attempted to create a schism in the Buddhist saṅgha.

## Kaṭapūtanā
*lus srul mo*, Skt. *kaṭapūtanā*, One of the great mātṛs.

## kaṭapūtanī
A female kaṭapūtana.

## kaṭapūtana
*lus srul po*, Skt. *kaṭapūtana*, A subgroup of pūtanas, a class of disease-causing spirits associated with cemeteries and dead bodies. The name probably derives from the Skt. pūta, “foul-smelling,” as reflected also in the Tib. srul po. The smell of a kaṭapūtana, as its name suggests, could resemble a corpse (kaṭa). The morbid condition caused by pūtanas comes in various forms, with symptoms such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, skin eruptions, and festering wounds, the latter possibly explaining the association with bad smells.

## kaṭapūtana graha
A type of “possessor,” or demon.

## kaṭavāsinī
*lus chags ma*, Skt. *kaṭavāsinī*, A class of supernatural beings.

## Kṛṣṇabandhu
*nag po’i phyogs*, Skt. *kṛṣṇabandhu*, Lit. “Friend of the Dark.” An epithet of Māra.

## Kacaṅgalā
*ka tsang ga la*, Skt. *kacaṅgalā*, A woman who was the Buddha’s mother in a former life.

## Kacaṅkalā
*ka tsang ka la*, Skt. *kacaṅkalā*, A woman who, because she had previously been the Buddha’s mother for five hundred lifetimes, saw him as her son and ran to embrace him. Then, hearing the Dharma from him, she became ordained and manifested arhatship, and the Buddha declared her foremost among nuns who interpret the sūtras.

## Kacchapī
*rus sbal can*, Skt. *kacchapī*, A river queen.

## kachnar
*a ti muk ta ka*, Skt. *atimuktaka*, Phanera variegata. One of the most beautiful and aromatic of Indian trees, also known as orchid tree, mountain ebony, and camel’s foot tree.

## Kañcika
*kon tsi*, Skt. *kañciku (gilgit ms.)*, Appears to mean “a person from Kañci.” Unidentified. Possibly a description of Pūrna, who is next in the list of the Buddha’s disciples. Alternatively this may be Kaccāna, also known as Kaccāyana, but principally as Katyayāna, one of the Buddha’s ten principal pupils.

## Kadampa
*bka' gdams pa*, the first of the schools of the [New Tradition](#new-tradition), which followed the teachings of [Atīśa](#atīśa). It stressed compassion, [study](#study) and pure discipline. Its teachings were continued by all other schools, in particular the [Gelugpa](#gelugpa), which is also known as the New Kadampa school.

## Kūṭadantī
*so brtsegs*, Skt. *kūṭadantī*, A fierce goddess. (Toh 555: so brtsegs ma)

## Kūṭadantinī
*so brtsegs ma*, Skt. *kūṭadantinī*, A goddess in this sūtra.

## Kūṭadaṃṣṭra
*mche ba gtsigs*, Skt. *kūṭadaṃṣṭra*, A yakṣa general.

## ākāśa­dhātvaparyanta
*nam mkha’i khams mu med pa*, Skt. *ākāśa­dhātvaparyanta*, Lit. “limitless space element.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Kadru
The mother of nāgas. According to the brahmanical tradition, she is one of the daughters of the creator god Dakṣa Prajāpati, who gave her and twelve of her sisters in marriage to the sage Kaśyapa.

## Kaduścara
*mdzes spyod*, Skt. *kaduścara*, A lord of the asuras who prays to be Samudrareṇu’s attendant when he is the Buddha Śākyamuni, i.e., Ānanda.

## Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana
*gnyis ’thung nag po’i bu*, Skt. *kṛṣṇadvaipāyana*, A great ṛṣi.

## Ākāśagarbha
*nam mkha’i snying po*, Skt. *ākāśagarbha*, The titular figure of the present sūtra. An important bodhisattva, his name means “essence of space.” He is one of the “eight close sons of the Buddha.”

## Kṛṣṇagautama
*gau ta ma nag po*, Skt. *kṛṣṇagautama*, One of the sages (ṛṣi).

## Ākāśaghoṣa
*nam mkha’ sgrogs*, Skt. *ākāśaghoṣa*, A Licchavī youth.

## Kagyupa
*bka' brgyud pa* one of the schools of the [New Tradition](#new-tradition), which followed the teachings brought to Tibet from India by [Mārpa](#mārpa) the Translator in the 11th century and transmitted to [Milarepa](#milarepa). There are several branches of the Kagyu school.

## Kaṭha
One of the lineages within the Yajurveda branch of the brahmanical tradition.

## Kaṇṭhaka
*bsngags ldan*, Skt. *kaṇṭhaka*, Prince Siddhārtha’s horse.

## Kaṇṭhamāla
*mgul phreng*, Skt. *kaṇṭhamāla*, King of the “necklaces” (a class of asuras).

## Kaiṭabha
*shes gsal*, Skt. *kaiṭabha*, The study of the prescribed rules for Brahmanical rites. It is one of the subjects a learned brahmin is supposed to have mastered.

## Kaśika cloth
*ka shi ka nas byung ba’i gos*, Skt. *kāśikavastra*, Cotton from Vārāṇasī, the capital of the ancient kingdom of Kashi, renowned as the best.

## Kailāśa
*ti se*, Skt. *kailāśa*, Mount Kailash, often considered the earthly representation of Mount Meru, the central world-axis in numerous South Asian cosmographies. In its role as the center of the cosmos, Mount Kailash is considered to be the dwelling place of numerous Buddhist and non-Buddhist deities including the Hindu god Śiva, the tantric Buddhist god Cakrasaṃvara, Kubera, and others. The mountain is considered sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, and Bönpos.

## Kailāśa Horn
*ti se’i rwa*, Skt. *ti se’i rwa*, A mountain north of Jambudvīpa.

## Kailash
*ti se gangs*, Skt. *kailāsa*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Kailāsa
*ti se’i ri*, Skt. *kailāsa*, Mount Kailash, often considered the earthly representation of Mount Meru, the central world-axis in numerous South Asian cosmographies. In its role as the center of the cosmos, Mount Kailash is considered to be the dwelling place of numerous Buddhist and non-Buddhist deities including the Hindu god Śiva, the tantric Buddhist god Cakrasaṃvara, Kubera, and others. The mountain is considered sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, and Bönpos.

## Kailāsa­śikhara­vāsinī
*ti se yi ni rtse mo na*, Skt. *kailāsa­śikhara­vāsinī*, “Dwelling on the top of Sumeru”; it is not clear whether it refers here to Pārvatī or to one of the Buddhist goddesses.

## Kaṇima
One of the lineages within the Yajurveda branch of the brahmanical tradition.

## Kaineya
*kai ne ya*, Skt. *kaineya*, A clairvoyant sage who lived with five hundred devotees in the forests of the Adumā region and spent time on the banks of Lake Mandākinī. His nephew was the sage Śaila.

## Kaivartaputra
The name of a king.

## Śākaja
*shAkya’i skyes*, Skt. *śākaja*, An ally of King Śrī.

## kañjaru
An unidentified ritual ingredient.

## Ākāśa­jñānārtha­pradīpa
*nam mkha’i ye shes don gyi sgron ma*, Skt. *ākāśa­jñānārtha­pradīpa*, A buddha in the distant past.

## kakali
An unidentified ritual substance.

## kakkola
*ka k+ko la*, Skt. *kakkola*, A code word for the female genital organ. Taken literally, refers to an aromatic plant and the perfume made from it.

## Kakuda Kātyāyana
*ka tyA'i bu nog can*, Skt. *kakuda kātyāyana*, One of the six [tīrthika](#tīrthika) teachers contemporaneous with [Śākyamuni](#śākyamuni). Also rendered here as "Kakuda, a descendant of [Kātyāyana](#kātyāyana)."

## Kakutsunda
*’khor ba ’jig*, Skt. *kakutsunda*, One of the tathāgatas.

## kalā
A measure of time defined as consisting of sixteen kāṣṭhās. Thirty kalās make one nāḍikā, which means that the duration of one kalā is forty-eight seconds.

## Kalaśī
*bum pa can*, Skt. *kalaśī*, A great rākṣasī.

## Śākala
One of the lineages within the Ṛgveda branch of the brahmanical tradition.

## Kalaśa
*gA dA hA ya hi*, Skt. *kalaśa*, Unidentified.

## Kalahapriya
*’thab dga’ ba*, Skt. *kalahapriya*, A yakṣa general.

## kalala
*mer mer po*, Skt. *kalala*, The embryo in the first week of gestation.

## kalandaka bird
*bya ka lan+da ka*, Skt. *kalandaka*, A type of bird.

## Kalandaka Forest
*ka lan da ka*, Skt. *kalandaka*, A grove or forest within the Veṇuvana near Rājagṛha, where Buddha Śākyamuni spent several monsoon retreats and delivered many Great Vehicle teachings. In other texts it is known as the Kalandakanivāsa or °nivāpa, the dwelling place or feeding ground of kalandaka—crows or other birds according to Tibetan renderings, but some Sanskrit and Pali sources suggest flying squirrels.

## Kalandakanivāpa
*ka lan da ka'i gnas*, Skt. *kalandakanivāpa*, A place where the [Buddha](#buddha) often resided, within the [Bamboo Park](#bamboo-park) (Veṇuvana) outside Rajagṛha that had been donated to him. The name is said to have arisen when, one day, King [Bimbisāra](#bimbisāra) fell asleep after a romantic liaison in the [Bamboo Park](#bamboo-park). While the king rested, his [consort](#consort) wandered off. A snake (the reincarnation of the [park](#park)'s previous owner, who still resented the king's acquisition of the [park](#park)) approached with malign intentions. Through the king's tremendous [merit](#merit), a gathering of kalandaka‍—crows or other birds according to Tibetan renderings, but some Sanskrit and Pali sources suggest flying squirrels‍—miraculously appeared and began squawking. Their clamor alerted the king's [consort](#consort) to the danger, who rushed back and hacked the snake to pieces, thereby saving the king's life. King [Bimbisāra](#bimbisāra) then named the spot Kalandakanivāpa ("Kalandakas' Feeding Ground"), sometimes (though not in the Vinayavastu) given as Kalandakanivāpa ("Kalandakas' Abode") in their honor. The story is told in the Saṅghabhedavastu (Toh 1, ch.17, Degé Kangyur vol.4, folio 77.b et seq.).

## Kalandaka­nivāpa
*bya ka lan da ka’i gnas pa*, Skt. *kalandaka­nivāpa*, Literally, “The Squirrel Feeding Ground.” A location within the Veṇuvana where the Buddha stayed. The place received its name from the many squirrels living there, being fed by humans. It should be noted that Tibetan translations misunderstand the Sanskrit term kalandaka to be a kind of bird (Tib. bya).

## Kalanda­kanivāpa
*bya ka lan da ka gnas*, Skt. *kalanda­kanivāpa*, Literally, “The Squirrel Feeding Ground.” A location within the Veṇuvana where the Buddha stayed. The place was given its name by King Bimbisāra after being saved from being attacked by a snake there by the squawking of many kalandaka—flying squirrels, Sanskrit and Pali sources suggest, but crows or other birds according to the Tibetan rendering.

## Kalandakanivāpa in the Veṇuvana
*’od ma’i tshal bya ka lan da ka gnas pa*, Skt. *veṇuvana kalandakanivāpa*, Kalandaka­nivāpa means “feeding place of the kalandakas,” and kalandaka may refer either to a flying squirrel or to a bird, as explained by differing sources. The Kalandakanivāpa was a place within the bamboo grove near Rājagṛha where the Buddha regularly stayed and gave teachings. It was situated on land donated by King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha and, as such, was the first of several landholdings donated to the Buddhist community during the time of the Buddha.

## Kalandakanivāsa
*bya ka lan da ka gnas pa*, Skt. *kalandakanivāsa*, Literally “the dwelling place of kalandakas.” A location within the Bamboo Grove where the Buddha stayed. The alternative Sanskrit Kalandakanivāpa means “where food offerings are made to kalandakas.” It is said that the place was given its name by King Bimbisāra after he was rescued from a snake attack there. Pali sources suggest he was saved by the squawking of many kalandaka or flying squirrels. In Tibetan translation these were called “kalandaka birds” (bya).

## Kalaśoda
*bum chu can*, Skt. *kalaśoda*, One of the kings of the nāgas.

## Kalaśodarī
*bum lto ma*, Skt. *kalaśodarī*, A great piśācī.

## Kalaśodara
*bum pa’i lto*, Skt. *kalaśodara*, A yakṣa general.

## kalaviṅka
*ka la ping ka*, Skt. *kalaviṅka*, An Indian bird renowned for its beautiful song. There is some uncertainty regarding the identity of the kalaviṅka, as some dictionaries declare it to be a type of Indian cuckoo (probably Eudynamys scolopacea, also known as the asian koel) or a red and green sparrow (possibly Amandava amandava, also known as the red avadavat). Within the Buddhist sūtras, the bird is usually linked to its pleasing or striking voice. In some cases, it has also taken on mythical characteristics, being described as part human, part bird.

## kalaviṅka bird
Skt. *kalaviṅka*, In Buddhist literature refers to a mythical bird with the head of a human and the body of a bird. The kalaviṅka’s call is said to be far more beautiful than that of all other birds and so compelling that it could be heard even before the bird has hatched. The call of the kalaviṅka is also used as an analogy to describe the voice of the Buddha.

## Kale
The name of a king.

## Kali
*ka ling*, Skt. *kali*, An evil king.

## Kaliṅga
The name of a country along the eastern coast of the Indian subcontinent, roughly corresponding to the present-day state of Orissa.

## Kaliṅgarāja
*ka ling ga’i rgyal po*, Skt. *kaliṅgarāja*, A buddha.

## Kaliṅgavana
*ka ling ga’i nags tshal*, Skt. *kaliṅgavana*, A town in South India.

## Kaliyuga
The fourth in a repeating cycle of four eons, in which the lives of beings are short and the world is afflicted by famine, illness, and war. This is our current eon.

## Kalmāṣadamya
*khra bo ’dul*, Skt. *kalmāṣadamya*, A village.

## Kalmāṣapada
*rkang bkra*, Skt. *kalmāṣapada*, The cannibal prince who was born from the rape of king Sudāsa by a ferocious lioness and developed a taste for the flesh of human children. In the story alluded to here, the cannibal prince sets out to imprison one thousand princes to slaughter, but the bodhisattva Prince Candra intervenes and manages to turn the cannibal prince’s mind toward virtue so that he releases all his captives. This version of the story is found in Āryaśūra’s Jātakamālā, Jātaka 31, Toh 4150, folio 118.a.

## Kalmāṣapāda
*rkang bkra po*, Skt. *kalmāṣapāda*, A yakṣa general.

## Kalpa
*bskal pa*. A great kalpa, which corresponds to a cycle of formation and destruction of a universe, is divided into eighty intermediate kalpas. An intermediate kalpa is composed of one small kalpa during which the span of life, etc., increases and one small kalpa during which it decreases.

## Kalyāṇacūḍa
*dge ba’i gtsug*, Skt. *kalyāṇacūḍa*, The 804th buddha in the first list, 803rd in the second list, and not listed in the third list.

## Kalyāṇaka
One of six wicked mendicants in the distant past, during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin.

## kalyāṇamitra
*dge ba’i bshes gnyen*, Skt. *kalyāṇamitra*, The Sanskrit can mean “good friend” or “beneficial friend.” The Tibetan can mean “virtuous friend” or “friend of virtue.” A title for a teacher of the spiritual path.

## Kamala
*pad+ma*, Skt. *kamala*, One of the vidyārājas dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## kaśmala
*sdig pa’i sems dang ldan pa*, Skt. *kaśmala*, A class of impure spirits.

## Kamala­dala­vimala­nakṣatra­rāja­saṃkusumitābhi­jña
*pad ma’i ’dab ma dri ma med pa skar ma’i rgyal po me tog kun tu rgyas pa*, Skt. *kamala­dala­vimala­nakṣatra­rāja­saṃkusumitābhi­jña*, A buddha in a realm far away in the eastern direction.

## Kamala­dala­vimala­nakṣatra­rāja­saṃkusumitā­bhijña
*pad ma’i ’dab ma ltar dri ma med pa rgyu skar rgyal po mngon par shes pa’i me tog shin tu rgyas pa*, Skt. *kamala­dala­vimala­nakṣatra­rāja­saṃkusumitā­bhijña*, One of the bodhisattva great beings.

## Kamalagupta
*ka ma la gub ta*, Skt. *kamalagupta*, An Indian scholar who was involved in a number of translations during the eleventh century in Tibet.

## Kamalaśīla
*ka ma la shI la*, Skt. *kamalaśīla*, Indian Buddhist master (713–763) who came to Tibet in the late 8th century. Said to have been assassinated after a debate with the representatives of Chinese Buddhism. A later legend has him return to India and come back in another body in the eleventh century as the master Padampa Sangye.

## Kamalalocanī
*pad+ma’i mig can ma*, Skt. *kamalalocanī*, ‟Lotus-Eyed One,” one of the eight demonesses who inhabit the eight great charnel grounds.

## Kamalapāṇi
*phyag na pad+ma*, Skt. *kamalapāṇi*, One of the vidyārājas dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Kamalaraśmi
*pad+ma’i ’od*, Skt. *kamalaraśmi*, One of the uṣṇīṣa kings attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Kamalākṣī
*pad+ma’i spyan*, Skt. *kamalākṣī*, The name of a female Buddhist deity, meaning “Lotus-Like Eyes,” here used as an epithet of Sitātapatrā.

## Kamaloṣṇīṣa
*pad+ma’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *kamaloṣṇīṣa*, One of the eight uṣṇīṣa kings.

## Kambalā
*la ba can*, Skt. *kambalā*, Name of a rākṣasī and Dharma protector.

## Kambala
Skt. *kambala*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Kambaleśvara
*snam bu’i dbang phyug*, Skt. *kambaleśvara*, A nāga king. This might be another name for the attested nāga king Upakambala. See Edgerton (1985).

## Kambojī
*g.yo ldan ma*, Skt. *kambojī*, One of the goddesses invited to partake in the oblation offering; one of the four guardian goddesses who can be indicated to a fellow practitioner by her pledge sign.

## Kamboja
*kam bo dza*, Skt. *kamboja*, A land in the north of Jambūdvīpa, included in some Pali texts as one of the sixteen great kingdoms of ancient India at the time of the Buddha. Also attested in early non-Buddhist literature as a land corresponding to part of contemporary Afghanistan. In this text, the term kāmbojikā, “from Kamboja,” is used to describe a group of girls (kanyā).

## Kambudhāra
*dung thogs*, Skt. *kambudhāra*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Kambugrīvā
*dung mgrin ma*, Skt. *kambugrīvā*, A great piśācī.

## kambukāminī
*lus chags ma*, Skt. *kambukāminī*, A class of supernatural beings.

## ākāśamūli
An unidentified ritual ingredient. Possibly a plant of the Pistia genus.

## Kṣamottara
*bde mchog*, Skt. *kṣamottara*, The name of an eastern buddha realm.

## Kampa
*sa ’gul*, Skt. *kampa*, God of earthquakes.

## Kampila
*’ug pa*, Skt. *kampila*, One of the monks attending this teaching in Śrāvastī, at Jeta’s Grove. He was one of the Buddha’s arhat disciples, a former king, renowned as foremost among those who teach monks. This spelling is attested in the present text but in other texts his name is spelled Mahākapphiṇa, Kapphiṇa, Kapphina, Kaphiṇa, Kasphiṇa, Kaṃphina, Kaphilla, or Kaphiṇḍa.

## Kampilya
*g.yo ba ’dzin*, Skt. *kampilya*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Kaśmīra
*kha che’i yul*, Skt. *kaśmīra*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## ākāśamātṛ
*nam mkha’i ma mo*, Skt. *ākāśamātṛ*, “Sky mother”; a class of female spirits.

## Kanaka

*gser gyi lag pa’i dbang*, Skt. *kanakabhujendra*, A son of the king Suvarṇa­bhujendra.

*gser gyi ’od*, Skt. *kanaka­prabhā­svara*, A son of the king Suvarṇabhujendra.

*gser gyi phung po*, Skt. *kanakarāśi*, One of the uṣṇīṣa kings attending the delivery of the MMK.

*gser ltar dri ma med pa’i ’od kyi rgyan*, Skt. *kanaka­vimala­prabhā­vyūha*, A world realm in the eastern direction. Also called Kanaka­vimala­prabhā.

*gser gyi dpung pa’i dbang*, Skt. *kanakendra*, A son of the king Suvarṇabhujendra.

*gser mdog gzi brjid dri ma med pa rnam par dag pa*, Skt. *kanakārciḥ­śuddha­vimala­tejas*, A bodhisattva present in the Buddha’s assembly.

## Kanakāvatī
*gser can*, Skt. *Kanakāvatī*, “Golden One.” The royal capital from which King Kanakavarṇa ruled over the whole of Jambudvīpa in the distant past.

*’gugs byed ma*, Skt. *ākarṣaṇī*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## kṛśara oil
*snying po gsum gyi mar*, Skt. *kṛśara*, The Sanskrit term kṛśara (or kṛsara) refers to a dish made of sesame together with a mixture of rice, peas, and spices. The Tibetan seems to understand this as a type of oil (Tib. mar) and appears to have preserved a corrupted reading that reflects the Sanskrit back-translation *trisara.

## Ākarṣaṇa­dhāriṇī
*’gugs par byed pa’i gzungs ma*, Skt. *ākarṣaṇa­dhāriṇī*, One of the dhāraṇī goddesses present at the delivery of the MMK.

*lo thang spyod*, Skt. *karabhuja*, The first of the five young brahmin attendants of the brahmin Samudrareṇu. The Buddha Ratnagarbha prophesies that he will be the Buddha Dṛḍhasvara, the thousandth of the 1,005 buddhas in the Bhadraka eon.

## karada
*ka ra da*, Skt. *karada*, A bird of a red color whose voice has been described as like thunder or the sound of a drum.

## Karadharavikrama
*sku mchog rnam par gnon*, Skt. *karadharavikrama*, A buddha in a western buddha realm.

*shing ka ra hA Ta*, Skt. *karahāṭa*, Meyna spinosa.

*lag rna*, Skt. *karakarṇī*, A son of King Ikṣuvāku.

The son of Pema Tensung and father of Ngu Chödorwa.

An unidentified ritual ingredient.

## kardoñjana
The identity of this substance is not clear.

## Karṇika

Pterospermum acerifolium. The bayur tree.

*sbal ba*, Skt. *karkaṭaka*, Cancer (zodiac sign and constellation).

*ke ke ru*, Skt. *karketana*, A stone sometimes identified as cat’s eye.

## Karkoṭa
*kak+ko Ta*, Skt. *karkoṭa*, A nāga king.
