*don mdzad gzigs*, Skt. *kṛtārthadarśin*, The 188th buddha in the first list, 187th in the second list, and 187th in the third list.

## Kṛttikā
*smin drug*, Skt. *kṛttikā*, A constellation in the east, personified as a semidivine being. Here called upon for protection.

## Kṛtāvin level
*byas pa rtogs pa can gyi sa*, Skt. *kṛtāvibhūmi*, Lit. “Have Done the Work to Be Done.” The seventh of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the level of an ordinary person until reaching buddhahood. It is equivalent to the level of a worthy one. See “ten levels.”

## kṛtyā
A class of nonhuman being, often female, who are ritually summoned to perform injurious acts against the target of the rite. They are often mentioned together with khākorḍas, who serve a similar function.

## kṛtyā rite
*bsgyur ba’i las*, Skt. *kṛtyākarma*, Rites of hostile magic that employ kṛtyās, a type of supernatural being, as magical agents. Taken literally, the Tibetan term sgyur ba’i las would mean “the karma/activities of transformation.”

## kṛtyā rites
*bsgyur ba’i las*, Skt. *kṛtyākarma*, Rites of hostile magic that employ kṛtyās, a type of supernatural being, as magical agents.

## kṛtya
*gshed byed*, Skt. *kṛtya*, A spirit one can request, by making offerings, to destroy others. Usually female, with this sūtra having the sole instance of a male entity. There are also references to humans who have this power.

## Kātyarṣabha
*brtson pa’i khyu mchog*, Skt. *kātyarṣabha*, A lay brother living in Nādikā.

## kātyāyanī
*ka ta ya na*, Skt. *kātyāyanī*, Usually an epithet of the goddess Durgā, in the Bhūtaḍāmara Tantra this term refers to a class of wild and powerful female spirits.

## Kātyāyana
Indian [Arhat](#arhat) who was a [disciple](#disciple) of the [buddha](#buddha) and wrote down one [section](#section) of the [Abhidharma](#abhidharma).

## Kātyāyana Who Gathers
*’dus pa’i kA tyA ya na*, Skt. *’dus pa’i kA tyA ya na*, See “Kātyāyana.”

## Kātyāyanaputra
*kA tyA ya na’i bu*, Skt. *kātyāyanaputra*, See “Kātyāyana.”

## Kātyāyanīputra
*kA t+yA’i bu*, Skt. *kātyāyanīputra*, See “Kātyāyanī.”

## Kātyāyanīya
The name of a family lineage.

## Kuśa
*ku sha*, Skt. *kuśa*, A prince who was the Buddha in a former life.

## kuśa grass
*ku sha*, Skt. *kuśa*, Desmostachya bipinnata. A type of grass often used for religious ceremonies.

## Kuṇḍalahāriṇī
*rna can ma*, Skt. *kuṇḍalahāriṇī*, One of the eight great bhūtinīs.

## Kuṇḍala­kātyāyanī
*ka ta ya na rna cha can*, Skt. *kuṇḍala­kātyāyanī*, ‟Kātyāyanī with Earrings,” one of the eight kātyāyanī spirits.

## Kuśalaprabha
*dge ba’i ’od*, Skt. *kuśalaprabha*, The 704th buddha in the first list, 703rd in the second list, and 693rd in the third list.

## Kuśalapradīpa
*dge ba’i sgron ma*, Skt. *kuśalapradīpa*, The 858th buddha in the first list, 857th in the second list, and 847th in the third list.

## Kuṇḍalin
*thab sbyor can*, Skt. *kuṇḍalin*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Kuṇapa
*ro myogs*, Skt. *kuṇapa*, “Rotting Corpse,” one of the cold hells.

## Kubala Grove
*ku ba la’i tshal*, Skt. *kubala*, A grove in Promotion

## Kubera
Skt. *kubera*, The king of yakṣas and an important wealth deity, he is also one of the Four Great Kings in Buddhist cosmology. In this capacity he is commonly known as Vaiśravaṇa, the guardian of the northern quarter.

## Kuberakāntā
*ku be ra’i snying du sdug ma*, Skt. *kuberakāntā*, One of the names of Śrī Mahādevī.

## Kublai Khan
Kublai Khan (1215–94) reigned over the Mongol empire from 1260 to 1294 and founded the Yuan dynasty in China. Based on his priest-patron (mchod yon) relationship, he entrusted both political and religious authority over Tibet to the head of the Sakya school of Tibetan Buddhism, Drogön Chögyal Phakpa.

## Kuśāgrapura
*ku sha’i mchog gi grong*, Skt. *kuśāgrapuri*, The one-time capital of ancient Magadha.

## Kuhā
*gya gyu*, Skt. *kuhā*, A river queen.

## Kuṇṭhā
*gtum mo*, Skt. *kuṇṭhā*, A great rākṣasī.

## Kuṣṭha
*mdze*, Skt. *kuṣṭha*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Kuhara
The name of a mountain.

## Kuṭi
*khang khyim can*, Skt. *kuṭi*, The hamlet from which Maitreya comes.

## kuśika
*ku shi kA*, Skt. *kuśika*, A class of vidyādharas.

## Kuśinagarī
*ku sha’i grong khyer*, Skt. *kuśinagarī*, Village in the country of Mallā where the Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa.

## Kuśinagara
*ku shi na*, Skt. *kuśinagara*, The capital of the Malla kingdom, in the vicinity of which the Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa.

## Kuñjara
*glang po che*, Skt. *kuñjara*, One of the rāśis.

## Kuñjaramati
*ba lang mo’i blo gros*, Skt. *kuñjaramati*, ‟Excellent Mind,” the name of a female spirit summoned in a sādhana.

## Kuñjaro
*kuny+dza ro*, Skt. *kuñjaro*, A mountain in the sea south of Jambudvīpa.

## Kuśākṣī
*ku sha lta bu’i mig can*, Skt. *kuśākṣī*, A great rākṣasī.

## Kukkuṭapādaka
*ri bya gag rkang*, Skt. *kukkuṭapādaka*, A mountain.

## Kukkuṭācīra
*kuk+ku TA tsI ra*, Skt. *kukkuṭācīra*, A forest on Forest Garlands.

## Kukkuripa
*ku ku ri pa*, Skt. *kukkuripa*, Counted among the most famous of the Indian Buddhist Mahāsiddhas and renowned for his association with packs of dogs (kukkura), he is a central figure in a number of tantric lineages, specifically of the Guhya­samāja Tantra and Mahā­māyā Tantra. He was active sometime between the eighth and tenth centuries.

## Kukūla
*mas ma me mur*, Skt. *kukūla*, One of the hells.

## kuṇāla
*ku na la*, Skt. *kuṇāla*, Bird with beautiful eyes that lives on Mount Sumeru.

## Kulakā
*ku la kA*, Skt. *kulakā*, A rākṣasī living in Ramayo.

## Kulasundarī
*rigs mdzes ma*, Skt. *kulasundarī*, One of the goddesses associated with Amoghapāśa; also a tantric goddess prominent in the Śrīvidyā tradition.

## Kulatā
*ku lu tA*, Skt. *kulatā*, One of the auxiliary charnel grounds.

## Kuleśvara
*rigs sngags kyi dbang phyug*, Skt. *kuleśvara*, ‟Lord of the Family,” one of the eight bhūta kings.

## Kuliśavatī
*rdo rje ldan ma*, Skt. *kuliśavatī*, One of the great dūtīs attending upon Lord Vajrapāṇi.

## Kuliśika
*rdo rje can*, Skt. *kuliśika*, One of the kings of the nāgas.

## Kulika
*rigs ldan*, Skt. *kulika*, The name of one of the eight nāga kings who obey the eight deities in Gaṇapati’s nine-section maṇḍala.

## Kulikeśvarī
One of the eight yoginīs in the Mahākāla maṇḍala described in Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra.

## kulmāṣa
*zan dron*, Skt. *kulmāṣa*, Sour gruel.

## kuṣmāṇḍa
*grul bum*, Skt. *kuṣmāṇḍa*, Another name for kumbhāṇḍa, a class of nonhuman beings.

## kumbhāṇḍā
A female kumbhāṇḍa.

## kumbhāṇḍī
A female kumbhāṇḍa.

## Kumbha
*bum pa*, Skt. *kumbha*, One of the kings of rākṣasas; Aquarius (the zodiac sign and the constellation); a south Indian king contemporary with Mahendra.

## kumbhāṇḍa
*grul bum*, Skt. *kumbhāṇḍa*, A class of dwarf beings subordinate to Virūḍhaka, one of the Four Great Kings, associated with the southern direction. The name uses a play on the word āṇḍa, which means “egg” but is also a euphemism for a testicle. Thus, they are often depicted as having testicles as big as pots (from khumba, or “pot”).

## Kumbhaka
Skt. *kumbhaka*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Kumbhakarṇa
*bum rna*, Skt. *kumbhakarṇa*, One of the kings of the rākṣasas.

## Kumbhakārī
*rdza byed ma*, Skt. *kumbhakārī*, One of the ten girls who attended upon Prince Siddhārtha while he was practicing austerities.

## Kumbhodara
*bum lto bo*, Skt. *kumbhodara*, A yakṣa general.

## Kumbhīrā
Skt. *kumbhīrā*, The name of a mātṛkā in Great Cool Grove.

## Kumbhīra
*chu srin kun b+hi ra*, Skt. *kumbhīra*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Kumbhīramukha
*chu srin kun b+ha ra’i gdong*, Skt. *kumbhīramukha*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Kumārī
A general term for a young girl or an epithet for the goddess Durgā. Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra refers to a group of kumārīs who can be depicted on a cloth canvas and then worshiped (see “seven kumārīs”).

## kumāra
*gzhon nu*, Skt. *kumāra*, Apart from the usual meaning and usages (such as being a title of Mañjuśrī, etc.), this also seems to be the name of a class of nonhuman beings. The term is rendered elsewhere in this translation as “divine youth.”

## Kumārabhṛta
*gzhon nu’i tshul*, Skt. *kumārabhṛta*, One of the previous incarnations of Māra.

## Kumārabhṛta, the physician
*'tsho byed gzhon nu*, Skt. *jīvaka kumārabhṛta*, Jīvaka is a title meaning "physician." Kumārabhṛta [means](#means) "raised by the prince," in this case Prince Abhaya, who was said to have fostered the future physician. He was personal physician to King [Bimbisāra](#bimbisāra) and the [Buddha](#buddha). He asked that ill persons would not be accepted into the order, for it would prove too great a burden on the king's treasury, which paid for all the treatment he administered, and his own health.

## Kumārajīva
*kumārajīva*, Skt. *kumārajīva*, A Buddhist monk and scholar from the Kingdom of Kucha, who was active in China. One of the greatest translators of Buddhist texts. He lived between 344–413 ce.

## Kumārakalaśa
*ku mA ra ka la sha*, Skt. *kumārakalaśa*, The name of an Indian preceptor and teacher who lived during the early Sarma (gsar ma) period (c. 11th century) and worked on the Tibetan translation of the Mañjuśrī­mūla­tantra.

## Kumārakāśyapa
*gzhon nu ’od srung gi bu*, Skt. *kumārakāśyapa*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Kumāravardhana
*yul gzhon nu bskyed pa*, Skt. *kumāravardhana*, A country. See also .

## kumuḍa flesh
The identity of this type of meat is not clear.

## Kumuda
*ku mu da*, Skt. *ku mu da*, Attendant of the buddha Gaganasvara.

## Kumuda Essence
*ku mu da yi snying po*, Skt. *ku mu da yi snying po*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Dṛḍhasvara.

## Kumuda Flowers
*me tog ku mu da*, Skt. *kumuda*, A river in Dwelling on Summits.

## Kumuda­vicitramaha
*ku ma dA’i dus ston sna tshogs can*, Skt. *kumuda­vicitramaha*, A certain bird that lived on Gandhamādana Mountain, who died with thoughts of joy toward the Buddha and therefore took rebirth as a god.

## Kumudākara
*ku mu da’i ’byung gnas*, Skt. *kumudākara*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Kundaśrī
*me tog kun da’i dpal*, Skt. *kundaśrī*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## kundhalicilī
An unidentified ritual ingredient.

## Kunga Lekrin
*kun dga’ legs rin*, Skt. *kun dga’ legs rin*, A fifteenth century Sakya scholar, nephew of Ngorchen Kunga Zangpo.

## Kunikaṇṭha
*mgrin ngan*, Skt. *kunikaṇṭha*, A yakṣa who is a “Dharma brother” of Vaiśravaṇa.

## kunāla
*ku na la*, Skt. *kunāla*, Himalayan bird with beautiful bright eyes.

## Kunpang Chödrak Palzang
*kun spangs chos grags dpal bzang*, Skt. *kun spangs chos grags dpal bzang*, A great fourteenth century Jonangpa scholar, practitioner, and translator (1283–1363), who had earlier studied at Sakya, with Butön at Zhalu, and with Tharpa Lotsāwa at Sangphu, before becoming the first major disciple of Dolpopa.

## Kuntī
*mdung can*, Skt. *kuntī*, A rākṣasī known only from this sūtra.

## Kunta
*bdung*, Skt. *kunta*, Another name of the king Ājita.

## Kuntadaṃṣṭrā
*me tog kun da’i mche ba can*, Skt. *kuntadaṃṣṭrā*, A great rākṣasī.

## Kuntalā
*ku ta la*, Skt. *kuntalā*, A yakṣiṇī in the maṇḍala of Ekajaṭā.

## Kuṇḍopadāna
*yul chu mig can*, Skt. *kuṇḍopadāna*, A country.

## Kṣuradhārā
*spu gri so*, Skt. *kṣuradhārā*, “Razor Blade,” one of the hells.

## Kurava
*sgra mi snyan*, Skt. *kurava*, In ancient Buddhist cosmology, the northern of the four continents in the cardinal directions, that of “Unpleasant Sound.”

## kurchi
Holarrhena pubescens.

## Kurkuṭārāma Gardens
*khyim bya ba’i kun dga’ ra ba*, Skt. *kurkuṭārāma*, A garden frequented by Devadatta and his followers.

## Kuru
The name of a region in the north of the Indian subcontinent, situated among the plains of the Yamunā River to the east of present-day Delhi.

## Kurukṣetra
*sgra ngan zhing*, Skt. *kurukṣetra*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Kurukullā
*ku ru kulle*, Skt. *kurukullā*, A deity in the maṇḍala of Yamāri. Her practice is taught in The Tantra of Black Yamāri.

## Kurukulla
*ku ru ku la*, Skt. *kurukulla*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Kurutararka
*rgyal ngan rgyal gnyi*, Skt. *kurutararka*, A yakṣa general.

## Kusa
*ku sha*, a kind of grass considered auspicious, because the [Buddha](#buddha) sat on a cushion of it when he attained [enlightenment](#enlightenment).

## Kusumā
*me tog ma*, Skt. *kusumā*, One of the great yakṣiṇīs; also, a goddess of flowers invoked in a mantra.

## Kusuma
*me tog*, Skt. *kusuma*, The 10th buddha in the first list, 10th in the second list, and 10th in the third list.

## Kusumadatta
*me tog byin*, Skt. *kusumadatta*, The 244th buddha in the first list, 243rd in the second list, and 243rd in the third list.

## Kusumadeva
*lha yi me tog*, Skt. *kusumadeva*, The 104th buddha in the first list, 104th in the second list, and 105th in the third list.

## Kusumadhvaja
*me tog rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *kusumadhvaja*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## Kusumagaṇi
*me tog tshogs can*, Skt. *kusumagaṇi*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## Kusumagarbha
*me tog mchog*, Skt. *kusumagarbha*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Kusumaketu
*me tog dpal*, Skt. *kusumaketu*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## kusuma­kośa
*me tog gi mdzod*, Skt. *kusuma­kośa*, A magical tree, the name of which means “treasure of flowers.”

## Kusumanetra
*me tog spyan*, Skt. *kusumanetra*, The 197th buddha in the first list, 196th in the second list, and 196th in the third list.

## Kusumanilayā
*ku mud la gnas ma*, Skt. *kusumanilayā*, One of the names of Śrī Mahādevī.

## Kusumaparvata
*me tog ri bo*, Skt. *kusumaparvata*, The 164th buddha in the first list, 163rd in the second list, and 163rd in the third list.

## Kusumaprabha
*me tog ’od*, Skt. *kusumaprabha*, The 842nd buddha in the first list, 841st in the second list, and 831st in the third list.

## Kusumapura
*me rtog can*, Skt. *kusumapura*, Another name of Pāṭaliputra.

## Kusuma­pura­vāsinī
*me tog gi grong khyer la gnas ma*, Skt. *kusuma­pura­vāsinī*, One of the great yakṣiṇīs.

## Kusumaśrī
*me tog dpal*, Skt. *kusumaśrī*, A tathāgata mentioned here as one of the thirty-five buddhas of confession.

## Kusumaraśmi
*me tog ’od zer*, Skt. *kusumaraśmi*, The 53rd buddha in the first list, 53rd in the second list, and 54th in the third list.

## Kusuma­śrī­garbha
*me tog rgyas pa dpal gyi snying po*, Skt. *kusuma­śrī­garbha*, A bodhisattva mahāsattva.

## Kusumarāśi
*me tog brtsegs*, Skt. *kusumarāśi*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Kusumarāṣṭra
*yul ’khor me tog*, Skt. *kusumarāṣṭra*, The 412th buddha in the first list, 411th in the second list, and 405th in the third list.

## Kusuma­tala­garbha­vyūhālaṃkāra
*gzhi me tog gi snying po’i rgyan gyis brgyan pa*, Skt. *kusuma­tala­garbha­vyūhālaṃkāra*, An ocean of universes that includes our Sahā universe of a thousand million worlds and the even greater assembly of universes called Prabhāsa­vairocana. It has elsewhere been interpreted to be an alternative name for the Sahā universe.

## Kusumavicitra
*me tog sna tshogs*, Skt. *kusumavicitra*, The name of an eastern buddha realm.

## Kusumbharatnā
*le brgan rtsi dang rin chen ma*, Skt. *kusumbharatnā*, The name of a female Buddhist deity, meaning “Saffron Jewel,” here used as an epithet of Sitātapatrā.

## kusumābhikīrṇa
*me tog bkram pa*, Skt. *kusumābhikīrṇa*, Lit. “on account of which flowers have been strewed.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Kusumeśvarā
*me tog gi dbang phyug ma*, Skt. *kusumeśvarā*, One of the names of Śrī Mahādevī.

## Kusumottama
A future buddha whose name is attested in the Mañjuśrī­mūlakalpa.

## Kusumottara­jñānin
*me tog dam pa’i ye shes*, Skt. *kusumottara­jñānin*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## Kusumārci­sāgara­pradīpa
*me tog ’od ’phro rgya mtsho sgron*, Skt. *kusumārci­sāgara­pradīpa*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Kusumāvatī
*me tog dang ldan pa*, Skt. *kusumāvatī*, “Rich in Flowers,” one of the pure abodes presided over by the tathāgata Saṃkusumita Rajendra; in the MMK it is also the abode of Mañjuśrī.

## Kuśāvatī
*rtswa can*, Skt. *kuśāvatī*, A city.

## ākāśāvasthita
*nam mkha’i gnas la gnas pa*, Skt. *ākāśāvasthita*, Lit. “abiding in space.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Kāvelī
Skt. *kāvelī*, A river queen.

## Kāverī
*kA be rI*, Skt. *kāverī*, A river in Jambudvīpa.

## Kāviśa
*mang yul*, Skt. *kāviśa*, This seems to be one of the Himalayan countries; the Tibetan translation essentially means the front range of the Himalayas.

## Kāṇvāyana
*mig mi ’dzums kyi bu*, Skt. *kāṇvāyana*, The descendants of the ṛṣi Kaṇva.

## Kāya
*sku*, see [three kāyas](#three-kāyas), [four kāyas](#four-kāyas), [five kāyas](#five-kāyas).

## Kāṣāya
*ngur smrig*, Skt. *kāṣāya*, A realm to the north of the Buddha Ratnagarbha’s realm in which resides the Buddha Lokeśvararāja.

## Śākya
*shakya*, Skt. *śākya*, Name of the ancient tribe in which the Buddha was born as a prince; their kingdom was based to the east of Kośala, in the foothills near the present-day border of India and Nepal, with Kapilavastu as its capital.

## Śākya Ö
Tibetan monk and translator of this sūtra.

## Śākya clan
The clan into which the Buddha was born.

## Śākya followers
*shAkya pa*, Skt. *shAkya pa*, In the sūtra this term used by non-Buddhists to refer to Buddhists.

## Śākya Gomīrāja
*shAkya btsun pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *śākya gomīrāja*, A buddha.

## Śākya Lodrö
*shAkya blo gros*, Skt. *(not in the skt. source of the mmk)*, The name of an important translator who was active during the early Sarma (gsar ma) period (c. 11th century).

## Śākya Suprabuddha
*shAkya rab sad*, Skt. *śākya suprabuddha*, King of Vṛji, father of Buddha Śākyamuni’s mother Mahā­māyā. See “Suprabuddha.”

## Śākya Yeshé
Śākya Yeshé, commonly known as Drokmi Lotsāwa (’brog mi lo tsā ba), was a Tibetan translator from Lhatsé in Western Tsang and an important figure in the Lamdré (Tib. lam ’bras) lineage. Drokmi’s dates are uncertain, but Tibetan literature offers a range of possible dates, beginning in 990 ce and ending in 1074 ce. One of his principal teachers was the Indian paṇḍita Gayādhara.

## Śākyaṛṣabha
*shA kya mkhyu mchog*, Skt. *śākyaṛṣabha*, Literally, “the Bull of the Śākyas.” This is similar to Śākyamuni, “the Sage of the Śākyas,” the Śākyas being the Buddha’s clan.

## Kāṣāyadhvajā
*ngur smrig gi rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *kāṣāyadhvajā*, A buddha realm in the north.

## kāya­kali­saṃpramathana
*lus kyi skyon yang dag par sel ba*, Skt. *kāya­kali­saṃpramathana*, Lit. “overcomes physical flaws.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Śākyamuni
*sha kya thub pa*, the [Buddha](#buddha) of our time, who lived around the 5th century B.C.

## Śākyan
*shAkya*, Skt. *śākya*, In general, describes those belonging (like the Buddha Śākyamuni) to the Śākya people or lineage of the kingdom centered on Kapilavastu, but also used by extension as an epithet of monastics who are followers of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Kāśyapa
*'od srung*, the third of the thousand [Buddha](#buddha)s of this present [kalpa](#kalpa) the one before [Śākyamuni](#śākyamuni). Kāśyapa is also the name of one of [Śākyamuni](#śākyamuni)'s [Śrāvaka](#śrāvaka) [disciple](#disciple)s, who became the [Buddha](#buddha)'s successor on his passing.

## Kāśyapa (buddha)
*’od srung*, Skt. *kāśyapa*, Buddha of a previous age. Not to be confused with the monk Kāśyapa of Buddha Śākyamuni’s order, nor with Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, Nadī Kāśyapa, or Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, nor with Nirgrantha Kāśyapa, nor Foremost Kāśyapa.

## Kāśyapa (monk)
*’od srung*, Skt. *kāśyapa*, See “Mahā­kāśyapa.”

## Kāśyapa (Nirgrantha)
*’od srung*, Skt. *kāśyapa*, Given name of “Nirgrantha Kinsman of the Kāśyapas.” Not to be confused with Kāśyapa, buddha of a previous age; the monk Kāśyapa of Buddha Śākyamuni’s order; nor with Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, Nadī Kāśyapa, or Pūraṇa Kāśyapa; nor Foremost Kāśyapa.

## Kāśyapakumāra
*’od srung gzhon nu*, Skt. *kāśyapakumāra*, One of the elders mentioned in The Four Boys’ Absorption as being present at the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. He is to be distinguished from the disciple Mahākāśyapa who, it is said, was not present.

## Śākyaprabha
Skt. *śākyaprabha*, An Indian paṇḍita who was resident in Tibet during the late eighth and early ninth centuries.

## Śākyaśrī
A Kashmiri master, Śākyaśrībhadra (1127–1225) was the last abbot of the great Nālandā monastery in India. Later in his life he traveled to Tibet and taught a number of Tibetan students, including Sakya Paṇḍita. He is credited with authoring twenty-three texts that are included in the Tengyur.

## Śākyaśrībhadra
Skt. *śākyaśrībhadra*, 1127–1225, an influential Kashmiri paṇḍita who visited Tibet from 1204–13.

## Śākyasiṃha
*shAkya sing ha*, Skt. *śākyasiṃha*, An Indian scholar who was a contemporary of Kawa Paltsek. He was among the translators of The Sutra of Nandika into Tibetan. He also translated the Buddha­makuṭa­sūtra (Toh 274) along with the Tibetan translator Devendrarakṣita.

## Śākyavardhana
*shA kya ’phel*, Skt. *śākyavardhana*, A yakṣa that was the protective deity for the Śākya clan, which was the Buddha’s clan. The Śākyas had a temple devoted to him and he is represented in sculpture as being present at his birth.

## Kyo Öjung
The eleventh century Tibetan translator and adept involved in the translation of the present text and the transmission of Vajrabhairava/Yamāntaka lineages in Tibet.

## Kāṇḍyāyana
Skt. *kāṇḍyāyana*, A great ṛṣi.

## Śālā
*gnas ma*, Skt. *śālā*, One of the great dūtīs attending upon Lord Vajrapāṇi.

## laḍḍū
*la du*, Skt. *laḍḍū*, A kind of sweetmeat made of coarsely ground gram or other pulse or of corn flour, mixed with sugar and spices, and fried in ghee or oil (Monier-Williams).

## Lāḍa
*lA dA*, Skt. *lāḍa*, A country corresponding in area to modern Gujarat.

## Lāṭa
The name of a country.

## Śīla
*ngang tshul*, Skt. *śīla*, The king identified with Śīlāditya Dharmāditya I of the Maitraka dynasty.

*gzer nad*, Skt. *śūla*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

*shing sA la*, Skt. *śāla*, A widespread species of tall trees in forests of the Indian subcontinent, either Vatica robusta or Shorea robusta.

## laṭakī
An unidentified ritual ingredient.

*ming du btags*, Skt. *lokasaṃjñā*, Mahāvyutpatti 6558.

*tshul khrims bzang po*, Skt. *śīlabhadra*, A king in Jambudvīpa, Musulundha’s rebirth.

## śālabhañjikā
*sa la ’joms ma*, Skt. *śālabhañjikā*, A term used for a courtesan. In the Bhūta­ḍāmara Tantra this term refers to a class of nonhuman female beings.

## laboring class
*dmangs rigs*, Skt. *śūdravarṇa*, Fourth of the four classes of traditional Indian society.

## lac
*rgya skyegs*, Skt. *alaktaka*, The resinous secretion of the coccid or scale insect, which can be used for dyeing and as a wax.

## lac dye
*rgya skyegs kyi khu ba*, Skt. *lākṣa*, A dye made from the insect Laccifer lacca.

## lack of parsimony as preceptors
*slob dpon gyi dpe mkhyud med pa*, Skt. *anācāryamuṣṭi*, Literally “not being a tight-fisted teacher,” this term denotes a teacher who freely gives appropriate teachings to their disciples.

## lacking a self
*bdag med pa*, Skt. *anātman*, The view that there is no inherently existent self, whether dependent on or independent of the five aggregates.

## Śīladhvaja
*tshul khrims rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *śīladhvaja*, “Banner of Discipline;” the name of the person who sponsored the writing of the manuscript of the JAA.

## ladle

*sA la pho nya mo*, Skt. *śāladūtī*, One of the vidyā goddesses, possibly the same as Vajraśālavatī.

## Laṅgala
One of the sublineages connected with the Kautsa lineage of the brahmanical tradition.

## Lagna
One of the sublineages connected with the Kautsa lineage of the brahmanical tradition.

## Lañjanī

## Laṅkā
*lang ka*, Skt. *laṅkā*, Present-day Śrī Laṅkā; the capital city of this island.

## Laṅka
The name of an ancient kingdom located to the south of Mount Sumeru and commonly identified as the island of Śrī Laṅka.

## Lakṣaṇa­bhūṣita­gātra
*sku mtshan gyis rnam par brgyan pa*, Skt. *lakṣaṇa­bhūṣita­gātra*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Lakṣaṇa­meru
*mtshan gyi*, Skt. *lakṣaṇa­meru*, A buddha in the distant past. See mtshan gyi is in error for mtshan ri-->.

## Lakṣaṇa­parvata­vairocana
*mtshan gyi ri bo rnam par snang ba*, Skt. *lakṣaṇa­parvata­vairocana*, One of countless buddhas in a past kalpa.

## Lakṣaṇa­śrī­parvata
*mtshan gyi dpal ri bo*, Skt. *lakṣaṇa­śrī­parvata*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Lakṣaṇa­rucira­supuṣpitāṅga
*mtshan yid du ’ong ba’i me tog gi yan lag shin tu rgyas pa*, Skt. *lakṣaṇa­rucira­supuṣpitāṅga*, One of countless buddhas in a past kalpa.

## Lakṣaṇa­sūrya­cakra­samanta­prabha
*mtshan gyi nyi ma’i ’khor lo kun tu snang ba*, Skt. *lakṣaṇa­sūrya­cakra­samanta­prabha*, One of countless buddhas in a past kalpa.

*mtshan nyid ri rab*, Skt. *lakṣaṇa­sumeru*, A buddha in the distant past.

*mtshan gyi rnam par brgyan pa’i rgyal mtshan zla ba*, Skt. *lakṣaṇa­vibhūṣita­dhvaja­candra*, One of countless buddhas in a past kalpa.

## lakṣana­pariśodhaṇa
*mtshan nyid yongs su sbyong ba*, Skt. *lakṣana­pariśodhaṇa*, Lit. “purification of marks.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Laṅkapura
The name of a city and its surrounding territory. Traditionally identified as the land of the rākṣasas (srin yul).

## Laṅkapuri Rākṣasas
*lang ka’i grong khyer na nges par gnas pa’i srin po*, Skt. *lang ka’i grong khyer na nges par gnas pa’i srin po*, An island in the vicinity of Jambudvīpa.

## Lake Anavatapta
*ma dros pa*, Skt. *anavatapta*, The mythical Lake Anavatapta is said to be at the center of Jambudvīpa, the continent on which we reside. The great rivers of Jambudvīpa are said to flow from this lake. It is often associated with Lake Manasarovar in Tibet, which lies in close proximity to Mount Kailash.

## Lake Mandākinī
*mtsho dal gyis ’bab*, Skt. *mandākinī*, The Mandākinī river, which translates as “the slow-flowing” river, is the name of a specific tributary of the Ganges that flows through the Kedāranātha valley in the Himālayas, as well as a name that might be used for other rivers (Monier-Williams 788.2). The term is assumed to refer to a lake in this case (and not a river) because the Tibetan uses the term mtsho.

## Lake Mapham
Also known as Lake Mānasarovar, Lake Mapham is a high-altitude freshwater lake in the vicinity of Mount Tisé sacred to Bönpos, Buddhists, Jains, and Hindus.

## Lake Namtso Chukmo
One of the four famous lakes of Tibet. Located in Damshung (’dam gzhung) county, not far from Lhasa.

## Lake Nuptso
Also known as Yardrok Yumtso (yar ’brog g.yu mtsho), Lake Nuptso is located in present-day Nakartse (sna dkar rtse) county in Tibet. Its name derives from the Nub (snubs) clan that inhabited the surrounding regions.

## Lake of Jewels
*dbyig mtsho*, Skt. *dbyig mtsho*, An arhat monk whose past virtuous deeds ripened into countless glories both human and divine.

## Lake Tri Shö
Also known as Lake Kokonor or Qinghai Lake, meaning Blue Lake. Located in present-day Qinghai province, west of Xining. There appears to be a wide variety of alternative spellings for the lake’s name, which suggests its origin in pre-written oral culture. According to the Dungkar Dictionary, the name Tri Shö derives from an oral legend that the families living in that area numbered in the tens of thousands (khri) and as the lake appeared out of the earth they fell (shor) inside.

## Laṅkeśvara
*lang ka’i bdag*, Skt. *laṅkeśvara*, A yakṣa general.

*gla khe*, kind of tree with a sweet [bark](#bark).

## latecomer
*rgan zhugs*, Skt. *mahallaka*, This term refers to those who become monks or nuns after having a family. In ordinary Skt. usage mahallaka is used as a respectful direct address to an elder. In the Vinaya, these monastics are usually addressed as “latecomer” rather than as “venerable,” the customary address for ordained monks and nuns. This may suggest that “latecomers” occupied a special place within the saṅgha somewhat separate from those who joined before having a family.

## latent impulse
*bag la nyal ba*, Skt. *anuśaya*, The latent impulses are seven subconscious impulses or tendencies, namely attachment to sense pleasures (’dod pa’i ’dod chags), hatred (khong khro), attachment to existence (srid pa’i ’dod chags), pride (nga rgyal), ignorance (ma rig pa), views (lta ba), and doubt (the tshom).

## latent karmic tendencies

## latent tendency
*bag la nyal ba*, Skt. *anuśaya*, The first stage in the development and expression of afflictions (Skt. kleśa, Tib. nyon mongs), followed by “belief” (Skt. dṛṣṭi, Tib. lta ba smra ba) and “manifest affliction” (Skt. paryutthāna, Tib. kun nas ldang ba).

## laḍḍu
*la du*, Skt. *laḍḍu*, A round sweet ball. The Tantra of Great Gaṇapati describes a laḍḍu as a type of food containing the three sweets and the three fruits that is sprinkled with a delicious fragrance, rolled into a ball, and boiled in milk and butter.

## Laukākṣa
One of the lineages within the Sāmaveda branch of the brahmanical tradition and one of the sublineages connected with the Kauśika lineage of the brahmanical tradition.

## lava
A measure of time defined as consisting of two blinks of the eye. Eight lavas make one kāṣṭhā, which means that the duration of one lava is three hundred seventy-five milliseconds. Term lava is thus commonly used to refer to a brief moment in time. According to another time system, lava refers to a thirtieth part of a muhūrta, giving it a duration of one minute and thirty-six seconds. This is also how Vasubandhu defines lava in the Abhidharmakośa (III 88): thirty lavas make one muhūrta, and thirty muhūrtas make one full day and night.

## league

The Sanskrit literally means “yoking” or “joining.” It is the distance a yoked ox can travel in a day or before needing to be unyoked. Sources calculate the exact distance variably, somewhere between four and ten miles.

## lengthy period
Often translated as “intermediate age” or kalpa, the term can refer to the smallest division of a great age, of which there are said to eighty in the Abhidharmakośa, but the term is also used to refer to very lengthy periods of war, famine, or disease that result in mass losses of life.

## leper
Someone with leprosy (also known as Hansen’s disease). Longstanding leprosy may cause loss of the extremities due to nerve damage, as well as other unsightly signs, and throughout most of history has been associated with social stigma.

*mdze can*, Skt. *mdze can*, A type of worm (srin bu) that lives in and feeds on the body.

## Lesser Vehicle
*theg pa dman pa*, Skt. *hīnayāna*, This is a collective term used by proponents of the Great Vehicle to refer to the hearer vehicle (śrāvakayāna) and solitary buddha vehicle (pratyeka­buddha­yāna). The name stems from their goal‍—i.e. nirvāṇa and personal liberation‍—being seen as small or lesser than the goal of the Great Vehicle‍—i.e. buddhahood and the liberation of all sentient beings. See also “Great Vehicle.”

*sa*, Skt. *bhūmi*, The stages a bodhisattva must traverse before reaching perfect buddhahood; traditionally ten in number, though some systems present more.

## level of a crown prince
*gzhon nu’i sa*, Skt. *kumārabhūmi*, In general a term for bodhisattvas of higher levels, implying that they will soon be consecrated as buddhas, and more particularly for bodhisattvas awaiting their final rebirth as a buddha.

## level of a non-returner
*phyir mi ldog pa’i sa*, Skt. *avinivartanıya-bhūmi*, A level on the path to awakening at which point there is no danger of falling back into saṃsāra.

## level of [an arhat’s] spiritual achievement
*byas pa rtogs pa’i sa*, Skt. *kṛtakṛtyabhūmi*, Name of the seventh of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the state of an ordinary person up to buddhahood, distinct from the ten bodhisattva levels. See “ten levels.”

## level of attenuated refinement
*bsrabs pa’i sa*, Skt. *tanubhūmi*, Name of the fifth of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the state of an ordinary person up to buddhahood, distinct from the ten bodhisattva levels. See “ten levels.”

## level of bright insight
*dkar po rnam par mthong ba’i sa*, Skt. *śukla­vidarśanā­bhūmi*, Name of the first of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the state of an ordinary person up to buddhahood, distinct from the ten bodhisattva levels. In this text, it seems to equivalent to the level of ordinary people. See “ten levels.”

## level of buddha nature
*rigs kyi sa*, Skt. *gotra­bhūmi*, Name of the second level attainable by bodhisattvas. See .

## level of cultivation
*sgom pa’i sa*, Skt. *bhāvanābhūmi*, A stage in the path to awakening.

## level of dedicated conduct
An early stage in a bodhisattva’s career during which they have developed a degree of conviction that is not yet informed by direct experience. The level of dedicated conduct is said to comprise the first two of the five paths, those of accumulation and preparation, which lead up to the path of seeing.

## level of devoted conduct
*mos spyod pa’i sa*, Skt. *adhimukti­caryā­bhūmi*, The level of devoted conduct is said to comprise the first two of the five paths, those of accumulation and preparation, which lead up to the path of seeing. This level is also presented as the second of seven spiritual levels in the Bodhisattva­bhūmi, which follows the initial level of the spiritual potential (gotrabhūmi).

## level of dispassion
*’dod chags dang bral ba’i sa*, Skt. *vīta­rāga­bhūmi*, Name of the sixth level attainable by bodhisattvas, from which point there is no more rebirth. See .

## level of insight
*mthong ba’i sa*, Skt. *darśanabhūmi*, Name of the fourth of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the state of an ordinary person up to buddhahood, distinct from the ten bodhisattva levels. It is equivalent to entering the stream to nirvāṇa. See “ten levels.”

## level of no attachment
*’dod chags dang bral ba’i sa*, Skt. *vītarāgabhūmi*, Name of the sixth level of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the state of an ordinary person up to buddhahood, distinct from the ten bodhisattva levels. It is the level from which point there is no more rebirth in the desire realm. See “ten levels.”

## level of nonregression
*phyir mi ldog pa’i sa*, Skt. *﻿avaivartikabhūmi*, A term used to describe a stage on the path at which further progress is assured, with no further possibility of retrogressing to a previous stage.

## level of nonreturning
*phyir mi ’ong ba’i ’bras bu*, Skt. *anāgāmiphala*, The third of four levels of attainment in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, at which one will no longer be reborn in the desire realm.

## level of ordinary people
*so so’i skye bo’i sa*, Skt. *pṛthagjanabhūmi*, Name of the first of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the state of an ordinary person up to buddhahood, distinct from the ten bodhisattva levels. In this text, it seems to equivalent to the level of bright insight. See “ten levels.”

## level of seeing
Name of the fourth level of realization attainable by bodhisattvas, equivalent to entering the stream to nirvāṇa.

## level of the bodhisattvas
*byang chub sems dpa’i sa*, Skt. *bodhi­sattva­bhūmi*, Name of the ninth of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the state of an ordinary person up to buddhahood, distinct from the ten bodhisattva levels. See “ten levels.”

## level of the buddhas
*sangs rgyas kyi sa*, Skt. *buddhabhūmi*, The tenth and last of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the state of an ordinary person up to buddhahood, distinct from the ten bodhisattva levels. Also rendered here as “level of the perfectly complete buddhas.” See “ten levels.”

## level of the completely awakened buddhas
*yang dag par rdzogs pa’i sangs rgyas kyi sa*, Skt. *samyaksambuddha­bhūmi*, Name of the tenth of the levels of realization attainable by bodhisattvas. See .

## level of the family
*rigs kyi sa*, Skt. *gotrabhūmi*, One of the initial levels of realization on the path of the hearers. Depending on classification system it is either the first or the second level (when it is preceded by the Śuklavipaśyanā level).

## level of the genuinely perfect buddhas
*yang dag par rdzogs pa’i sangs rgyas kyi sa*, Skt. *samyak­sambuddha­bhūmi*, Name of the tenth of the levels of realization attainable by bodhisattvas. See .

## level of the perfectly complete buddhas
*yang dag par rdzogs pa’i sangs rgyas kyi sa*, Skt. *samyaksambuddha­bhūmi*, The tenth and last of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the state of an ordinary person up to buddhahood, distinct from the ten bodhisattva levels. Also rendered here as “level of the buddhas.” See “ten levels.”

## level of the pratyekabuddhas
*rang sangs rgyas kyi sa*, Skt. *pratyeka­buddha­bhūmi*, Name of the eighth of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the state of an ordinary person up to buddhahood, distinct from the ten bodhisattva levels. See “ten levels.”

## level of the spiritual family
*rigs kyi sa*, Skt. *gotrabhūmi*, Name of the second of the ten levels traversed by all practitioners, from the state of an ordinary person up to buddhahood, distinct from the ten bodhisattva levels. See “ten levels;” see also “spiritual family.”

## level of the spiritual potential
*rigs kyi sa*, Skt. *gotrabhūmi*, Name of the second level attainable by bodhisattvas. See The Transcendent Perfection of Wisdom in Ten Thousand Lines (Toh 11), 13.9.

## level of training
*slob pa’i sa*, Skt. *śaikṣabhūmi*, A stage in the path to awakening.

## Level of union
*zung 'jug gi go 'phang*, the level of [Vajradhara](#vajradhara). The union is that of [dharmakāya](#dharmakāya) and [rūpakāya](#rūpakāya).

## Levels
see [Bodhisattva levels](#bodhisattva-levels).

## lever
*’khor gtan*, Skt. *cakrikā*, Śīlapālita, in his commentary on The Minor Matters of Monastic Discipline (Toh 4115, F.21.b), explains, “The lever is a way to prevent the door panels from opening. A small wooden peg, one cubit long, is affixed in the center between two door panels. Because this piece of wood turns like a wheel in order to hold the doors in place, it is called a ‘lever.’ ” This is one of three fasteners, along with cross bolts (Tib. gnam gzer) and bars (Tib. phred gtan), that the Buddha allowed to bar doors.

## lexical explanations
*nges pa’i tshig*, Skt. *nirukta*, Lexical explanations here implies the exact knowledge of the primary and derivative definitions and explanations of names and words. It is also the third of the four kinds of exact knowledge; see “exact knowledge of language and lexical explanations.”

## lexical explanations, words, and syllables with respect to all phenomena
*chos thams cad nges pa’i sgra dang tshig dang ’bru*, Skt. *chos thams cad nges pa’i sgra dang tshig dang ’bru*, The twenty-fourth of the fifty-one meditative stabilities manifested to Sadāprarudita in chapter 73.

## Lāṅgala
A sublineage of the Sāmavedins.

## Lāṅgula
*’jug ma*, Skt. *lāṅgula*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Lhai Dawa
*lha’i zla ba*, Skt. *lha’i zla ba*, Prolific Tibetan translator active during the late eighth and early ninth centuries.

## Lhasé Tsangma
*lha sras gtsang ma*, A son of the king Mutik Tsenpo (Senalek), probably the eldest (born 800?); he may have been exiled to Bhutan, and did not reign himself.

## Lhasa
The capital of Tibet.

## Lhenkar Palace
*pho brang lhan dkar*, Skt. *pho brang lhan dkar*, A royal palace located in central Tibet, which is famous for giving its name to the catalog of translated canonical texts produced up to the early ninth century. Also called Denkar (ldan dkar).

## Lhodzong palace
The place in eastern Tibet where the Lhodzong Kangyur was housed.

## Lhundrup Teng
Lhundrup Teng is a monastery in Degé, also known as Degé Gonchen. It houses the renowned Degé printing house established by Tenpa Tsering. Originally a royal palace and temple, from the seventeenth century Lhundrup Teng became closely associated with the Ngor branch of the Sakya tradition. Until the mid-nineteenth century the kings of Degé were also often, as in the case of Tenpa Tsering, the throne holders (khri chen) or abbots of Lhundrup Teng.

## Lhunthup
The sixth Degé king, Pönchen Könchok Lhuntub (late sixteenth to mid-seventeenth century) was the head of the house of Degé in its thirty-sixth generation.

## āli kāli
*A li kA li*, Skt. *āli kāli*, The vowels (āli) and consonants (kāli) of the Sanskrit alphabet.

## liberated
*grol ba*, Skt. *mukta*, A quality or criterion applied in this text to authentic monks or practitioners that summarizes their having rid themselves of hindrances to awakening, paired with several different epithets describing their positive qualities; see “knowledge,” “coherent,” and “equipped”; see also . In later literature the liberation to which this term refers is usually explained as being from attachment, obstruction, and the obscuration of inferior outlook.

## Liberated Array
*rnam par grol ba’i bkod pa*, Skt. *rnam par grol ba’i bkod pa*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Siṃhadaṃṣṭra.

## liberated from the two factors
This commonly refers to being liberated from the obscurations of afflictive emotions and the obscurations of meditative attainment. The Skt. term can also be interpreted to mean “liberated through the two factors,” in which the two factors are meditative stability (dhyāna) and insight (prajñā). In this latter case, the term reflects a tension within the Indian Buddhist community regarding the value of scholarly knowledge and meditative experience alone or in combination.

## Liberated Intelligence
*blo gros rnam par grol ba*, Skt. *blo gros rnam par grol ba*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Puṇyabala.

## Liberated Mind
*sems grol ma*, Skt. *sems grol ma*, Mother of the buddha Hutārci.

## Liberating Concentration
*thar pa’i bsam gtan*, Skt. *thar pa’i bsam gtan*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Dṛḍha (795 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Liberating Conquest
*rnam par grol bas ’joms*, Skt. *rnam par grol bas ’joms*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Somaraśmi.

## liberating words
*thar pa’i tshig*, Skt. *mokṣapada*, One of ten different kinds of verbal phrase or statement (Skt. pada) mentioned in this text.

## Liberation
*thar pa*, Skt. *mokṣa*, 1. freedom from [saṃsāra](#saṃsāra), either as an [Arhat](#arhat) or as a [Buddha](#buddha). 2. occasionally, *bsgral las byed pa*, performing the action of liberation, a practice to liberate the consciousness of a malignant being into a [Buddhafield](#buddhafield).

## Liberation Faith
*thar pa dad*, Skt. *thar pa dad*, Mother of the buddha Anilavegagāmin.

## Liberation from All Sorrow and Harm
*mya ngan dang gnod pa thams cad las sgrol ba*, Skt. *mya ngan dang gnod pa thams cad las sgrol ba*, Name of the world system of the thus-gone one Branch Guru. Alternate name for the world system Beyond All Sorrow and Harm.

## Liberation Joy
*thar pa dga’*, Skt. *thar pa dga’*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Ratnavyūha.

## liberation through wisdom
Liberation involving only wisdom, instead of both meditative absorption and wisdom.

## Liberation without Attachment
*chags med rnam par grol*, Skt. *chags med rnam par grol*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Anuttarajñānin.

## liberations
*rnam par thar ba*, Skt. *vimokṣa*, This can include any method for liberation. The most commonly listed are the eight liberations: (1) form viewing form: the view of dependent origination and emptiness; (2) the formless viewing form: having seen internal emptiness, seeing the emptiness of external forms; (3) the view of the pleasant: seeing pleasant appearances as empty and contemplating the unpleasant; (4) seeing the emptiness of the formless meditation of infinite space; (5) seeing the emptiness of the formless meditation of infinite consciousness; (6) seeing the emptiness of the formless meditation of nothingness; (7) seeing the emptiness of the formless meditation of neither perception nor nonperception; and (8) seeing the emptiness of the state of cessation.

## liberative art
*thabs*, Skt. *upāya*, This is the expression in action of the great compassion of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas—physical, verbal, and mental. It follows that one empathetically aware of the troubles of living beings would, for his very survival, devise the most potent and efficacious techniques possible to remove those troubles, and the troubles of living beings are removed effectively only when they reach liberation. “Art” was chosen over the usual “method” and “means” because it has a stronger connotation of efficacy in our technological world; also, in Buddhism, liberative art is identified with the extreme of power, energy, and efficacy, as symbolized in the vajra (adamantine scepter): The importance of this term is highlighted in this sūtra by the fact that Vimalakīrti himself is introduced in the chapter entitled “Inconceivable Skill in Liberative Art”; this indicates that he, as a function of the nirmāṇakāya (incarnation-body), just like the Buddha himself, is the very incarnation of liberative art, and every act of his life is therefore a technique for the development and liberation of living beings. The “liberative” part of the translation follows “salvifique” in Lamotte’s phrase “moyens salvifique.”

## liberative meditative states, the attainments of concentration
In its most general sense, this term refers to the state of freedom from suffering and cyclic existence, or saṃsāra, that is the goal of the Buddhist path. More specifically, the term may refer to a category of advanced meditative attainment such as those of the “eight liberations.”

## Liberator
*thar byed*, Skt. *thar byed*, Liberator (one who sets others free), also the name of a son of the buddha Laḍitāgragāmin.

## Liberator from Existence
*srid mthar byed*, Skt. *srid mthar byed*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Candrārka.

## Liberator of Beings
*sems can sgrol*, The name of a bodhisattva.

## Libra
*srang*, Skt. *tula*, See “Tula.”

## Licchavī
*lits+tsha bI*, Skt. *licchavī*, A clan with its capital, Vaiśālī, in present-day Bihar, north of the Ganges. Their capital was a place where the Buddha had many followers when they were an independent republic.

## Licchavi
*lid tsa byi*, Skt. *licchavi*, The people of the city and region of Vaiśālī. The Licchavi were one of the clans making up the Vṛji confederacy, an early republic at the time of the Buddha.

## Licchavis
*lits+tsha bI*, Skt. *licchavi*, The name of a northern Indian clan and royal dynasty based in Vaiśālī, the capital of the Vṛji confederacy. The Buddha first visited the city in the fifth year after his awakening and spent his last rainy season retreat in the vicinity of Vaiśālī.

## lickers
*rab tu ldag byed*, Skt. *rab tu ldag byed*, Parasites that are said to live inside women’s wombs.

## licorice tree
*ma du ka*, Skt. *madhuka*, Glycyrrhiza glabra according to the Pandanus Database of Plants.

## life force
*srog*, Skt. *jīvita*, The life force present in all beings. Often this life force is associated with the breath (prāṇa).

## Life Isochronous with Death
*srog ’chi ba dang bcas pa*, Skt. *samṛtyujīvita*, One of sixteen realms that surround the Great Howling Hell. Alternatively referred to as Instant Revival Upon Death (shi ma thag tu ’tsho ba) in the Tibetan text.

## life of purity
In Mahāyāna understood as pure conduct in the sense of compassion and so on; in other traditions understood as chastity.

## life pillar
*srog shing*, Skt. *yaṣṭi*, The Sanskrit yaṣṭi may refer to a flagpole, especially one said to have adorned the capital cities of five former buddha, but more specifically, it refers to the “life pillar” in the center of a statue or stūpa

## life-force mantra
*srog sngags*, The name of a particular type of mantra.

## life-force’s most basic feeling
*srog gi mtha’ pa’i tshor ba*, Skt. *srog gi mtha’ pa’i tshor ba*, See .

## Life-Granting Golden Garland
*gser gyi phreng ba can tshe sbyin ma*, Skt. *gser gyi phreng ba can tshe sbyin ma*, A goddess.

## Life-Granting Vajra Garland
*rdo rje phreng ba tshe sbyin ma*, Skt. *rdo rje phreng ba tshe sbyin ma*, A goddess.

## lifelong medicines
*'tsho ba'i [bar](#bar) du bcang ba*, Skt. *yāvajjīvika*, There are no limits to the length of time monks are permitted to keep medicine proper. Hence those compounds commonly understood to be medicine proper are literally called "kept lifelong," that is "lifelong medicines." These are aimed at combating illnesses that arise from the confluence of factors such as [bile](#bile), [phlegm](#phlegm), and [wind](#wind). The texts describe these medicines as being made from roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and other plant materials.

## lifting of restrictions
*dgag dbye*, Skt. *pravāraṇāṃ pravārayitum*, During the rite of lifting restrictions, each monk extends an “invitation” or “lifts restrictions” (Tib. dgag dbye bya ba; Skt. pravāraṇam pravārayitum) to the other monks with whom he has passed the rains retreat. These other monks may then “prompt” (Tib. gleng ba; Skt. codanā) his memory of an offense he has failed to confess with evidence or well-grounded suspicion. The Pāli parallel pavāraṇā is generally translated with “inviting, invitation.” We generally use the English “lifting of restrictions” to reflect the Sanskrit original pravāraṇāṃ pravārayitum. Nevertheless, in The Chapter on Lifting Restrictions, “to lift restrictions” means “to invite” and the two can be used interchangeably; see, for instance, our translation of Kalyāṇamitra’s gloss of the term: “ ‘To invite,’ to give the opportunity for monks with whom one has pledged to settle for the rains to speak about what they have seen, heard, or suspected.” Kalyāṇamitra (F.313.a): dgag dbye zhes bya ba ni dbyar gnas par khas blangs pa’i dge slong rnams kyis mthong ba dang/ thos pa dang/ dgos pa’i gnas gsum gyis gleng pa’i skabs ’byed pa’o. Here are parallel uses from The Chapter on Lifting Restrictions in Skt., Tib., and Chinese Sanskrit Pravāraṇavastu (2.3.2.2): utsahase tvam evaṃnāmā saṃghasya pravāraṇāṃ pravārayitum iti. Tibetan (F.223.b): ming ’di zhes bya ba khyod dbyar gnas pa’i dge ’dun la dgag dbye byed par spro’am. Chinese (Taishō 1045a34: 汝某甲。頗能爲夏坐僧伽。以三事見聞疑。爲隨意不.

## lifting of restrictions ceremony
*skabs ’byed pa’i las*, Skt. *pravāraṇakarman*, Literally means “open an opportunity”; it refers to the pravāraṇa, or the “lifting of restrictions” ceremony held at the end of each summer rains retreat, in which monks are given an “opportunity,” otherwise prohibited, to oppose and debate what was heard, seen, or suspected while undertaking a rains retreat.

## lifting restrictions
*dgag dbye*, Skt. *pravāraṇa*, A ceremony in which restrictions adopted for the rains retreat are relaxed, marking its end. Also short for the Vinayavastu's third chapter on the same.

## liṅga
A physical representation of the god Śiva in the form of short cylindrical column that is rounded at the top and sits on a circular base. A “solitary liṅga” (ekaliṅga) is often listed among suitable sites for esoteric rituals and practices.

## Light
Light (illumination, brightness), also the name of a sage (ṛṣi). The Sanskrit could be Dīpta or Roca, the latter being attested in the Lalitavistara, the former in the Mañjuśrī­mūlakalpa.

## light array
*’od bkod pa*, Skt. *’od bkod pa*, The name of an absorption.

*glog chen sgron ma*, Skt. *glog chen sgron ma*, The name of a bodhisattva in the Buddha’s audience.

*mar me byed*, Skt. *mar me byed*, A buddha realm.

*’od skyong ma*, Skt. *’od skyong ma*, Mother of the buddha Sujāta.

*rdo rje’i ’od*, Skt. *rdo rje’i ’od*, Not in Negi. rdo rje ’od ma appears in Negi as Skt. Vajrābha.

## Light of All Good Qualities
The buddhafield of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra.

## Light of All Qualities
*yon tan kun gyi ’od*, Skt. *yon tan kun gyi ’od*, Birthplace of the buddha Jñānarata.

*bde ba’i ’od*, Skt. *bde ba’i ’od*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Anantarūpa.

*gzi brjid brtsegs ’od*, Skt. *gzi brjid brtsegs ’od*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Prabhaṃkara (46 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

*brtson ’grus ’od*, Skt. *brtson ’grus ’od*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Jagadraśmi.

*cho ga bzang zhes snang*, Skt. *cho ga bzang zhes snang*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Jyotiṣka.

*spos ’od*, Skt. *spos ’od*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Endowed with Great Ornament.

*dbang po’i rgyal mtshan ’od*, Skt. *dbang po’i rgyal mtshan ’od*, A Licchavi youth present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

*gzi brjid mtha’ yas ’od*, Skt. *gzi brjid mtha’ yas ’od*, Father of the buddha Tejorāja.

*gzi brjid mtha’ yas pa’i ’od*, Skt. *gzi brjid mtha’ yas pa’i ’od*, Birthplace of the buddha Devasūrya.

## limbs of awakening
*byang chub kyi yan lag*, Skt. *bodhyaṅga*, Traditionally there are seven limbs of awakening (saptabodhyaṅga) of an awakened one—mindfulness, discrimination, diligence, joy, pliability, absorption, and equanimity.

## limbs of enlightenment
*byang chub kyi yan lag*, Skt. *bodhyaṅga*, There are seven limbs of enlightenment: correct mindfulness, correct wisdom of the analysis of phenomena, correct diligence, correct joy, correct serenity, correct samādhi, and correct equanimity.

## limit of reality
*yang dag pa’i mtha’*, Skt. *bhūtakoṭi*, A synonym for ultimate reality, emptiness, dharmadhātu, and so forth—as either an ontological reality or a state of being—this compound is typically parsed as the “limit” or “frontier” (koṭi) of “reality” (bhūta), which is intended metaphorically, as it is consistently described, in a play on words, as “without limit” (akoṭi) or “infinite” (atyanta). This compound might also be parsed as the “final” or “true” (bhūta) “conclusion” or “goal” (koṭi), although the majority of cases and the Indian Buddhist commentarial tradition tend to support the former interpretation.

## line
*tshigs bcad*, Skt. *śloka*, The term usually refers to a unit of metrical verse, most commonly in Sanskrit literature a couplet of two sixteen-syllable lines (pāda), each of which can be subdivided into two half-lines of eight syllables. In the Tibetan translations a śloka is usually rendered as a four-line verse. However, the term is also used (especially in catalogs of canonical works) as a unit measuring the length of texts written in prose or in a mixture of prose and verse, in which case it simply measures thirty-two syllables. The titles of the principal Prajñā­pāramitā sūtras, most of which are written in prose, identify them by including mention of their length in ślokas, usually translated in English as “in nnn lines.” The original titles, even in their long form, include only the number itself, and that this refers to the length in ślokas is by convention inferred.

## lineage
*rigs*, Skt. *gotra*, Literally, the class, caste or lineage. In this context, it is the basic disposition or propensity of an individual which determines which kind of vehicle (śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, or bodhisattva) they will follow and therefore which kind of awakening they will obtain. However, in Buddhist literature of the third turning, this same term is used instead as a synonym of buddha-nature (tathāgata­garbha), ie, that all the beings are in fact endowed with the potential or geniture of a buddha’s awakening.

## śloka
*shlo ka*, Skt. *śloka*, The term usually refers to a unit of metrical verse, most commonly in Sanskrit literature a couplet of two sixteen-syllable lines (pāda) each of which can be subdivided into two half-lines of eight syllables. In the Tibetan translations a śloka is usually rendered as a four-line verse. However, the term is also used (especially in catalogues of canonical works) as a unit measuring the length of texts written in prose or in a mixture of prose and verse, in which case it simply measures thirty-two syllables. The titles of the principal Prajñā­pāramitā sūtras, most of which are written in prose, identify them by including mention of their length in ślokas, usually translated in English as “in nnn lines.” The original titles, even in their long form, include only the number itself, and that this refers to the length in ślokas is by convention inferred.

## lokeśvara
*’jig rten dbang phyug*, Skt. *lokeśvara*, “Lokeśvara” is the title applied to Avalokiteśvara and his male emanations, including Amoghapāśa; in the later tradition there are 108 lokeśvaras. In contexts where the literal meaning, “lord of the world,” is more relevant than the class name, the term has been translated as such (see corresponding glossary entry for “lord of the world”). It is capitalized when used as the title without the name, such as “the Lokeśvara” or “the Lord of the World.”

## Lokāyata
*’jig rten rgyang phan pa*, Skt. *lokāyata*, The materialist or “worldly” school, one of the many schools of the Indian śramaṇa movement around at the time of the Buddha. Today most of their literature and discourse has been lost, but their view can be compiled through secondary historical literature and the voices of their critics. According to this, they are claimed to have asserted a rigid materialist philosophy in which everything in the universe is composed of only four elements (earth, water, heat, and air). They rejected the moral causality associated with karma, and they rejected transmigration or rebirth. For more on the Lokāyata philosophy, see Chattopadhaya (1992), pp. 22–75.

## Longchenpa
*klong chen rab 'byams pa* (1308-1363), also called the Omniscient Sovereign or King of [Dharma](#dharma), one of the most extraordinary spiritual masters and scholars of the [Nyingmapa](#nyingmapa) school. He wrote more than 250 treatises covering almost all of Buddhist theory and practice up to the [Great Perfection](#great-perfection), of which he was among the greatest exponents. Among those that have survived are the famous *Seven [Treasure](#treasure)s (mdzod bdun)*, the *Nyingtik Yabzhi (snying tig ya bzhi)*, the *Trilogy of Rest (ngal gso skor gsum)*, the *Trilogy of Natural Freedom (rang grol skor gsum)*, the *Trilogy of Dispelling Darkness (mun sel skor gsum)* and the *Miscellaneous Writings (gsung thor bu)*.

## lord
*bcom ldan ’das*, Skt. *bhagavān*, “Lord” is chosen to translate the title Bhagavān because it is the term of greatest respect current in our “sacred” language, as established for the Deity in the Elizabethan version of the Bible. Indeed, the Skt. Bhagavān was given as a title to the Buddha, although it also served the non-Buddhist Indians of the day and, subsequently, it served as an honorific title of their particular deities. As the Buddha is clearly described in the sūtras as the “Supreme Teacher of Gods and Men,” there seems little danger that he may be confused with any particular deity through the use of this term [as indeed in Buddhist sūtras various deities, creators, protectors, etc., are shown in their respective roles]. Thus I feel it would compromise the weight and function of the original Bhagavān to use any less weighty term than “Lord” for the Buddha.

## love

Immeasurable love arises from the wish for all living beings to have happiness and the causes of happiness.

## loving kindness
*byams pa*, Skt. *maitra*, One of the four immeasurables of the Mahāyāna, known in early Buddhism as “pure abodes” (Skt. brahmavihāra), which comprise (1) loving kindness, (2) compassion, (3) empathetic joy, and (4) impartiality. Immeasurable loving kindness arises from the wish for all living beings to have happiness and the causes of happiness.

## Loving Mind
*rnam par brtse ba’i blo*, Skt. *rnam par brtse ba’i blo*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Puṇyapriya.

## loving-kindness
*byams pa*, Skt. *maitrī*, One of the four practices of spiritual practitioners, and one of the four immeasurables (the other three being compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity).

*nye ba’i dpung pa*, Skt. *nye ba’i dpung pa*, A type of worm (srin bu) that lives in and feeds on the body.

*ngan song*, the [hells](#hell), the [realm](#realm)s of [pretas](#preta) and of animals.

The garment covering the lower body. One of the three Dharma robes (tricīvara, chos gos gsum).

## Lui Gyaltsen
The Tibetan translator who, along with Jñānagarbha, revised the translation of The Prophecy of Dīpaṅkara.

## Lui Wangpo
*klu’i dbang po*, The Tibetan translator of this text, active during the late eight and early ninth centuries. Lui Wangpo was one of the first seven Tibetans to take monastic ordination at the founding of Samyé monastery. He was a member of the Khön family that would later achieve preeminence in Tibet as the leading family of the Sakya school.

## Lumbinī
*lum bi*, Skt. *lumbinī*, The place where the Buddha was born, located in what is now Southern Nepal.

## Lumbini
*lum bi ni*, Skt. *lumbini*, The grove where Śākyamuni was born.

## luminosity
*’od gsal ba*, Skt. *prabhāsvara*, In the context of the nature of mind, luminosity refers to the subtlest level of mind, i.e., the fundamental, essential nature of all cognitive events. Though ever present within all beings, this luminosity becomes manifest only when the gross mind has ceased to function. It is said that such a dissolution is experienced by ordinary beings, naturally, at the time of death, but it can also be experientially cultivated through certain meditative practices.

## luminosity radiates as they walk
*’od kyis gsal bar mdzad cing gshegs pa*, Skt. *prabhā­svara­gāmi­tā*, Sixty-fourth of the eighty minor marks.

## Luminous
*’od gsal*, Skt. *’od gsal*, Luminous (giving off light; bright), also the name of the buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Vidyutprabha (372 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and the pure realms, it is listed as the third of the three heavens that correspond to the second of the four concentrations.

*skar mda’ ’od*, Skt. *skar mda’ ’od*, Son of the buddha Sūryaprabha.

*lhun po’i ’od*, Skt. *lhun po’i ’od*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Siṃhabala.

*bdud rtsi gsal*, Skt. *bdud rtsi gsal*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Jñānakūṭa (598 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## lunar asterism
A constellation of stars through which the moon passes, also known as a lunar mansion.

## lunar day
A single day of the lunar calendar.

## lunar fortnight
One of two halves of the lunar month, either the “bright half” (śuklapakṣa), during which the moon waxes, or the “dark half” (kṛṣṇapakṣa), during which the moon wanes.

## lunar mansion
*rgyu skar*, Skt. *nakṣatra*, The twenty-seven or twenty-eight sectors along the ecliptic that exert influence on individuals and the world according to Indic astrological lore.

*zla ldan dbyangs*, Skt. *zla ldan dbyangs*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Asaṅgadhvaja (863 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

The name of a lunar mansion and a lunar month.

The name of a lunar mansion and a lunar month.

The name of a lunar mansion and a lunar month.
