## Maḍa
A place the north of Paṭṭikeraka with a king named Kamboja.

## Maṇḍa
The name of a city.

## Maṇḍala
*dkyil 'khor*, lit. center and circumference. 1. The universe with the palace of the [deity](#deity) at the center, as visualized in the practice of the [generation phase](#generation-phase). 2. The visualized ideal universe as an offering.

## maṇḍala of consecration in great gnosis
The name of the maṇḍala in The Noble Dhāraṇī of the Eight Goddesses.

## maṇḍala of liberation
*rnam par grol ba’i dkyil ’khor*, Skt. *vimokṣamaṇḍala*, This term seems to refer to any ritual device in itself sufficient to produce liberation; it may thus refer to the entire text of the AP, to an individual rite, to a mantra or a mudrā, or to a set of a corresponding mudrā and mantra.

## maṇḍala of powders
*rdul tshon dkyil ’khor*, Skt. *rajomaṇḍala*, A maṇḍala created with colored powders.

## maṇḍala of wind
Literally, a wheel or disk of wind. This term is found in Buddhist cosmology, where a world system is built on top of various layers, one of which is a vāyumaṇḍala, or a cosmic disk of wind; however, in The Prophecy for Bhadra the Illusionist, the term is used to describe the ten winds that will contribute to the conflagration and destruction of the trichiliocosm at the end of an eon. Also translated as “wind.”

## Maṇḍalin
*dkyil ’khor pa*, Skt. *maṇḍalin*, The shorter form of the name Mahāmaṇḍalin.

## Maṇḍalāsana
*dkyil ’khor stan*, Skt. *maṇḍalāsana*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Maṇḍana
One of the sublineages connected with the Kāśyapa lineage of the brahmanical tradition.

## Maṇḍapa
*’joms pa*, Skt. *maṇḍapa*, A yakṣa general.

## Maṇḍavī
*snying po thob byed*, Skt. *maṇḍavī*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Machik Labdrön
*ma cig lab sgron* (1031-1129), a [disciple](#disciple) of [Padampa Sangye](#padampa-sangye), she became the holder of his instructions on the [Cho](#cho) practice.

## Madā
*rgyags ma*, Skt. *madā*, A great piśācī.

## Madanā
*rgyags byed ma*, Skt. *madanā*, A great piśācī.

## Madanī
*rgyags ma*, Skt. *madanī*, A great rākṣasī.

## Madana
*rgyags pa*, Skt. *madana*, A great ṛṣi.

## Madanasundarī
*’dod pas mdzes ma*, Skt. *madanasundarī*, A deity in Vajrānaṅga’s maṇḍala.

## Madanotsukā
*’dod pa’i lcags kyu*, Skt. *madanotsukā*, A deity in Vajrānaṅga’s maṇḍala.

## Madaprahīṇa
*dregs spang*, Skt. *madaprahīṇa*, The 668th buddha in the first list, 667th in the second list, and 659th in the third list.

## madder
*leb rgan*, Skt. *māñjiṣṭha*, A distinctive shade of red now known as “rose madder,” common in ancient India and derived from the root of the madder plant (Rubia manjista/Rubia tinctorum). According to the Mahāvyutpatti, the Tibetan should be btsod.

## Madhu
*sbrang rtsi*, Skt. *madhu*, A brahmin statesman.

## Madhukara
*sbrang rtsir byed pa*, Skt. *madhukara*, A deity whose dagger is employed in the rituals described in this text. The word madhukara literally means “honey-maker” and the term can also refer to a bee.

## Madhumatī
*sbrang rtsi can*, Skt. *madhumatī*, A river queen.

## Madhura
*’jam snyan*, Skt. *madhura*, Gandharva king present at the teaching of the sūtra.

## Madhura­nirghoṣa
*dbyangs snyan*, Skt. *madhura­nirghoṣa*, One of Māra’s sons who developed faith in Prince Siddhārtha and tried to dissuade Māra from attacking him on the evening of his awakening.

## Madhurasvara
*dbyangs snyan*, Skt. *madhurasvara*, Gandharva king present at the teaching of the sūtra.

## Madhura­svara­rāja
*dbyangs snyan*, Skt. *madhura­svara­rāja*, The 395th buddha in the first list, 394th in the second list, and 388th in the third list.

## Madhusaṃbhava
*sbrang rtsi ’byung*, Skt. *madhusaṃbhava*, The name the merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika will bear when they become buddhas in the future.

## Madhuvaktra
*sbrang rtsi’i zhal*, Skt. *madhuvaktra*, The 487th buddha in the first list, 486th in the second list, and 480th in the third list.

## Madhuvāsiṣṭha
*gnas ’jog sbrang rtsi can*, Skt. *madhuvāsiṣṭha*, A disciple of the Buddha.

## Madhyadeśa
*dbus kyi yul*, Skt. *madhyadeśa*, The “central region,” which seems to refer to all the regions and countries between the Vindhya and Himālaya mountains.

## Madhyama
*bar ma*, Skt. *madhyama*, One of the rāśis.

## Madhyamaka
*dbu ma*, Skt. *madhya­maka*, Derived from the Sanskrit expression madhyamapratipad, meaning the “Middle Way” between the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, Madhyamaka is one of the most influential among the schools of Indian Buddhist philosophy since it emphasizes the deconstruction of all conceptual elaboration and the realization of emptiness. Various sub-schools evolved in India and Tibet, based on distinctions between relative and ultimate truth, the logical methodologies of reduction ad absurdum and syllogistic reasoning, and views concerning the nature of buddha attributes.

## Madhyamakīya
*dbu ma pa*, Skt. *madhyamakīya*, A yakṣa general.

## Madhyandina
*nyi ma’i gung*, Skt. *madhyandina*, A monk who is predicted by the Buddha to appear in the future.

## Madhyānta­vibhāga
*dbus mtha’ rnam ’byed*, Skt. *madhyānta­vibhāga*, The “Analysis of the Middle and the Extremes,” it is an important work of Vijñānavāda philosophy, said to have been received as a revelation from the future Buddha Maitreya by the great scholar and saint, Āryāsaṅga, after twelve years of meditation.

## Madotkaṭā
*rgyags byed ma’i shas che ma*, Skt. *madotkaṭā*, A great piśācī.

## Madrā
*ma drA*, Skt. *madrā*, A land in the south of Jambudvīpa.

## Madra
The name of a people in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent who were located between the Ravi and Chenab rivers in northern Punjab, with Bhadrakāra (or Bhadraṃkāra), present-day Sialkot, as their capital city.

## Madri
*ma dri*, Skt. *madri*, A wife of the bodhisattva in his former rebirth as Sudaṃṣṭra.

## Madtakaṭama
*mad ta ka Ta ma*, Skt. *madtakaṭama*, A peak upon Mount Sumeru.

## Magadha
*ma ga d'ha*, A kingdom on the banks of the Ganges (in the southern part of the modern day Indian state of Bihar), whose capital was at Pāṭaliputra (modern day Patna). During the life of [Śākyamuni](#śākyamuni) [Buddha](#buddha), it was the dominant kingdom in north central India and is home to many of the most important Buddhist sites, including Bodh Gayā, [Nālandā](#nālandā), and its capital [Rājagṛha](#rājagṛha).

## Magadhan
Belonging to Magadha, the region along the southern side of the Ganges River at Pāṭaliputra, covering the southern part of the present-day state of Bihar.

## Magadhan bushel
*ma ga dha’i bre bo*, Skt. *ma ga dha’i bre bo*, A unit of measurement for food and drink in the kingdom of Magadha, made using a container or bushel (Tib. bre bo) of a specific size.

## Magadhan measure
*yul dbus ’gyur tshal gyi bre tshad ma*, Skt. *yul dbus ’gyur tshal gyi bre tshad ma*, A quantity of food measured using a basket or container (Tib. bre) of a specific size, as designated by custom in the kingdom of Magadha.

## Maṅgalā
*bkra shis ma*, Skt. *maṅgalā*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Maṅgala
This seems to be referring to Tashi Lhundrup (bkra shis lhun grub, 1672–1739), the thirty-first abbot of Ngor monastery, whose name, Tashi, corresponds to the Sanskrit maṅgala, or “good fortune.”

## Maṅgalin
*bkra shis ldan*, Skt. *maṅgalin*, The 989th buddha in the first list, 988th in the second list, and 980th in the third list.

## Maṅgalāvahā
*bkra shis byed ma*, Skt. *maṅgalāvahā*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Maṅgalya
*bkra shis*, Skt. *maṅgalya*, A nāga king.

## Magandhari
The name of a market town.

## Maghā
*mchu*, Skt. *maghā*, A constellation in the south, personified as a semidivine being. Here called upon for protection.

## Maghavan
Skt. *maghavan*, “God of Bounty,” an epithet of Indra.

## magical abilities
Also rendered here as “magical powers.”

## magical accomplishment
*dngos grub*, Skt. *siddhi*, See “accomplishment.”

## magical creation
A noun derived from the verb mā, (“to create”) and connected to the term māyā (“magical illusion”).

## magical device
*’khrul ’khor*, Skt. *yantra*, A magical diagram; any mechanical tool or device.

## magical display
*sgyu ma*, Skt. *māyā*, Also translated here as “illusion.”

## Magical Display of Māra
*bdud rnam par ’phrul pa*, Skt. *bdud rnam par ’phrul pa*, A being in the Buddha’s assembly.

## magical display that ascertains perfect calm
*rab tu zhi ba rnam par nges pa’i cho ’phrul*, Skt. *rab tu zhi ba rnam par nges pa’i cho ’phrul*, An absorption.

## magical eye
*’phrul gyi mig*, Skt. *divyaṃ cakṣuḥ*, Pre-reform Tibetan term for lha’i mig (“divine eye,” “clairvoyance”) one of the six supramundane powers (Skt. abhijñā) and of the three knowledges (Skt. trividyā): the ability to see things that are far away, mind-made bodies (of enlightened beings and advanced meditators), and the destinies of all beings according to their actions.

## magical power
Various magical abilities developed as the byproduct of meditative concentration (dhyāna). These are closely related to the superknowledges (abhijñā), although knowledge of ṛddhi is listed as one of the five mundane superknowledges, in which case it specifically refers to the magical display of physical marvels such as walking on water, flying, bilocating, and so forth, while the other four refer to psychic abilities. See also “superknowledge.”

## magical powers
See “magical abilitites.”

## magical technique
See “magical abilities.”

## magical transformation
*rdzu ’phrul*, Skt. *ṛddhi*, See “miraculous power.”

## magically created being
A noun derived from the verb mā (“to create”) and connected to the term māyā (“magical illusion”).

## magically created form
Derived from the Sanskrit verb mā (“to measure out”, “to form”, “to create”, “to exhibit”), and thus probably connected to the term māyā (“magical illusion”), a nirmita in this sense is an object or image, often a replica of a person, that has been created through the superhuman power of creating magical illusions.

## Magnificent
*kun nas mdzes pa*, Skt. *kun nas mdzes pa*, Magnificent (impressively beautiful or grand), also the name of a king.

## magnificent sapphires
*mthon ka chen po*, Skt. *mahānīla*, A large and/or deep-blue sapphire.

## magnifying glass
*me shel*, Skt. *arkakānta*, Literally, a “sunstone” or “sun-crystal.” See also .

## magnolia
*tsam pa ka*, Skt. *campaka*, Magnolia campaca.

## Mahī
*chu bo chen po*, Skt. *mahī*, The river Gandakī (a tributary of the Gaṅgā).

## Maha (yoga)
the first of the three higher [yogas](#yoga) according to the classification of the [Dharma](#dharma) into nine [vehicle](#vehicle)s. In this [yoga](#yoga), the main stress is put on the [generation phase](#generation-phase) (*bskyed rim*).

## Mahaka
*chen po pa*, Skt. *mahaka*, One of [Upananda](#upananda)'s two [novice](#novice)s whose homoerotic play led the [Buddha](#buddha) to forbid allowing two [novice](#novice)s to live together.

## Mahāśaṅkha
*dung chen*, Skt. *mahāśaṅkha*, “The great conch shell.” One of the four great treasures and the being who presides over it.

## Mahāśakunī
*bya ma chen mo*, Skt. *mahāśakunī*, One of the great mātṛs.

## Mahāśakuna
*bya chen po*, Skt. *mahāśakuna*, One of the garuḍa kings.

## Mahāśakuni
*la nye can chen po*, Skt. *mahāśakuni*, Another name of Śakuna.

## Maharddhika
*rdzu ’phrul chen po*, Skt. *maharddhika*, One of the kinnara kings.

## Maha­rddhi­prāpta
*’phrul chen thob*, Skt. *maha­rddhi­prāpta*, One of the four garuḍa kings, present at the teaching of the sūtra.

## Mahāśarīra
*lus chen*, Skt. *mahāśarīra*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahauṣadha
*sman chen*, Skt. *mahauṣadha*, Name of a bodhisattva, a hero of a jātaka who was a learned advisor to a king. In the Ummagga jātaka, he skillfully employs violence, but only when it is absolutely necessary to safeguard his country and its people.

## Mahauṣadhi
*sman chen*, Skt. *mahauṣadhi*, The 534th buddha in the first list, 534th in the second list, and 527th in the third list.

## mahābalā
*mthu chen*, Skt. *mahābalā*, A group of goddesses connected to Vajrapāṇi; also, a group of mātṛs attending upon Skanda.

## Mahābala
*stobs pa che*, Skt. *mahābala*, Name of the Buddha Śākyamuni in a past life, when he was a king practicing bodhisattva conduct.

## Mahābalavegadhārin
*stobs chen shugs ’chang*, Skt. *mahābalavegadhārin*, The youngest of the thousand young Veda-reciting pupils of the brahmin Samudrareṇu. The Buddha Ratnagarbha names him the bodhisattva Bhaiṣajya­rāja­jyotirvi­mala and prophesies that he will be the Buddha Roca, the last buddha in the Bhadraka eon, the 1,005th buddha of the eon.

## Mahā­bala­vega­sthāma
*shugs drag stobs chen*, Skt. *mahā­bala­vega­sthāma*, Lord of the garuḍas. Also called Mahāvegadhārin.

## Mahābhadrika
*skal bzang yod chen po*, Skt. *mahābhadrika*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Mahābhairava
An epithet for the deity Mahākāla, as well as the name of a wrathful form of Śiva.

## Mahābhañjapuri
The name of a town.

## Mahābhaya
“Great Peril.” The name of a muhūrta.

## Mahābhāgā
*skal chen*, Skt. *mahābhāgā*, A goddess in this sūtra.

## Mahābhāga
*skal ba chen po*, Skt. *mahābhāga*, A yakṣa king.

## Mahābhāgīratha
*shing rta skal ldan chen po*, Skt. *mahābhāgīratha*, A buddha in the past.

## Mahābhijñā­jñānābhi­bhū
*mngon par shes pa’i ye shes chen pos zil gyis gnon pa*, Skt. *mahābhijñā­jñānābhi­bhū*, A buddha in the distant past. Also the name of a prince in the distant past.

## Mahābhogavatī
*longs spyod che ldan ma*, Skt. *mahābhogavatī*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Mahābāhu
*lag chen*, Skt. *mahābāhu*, The 13th buddha in the first list, 13th in the second list, and 13th in the third list.

## Mahābhuja
*lag pa chen po*, Skt. *mahābhuja*, A yakṣa general.

## Mahābhujaṃga
*lag gis ’gro chen po*, Skt. *mahābhujaṃga*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahābhujaṃgama
*lag ’gro chen po*, Skt. *mahābhujaṃgama*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahābrahmā
*tshangs pa chen po*, Skt. *mahābrahmā*, Lit. “Great Brahmā.” The third of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and pure abodes‍, or Śuddhāvāsa, it is listed as the third of the three heavens that correspond to the first of the four concentrations. See also “Brahmapārṣadya.”

## Mahā­brahmā
*tshangs pa chen po*, Skt. *mahā­brahmā*, Third god realm of form, meaning “great Brahmā.”

## Mahā-Brahmā Heaven
*tshangs chen*, Skt. *mahā­brahmā*, The third of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and the pure realms, it is listed as the third of the three heavens that correspond to the first of the four concentrations.

## Mahābrahma
*tshangs chen*, Skt. *mahābrahma*, The highest of the three paradises that correspond to the first dhyāna in the form realm.

## Mahābrahman
*tshangs pa chen po*, Skt. *mahābrahman*, A class of gods who inhabit the third heaven of the realm of form.

## Mahācakravāḍa
*khor yug chen po*, Skt. *mahācakravāḍa*, This appears to refer to the great circles of mountains that enclose a thousand worlds, each with its own Cakravāḍa.

## Mahācakravāḍa Mountains
Name of a mountain range in Buddhist cosmology.

## Mahācakravartin
*’khor los sgyur ba chen po*, Skt. *mahācakravartin*, One of the mantra deities.

## Mahācakravāla
*khor yug chen po*, Skt. *mahācakravāla*, “Great Cakravāla,” an epithet for the ring of mountains forming the periphery of a world system in Buddhist cosmology.

## Mahācandanagandha
*tsan dan gyi dri chen po*, Skt. *mahā­candana­gandha*, One of the tathāgatas.

## Mahācandra
*zla ba chen po*, Skt. *mahācandra*, A being in this sūtra.

## Mahāceṭī
*bran mo chen mo*, Skt. *mahāceṭī*, ‟Great Servant,” a bhūtinī.

## Mahācīna
*rgyal yul che*, Skt. *mahācīna*, China.

## Mahācunda
*skul byed chen po*, Skt. *mahācunda*, One of the Buddha’s foremost hearer disciples.

## Mahādaṇḍā
*dbyug pa chen mo ma*, Skt. *mahādaṇḍā*, One of the great dūtīs attending upon Lord Vajrapāṇi.

## Mahādaṇḍadharā
*be con ’dzin chen mo*, Skt. *mahādaṇḍadharā*, A being in this sūtra.

## Mahādarśana
*gzigs pa che*, Skt. *mahādarśana*, The 744th buddha in the first list, 743rd in the second list, and 733rd in the third list. The translation is tentative; gzigs pa che and gzigs pa chen po found in list one and three correspond to Mahādarśana, but gzi brjid chen po found in list two would expect *Mahātejas.

## Mahādatta
*phal chen byin pa*, Skt. *mahādatta*, The 247th buddha in the first list, 246th in the second list, and 246th in the third list.

## Mahādevī
*lha mo chen mo*, Skt. *mahādevī*, One of the goddesses associated with Amoghapāśa.

## Mahādeva
*lha chen po*, Skt. *mahādeva*, A wheel-turning king who was the Buddha in a former life. It is also the name of his eldest son and the other eighty-four thousand eldest sons in his line of succession.

## Mahā­deva (Śiva)
*lha chen po*, Skt. *mahā­deva*, An epithet of the god Śiva. Though not in this text, in other texts this term may also appear as an epithet of the Buddha. Alternatively a certain king of Mithilā who lived before the time of Buddha Śākyamuni, see “Mahā­deva (the king).”

## Mahā­deva Mango Grove
*lha chen po’i a mra’i tshal*, Skt. *mahā­deva āmravana*, A certain mango grove in the country of Mithilā where the Buddha once stayed.

## Mahā­deva (the king)
*lha chen po*, Skt. *mahā­deva*, In former times, the king of the city of Mithilā. His two chief ministers were Nanda and Upananda. In other contexts, sometimes an epithet of the god Śiva, see “Mahā­deva.”

## Mahādharaṇīdhara
*sa ’dzin chen po*, Skt. *mahādharaṇīdhara*, “Great Earth Bearer.” One of the bodhisattvas in the entourage of the Buddha Śākyamuni when he taught the girl Vimalaśraddhā.

## Mahādharma
*chos chen*, Skt. *mahādharma*, One of the four kinnara kings.

## Mahādīpaṃkara
*mar me mdzad chen po*, Skt. *mahādīpaṃkara*, One of the most renowned of former Buddhas.

## Maheśākhya
*che bar grags*, Skt. *maheśākhya*, A certain yakṣa, a friend of the Buddha.

## Mahendra
*dbang phyug chen po*, Skt. *mahendra*, Epithet applied to various gods. When used in the plural it refers to a class of gods; also the name of various kings (dealt with in separate entries).

## mahendra fever
A type of powerful fever that is said to be curable only by religious, rather than medical means.

## Mahendradeva
*dbang phyug lha*, Skt. *mahendradeva*, The name of a future buddha in this kalpa.

## Mahendrasena (future king of Kauśāmbī)
*dbang chen sde*, Skt. *mahendrasena*, Foretold as the name of a future monarch of Kauśāmbī, during the time of the Dharma’s disappearance from our world. In either case not to be confused with Mahendra or Mahā­sena, neither Mahendrasena, the King of Videha; Mahendrasena, the prince of Potalaka; or Mahendrasena, the king of Vārāṇasī.

## Mahendrasena (king of Videha)
*dbang chen sde*, Skt. *mahendrasena*, Typically given as the name of the King of Videha, son of King Mahendra, and a previous incarnation of the Buddha. Not to be confused with Mahendra or Mahā­sena; or with Mahendrasena, a future monarch of Kauśāmbī; Mahendrasena, the prince of Potalaka; or Mahendrasena, the king of Vārāṇasī.

## Mahendrasena (king of Vārāṇasī)
*dbang chen sde*, Skt. *mahendrasena*, King of Vārāṇasī, a previous incarnation of the Buddha.

## Mahendrasena (prince of Potalaka)
*dbang chen sde*, Skt. *mahendrasena*, A previous incarnation of the Buddha, who was son of King Mahendra, the ruler of the city of Potalaka. Not to be confused with Mahendra or Mahā­sena., or with Mahendrasena, a future monarch of Kauśāmbī; Mahendrasena, the king of Videha; or Mahendrasena, the king of Vārāṇasī.

## Mahendrasena (queen of Videha)
*dbang chen sde*, Skt. *mahendrasena*, Queen and wife of King Mahendrasena of Videha

## Maheśvarī
One of the eight yoginīs in the Mahākāla maṇḍala described in Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra.

## Mahe­śvara
*dbang phyug chen po*, Skt. *mahe­śvara*, A god who rules over the heavenly pure abodes.

## Maheśvara
*dbang phyug chen po*, Skt. *maheśvara*, One of the most frequently used names for Śiva. A deity of the jungles, named Rudra in the Vedas, he rose to prominence in the Purāṇic literature at the beginning of the first millennium. Often synonymous with Īśvara, but sometimes presented as a separate deity.

## Maheśvara-Mahādeva
*dbang phyug chen po’i lha chen po*, Skt. *maheśvara-mahādeva*, ‟Great Lord Mahādeva,” one of the epithets of Śiva.

## Maheśvaraśrī
*dbang phyud chen po’i dpal*, Skt. *maheśvaraśrī*, A tathāgata.

## Maheśvarāntaś­cara
*dbang phyug chen po’i nang spyod*, Skt. *maheśvarāntaś­cara*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Maheśvāsa
*dbugs ’byin chen po*, Skt. *maheśvāsa*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Mahāgaṇapati
*tshogs kyi bdag po chen po*, Skt. *mahāgaṇapati*, An epithet of Gaṇeśa, the elephant-headed god invoked to remove obstacles.

## Mahāgandhakusuma
*me tog dri chen*, Skt. *mahāgandhakusuma*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahāgaurī
*dkar sham chen mo*, Skt. *mahāgaurī*, Here a Buddhist goddess, possibly related to the Śaiva goddess Gaurī.

## Mahāgayākāśyapa
*ga ya ’od srung chen po*, Skt. *mahā­gayākāśyapa*, Alternate name of Gayākāśyapa, the brother of Nadīkāśyapa and Uruvilvākāśyapa. A practitioner of fire offering at Uruvilvā (Bodhgaya), he and his two hundred pupils were converted to becoming bhikṣus (monks) under the Buddha. He and his brothers and their pupils were the third group to become followers of the Buddha Śākyamuni after his awakening.

## Mahāghoṣa
*sgra chen*, Skt. *mahāghoṣa*, A nāga king. (Toh 555: sgra bo che)

## Mahā­ghoṣa­svara­rāja
*sgra chen po’i dbyangs kyi rgyal po*, Skt. *mahā­ghoṣa­svara­rāja*, A great bodhisattva.

## Mahāghora
*drag po chen po*, Skt. *mahāghora*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahāgiri
*ri bo chen po*, Skt. *mahāgiri*, Name of a yakṣa.

## Mahā­govinda
*khyab ’jug chen po*, Skt. *mahā­govinda*, See “Guardian of the Flame Govinda.”

## Mahāgrāsa
*kham po che*, Skt. *mahāgrāsa*, A yakṣa king. (Toh 557: kam po ji (corrupt), Toh 555: mchog tu rgyal ba)

## Mahiṣī
*ma he mo*, Skt. *mahiṣī*, A great rākṣasī.

## Mahiṣa
*ma he*, Skt. *mahiṣa*, One of the rāśis.

## Mahikṣikā
*ma hi ShI kA*, Skt. *mahikṣikā*, A land to the north of Jambudvīpa.

## Mahiṣmatī
*ma he ldan*, Skt. *mahiṣmatī*, A city.

## Mahindhara
*sa ’dzin*, Skt. *mahindhara*, One of the sixteen gods guarding the seat of awakening.

## Mahita
*mchod pa*, Skt. *mahita*, The 255th buddha in the first list, 254th in the second list, and 254th in the third list.

## Mahājana
*ma hA dza na*, Skt. *mahājana*, A Kashmiri paṇḍita active in Tibet in the eleventh century.

## Mahākṛṣṇa
*nag po chen po*, Skt. *mahākṛṣṇa*, A nāga king.

## Mahākapila
*ser po chen po*, Skt. *mahākapila*, The name of a bodhisattva present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahākapphiṇa
*ka pi la na chen po*, Skt. *mahākapphiṇa*, One of the monks attending this teaching in Śrāvastī, at Jeta’s Grove.

## Mahākara
*’od zer chen po*, Skt. *mahākara*, A buddha in the past.

## Mahākarṇa
*rna bo che*, Skt. *mahākarṇa*, Name of a yakṣa general.

## Mahākaruṇa
*thugs rje chen po*, Skt. *mahākaruṇa*, Name of a thus-gone one.

## Mahā­karuṇa­megha­dhvaja
*thugs rje chen po’i sprin gyi rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *mahā­karuṇa­megha­dhvaja*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Mahā­karuṇa­megha­śrī
*snying rje chen po’i sprin gyi dpal*, Skt. *mahā­karuṇa­megha­śrī*, The seventieth buddha in a kalpa in the distant past. BHS in verse: Mahā­karuṇa­megha­śirī.

## Mahā­karuṇā­candrin
*snying rje cher sems*, Skt. *mahā­karuṇā­candrin*, One of the bodhisattvas attending this teaching in Śrāvastī, at Jeta’s Grove.

## Mahā­karuṇā­cinta
*snying rje cher sems*, Skt. *mahā­karuṇā­cinta*, A bodhisattva great being present in the audience of this sūtra.

## Mahā­karuṇā­cintin
*snying rje chen po sems*, Skt. *mahā­karuṇā­cintin*, A prince who was a pupil of Buddha Abhāva­samudgata countless eons ago.

## Mahā­karuṇānaya­megha­nigarjita­ghoṣa
*snying rje chen po’i tshul gyi sprin rab tu sgrog pa’i dbyangs*, Skt. *mahā­karuṇānaya­megha­nigarjita­ghoṣa*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## Mahā­karuṇā­siṃha
*thugs rje chen po’i seng ge*, Skt. *mahā­karuṇā­siṃha*, The third of five hundred buddhas in a future kalpa.

## Mahā­karuṇā­vairocana­saumya
*snying rje chen po rnam par snang byed*, Skt. *Mahā­karuṇā­vairocana­saumya*, Literally “The Peaceful Illumination of Great Compassion.”A bodhisattva who was the kalyāṇamitra and benefactor of the tathāgata Ratnagarbha. He now resides in the world realm Aṅguṣṭhā.

## Mahākauṣṭhila
*mdzod ldan chen po*, Skt. *mahākauṣṭhila*, One of the foremost śrāvaka disciples of the Buddha, known for his analytical reasoning.

## Mahākauṣṭhilya
*gsus po che*, Skt. *mahākauṣṭhilya*, A great śrāvaka included in the audience of this sūtra.

## Mahāketu
*me tog chen po*, Skt. *mahāketu*, Lit. “Great Flower.” Name that three hundred monks will bear when they become buddhas, during the eon called Tārakopama, due to dressing the body of the Buddha and producing the thought of awakening while attending this teaching.

## Mahāketudhvaja
*tog chen po’i rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *mahāketudhvaja*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahākhya
*grags pa chen po*, Skt. *mahākhya*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Mahākālī
*nag mo che*, Skt. *mahākālī*, One of the goddesses invited to partake in the oblation offering.

## Mahākāla
*nag po chen po*, Skt. *mahākāla*, Mahākāla is a wrathful Buddhist protector deity. In Tibetan, the name Mahākāla was mostly translated literally with nag po chen po (“Great Black One”) but on occasion it was rendered mgon po nag po (“Black Lord”). In Toh 440, for which the Sanskrit is extant, we have an attested example of this. Hence we have rendered both Tibetan terms in this text as Mahākāla. Outside the Buddhist tradition, Mahākāla is also a name for a wrathful form of Śiva.

## Mahākāla Who Controls the Life Breath of Living Beings
*skye ’gro sems can rnams kyi srog dbugs la dbang byed pa’i nag po chen po*, An epithet for the deity Mahākāla.

## Mahākośa
*mdzod mang po*, Skt. *mahākośa*, The cakravartin king who was the father of Buddha Mahābhijñā­jñānābhi­bhū.

## Mahākoṣavatī
*mdzod chen por gnas*, Skt. *mahākoṣavatī*, This appears to be an epithet of Paṇḍaravāsinī, the consort of Amitābha.

## Mahākrodha
*khro bo chen po*, Skt. *mahākrodha*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi; an epithet of Yamāntaka; an epithet of Yamāri; the name of a boar-faced emanation of Mañjuśrī.

## Mahākāruṇika
*thugs rje chen po dang ldan pa*, Skt. *mahākāruṇika*, The bodhisattva name given to the brahmin Samudrareṇu (who would eventually become the Buddha Śākyamuni) on account of his great compassion for beings. It means “One Who Has Great Compassion.”

## Mahākātyāyanī
*ka ta ya na chen mo*, Skt. *mahākātyāyanī*, ‟Great Kātyāyanī,” one of the eight kātyāyanī spirits.

## Mahākātyāyana
*ka tya’i bu chen po*, Skt. *mahākātyāyana*, (also Kātyāyana). Disciple of the Buddha noted for his skill in analysis of the Buddha’s discourses and, traditionally, the founder of the Abhidharma.

## Mahā­kātyāyana
*kA tyA’i bu chen po*, Skt. *mahā­kātyāyana*, One of the hearers present during the delivery of the sūtra.

## Mahākātyāyanaputra
One of the ten principal pupils of the Buddha, he was renowned for his ability to understand and explaining the Buddha’s teachings.

## Mahākāya
*lus chen*, Skt. *mahākāya*, One of the garuḍa kings present at the teaching of the sūtra.

## Mahākāśyapa
*'od srung chen po*, one of the foremost [śrāvaka](#śrāvaka) [disciple](#disciple)s of [Buddha](#buddha) [Śākyamuni](#śākyamuni), and chief among the first compilers of the [Abhidharma](#abhidharma). After the [Buddha](#buddha) had left this world, he became the first patriarch of the [Dharma](#dharma), entrusted with the responsibility for maintaining the teachings and the [Saṅgha](#saṅgha).

## Mahā­kāśyapa
*’od srung chen po*, Skt. *mahā­kāśyapa*, A monk of Buddha Śākyamuni’s order who was first in the apostolic succession that carried on Lord Buddha’s teaching after his parinirvāṇa. Also rendered here simply as “Kāśyapa.” Not to be confused with Buddha Kāśyapa, nor with Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, Nadī Kāśyapa, or Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, nor with Nirgrantha Kāśyapa, nor Foremost Kāśyapa.

## Mahāla
*smra ’dzin*, Skt. *mahāla*, One of the twelve great yakṣa generals who protect and serve those who bear, read, recite, copy, or commission a copy of the Bhaiṣajya­guru­vaiḍūrya­prabha­rāja­sūtra.

## Mahāśūla
*gzer nad chen po*, Skt. *mahāśūla*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Mahālakṣmī
*dpal chen mo*, Skt. *mahālakṣmī*, One of the vidyās attending upon Mañjuśrī.

## Mahālakuṭa
*dbyig pa chen po*, Skt. *mahālakuṭa*, One of the kings of the nāgas.

## Mahāmaṇḍalika
*dkyil ’khor chen po can*, Skt. *mahāmaṇḍalika*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahāmaṇḍalin
*dkyil ’khor chen po*, Skt. *mahāmaṇḍalin*, One of the nāga kings.

## Mahāmaṇicūḍa
*gtsug na nor bu chen po*, Skt. *mahāmaṇicūḍa*, A great nāga king.

## Mahā­maitryudgata
*byams pa chen pos ’phags pa*, Skt. *mahā­maitryudgata*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## mahāmañjūṣaka
*man dzu sha ka chen po*, Skt. *mahāmañjūṣaka*, A large celestial tree famed for its fragrance and beautiful flowers.

## Mahāmanasvin
*gzi can chen po*, Skt. *mahāmanasvin*, A nāga king.

## mahāmandārava
*man dA ra ba chen po*, Skt. *mahāmandārava*, Great coral tree.

## Mahāmati
*blo gros chen po*, Skt. *mahāmati*, A bodhisattva present during the delivery of the King of the Array of all Dharma Qualities.

## Mahāmati (the king)
*blo gros chen po*, Skt. *mahāmati*, A king in the distant past.

## Mahāmati (the upāsaka)
*blo gros chen po*, Skt. *mahāmati*, An upāsaka in Dhanyākara.

## Mahāmaudgalyāyana
One of the two chief śrāvaka disciples of the Buddha Śākyamuni, along with Śāriputra. He is also referred to as Maudgalyāyana. According to Pāli sources Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra were both older than the Buddha and childhood friends. They together renounced the world and became mendicants, spending much of their life searching for a teacher until Śāriputra encountered the Buddha’s disciple Aśvajit and heard the famous ye dharmā verse (see The Sūtra on Dependent Arising, Toh 212, ). Śāriputra immediately attained the path of a stream enterer (srota-āpanna), and when he repeated the verse to Maudgalyāyana the latter attained it as well. The two soon went forth in the Buddha’s teachings, becoming arhats and the two chief disciples of the Buddha. Mahāmaudgalyāyana is considered foremost among the Buddha’s disciples in terms of his ability in magical powers (ṛddhi), and there are many accounts describing his magical displays such as flying and creating multiple forms of himself. Maudgalyāyana is an interlocutor in many Mahāyāna sūtras. Pali: Mahāmoggallāna

## Mahā­maudgalyāyana
*maud gal gyi bu chen po*, Skt. *mahā­maudgalyāyana*, One of the two principal pupils of the Buddha, along with Śariputra. He was renowned for miraculous powers. He was assassinated during the Buddha’s lifetime.

## Mahā­maudgalyā­yana
*maud gal gyi bu chen po*, Skt. *mahā­maudgalyā­yana*, One of the Buddha’s foremost hearer disciples. Also known as Maudgalyāyana.

## Mahā­maud­galyā­yana
*maud gal gyi bu*, Skt. *maud­galyā­yana*, A close hearer disciple of the Buddha, reknowned for his miraculous powers. Also rendered here just as “Maud­galyā­yana.”

## Mahāmegha
*sprin chen po*, Skt. *mahāmegha*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Mahāmeghagarbha
*sprin chen snying po*, Skt. *mahāmeghagarbha*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahāmeghaśrī
*sprin chen po’i dpal*, Skt. *mahāmeghaśrī*, A tathāgata.

## Mahāmeghāmbuda
*chu sbyin sprin chen*, Skt. *mahāmeghāmbuda*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahāmekhalā
*’og pag chen mo*, Skt. *mahāmekhalā*, One of the goddesses in one of the paintings of Mañjuśrī.

## Mahāmeru
*lhun po chen po*, Skt. *mahāmeru*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## Mahā­meru­prabhāsa
*lhun po chen po snang ba*, Skt. *mahā­meru­prabhāsa*, Name of a tathāgata.

## Mahāmitra
*bshes gnyen chen po*, Skt. *mahāmitra*, The 879th buddha in the first list, 878th in the second list, and 869th in the third list.

## Mahāmānāsī
*yid las byung chen po*, Skt. *mahāmānāsī*, A being in this sūtra.

## Mahāmārī
*’ching chen po*, Skt. *mahāmārī*, A goddess of pestilence; pestilence personified.

## Mahāmucilinda
*btang bzung chen po*, Skt. *mahāmucilinda*, An unidentified mountain mentioned in a number of sūtras, not apparently connected to the well known nāga of that name (who is also known as Mucilinda), but perhaps to the sacred mucilinda tree, known in English mainly as the bayur tree.

## Mahā­muci­linda
*btang bzung chen po*, Skt. *mahā­muci­linda*, One of ten “kings of mountains” according to Abhidharma cosmology.

## Mahāmudrā
*phyag rgya chen po*, lit. Great Seal. The Great Seal [means](#means) that the seal of the absolute nature is on everything, that all phenomena belong to the [wisdom](#wisdom) [maṇḍala](#maṇḍala). This term can be used to denote the teaching, meditation practice or [supreme accomplishment](#supreme-accomplishment). See [practics instructions](https://www.lotsawahouse.org/indian-masters/tilopa/ganges-mahamudra-instruction)

## mahāmudrā siddhi
This term refers to spontaneous union with the deity and the transformation of one’s own body, speech, and mind into a the body, speech, and mind of the deity.

## mahāmudra
*phyag rgya chen po*, Skt. *mahāmudra*, A very advanced practice that combines wisdom and means.

## Mahāmāyā
*sgyu ’phrul chen mo*, Skt. *mahāmāyā*, The female central deity of the Mahā­māyā Tantra who appears in the form of the male Heruka. She was also a popular form of the Brahmanical great goddess (Mahādevī), to whom the Buddhist figure is intimately related. Also rendered here as “Great Illusion.”

## Mahā­māyā
*sgyu ’phrul chen mo*, Skt. *mahā­māyā*, Buddha Śākyamuni’s mother. She and her sister Māyā both married King Śuddhodana of Kapilavastu. Here she is said to be the daughter of Śākya Suprabuddha. In other stories, Mahā­māyā is alternatively said to be the daughter of King Āñjāna of Devaḍaha. Also called “Mahā­māyādevī” and “Māyādevī.”

## Mahāmāyādevī
*lha mo sgyu ’phrul chen mo*, Skt. *mahāmāyādevī*, The mother of the Buddha.

## Mahā­māyādevī
*lha mo sgyu ’phrul chen mo*, Skt. *mahā­māyādevī*, See “Mahā­māyā.”

## Mahāmāyūrī
*rma bya chen mo*, Skt. *mahāmāyūrī*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode; one of the five Pañcarakṣā goddesses.

## Mahānanda
*dga’ byed chen po*, Skt. *mahānanda*, The name of a garuḍa in his past life as a monk-student of the Buddha Kanakamuni.

## Mahānandi
The name of a goddess in the Mahākāla maṇḍala described in Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra.

## Mahānarthā
Skt. *mahānarthā*, One of the great dūtīs attending upon Lord Vajrapāṇi.

## Mahānāga
*klu chen*, Skt. *mahānāga*, A deity.

## Mahānirnādanādin
*cher sgrogs*, Skt. *mahānirnādanādin*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahānāma
*ming chen*, Skt. *mahānāma*, One of the monks attending this teaching in Śrāvastī, at Jeta’s Grove. He was one of the five companions who joined Prince Siddhārtha while practicing austerities and attended his first turning of the wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park, after the Buddha’s awakening.

## Mahānāman
*ming chen*, Skt. *mahānāman*, One of the Five Excellent Companions, with whom Siddhārtha Gautama practiced asceticism near the Nairañjanā River and who later heard the [Buddha](#buddha) first teach the Four Noble Truths at the Deer [Park](#park) in Sarnath.

## Mahā­nārāyaṇa
*sred med kyi bu chen po*, Skt. *mahā­nārāyaṇa*, A powerful deity of the desire realm, more commonly known as Viṣṇu.

## mahāntara
An unidentified ritual ingredient.

## Mahoṣadhī
*sman chen po*, Skt. *mahoṣadhī*, A pore on Avalokiteśvara’s body.

## Mahodaya
Skt. *mahodaya*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Mahoja
*gzi brjid chen po*, Skt. *mahoja*, One of the kinnara kings; one of the rāśis.

## Mahojas
*gzi brjid chen po*, Skt. *mahojas*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Mahojaska
*gzi brjid chen po can*, Skt. *mahojaska*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

*sgron ma chen po ’dzin pa*, Skt. *maholkādhārin*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Mahollūkhala
*gtum chen*, Skt. *mahollūkhala*, A yakṣa general.

## mahoragī
A female mahoraga.

## mahoraga
*lto ’phyed*, Skt. *mahoraga*, Literally “large serpent.” A semidivine being that takes the form of a large serpent, sometimes with a human torso and head. They are a class of subterranean geomantic spirits whose movement through the seasons and months of the year is deemed significant for construction projects.

## Mahoraska
*brang chen po*, Skt. *mahoraska*, One of the kinnara kings.

## mahorāga
*lto ’phye chen po*, Skt. *mahorāga*, Literally “large serpent.” A nonhuman being that takes the form of a large serpent, sometimes with a human torso and head. They make up a class of subterranean geomantic spirits whose movement through the seasons and months of the year is deemed significant for construction projects.

## Mahotsāha
*spro ba che ba*, Skt. *mahotsāha*, One of the bodhisattva great beings.

## Mahāpāśa
*zhags pa chen po*, Skt. *mahāpāśa*, Mahāpāśa (“Great Noose”) seems to be another epithet of Amoghapāśa.

## Mahāpadmā
*pad chen*, Skt. *mahāpadmā*, ‟The Great Lotus,” one of the eight great bhūtinīs.

## Mahāpadma
*pad ma chen po*, King of [Magadha](#magadha) at the time of the [Buddha](#buddha)’s birth, husband of Queen [Bimbī](#bimbī), and father of [Bimbisāra](#bimbisāra).

## Mahāpadminī
*ma hA pad+ma ma Ni*, Skt. *mahāpadminī*, One of the eight nāga queens.

*yongs su mya ngan las ’das pa chen po*, Skt. *mahāparinirvāṇa*, Synonym of “parinirvāṇa.”

## mahā­parinirvāṇa
*yongs su mya ngan las ’das pa chen po*, Skt. *mahā­parinirvāṇa*, A specialized term for nirvāṇa when it is used in reference to the apparent passing away of a physical body of a buddha.

## Mahāpaśupati
*phyugs bdag chen po*, Skt. *mahāpaśupati*, An epithet of Śiva.

## Mahāpaśyinī
*mthong ldan chen mo*, Skt. *mahāpaśyinī*, One of the great dūtīs attending upon Lord Vajrapāṇi.

*gdengs ka chen*, Skt. *mahāphaṇaka*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

*chos skyong*, Skt. *mahāpāla*, A yakṣa king.

*gru bzang*, Skt. *mahāpota*, Another name of the king Mahendra.

*rdzogs chen*, Skt. *mahāpūrṇa*, One of the four garuḍa kings, present at the teaching of the sūtra.

## Mahāprabha
*rgya chen po’i ’od*, Skt. *mahāprabha*, The name of one of the bodhisattvas in the Buddha Śākyamuni’s presence in Śrāvastī in chapter 1 (where it is translated as rgya chen po’i ’od), and the name of the king, one of Sudhana’s kalyāṇamitras, in chapter 22 (where it is translated as ’od chen po).

*’od chen po*, Skt. *mahāprabhasa*, A city in South India.

*rab tu cher gtums*, Skt. *mahāpracaṇḍa*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

*smon lam chen po shugs kyi dpal*, Skt. *mahā­praṇidhi­vega­śrī*, The ninety-eighth buddha in a kalpa in the distant past. BHS in verse: Mahā­praṇidhi­vega­śiri.

*smon lam chen po*, Skt. *mahāpraṇidhāna*, A great bodhisattva.

## Mahāpāraṇika
*pha rol tu ’gro ba chen po*, Skt. *mahāpāraṇika*, One of the monks attending this teaching in Śrāvastī, at Jeta’s Grove.

## Mahāprajñā
*shes rab chen mo*, Skt. *mahāprajñā*, An upāsikā in Dhanyākara.

## Mahāprajña
*shes rab chen po*, Skt. *mahāprajña*, An upāsaka in Dhanyākara.

## Mahāprajāpatī
*skye dgu’i bdag mo chen mo*, Skt. *mahāprajāpatī*, The Buddha’s mother’s sister and his stepmother. She was also the mother of Nanda, whom the Buddha later inspired to become a monk, as recorded in two sūtras bearing his name and elsewhere. She became the first bhikṣuṇī after the death of the Buddha’s father.

## Mahā­prajāpatī
*skye dgu’i bdag mo chen mo gau ta mI*, Skt. *mahā­prajāpatī gautamī*, See “Mahā­prajāpatī Gautamī.”

## Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī
*skye dgu’i bdag mo chen mo gau ta mI*, Skt. *mahāprajāpatī gautamī*, The Buddha’s mother’s sister and his step-mother. She was the mother of Nanda. She became the first bhikṣuṇī after the death of the Buddha’s father. Gautamī is the family name, the female equivalent to Gautama. The family line is said to descend from the Gautama who was one of the seven rishis that established the religion and culture of India. His sūtra specifies that a renunciant should be called a bhikṣu, have a shaved head, and wear yellow robes. Also rendered here simply as “Mahāprajāpatī.”

## Mahā­prajāpatī Gautamī
*skye dgu’i bdag mo chen mo gau ta mI*, Skt. *mahā­prajāpatī gautamī*, Siddhārtha Gautama’s aunt, who raised him following his mother’s death and who later became the first woman to go forth as a member of Buddha Śākyamuni’s monastic saṅgha. Also rendered here as “Mahā­prajāpatī.”

## Mahā­prajñā­tīrtha
*shes rab chen po’i stegs*, Skt. *mahā­prajñā­tīrtha*, The 747th buddha in the first list, 746th in the second list, and 736th in the third list.

## Mahāpraṇālin
*yur chen can*, Skt. *mahāpraṇālin*, A yakṣa king. (Toh 556 Degé: yul chen can; Toh 557 Degé: yul chen can; Toh 555: pra na li chen)

## Mahāprasandaya
*rab tu che bstsags*, Skt. *mahāprasandaya*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## Mahāpratibhāna
*spobs pa chen po*, Skt. *mahāpratibhāna*, A bodhisattva who appears mainly in chapters 11 and 12 of this sūtra. In the Chinese version, like other bodhisattvas who appear in the second half of the sūtra, considered to be of a later date than the first half, he is not in the initial list of bodhisattvas given in the first chapter.

## Mahāpratisarā
*ma hA pR ti sA re*, Skt. *mahāpratisarā*, In the Sampuṭodbhava, this deity is invoked to help obtain a son.

## Mahāpravarṣaka
*rab tu char ’bebs chen po*, Skt. *mahāpravarṣaka*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Mahāpriya
*dgyes chen*, Skt. *mahāpriya*, The 462nd buddha in the first list, 461st in the second list, and 455th in the third list.

## Mahāpura
*grong khyer che*, Skt. *mahāpura*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Mahāpuruṣasamaya
*skyes bu chen po’i dam tshig*, Skt. *mahā­puruṣa­samaya*, An epithet or name of a bhagavat in The Tantra of Black Yamāri.

## Mahāśrī
*dpal chen mo*, Skt. *mahāśrī*, Name of a goddess more prevalent in the brahmanical tradition, where she is a consort of Viṣṇu. She is the subject of The Sūtra of Mahāśrī and The Twelve Names of the Goddess Śrī (Toh 741/1006), where twelve of her epithets are listed.

## Mahāraśmi
*’od zer che*, Skt. *mahāraśmi*, The 377th buddha in the first list, 376th in the second list, and 371st in the third list.

## Mahā­raśmi­jālāvabhāsa­garbha
*’od zer gyi dra ba chen po rab tu snang ba’i snying po*, Skt. *mahā­raśmi­jālāvabhāsa­garbha*, A bodhisattva mahāsattva.

## Mahāraśmiskandha
*’od zer gyi phung po chen po*, Skt. *mahā­raśmi­skandha*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Mahāratha
*The king of siddha*, Skt. *mahāratha*, The king of siddhas (semidivine beings).

## Mahāratnī
*rin po che*, Skt. *mahāratnī*, ‟The Great Jewel,” one of the eight great bhūtinīs.

## Mahāratnaketu
*rin po che’i tog chen po*, Skt. *mahāratnaketu*, A bodhisattva. (Toh 555: Mahāratnadhvaja; rin po che’i rgyal mtshan chen po)

## Mahāraurava
*ngu ’bod chen po*, Skt. *mahāraurava*, The fourth of the hot hells in Buddhism. The name in Tibetan means “weeping and wailing.”

## Mahārciskandha
*’od ’phro’i phung po chen po*, Skt. *mahārciskandha*, Name of a tathāgata.

## Mahārciskandhin
*’od ’phro chen po’i phung po*, Skt. *mahārciskandhin*, A thus-gone one to whom the Bodhisattva made offerings in a past life.

## Mahāśrīdevī
*dpal gyi lha mo chen mo*, Skt. *mahāśrīdevī*, Epithet of Lakṣmī, Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity and consort of Viṣṇu.

## Mahārhata
*mang pos mchod ’os*, Skt. *mang pos mchod ’os*, A merchant (lit. “Fit to be Honored by Many”). Identical with Rūpavati.

## Mahāśāriputra
*shA ri’i bu chen po*, Skt. *mahāśāriputra*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Mahāśriyā
*dpal byed chen mo*, Skt. *mahāśriyā*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Mahārājā
*rgyal po che*, Skt. *mahārājā*, One of the eight goddesses in the north, called upon to grant protection.

## mahārāja
*rgyal po chen po*, Skt. *mahārāja*, Literally means “great king.” In addition to referring to human kings, this is also the epithet for the four deities on the base of Mount Meru, each one the guardian of his direction: Vaiśravaṇa in the north, Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east, Virūpākṣa in the west, and Virūḍhaka in the south.

## Mahā­rāja
*rgyal po chen po*, Skt. *mahā­rāja*, Four deities at the base of Sumeru, each one the guardian of his direction: Vaiśravaṇa in the north, Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east, Virūpākṣa in the west, and Virūḍhaka in the south.

## Mahārājamati
*rgyal chen blo gros*, Skt. *mahārājamati*, A bodhisattva.

## Mahārūpa
*gzugs chen po*, Skt. *mahārūpa*, “Great Form.” The name of a past eon.

## Mahārti
*nyam thag pa chen po*, Skt. *mahārti*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## mahāśrāvaka
*nyan thos chen po*, Skt. *mahāśrāvaka*, An epithet for the Buddha’s principal students who had attained the goal of the path.

## Mahāsaṃbhavā
*cher ’byung ba*, Skt. *mahāsaṃbhavā*, A world realm in the distant past.

## Mahāsaṃbhava
*’byung ba chen po*, Skt. *mahāsaṃbhava*, A town in the south of India.

## Mahāsaṅghika order
*phal chen gyi sde*, Skt. *mahā­saṅghika*, One of the four main monastic orders of Indian Buddhism.

## Mahāsama
One of the lineages within the Sāmaveda branch of the brahmanical tradition.

## Mahāsamantabhadra
*kun tu bzang po chen po*, Skt. *mahā­samantabhadra*, A being in this sūtra.

## Mahāsamaya
*dam tshig chen po*, Skt. *mahāsamaya*, A being in this sūtra.

## Mahā­samayoṣṇīṣa
*dam tshig thogs pa med pa gtsug tor*, Skt. *mahā­samayoṣṇīṣa*, One of the mantra deities.

## Mahāsammata
Meaning "the Great Elect," they are the first farmer monarch of the world in Buddhist tradition. Elected by the people to rule according to Dhamma, they founded the dynasty of the historical [Buddha](#buddha), established state order, and compiled the first law treatise.

## Mahāsannipāta
*’dus pa chen po*, Skt. *mahāsannipāta*, A collection of seventeen sūtras on a range of themes, compiled as a separate collection. Today, this collection only exists in Chinese translation, although several of the individual scriptures exist in Sanskrit and in Tibetan translation.

## Mahāsanārcis
*’od ’phro chen pos bzhugs pa*, Skt. *mahāsanārcis*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## mahāsattva
*sems dpa’ chen po*, Skt. *mahāsattva*, In chapter 4 of this text (see ) the Buddha Ratnagarbha states that bodhisattvas who have vowed to attain awakening under relatively easier circumstances do not deserve the title mahāsattva, which should be reserved for those like Mahākāruṇika who have vowed to attain awakening only in the most degenerate and difficult times and places. However, this statement is best taken as highlighting a specific point of perspective rather than as a general gloss, since throughout the text the term is nevertheless used—just as it is in most Mahāyāna sūtras—as an epithet for bodhisattvas in general regardless of their individual status, qualities, or aspirations.

## Mahāsenā
*sde chen ma*, Skt. *mahāsenā*, (1) The wife of the householder Mahāsena and lay follower of the Buddha. (2) The wife of a householder in a former life of a person with the same name.

## Mahāsena
*sde chen*, Skt. *mahāsena*, (1) A householder and lay follower of the Buddha. (2) A householder in a former life of a person with the same name.

## Mahā­sena
*sde chen po*, Skt. *mahā­sena*, King of the city of Ayodhyā before the time of Buddha Śākyamuni. Not to be confused with Mahendra or Mahendrasena.

## Mahāsāṃghika
*dge ’dun phal chen po’i sde*, Skt. *mahāsāṃghika*, One of the early schools of Buddhism, within which views such as the transcendence of the Buddha formed the basis for the rise of Mahāyāna.

## Mahāsiddha
*grub chen*, a [yogī](#yogī-or-yoginī) who has reached the [supreme accomplishment](#supreme-accomplishment).

## Mahā­siṃha­tejas
*seng ge’i gzi brjid chen po*, Skt. *mahā­siṃha­tejas*, A buddha in the past.

## Mahāskandha
A buddha in the distant past.

## Mahāskhanda
*dpung mgo chen po*, Skt. *mahāskhanda*, A buddha.

## Mahāsārathi
“Great Charioteer.” A bodhisattva in the Buddha’s retinue.

## Mahāsārthavāha
*ded dpon chen po*, Skt. *mahāsārthavāha*, A great bodhisattva.

## Mahāsthāman
*mthu chen*, Skt. *mahāsthāman*, The 372nd buddha in the first list, 371st in the second list, and 366th in the third list.

## Mahāsthāmaprāpta
*mthu chen thob*, Skt. *mahāsthāmaprāpta*, One of the two principal bodhisattvas in Sukhāvatī and prominent in Chinese Buddhism. In Tibetan Buddhism he is identified with Vajrapāṇi, though they are separate bodhisattvas in the sūtras. The second of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin, on becoming a bodhisattva, is given the name Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and as such in the future will be in Sukhāvatī as that bodhisattva when his father becomes the Buddha Amitābha. He will eventually become the Buddha Supra­tiṣṭhita­guṇa­maṇikūṭa­rāja in that realm.

## Mahāsthāma­prāpta
*mthu chen po thob pa*, Skt. *mahāsthāma­prāpta*, One of the two principal bodhisattvas in Sukhāvatī and prominent in Chinese Buddhism. In Tibetan Buddhism he is identified with Vajrapāṇi, though they are separate bodhisattvas in the sūtras.

## Mahāvastu
Skt. *mahāvastu*, The Mahāvastu or “Great Chapter” is a lengthy work of the Lokottaravāda (Proponents of the Supramundane) subsect of the Mahāsāṃghika (Great Saṅgha) tradition, which some scholars have regarded as a precursor of Mahāyāna Buddhism. It is written in mixed Sanskrit, Pāli, and Prakrit and is regarded as the earliest Sanskrit biography of the Buddha. The work belongs to the Vinayapiṭaka and in fact describes itself as a historical preface to the Buddhist monastic codes (Skt. vinaya). In this regard, it does correspond loosely to the Mahāvagga section of the Khandhaka in the Pāli Vinayapiṭaka. Over half the text comprises avadānas and jatakas (some having no Pāli antecedent), which tell of past lives of the Buddha when he was a bodhisattva on the path to awakening.

## majestic power
Specifically that of the Buddha, in most instances of the term, but used more generally, too, of the sun and the moon, as well as various beings in the phrase “great superhuman power and great majestic power” (mahārddhiko mahānubhāvaḥ). The term has the sense of the power that comes from the mere presence or nature of the thing, something like the classical sense of the term charisma.

## Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta
*’jam dpal gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *mañjuśrī kumārabhūta*, Evolved from the gandharva Pañcaśikha in early Buddhism, which remains one of Mañjuśrī’s alternate names. Pañcaśikha was a gandharva who lived on a five-peaked mountain, and who brought the Buddha information on what was occuring in the paradises. Mañjuśrī is the first prominent bodhisattva after Maitreya in the early Mahāyāna sūtras, where he is known as Mañjughoṣa (“Having a Beautiful Voice”). He came to embody wisdom, and became one of the eight great bodhisattvas. In the early tantras he was the lord of one of the three buddha families. In the Sanskrit version of the sūtra, Kumārabhūta is a separate word rather than a compound with his proper name. This means that it could be the second of his names, and it is glossed as meaning “always young.” Alternatively it could be treated simply as an adjective, as in “the youth Manjuśrī.”

## Mañjuśrī Kumāra­bhūta
*’jam dpal gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *mañjuśrī kumāra­bhūta*, Also rendered here as “Mañjuśrī.”

*many+dzu shrI gar+b+ha*, Skt. *mañjuśrīgarbha*, A translator of canonical texts.

*’jam dpal gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *mañjuśrī­kumārabhūta*, Another name for the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, it means in full “the youthful Mañjuśrī.”

*’jam dpal gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *mañjuśrī­kumāra­bhūta*, An epithet of the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, meaning “the youthful Mañjuśrī.” Mañjuśrī is one of the eight “close sons” of the Buddha and the embodiment of wisdom.

## Mañjuśrīmitra

Eighth- to ninth-century Tibetan translator also known by his Tibetan name, Gajam Gocha (dba ’jam dpal go cha).

*’jam dbyangs*, Skt. *mañjusvara*, Meaning “gentle or beautiful voice,” this is an alternative name for Mañjuśrī. It is synonymous with Mañjughoṣa, which is also translated into Tibetan as ’jam dbyangs. See also “Mañjuśrī.”

## Mañjuvajra

*’jam pa’i dbyangs*, Skt. *mañjuvara*, An epithet of Mañjuśrī.

## makara
*chu srin*, Skt. *makara*, A fabled sea monster, the front part of which is a mammal. It is said to be the largest animal in the world, with the strongest bite. Its head is said to be a combination of the features of an elephant, a crocodile, and a boar. The name is also applied to the dugong, the crocodile (in particular the Mugger crocodile, whose name is even derived from makara ), and the dolphin, particularly the Ganges dolphin, because the Ganges goddess is said to ride on a makara.

## Makaradhvaja
*chu srin rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *makaradhvaja*, A yakṣa general.

## Makaraketu

*chu srin ’dul*, Skt. *makarandama*, A yakṣa general.

## make amends
*phyir bya*, Skt. *prati√kṛ*, Lit. “should make amends.” Monks and nuns must confess offenses and “make amends” for them. The proper procedure for making amends for offenses is described in The Chapter on the Restoration Rite (Toh 1, ch. 2, ), where the monastic acknowledges the fault and then resolves to refrain from such behavior in the future. In the Tengyur, the Tibetan verb is usually given as phyir bcos pa. In The Chapter on Lifting Restrictions, the Skt. pratikartavyā is rendered in Tibetan as slar bgyi’o, as in the oft-repeated statement, “If I know of or see an offense, I will properly make amends for that offense in accord with the Vinaya” (Toh 1, ch. 3, : ltung ba shes zhing mthong na chos bzhin ’dul ba bzhin slar bgyi’o; Skt. jānaṃ paśyann āpattiṃ yathādharmaṃ yathāvinayaṃ pratikariṣye).

## male lay disciple
An unordained male practitioner who observes the five precepts not to kill, lie, steal, be intoxicated, or commit sexual misconduct.

## male lay vow holder
*dge bsnyen*, Skt. *upāsaka*, A Buddhist lay vow holder who pledges to refrain from at least one but often all five actions of killing, stealing, pretending to superhuman qualities, committing sexual misconduct, and imbibing intoxicants like alcohol. An additional, optional pledge can be made to complete celibacy.

## male novice
*dge tshul*, Skt. *śrāmaṇera*, A male who has been inducted into the novitiate (Tib. dge tshul nyid du bsgrub). Male novices in the Mūlasarvāstivādin tradition take ten precepts.

## malevolent female spirit
*phra men ma*, Skt. *ḍākinī*, The term phra men ma (also spelled phra man ma in some texts) is one of the two translations of the word ḍākinī found in canonical works. In this case—as in many of the cases where phra men ma rather than the other Tibetan translation of ḍākinī, mkha’ ’gro ma is employed—it refers to a class of malevolent female spirits. The higher tantras of the Nyingma tradition feature phra men (ma) as a class of protective deities on the periphery of the maṇḍala of wrathful deities in the Shitro (zhi khro) maṇḍala of peaceful and wrathful deities. They have female bodies, animal heads, and often appear as a set of eight.

## malevolent female spirits
*phra men ma*, Skt. *ḍākinī*, The term phra men ma is one of the two translations of the word ḍākinī found in canonical works. In this case—as in many of the cases where phra men ma rather than the other Tibetan translation of ḍākinī, mkha’ ’gro ma, is employed—it refers to a class of malevolent female spirits. The higher tantras of the Nyingma tradition feature phra men (ma) as a class of protective deities on the periphery of the maṇḍala of wrathful deities in the Shitro (zhi khro) maṇḍala of peaceful and wrathful deities. They have female bodies, animal heads, and often appear as a set of eight.

In the summer it is covered in large crimson flowers, which are believed to also grow in Indra’s paradise. The coral tree is the most widespread species of Erythrina or mandārava, taller than the others, and all are collectively known as coral trees.

## Mantra
*sngags*, manifestation of supreme [enlightenment](#enlightenment) in the form of sounds. Syllables which, in the sādhanas of the [Secret Mantrayāna](#secret-mantrayāna), protect the mind of the practitioner from ordinary [perceptions](#perceptions) and invoke the [wisdom](#wisdom) deities.

## Manu
*shed*, Skt. *manu*, In the Indian tradition, Manu, similar to Noah in the Biblical tradition, was the survivor of a flood that covered the world, and so is the ancestor of all humans. On divine advice, he built a boat in which he saved his family and all the plants, seeds, and animals necessary to reintroduce to the world after the flood had diminished.

## mark
*mtshan ma*, Skt. *nimitta*, A polyvalent term, it generally refers to the characteristic features of an object or image. Nimitta can refer to features of an object that attract the mind’s attention, engage with it more deeply, and develop emotional responses to it. Such marks or features are often considered to be ultimately false and deceptive. In a more positive sense nimitta can refer to the focus of meditation practice. The term applies to both external objects and visualized images that are used to deepen meditative concentration and absorption. Also translated here as “sign” and “feature.”

## marks of a great being
The thirty-two physical characteristics that identify both buddhas and universal monarchs. This set is often combined with the eighty excellent signs.

## marks of a great person
The physical characteristics or attributes of the human body possessed by wheel-turning kings and perfect buddhas and of which there are said to be thirty-two.

## Marpa Chökyi Lodrö
*mar pa chos kyi blo gros*, Skt. *-*, (1012–1097) Tibetan translator and lay practitioner from Lhodrak. Traveled several times to Nepal and India to receive tantric Buddhist teachings, notably from Nāropa and Maitripā, and in Tibet established an important set of lineages through his “four pillar” disciples, Milarepa, Ngoktön Chöku Dorje, Tshurtön Wangki Dorje, and Metön Tshönpo.

## mastery
*dbang phyug*, Skt. *aiśvarya*, The Sanskrit aiśvarya can be variously rendered as “sovereignty or supremacy, mastery, or might, superhuman power, or omnipotence, etc.” The term refers to the mastery or sovereignty of a buddha gained through the training on the Buddhist path to awakening and through the development of superhuman abilities or superknowledges (abhijñā) thereby, such as clairvoyance, the ability to read others’ minds, and other magical powers like the ability to walk through solid objects.

## mastery over the senses
*zil gyis gnon pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *abhibhvāyatana*, Eight stages of mastery over the senses is a classic formula describing the process of stabilizing the mind through meditation. They are divided by form (attractive, unattractive, good, and bad) and color (white, red, yellow, and blue).

## materialist
*’jig rten rgyang phen pa*, Skt. *lokāyata*, An ancient Indian tradition of thought and practice that denies the existence of past and future lives.

## materialist doctrine
A reference to the materialist doctrines espoused by the Lokāyatas, an ancient Indian school that only accepted the direct evidence of the senses and rejected the existence of a creator deity and other lifetimes.

## materialists
*’jig rten rgyang pan pa*, Skt. *lokāyata*, A philosophical school founded by the legendary Bṛhaspati and headed by Ajita Keśakambalin at the time of the historical Buddha. The school taught that all phenomena in the universe are produced by the five main elements—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—and that all events occur randomly through the interaction of the elements’ properties. The highest goal in life can thus only be the maximization of sensual pleasure; since no human action can influence the course of nature, striving for virtuous behavior and better rebirth is denied as fruitless. See also Jamgön Kongtrül’s Light of the Sun, folios 3.a–3.b.

## materiality
*’jig tshogs*, Skt. *satkāya*, Object of egoistic or materialist interest (satkāyadṛṣṭi). See “egoistic views.”

## matter
*gzugs*, Skt. *rūpa*, The first of the five aggregates, defined in Abhidharma literature as anything comprised of the four major elements (earth, air, fire, and water), either alone or in combination. Also rendered here as “material form.”

## matter at hand
*dris pa’i tshig*, Skt. *pṛṣṭavācika*, Before a formal gathering of the saṅgha, the matter at hand requiring the monks’ presence is announced. After this the gaṇḍī beam is struck to summon the monks to the meeting.

## maturity
*skyon ma mchis pa*, Skt. *niyāma*, Used with respect to bodhisattva great beings. While “immaturity” (āma, skyon) suggests rawness—something that is uncooked, unrefined, and flawed—here the term “maturity” implies certitude, refinement, cooking, softening, and flawlessness. This rendering of skyon med pa incorporates the creative etymology of nyāma from ni plus āma (“raw”) rather than niyāma (“certainty”).

## maturity with respect to all phenomena
*chos skyon med pa nyid*, Skt. *dharmanyāmatā*, See “maturity.”

## Maudgalyagotra
*maud gal rigs*, Skt. *maudgalyagotra*, “Of the family of Mudgala.” Alternative name for Maudgalyāyana (descendant of Mudgala). One of the two principal pupils of the Buddha.

## Maudgalyāyana
*mo'u 'gal gyi bu*, one of the two foremost [śrāvaka](#śrāvaka) [disciple](#disciple)s of [Śākyamuni Buddha](#śākyamuni). He was said to be the one who had the greatest miraculous powers. His relatives named him Maudgalyāyana in honor of his being a descendant of Mudgala. He is respectfully referred to as Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

## Maudgalyā­yana
*maud gal gyi bu*, Skt. *maudgalyā­yana*, One of the principal hearer disciples of the Buddha, paired with Śāriputra, he was renowned for his miraculous powers. His family clan was descended from Mudgala, hence his name Maudgalyā­yana, “the son of Mudgala’s descendants.” Respectfully referred to as Mahā­maudgalyā­yana.

## Maudgalyāyana the Great
One of the main disciples of the Buddha, perhaps best known for being paired with Śāriputra as one of the Buddha’s two chief disciples in some texts and for being acknowledged by the Buddha as foremost among his disciples in regard to superhuman powers.

## Maudgalyāyanīya
The name of a family lineage.

## Means
*thabs*, see [skilful means](#skilful-means).

## means for gathering disciples
*bsdu ba’i dngos po*, Skt. *saṅgrahavastu*, Four things that a bodhisattva practices to bring living beings into their circle and to care for them spiritually: generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and conduct that accords with what they teach.

## means of attracting disciples
The four methods of attracting disciples are generosity (Tib. sbyin pa, Skt. dāna), pleasant speech (Tib. snyan par smra ba, Skt. priyavādita), helpfulness (Tib. don spyod pa, Skt. arthacaryā), and acting in a way that accords with the teachings (Tib. don ’thun pa, Skt. samānārthatā).

## means of attraction
*bsdu ba*, Skt. *saṃgraha*, The means of attracting disciples: generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and conduct that accords with the wishes of disciples.

## means of drawing others to oneself
A traditional list of four qualities by means of which buddhas and bodhisattvas build a group followers: giving gifts (dāna), kind speech (priyavādita), acting for their benefit (arthacārya), and having the same goals as they do (samānārthatā)

## means of magnetizing
*bsdu ba’i dngos po*, Skt. *saṅgrahavastu*, These are traditionally listed as four: generosity, kind talk, meaningful actions, and practicing what one preaches.

## means of unification
*bsdu ba’i dngos po*, Skt. *saṃgrahavastu*, Four ways in which a bodhisattva forms a group of people united by the common aim of practicing the Dharma: giving (dāna); pleasant speech (priyavaditā); accomplishment of the aims (of others) by teaching Dharma (arthacaryā); and consistency of behavior with the teaching (samānārthatā).

## measure
*bre’u chung*, Skt. *mānikā*, The Sanskrit mānikā is also a term used as a measure of weight for grains. It is usually defined as equal to two kuḍavas or eight palas, which is equivalent to about four hundred grams. In this text, however, it probably just refers to a “small amount,” as reflected in the Tibetan bre’u chung.

*lta ba tshod*, Skt. *lta ba tshod*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Padmagarbha.

*sman sbyin*, Skt. *sman sbyin*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Dhārmika.

## Meditate, meditation
*sgom pa*, to let the mind rest on an object of contemplation or reflection, or to maintain the flow of the authentic [view](#view).

## meditation
*bsam gtan*, Skt. *dhyāna*, Also called “(meditative) concentration,” “meditative state,” and a state of mind in which one is able to focus one’s attention single-pointedly on any suitable virtuous object without wavering (Rigzin 455). Closely related to meditative stabilization (samādhi). The term “meditation” has also been used in this translation to render sgom pa (meditation training) and ting nge ’dzin (meditative stabilization).

## Meditation Joy
*bsam gtan dga’*, Skt. *bsam gtan dga’*, Father of the buddha Gautama.

## meditation manager
*spong ba’i zhal ta byed pa*, Skt. *prahāṇa­pratijāgraka*, This monk manages the meditation residence. Their duties include sprinkling the floor of the meditation hall with water, sweeping it, spreading a fresh paste of dung over it, laying out the seats, cleaning the toilets, sprinkling water over their floor, sweeping them out, spreading a fresh paste of dung over them, and setting out piles of leaves, clods of dirt, earth, and water.

## meditation residence
*spong khang*, Skt. *prahāṇaśālā*, This term refers both to the dwellings and communal structures like a meditation hall at a monastic site. More literally “shelter for exertion”, Kalyāṇamitra describes this as a “place for the cultivation of samādhi” (F.309.a: spong khang zhes bya ba ni bsam gtan sgom pa’i gnas so). Asaṅga’s Abhidharma­samuccaya uses the Skt. prahāṇa (Tib. spong ba) as “meditation” in the phrase samyakprahāṇa; Tib. yang dag par spong ba. On the Pāli correlate, padhāna, see Paravahera Vajirañāṇa Mahāthera 2022, p. 22.

## meditation training
*sgom pa*, Skt. *bhāvanā*, Acquainting the mind with a virtuous object or mentally contemplating the Buddha’s teachings (Rigzin 75). Also translated here as “meditation.”

## meditation walkway
*’chag pa*, Skt. *caṃkrama*, This is a straight walkway used for walking meditation, usually around forty feet long and often raised above the level of the ground. Monks walk up and down the length of it.

## meditative absorption
*bsam gtan*, Skt. *dhyāna*, Designates mental states of deep concentration and the specific meditative practices leading to them. These states are characterized by a gradual withdrawal of one’s awareness from external sense data. There are four meditative absorptions associated with the form realm and four meditative absorption associated with the formless realm. In the course of the four meditative absorptions associated with the form realm, the meditator gradually eliminates the five hindrances (sensuous desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, and doubt) and cultivates the seven constituents of enlightenment (Skt. bodhyaṅga). In the four meditative absorptions associated with the formless realm, the meditator gradually refines the object of the fourth meditative absorption associated with the form realm to the point of the complete dissolution of subject-object differentiation.

## meditative absorption of neither perception nor non-perception
*’du shes med min gyi snyoms ’jug*, Skt. *naiva­saṃjñā­saṃjñāyatana*, Fourth of the four meditative absorptions.

## meditative absorption of the sense field of infinite consciousness
*rnam shes mtha’ yas skye mched kyi snyoms ’jug*, Skt. *vi­jñānāntyāyatana*, Second of the four formless meditative absorptions.

## meditative absorption of the sense field of infinite space
*nam mkha’ mtha’ yas skye mched kyi snyoms ’jug*, Skt. *ākāśānantyāyatana*, First of the four meditative absorptions.

## meditative absorption of the sense field of nothing-at-all
*ci yang med pa’i skye mched kyi snyoms ’jug*, Skt. *a­kiṃ­canyāyatana*, Third of the four meditative absorptions.

## meditative attainment
One of the synonyms for the meditative state, in terms of both the state itself and the various meditative states that serve as attainments along the path.

## meditative calm
*zhi gnas*, Skt. *śamatha*, One of the basic forms of Buddhist meditation that focuses on calming the mind. Often presented as part of a pair of meditation techniques, the other being meditative insight (vipaśyanā; lhag mthong).

## meditative concentration
*bsam gtan*, Skt. *dhyāna*, Meditative concentration is defined as the one-pointed abiding in an undistracted state of mind free from afflicted mental states. It is an advanced form of calm abiding, where often both calm abiding and penetrative insight may be present in perfect union. Four states of meditative concentration are identified as being conducive to birth within the world system of form, each of which has three phases of intensity. However, in the context‌ of the Great Vehicle, meditative concentration is the fifth of the six transcendent perfections. See also “four meditative concentrations” and .

## meditative concentration hand-mudrā
*ting nge ’dzin phyag rgya*, Skt. *samādhimudrā*, A hand gesture that signifies the attainment of meditative concentration.

## meditative concentration of valiant progress
*dpa’ bar ’gro ba’i ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *śuraṅgama­samādhi*, A special type of samādhi (meditative absorption).

## meditative equipoise
*mnyam par bzhag pa*, Skt. *samāhita*, A state of deep concentration in which the mind is absorbed in its object to such degree that conceptual thought is suspended. It is sometimes interpreted as settling (āhita) the mind in equanimity (sama).

## Meditative Movement
*bsam gtan ’gro*, Skt. *bsam gtan ’gro*, Son of the buddha Vajrasaṃhata.

## meditative seclusion
*nang du yang dag ’jog*, Skt. *pratisaṃlayana*, This term can mean both physical seclusion and a meditative state of withdrawal. It often refers specifically to the practice of calm abiding (śamatha) and special insight (vipaśyanā).

## meditative stability
*ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *samādhi*, A generic name for the meditative stabilities enumerated in the present sūtra. There are several sets of named meditative stabilities in the text: (a) an abbreviated set of 32 in chapter 4, -->; (b) a longer list of 119 in chapter 6, -->; (c) a similar list in chapter 8, -->, followed by an explanation of each; (d) a list of 51 manifested by Sadāprarudita in chapter 73, in -->; and (e) a further 24 in which Sadāprarudita establishes certainty in chapter 75, -->). Additional meditative stabilities are mentioned in other places in the text. These lists differ slightly from their equivalents in the other long Prajñā­pāramitā sūtras.

## meditative stability devoid of both ideation and scrutiny
*mi rtog mi dpyod pa’i ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *avitarko’vicāra­samādhi*, Third of the second set of three meditative stabilities, see .

## meditative stability endowed with ideation and scrutiny
*rtog pa dang bcas dpyod pa dang bcas pa’i ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *savitarka­savicāra­samādhi*, First of the second set of three meditative stabilities, see .

## meditative stability free from both ideation and scrutiny
*mi rtog mi dpyod pa’i ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *a­vi­tarko'vi­cāra­samādhi*, Third of the three meditative stabilities.

## meditative stability free from ideation and endowed merely with scrutiny
*rtog pa med la dpyod pa tsam gyi ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *avitarka­savicāra­mātra­samādhi*, Second of the second set of three meditative stabilities, see -->.

## meditative stability free from ideation and merely endowed with scrutiny
*rtog pa med la dpyod pa tsam gyi ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *a­vi­tarka­savicāra­mātra­samādhi*, Second of the three meditative stabilities.

## meditative stabilization
*ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *samādhi*, Also called “(meditative) concentration,” the ability of the mind to concentrate on a specific object of cognition for a length of time (Rigzin 144). Closely related to dhyāna. Also rendered here as “meditation.”

## meditative stabilization like a flash of lightning
*glog lta bu’i ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *vidyutopama­samādhi*, Name of a meditative stabilization.

## meditative stabilization with applied and sustained thought
*rtog pa dang bcas dpyod pa dang bcas pa’i ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *sa­vitarka­savicāra­samādhi*, See “meditative stabilization.”

## meditative stabilization without applied thought but with sustained thought
*rtog pa med cing dpyod pa’i ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *a­vitarka­vicāra­mātra­samādhi*, See “meditative stabilization.”

## meditative stabilization without either applied or sustained thought
*rtog pa yang med dpyod pa yang med pa’i ting nge ’dzin*, Skt. *a­vitarkāvicāra­samādhi*, See “meditative stabilization.”

## meditative state
*mnyam par bzhag pa*, Skt. *samāhita*, Literally meaning correct (samyak) acquisition (āpatti) of truth or reality, this is a term used in early Buddhism to refer to the succession of meditative states leading to the attainment of nirvāṇa.

## meditative state of totality
*rgyas pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *kṛtsnāyatana*, There are ten of these meditative states in the Śrāvakayāna: through meditating individually on the four elements of earth, water, fire, and air, on the four colors blue, yellow, red, and white, on space, and on consciousness, one meditates that everything that exists becomes that element, or that color, or space, or consciousness. Elsewhere, including the Mahāvyutpatti, this is translated as zad par gyi skye mched. The Sanskrit kṛtsna means “totality,” while rgyas pa means “spread,” or “pervade,” and zad par means cessation, in that everything ceases within that element, color, etc.

## meditator
*spong ba pa*, Skt. *prahāṇika*, A monastic engaged in the practice of “renunciation” or “abandonment” (Tib. spong ba, Skt. prahāṇa), which is taken to be a synecdoche for “meditation.” In this Chapter on the Restoration Rite, the meditation in question takes the form of a meditation on the impurity of the human body. See also .

## medium dichiliocosm
*’jig rten gyi khams ’bring po stong gnyis pa*, Skt. *dvisāhasra lokadhātu*, A second-order universe comprising one thousand chiliocosms, according to traditional Indian cosmology. See also .

## Megha
Lit. “Cloud.” A brahmin boy, a past life of the Buddha Śākyamuni during the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, from whom he received a prophecy of his future awakening. In other iterations of the story he is known in Sanskrit as Sumati, and in Pali as Sumedha.
