*ni tsu lun+da ’bab pa*, Skt. *niculundha*, A river on Flocking Peacocks.

## Nidhisaṃdarśana
*gter ston*, Skt. *nidhisaṃdarśana*, A previous life of Śākyamuni as a nāga king.

## nidāna
*gleng gzhi*, Skt. *nidāna*, As one of the twelve aspects of the Dharma, it means the introductions to teachings. See also “twelve wheels of the Dharma.”

## Nigama
*grong brdal*, Skt. *nigama*, A world system.

## night is fading
*nam nangs*, Skt. *nirgacchantī rātriḥ*, The translation follows the Sanskrit: nirgacchati ratri. The Tibetan might be rendered “first light.”

## night lotus
*ku mu da*, Skt. *kumuda*, Nymphaea pubescens. This night-blossoming water lily, which can be red, pink, or white, is not actually a lotus, since it does not have the lotus’s distinctive pericarp. Nevertheless it is commonly called the “night lotus.” It is also known as hairy water lily, because of the hairs on the stem and the underside of the leaves.

## night-flowering jasmine
*yongs ’dus*, Skt. *pārijāta*, Nyctanthes arbor-tristis. Presently in Hindi called parijat, pārijāta in Kannada, and so on. It features prominently in Indian legends and is one of the earthly trees that are are said to be in paradise. Some dictionaries equate it with the coral tree (māndārava).

*tshar gcod pa’i gzungs ma*, Skt. *nigrahadhāraṇī*, One of the dhāraṇī goddesses present at the delivery of the MMK.

## Nihata­dhīra
*brtson ’grus ma nyams pa*, Skt. *nihata­dhīra*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Nihata­rāga­rajas
*’dod chags rdul bcom pa*, Skt. *nihata­rāga­rajas*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Nihata­tejas
*gzi brjid mnyam pa*, Skt. *nihata­tejas*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Niṣṭhāgata
*mthar thug*, Skt. *niṣṭhāgata*, A pure realm.

## Nihilism
*chad par lta ba*, Skt. *vibhava dṛṣṭi*, materialism, the [view](#view) which denies the existence of past and future lives, the [principle of cause and effect](#principle-of-cause-and-effect), and so on.

## Nihilism Relinquished

## nihilist
*med par smra ba*, Skt. *nāstikyavādin*, In Buddhist terms, a view or outlook that rejects the validity or truth of the law of karma and rebirth (see “wrong view of nihilism”).

*ma nyams pa’i yon tan ’byung ba*, Skt. *nihita­guṇodita*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

*mi g.yo ba*, Skt. *āniñjya*, Lit. “immovable.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## nāḍikā
A measure of time defined as consisting of thirty kalās. It is measured by means of a water container fitted with a “tube” (nālika). Two nāḍikās make one muhūrta, which means that the duration of one nāḍikā is twenty-four minutes.

*sel byed*, Skt. *nikarṣa*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

*gnas can rtag pa*, Skt. *nilayadhruva*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## nimb tree
*nim ba*, Skt. *nimba*, Azadirachta indica.

## Nimi
*mu khyud*, Skt. *nimi*, The second of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin, who in becoming a bodhisattva is given the name Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and as such in the future will be in Sukhāvatī as that bodhisattva when his father becomes the Buddha Amitābha. He will eventually become in that realm the Buddha Supra­tiṣṭhita­guṇa­maṇikūṭa­rāja.

## Nimiṃdhara

## Nimindhara
The name of a universal monarch, a future life of the queen Moonlit, as prophesied by the Buddha.

## Nimnaga
Skt. *nimnaga*, One of the rāśis.

## nine abodes of beings
*sems can gyi gnas dgu*, Skt. *sems can gyi gnas dgu*, The dung dkar tshig mdzod chen mo lists the nine as (1) among those with different (tha dad) bodies and perceptions, such as humans and some gods, (2) among those with different bodies and a single perception, such as the Brahmakāyika gods, (3) among those with a single body and different perceptions, such as the Ābhāsvara gods, (4) among those with a single body and a single perception, such as the Śubhakṛtsna gods, and (5) among beings in Asaṃjñisattva, (6) in the station of endless space, (7) in the station of endless consciousness, (8) in the station of nothing-at-all, and (9) in the station of neither perception nor nonperception.

## nine abodes of sentient beings
The dung dkar tshig mdzod chen mo lists the nine as (1) among those with different (tha dad) bodies and perceptions, such as humans and some gods, (2) among those with different bodies and a single perception, such as the Brahmakāyika gods, (3) among those with a single body and different perceptions, such as the Ābhāsvara gods, (4) among those with a single body and a single perception, such as the Śubhakṛtsna gods, and (5) among beings in Asaṃjñisattva, (6) in the abode of limitless space, (7) in the abode of limitless consciousness, (8) in the abode of nothing whatsoever, and (9) in the abode of neither perception nor nonperception.

## nine categories of discourses
*yan lag dgu’i mdo*, Skt. *navāṅgaśāsana*, Nine divisions of the Buddhist scriptures.

## nine causes of antagonism
*kun nas mnar sems kyi dngos po dgu*, Skt. *navā­ghātavastūni*, Thinking that someone harms oneself, harms someone dear to oneself, or benefits someone dear to oneself, each in the present, past, or future.

## nine causes of irritation
*kun nas mnar gsems kyi dngos po dgu*, Skt. *āghātavastu*, These consist of various mental distractions caused by the nine considerations “He has caused, causes, will cause wrong to me. He has caused, causes, will cause wrong to one dear to me. He has served, serves, will serve my enemies.”

## nine causes of resentment
*mnar sems kyi dngos po dgu*, Skt. *navāghāta­vastu*, The nine causes of resentment are thinking that someone has done, is doing, or will do injury to oneself; thinking that someone has done, is doing, or will do injury to someone dear to oneself; and thinking that someone has done, is doing, or will do a favor to someone who is hateful to oneself.

## nine contemplations of impurity
*’du shes dgu*, Skt. *nava­saṃjñā*, The nine contemplations of impurity, as described in , are as follows: (1) contemplation of a bloated corpse, (2) contemplation of a worm-infested corpse, (3) contemplation of a bloody corpse, (4) contemplation of a putrefied corpse, (5) contemplation of a blue-black corpse, (6) contemplation of a devoured corpse, (7) contemplation of a dismembered corpse, (8) contemplation of a skeleton, and (9) contemplation of an immolated corpse. For Pāli and Sanskrit sources relevant to the nine contemplations of impurity, see Dayal (193)2: 93–94.

## nine dramatic moods
*gar gyi cha byad dgu*, Skt. *navanāṭyarasa*, The nine dramatic moods, contained in the sixty-four crafts, comprise those of (1) grace (śṛṅgāra, sgeg pa); (2) heroism (vīra, dpa’ ba); (3) ugliness (bībhatsa, mi sdug pa); (4) ferocity (raudra, drag shul); (5) joviality (hāsya, bzhad gad); (6) fearsomeness (bhayānaka, ’jigs rung); (7) compassion (karuṇā, snying rje); (8) awesomeness (adbhūta, rngam pa); and (9) peace (śānta, zhi ba). On all these and related matters, see Jamgon Kongtrul TOK Book 6, Pt.1: 311–315.

## nine dramatic sentiments
The nine dramatic sentiments are borrowed from South Asian performance theory (nāṭyaśāstra), where they signify nine modes of performance that evoke the specific emotional responses from an audience. The traditional list of nine includes the erotic (sgeg pa, śrṅgāra), heroic (dpa’ ba, vīra), disgusting (mi sdug pa, bībhatsa), comical (dgod pa, hāsya), wrathful (drag zhul, raudra), terrifying (’jigs su rung ba, bhayānaka), compassionate (snying rje, karuṇā), wonderous (rngam pa, adbhūta), and peaceful (zhi ba, śānta) sentiments.

## Nine Expanses
*klong dgu*, nine subdivisions of the Expanse [Section](#section) (*klong sde*) in the teachings of the [Great Perfection](#great-perfection).

## nine gradual attainments
*mthar gyis gnas pa’i snyoms par ’jug pa dgu*, Skt. *navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*, Nine states of concentration that one may attain during a human life, corresponding to the four concentrations found in the form realm, the four concentrations found in the formless realm, and the attainment of the state of cessation.

## nine malicious intentions
See “nine types of harmful acts.”

## nine mundane contemplations
*’du shes dgu*, Skt. *navasaṃjñā*, The nine contemplations of impurity, as described in are as follows: (1) contemplation of a bloated corpse, (2) contemplation of a worm-infested corpse, (3) contemplation of a putrefied corpse, (4) contemplation of a bloody corpse, (5) contemplation of a blue-black corpse, (6) contemplation of a devoured corpse, (7) contemplation of a dismembered corpse, (8) contemplation of a skeleton, and (9) contemplation of an immolated corpse. For Pāli and Sanskrit sources relevant to the nine contemplations of impurity, see Dayal (1932): 93–94.

## nine perceptions
*’du shes dgu*, Skt. *navasaṃjñā*, The nine perceptions of impurity, as described in , are as follows: (1) perception of a bloated corpse, (2) perception of a worm-infested corpse, (3) perception of a putrefied corpse, (4) perception of a bloodied corpse, (5) perception of a black-and-blue corpse, (6) perception of a chewed-up corpse, (7) perception of a dismembered corpse, (8) perception of bones, and (9) perception of an immolated corpse. For Pali and Sanskrit sources relevant to the nine perceptions of impurity, see Dayal 1932: 93–94.

## nine places beings live
*sems can gyi gnas dgu*, Skt. *sems can gyi gnas dgu*, The dung dkar tshig mdzod chen mo lists the nine as (1) among those with different (tha dad) bodies and perceptions, such as humans and some gods, (2) among those with different bodies and a single perception, such as the Brahmakāyika gods, (3) among those with a single body and different perceptions, such as the Ābhāsvara gods, (4) among those with a single body and a single perception, such as the Śubhakṛtsna gods, and (5) among beings in Asaṃjñisattva, (6) in the station of endless space, (7) in the station of endless consciousness, (8) in the station of nothing-at-all, and (9) in the station of neither perception nor nonperception. See also .

## Nine Preeminent Dabren Medicine Ladies
A group of deities or spirits who cause illness.

## nine serial absorptions
*mthar gyis gnas pa’i snyoms par ’jug pa dgu*, Skt. *navānupūrva­vihāra­samāpatti*, Nine states of concentration that one may attain during a human life, namely the four concentrations corresponding to the form realm, the four formless absorptions, and the attainment of the state of cessation.

## nine serial steps of meditative absorption
*mthar gyis gnas pa’i snyoms par ’jug pa dgu*, Skt. *navānupūrva­vihāra­samāpatti*, The nine levels of meditative absorption that one may attain during a human life, namely the four meditative concentrations corresponding to the realm of form (caturdhyāna), the four formless meditative absorptions (caturārūpya­samāpatti), and the attainment of the state of cessation. For an explanation of the nine serial steps of meditative absorption in this text, see . These are also summarized in Jamgon Kongtrul, The Treasury of Knowledge, Book 6, Pt. 2: pp. 428–29.

## nine stages of meditative absorption
*mthar gyis gnas pa'i snyoms par 'jug pa dgu*, Skt. *navānupūrvavihārasamāpattaya*, The four dhyānas, the four absorptions of the formless [realm](#realm), and absorption in cessation.

## nine states of beings
*sems can gyi gnas dgu*, Skt. *navasattvāvāsa*, The nine states of beings (navasattvāvāsa, sems can gyi gnas dgu, Degé Tengyur vol. 91, F.41.a ) comprise (1) human beings and certain gods exemplifying those who have different bodies and different perceptions (lus tha dad cing ’du shes tha dad pa dag dper na mi rnams dang lha kha cig); (2) the gods appearing in the first tier of the Brahmakāyika realms, exemplifying those who have different bodies and identical perceptions (lus tha dad pa la ’du shes gcig pa dag dper na tshangs ris kyi lha dag dang po ’byung ba), (3) the gods of the Ᾱbhāsvara realms, exemplifying those who have identical bodies and different perceptions (lus gcig la ’du shes tha dad pa dag dper na ’od gsal ba rnams); (4) the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna realms, exemplifying those who have identical bodies and identical perceptions (lus gcig la ’du shes gcig pa dag dper na dge rgyas kyi lha rnams); (5) the activity field of infinite space (nam mkha’ mtha’ yas skye mched); (6) the activity field of infinite consciousness (rnam shes mtha’ yas skye mched); (7) the activity field of nothing-at-all (ci yang med pa’i skye mched); [(8) the activity field of neither perception nor nonperception (’du shes med ’du shes med min gyi skye mched)]; and (9) the activity field of nonperception (’du shes med pa’i skye mched). The missing one is included in Nordrang Orgyan, pp. 2034–35.

## nine successive meditative absorptions
*mthar gyis gnas pa’i snyoms par ’jug pa dgu*, Skt. *navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*, (1–4) the four meditative states, (5–8) the four absorptions within the formless realm (caturārūpyasamāpatti, gzugs med [snyoms ’jug] bzhi), and (9) the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti, ’gog pa’i snyoms ’jug).

## nine successive states of absorption
Nine meditative absorptions in a series: four in the form realm, four in the formless realms, and finally the absorption of cessation.

## nine successive states of meditative attainment
The four attainments corresponding to the form realm, the four formless absorptions, and the attainment of the state of cessation.

## nine things that harm
*gnod pa’i dngos po dgu*, Skt. *āghātavastu*, Nine points of reference that inflame one’s anger and hostility: (1) my enemy has harmed me, (2) is harming me, and (3) will harm me; (4) my enemy has harmed my friend, (5) is harming my friend, and (6) will harm my friend; (7) my enemy has assisted other enemies, (8) is assisting other enemies, and (9) my enemy will assist my other enemy.

## nine things that inspire aggression
*kun nas mnar sems kyi dngos po dgu*, Skt. *navāghātavastūni*, In his Gateway to Knowledge, Mipham identifies three groups of three [thought](#thought)s that inspire aggression: (1–3) the [thought](#thought)s, "This has hurt me," "This is hurting me," and "This will hurt me"; (4–6) the [thought](#thought)s "This has hurt someone dear to me," "This is hurting someone dear to me," and "This will hurt someone dear to me"; and (7–9) the [thought](#thought)s, "This has helped my enemy," "This helps my enemy," and "This will help my enemy" (mi pham rgyam mtsho 1978, p. 74).

## nine things that torment the mind
*mnar sems kyi dngos po dgu*, Skt. *mnar sems kyi dngos po dgu*, That one has been harmed by an enemy, that one’s loved ones have been harmed, or that one’s enemies have been helped, each in the past, present, or future respectively.

## nine types of harmful acts
Thinking “I have been treated unjustly” and giving rise to animosity, thinking “I am being treated unjustly” and giving rise to animosity, thinking “I will be treated unjustly” and giving rise to animosity, thinking “my dear ones have been, are being, or will be treated unjustly” and giving rise to animosity, and thinking “my enemy has gained, is gaining, or will gain an advantage” and giving rise to animosity.

## nine vindictive attitudes
*mnar sems kyi dngos po dgu*, Skt. *mnar sems kyi dngos po dgu*, Thinking that one’s enemy has harmed, is harming, or will harm oneself; thinking that one’s enemy has harmed, is harming, or will harm one’s friend; and thinking that someone has helped, is helping, or will help one’s enemy.

## Nine-Headed Snake
The name of a king of the kumbhāṇḍas.

## niradhiṣṭhāna
*gnas su bya ba med pa*, Skt. *niradhiṣṭhāna*, Lit. “without anything to rest on” (Conze: “All Stability Stopped”). Name of a meditative stabilization.

## nirarbuda
*chu bur rdol*, Skt. *nirarbuda*, A word for a high number (one hundred million). A variant of the Skt. nyarbuda. Also translated as “Bursting Blister Hell” when it designates one of the eight cold hells. See also .

## nirargaḍa
A more elaborate and “unrestrained” (nirargaḍa) form of the Vedic ritual of horse sacrifice.

## Nir­avadya­sthāna­vāsinī
*kha na ma tho ba med pa’i gnas na ’dug ma*, Skt. *nir­avadya­sthāna­vāsinī*, One of the names of Śrī Mahādevī.

## Niravagraha
*’dzin med*, Skt. *niravagraha*, A buddha realm.

## Nirbhaya
*mi bsnyengs*, Skt. *nirbhaya*, The 49th buddha in the first list, 49th in the second list, and 50th in the third list.

## Nirdhūtarāja
*nges par g.yo bar byed pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *nirdhūtarāja*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Nirghautālaya
*gzhi shin tu sbyangs pa*, Skt. *nirghautālaya*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Nirghoṣa
*rab sgrogs*, Skt. *nirghoṣa*, A buddha realm.

## Nirghoṣamati
*dbyangs kyi blo gros*, Skt. *nirghoṣamati*, The hundred-and-fourth buddha in a kalpa in the distant past.

## Nirghāta
Skt. *nirghāta*, Hurricane or earthquake personified.

## nirgrantha
*gcer bu pa*, Skt. *nirgrantha*, The Tibetan means “naked one,” and the Sanskrit “without possessions” or “without ties.” A nirgrantha is a non-Buddhist religious mendicant who eschews clothing and possessions, the term usually referring to Jains, including both ascetics and anyone otherwise following the tradition, such as householders.

## Nirgrantha Jñatiputra
*gcer bu pa nye du’u bu*, Skt. *nirgrantha jñatiputra*, Also known as the Mahāvīra, the founder of the Jaina sect.

## Nirgrantha Jñātiputra
*gcer bu pa gnyen gyi bu*, Skt. *nirgrantha jñātiputra*, One of the six philosophical extremists who lived during the time of Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Nirgrantha Jñāti­putra
*gcer bu gnyen gyi bu*, Skt. *nirgrantha jñāti­putra*, One of the six outsider teachers.

## Nirgrantha Kinsman of the Kāśyapas
*gcer bu pa ’od srung dang rus gcig pa*, The son of a poor brahmin farmer who lived outside of Rājagṛha, he mistook Nirgrantha Jñātiputra for Buddha Śākyamuni and became Nirgrantha Jñātiputra’s student. He then took refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha shortly before his death. Also called “Nirgrantha Kāśyapa,” or simply “Kāśyapa,” his given name.

## Nirgrantha Kāśyapa
*gcer bu pa ’od srung*, Skt. *nirgrantha kāśyapa*, See “Nirgrantha Kinsman of the Kāśyapas.”

## Nirjvara
*rims med*, Skt. *nirjvara*, The 241st buddha in the first list, 240th in the second list, and 240th in the third list.

## Nirmāṇa
*sprul pa*, Skt. *nirmāṇa*, A god.

## nirmāṇa cakra
*sprul pa’i ’khor lo*, Skt. *nirmāṇacakra*, The energy center (cakra) in the navel.

## Nirmadakarā
*rgyags pa med pa*, Skt. *nirmadakarā*, One of the names of Śrī Mahādevī.

## Nirmāṇakāya
*sprul sku*, body of manifestation, the aspect of Buddhahood which manifests out of compassion to help ordinary beings.

## Nirmalā
*dri ma med pa*, Skt. *nirmalā*, One of the vidyārājñīs attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Nirmāṇarata
*’phrul dga’*, Skt. *nirmāṇarata*, The fifth (counting from the lowest) of the six paradises in the desire realm.

## Nirmāṇa­rata
*’phrul dga’*, Skt. *nirmāṇa­rata*, Fifth god realm of desire, meaning “delighting in emanation.”

## Nirmāṇarati
*’phrul dga’*, Skt. *nirmāṇarati*, Lit. “Those Who Enjoy Magically Produced Creations.” The fifth of the six heavens of the desire realm; also the name of the gods living there. Its inhabitants magically create the objects of their own enjoyment.

## Nirmāṇaratin
*’phrul dga’*, Skt. *nirmāṇaratin*, The fifth (counting from the lowest) of the six paradises in the desire realm.

## Nirmitā
Skt. *nirmitā*, One of the great dūtīs attending upon Lord Vajrapāṇi.

## Nirmita
*sprul pa bzang po*, Skt. *nirmita*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Nirmita­megha­garjanayaśaḥ­śrī
*sprul ba’i ’brug sgra snyan pa’i dpal*, Skt. *nirmita­megha­garjanayaśaḥ­śrī*, A tathāgata.

## Nirmita­megha­susvara­śrī
*sprul pa’i sprin sgra snyan pa’i dpal mnga’*, Skt. *nirmita­megha­susvara­śrī*, A buddha in the distant past. BHS in verse: Nirmita­megha­susvara­śiri.

## Nirnaṣṭa
*mi snang byed*, Skt. *nirnaṣṭa*, One of the grahas.

## Nirodha
*gsal*, Skt. *nirodha*, A thus-gone one to whom the Bodhisattva made offerings in a past life.

## Nirodhanimna
*’gog par gzhol ba*, Skt. *nirodhanimna*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Nirārambha
A bodhisattva and interlocuter in The Dharma Council.

## Nirāsravarati
*zag pa med par ’gro ba*, Skt. *nirāsravarati*, The mansion within the city of Mānasaṅkalpa in the Heaven of Joy in which the bodhisattva Maitreya lives.

## Nirṛti
*srin po*, Skt. *nirṛti*, The deity governing the eastern direction.

## nirukti­nirdeśa­praveśa
*nges pa’i tshig bstan pa la ’jug pa*, Skt. *nirukti­nirdeśa­praveśa*, Lit. “entry into the exposition of etymologies.” Name of a meditative stabilization. (Ghoṣa has niruktāniyata­praveśa.)

## nirukti­niyata­praveśa
*nges pa’i tshig la gdon mi za bar ’jug pa*, Skt. *nirukti­niyata­praveśa*, Lit. “entry into certainty about the etymologies.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Nirvāṇa
*mya ngan las 'das pa*, the state beyond suffering. The conception of nirvāṇa differs in the [Śrāvakayāna](#śrāvakayāna), [Mahāyāna](#mahāyāna) and [Vajrayāna](#vajrayāna).

## nirvāṇa without any remainder of the aggregates
*lhag ma med pa’i mya ngan las ’das pa*, Skt. *nir­upadhi­śeṣa­nirvāṇa*, The attainment of nirvāṇa without any remainder of the physical and mental aggregates.

## nirvāṇa without remainder
*lhag med mya ngan ’das pa*, Skt. *anupadhiśeṣa­nirvāna*, The mode of nirvāṇa in which all physical and mental attributes have been relinquished. This mode occurs after death, as some physical and mental attributes remain when an awakened being is still alive.

## nirvāṇa without remaining aggregates
*phung po’i lhag ma med pa’i mya ngan las ’das pa*, Skt. *nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*, The attainment of nirvāṇa without any remainder of the physical and mental aggregates.

## Nirviṇṇā
*yid ’byung ma*, Skt. *nirviṇṇā*, One of the female śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Nirvikalpadharmanirdeśakuśala
*rnam par rtog med chos ston mkhas pa*, Skt. *nirvikalpadharmanirdeśakuśala*, Name of a bodhisattva; “Skilled in Teaching the Dharma of Nonconceptuality.”

## Nirvikalpamahāmaitrīśvara
*rnam par rtog med byams pa chen po dbang phyug*, Skt. *nirvikalpamahāmaitrīśvara*, Name of a bodhisattva; “Lord of Nonconceptual Great Love.”

## Nirvikalpamati
*rnam par rtog med blo gros*, Skt. *nirvikalpamati*, Name of a bodhisattva; “Wise in Nonconceptuality.”

## Nirvikalpanāda
*rnam par rtog med nga ro*, Skt. *nirvikalpanāda*, Name of a bodhisattva; “Roar of Nonconceptuality.”

## Nirvikalpaspharaṇa
*rnam par rtog med khyab byed*, Skt. *nirvikalpaspharaṇa*, Name of a bodhisattva; “Pervading Nonconceptuality.”

## Nirvikalpasvabhāva
*rnam par rtog med ngo bo nyid*, Skt. *nirvikalpasvabhāva*, Name of a bodhisattva; “Having the Nature of Nonconceptuality.”

## Nirvikalpasvara
*rnam par rtog med dbang phyug*, Skt. *nirvikalpasvara*, Name of a bodhisattva; “Lord of Nonconceptuality.”

## Nirvikalpavīra
*rnam par rtog med dpa’ bo*, Skt. *nirvikalpavīra*, Name of a bodhisattva; “Hero of Nonconceptuality.”

## Niryāṇa
*nges ’byung*, Skt. *niryāṇa*, A great bodhisattva.

## Niryūhavijṛṃbhita
*ba gam gyis bsgyings pa*, Skt. *niryūhavijṛṃbhita*, A realm to the south of the Buddha Ratnagarbha’s realm in which resides the Buddha Siṃhavijṛṃbhiteśvararāja.

## Nisumbha
*nges par gnod mdzes*, Skt. *nisumbha*, The name of an asura.

## nisundara
An unidentified ritual substance.

## nityajvarā
*rtag pa’i rims*, Skt. *nityajvarā*, A class of spirits causing continuous fever.

## Nitya­pari­nirvṛta
*rtag par yongs su mya ngan las ’das pa*, Skt. *nitya­pari­nirvṛta*, A buddha in the southern direction.

## Nityaprahasitapramuditendriya
*rtag tu rgod dga’ dbang po*, Skt. *nityaprahasita­pramuditendriya*, The name of a bodhisattva meaning “Faculty of Ever-Joyous Excitement.”

## Nityapramūdita
*rtag tu rab dga’*, Skt. *nityapramūdita*, Lit. “Always a Joy.” Name of one of four gardens in the residence of the bodhisattva great being Dharmodgata, in the city of Gandhavatī.

## Nityapramudita
*rtag par rab tu dga’ ba*, Skt. *nityapramudita*, Name of one of four gardens in the residence of the bodhisattva great being Dharmodgata, in the city of Gandhavatī.

## Nityaprayukta
*brtson pa mi gtong*, Skt. *nityaprayukta*, A bodhisattva great being present in the audience of this sūtra.

## Nityaujohara­druma­rāja
*rtag tu mdangs ’phrog pa sdong po’i rgyal po*, Skt. *nityaujohara­druma­rāja*, A rākṣasa lord.

## Nityayukta
*rtag tu sbyor ba*, Skt. *nityayukta*, Name of a bodhisattva.

## Nityodyukta
*rtag tu brtson pa*, Skt. *nityodyukta*, A bodhisattva present during the delivery of the King of the Array of all Dharma Qualities.

## Nityo­dyukta
*rtag tu brtson*, Skt. *nityo­dyukta*, A great bodhisattva.

## Nityotkaṇṭhita
A bodhisattva in the Buddha’s retinue.

## Nityotkṣiptahasta
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra whose name is attested in the Vimalakīrti­nirdeśa.

## Nityotkṣipta­hasta
*rtag tu phyag brkyang*, Skt. *nityotkṣipta­hasta*, A bodhisattva great being present in the audience of this sūtra.

## Nityotpalakṛtahasta
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra whose name is attested in the Vimalakīrti­nirdeśa.

## Nityāvabhāsa
*rtag par snang ba*, Skt. *nityāvabhāsa*, “Permanent Luster.” The name of the future eon in which the girl Vimalaśraddhā will become a buddha.

## Nivartana
*ldog par gnas*, Skt. *nivartana*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Niyatā
*nges pa*, Skt. *niyatā*, Lit. “Certain.” Name of four lotus ponds, each located in one of the four gardens of the residence of the bodhisattva great being Dharmodgata, in the city of Gandhavatī.

## Niyatabuddhi
*nges pa’i blo*, Skt. *niyatabuddhi*, The 177th buddha in the first list, 176th in the second list, and 176th in the third list.

## niyata­dhvaja­ketu
*nges pa’i rgyal mtshan tog*, Skt. *niyata­dhvaja­ketu*, Lit. “crest of the victory banner of certainty.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Nīlā
*sngon mo*, Skt. *nīlā*, A great rākṣasī.

## Nīla
*sngo ba*, Skt. *nīla*, One of the kings of the nāgas.

## Nīlabhūti
*sngor gyur*, Skt. *nīlabhūti*, A brahmin.

## Nālada
*na la da*, Skt. *nālada*, [Śāriputra](#śāriputra)'s birthplace in [Magadha](#magadha). King [Bimbisāra](#bimbisāra) granted [Śāriputra](#śāriputra)'s grandfather [Māṭhara](#māṭhara) and father [Tiṣya](#tiṣya) rights to this village as a victor's spoils after debates held in his presence.

## Nīlakaṇṭha
Skt. *nīlakaṇṭha*, An epithet of Śiva (lit. “blue-throated one”), here apparently understood as a form of Avalokiteśvara. This epithet references the Purāṇic narrative in which Śiva drank the poison that arose when the gods churned the cosmic ocean, thus saving the world. Śiva did not die, but his neck turned blue. There are many parallels between Śiva and Avalokiteśvara, and here the text appears to explicitly understand Śiva as a form of Avalokiteśvara.

## Nālandā
the birthplace near [Rājagṛha](#rājagṛha) of the [Buddha's](#buddha) [disciple](#disciple) [Śāriputra](#śāriputra), which much later, starting in the time of the Gupta kinds (5th century), became one of the great centers of learning in Buddhist India. It was destroyed around 1200 A.D.

## noble (one)
*’phags pa*, Skt. *ārya*, An honorific term used to refer to anything of exalted status. Thus, it can refer to a noble person, one of a higher class or caste. In the context of Buddhism, it refers to one who has gained realization on the path of seeing and thus understands selflessness.

## noble one

*’phags pa’i lam*, Skt. *āryamārga*, The noble eightfold path, enumerated in , comprises (1) right view, (2) right idea, (3) right speech, (4) right conduct, (5) right livelihood, (6) right effort, (7) right mindfulness, and (8) right meditative stabilization.

## noble truths
*’phags pa’i bden pa*, Skt. *āryasatya*, Also explained as the truths of the noble ones (ārya), a paradigmatic set of teachings traditionally believed to have been taught by the Buddha in the first sermon. They are the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path that leads to the cessation of suffering.

## non-Buddhist
*mu stegs pa*, Skt. *tīrthika*, Those of religious or philosophical orders that were contemporary with the early Buddhist order, including Jains, Jaṭilas, Ājīvikas, and Cārvākas. Initially, the term tīrthika or tīrthya may have referred to non-brahmanic ascetic orders. Tīrthika (“forder”) literally translates as “one belonging to or associated with (possessive suffix -ika) stairs for landing or for descent into a river,” or “a bathing place,” or “a place of pilgrimage on the banks of sacred streams” (Monier-Williams). The term may have originally referred to temple priests at river crossings or fords where travelers propitiated a deity before crossing. The Sanskrit term seems to have undergone metonymic transfer in referring to those able to ford the turbulent river of saṃsāra (as in the Jain tīrthaṅkaras, “ford makers”), and it came to be used in Buddhist sources to refer to teachers of rival religious traditions. The Sanskrit term is closely rendered by the Tibetan mu stegs pa: “those on the steps (stegs pa) at the edge (mu).”

## non-Buddhist schools
*mu stegs can*, Skt. *tīrthika*, The non-Buddhist spiritual traditions of ancient India, which according to the Buddhist view are generally said to fall into one of two categories of erroneous views: the view of eternalism or the view of nihilism.

## nonduality
*gnyis su med pa*, Skt. *advayatvā*, This is synonymous with reality, voidness, etc. But it must be remembered that nonduality does not necessarily mean unity, that unity is only one of the pair unity-duality; hence nonduality implies nonunity as well. This point is obscured by designating this nondual philosophy as “monism,” as too many modern scholars have done.

## Non-dwelling nirvāṇa
*mi gnas pa'i myang 'das*, [total enlightenment](#total-enlightenment), beyond both [saṃsāra](#saṃsāra) and [nirvāṇa](#nirvāṇa), not "dwelling" in either of them.

## nonentity
*dngos po med pa*, Skt. *abhāva*, Generally refers to nonexistence.

*brjed pa med pa*, Skt. *asaṃpramoṣa*, One of the three qualities of mindfulness (dran pa; smṛti) including familiarization (’dris pa’i dngos po; samstute vastuni) and nondistraction (mi g.yeng ba; avikṣipta). See, for example, Jaini 1992 (pp. 47–59) on asaṃpramoṣa in Abhidharma literature. The “absorption of nonforgetfullness” (asaṃpramoṣo nāma samādhiḥ) is listed in the Mahāvyutpatti §526.

(See also ).

## nonregressing level
*phyir mi ldog pa’i sa*, Skt. *avaivartya­bhūmi*, A level of no retrogression, the attainment of which assures further progress. Such a state is associated variously with different stages of the path or bodhisattva levels, as well as with pure lands such as Sukhāvatī or, in this case, Tuṣita heaven.

## nonregressing wheel
*phyir mi ldog pa’i ’khor lo*, The realm of phenomena just as it is. Having the characteristic of space because it accompanies everything, the nonregressing wheel denotes ultimate reality and the irreversible awakening that results from realizing it.

## nonregressing wheel of Dharma
*phyir mi ldog pa’i sa’i chos kyi ’khor lo*, Skt. *avaivartya­bhūmi­dharmacakra*, See nonregressing level.

## non-regression
*phyir mi ldog pa*, Skt. *avaivartikatva*, A stage in the bodhisattva path where the practitioner will never turn back.

## nonregression
*phyir mi ldog pa*, Skt. *avaivartika*, A stage on the bodhisattva path where the practitioner will never turn back, or be turned back, from progress toward the full awakening of a buddha.

## non-residual nirvāṇa
*lhag ma med pa’i mya ngan las ’das pa*, Skt. *nir­upadhi­śeṣa­nirvāṇa*, One of the different types of nirvāṇa, where the aggregates have also been consumed within emptiness. See also “final nirvāṇa.”

## nonresidual nirvāṇa
*phung po ma lus pa’i mya ngan las ’das pa*, Skt. *nirupadhi­śeṣa­nirvāṇa*, One of the different types of nirvāṇa, where the aggregates have also been consumed within emptiness. See also “final nirvāṇa.”

## non-returner
*phyir mi ’ong ba*, Skt. *anāgāmin*, There are four kinds of “noble persons” (Skt. āryapudgala) according to the Śrāvakayāna path, characterized by a gradual abandonment of ten kinds of fetters (Skt. saṃyojana) that bind one to saṃsāra. This is the third of the four (or eight) stages of the realization of the supermundane path (and fruit) leading to awakening.

## nonreturner
*phyir mi ’ong ba*, Skt. *anāgāmin*, The third level of noble ones when practicing the path of the hearers (bound to never be reborn).

## non-returning
*phyir mi ’ong ba*, Skt. *anāgāmin*, One who will not be reborn again. Third of the four fruitions.

## non-self
*bdag med pa*, Skt. *an­ātman*, The view that there is no self existing independent of the five psycho-physical aggregates. Also translated here as “selflessness” and “absence of self.”

## nonself

## notions
*’du shes*, Skt. *saṃjñā*, Often this term is translated as “perception” or “discrimination” when it is included as the third of the five aggregates, in which case it refers to the mental function of differentiating and identifying objects according to their qualities. Thus it does not refer to the perceptions of the senses but to the conceptual notions or labels that are ascribed to sense perceptions before they may be conceived by the rational mind. In this sense, they are not really concepts or thoughts either, but rather the fundamental units ascribed to phenomena by the dualistic mind in order to form conceptual thoughts about them. Thus we have translated this as a “notion,” as the verses of the Bhava­saṅkrānti­sūtra emphasize the insubstantiality of the names as mere notions ascribed to phenomena, which exist as nothing other than a designation imputed by the mind.

## notions about characteristics
*mtshan ma’i ’du shes*, Skt. *nimittasaṃjñā*, This refers to the conceptual designation of things using linguistic signs.

## nourishing being
*gso ba*, Skt. *poṣa*, Edgerton favors the theory according to which poṣa/posa should be derived from puruṣa; however, the Tibetan translation reflects a different etymologization of the term that must have been current at the time of the Tibetan translations of Sanskrit texts. Pāli etymologies also suggest a link to the idea of “nourishing” (attabhāvassa posanato poso), and therefore we have preferred to follow traditional etymologies that better reflect how the South Asian and Tibetan masters understood the term.Distinctly Ascertaining the Meanings into Tibetan (or to any other premodern Buddhist readership).-->

## Nārāyaṇa
*mthu bo che*, Skt. *nārāyaṇa*, An alternate name for Viṣṇu (khyab ’jug), which is also used for Brahmā and for Kṛṣṇa. The Sanskrit is variously interpreted as “the path of human beings” and “the son of man.” In Buddhist texts it is used for powerful beings such as Śakra. The usual Tibetan translation is sred med kyi bu, meaning “the son of Nāra,” with Nāra translated as “one without craving.” However, here it appears to be translated as mthu bo che (“great power”).

## Nyima Gyaltsen Palsangpo
A famous translator who lived during the fourteenth century ce. He is said to have spent fourteen years in Nepal and to have mastered the Sanskrit language to the degree that he was able to translate Indian works without the help of Indian paṇḍitas. He belonged to the Chel (dpyal) family, who owned Tharpaling (thar pa gling) monastery, a renowned translation center. Nyima Gyaltsen Palsangpo translated the “thirteen late-translated sūtras” with Ānandaśrī, as well as several tantras, tantra commentaries, hymns, and works on grammar and medicine. He was one of the most important teachers of Butön Rinchen Drup (bu ston rin chen grub, 1290–1364), the famous scholar and redactor of the Tibetan Buddhist canon.

## Nyima Gyaltsen Sangpo
*nyi ma rgyal mtshan bzang po*, Skt. *nyi ma rgyal mtshan bzang po*, A Tibetan translator active at the monastery of Tharpa Ling in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries, also widely known as Tharpa Lotsāwa (thar pa lo tsA ba). He was one of the teachers of Butön Rinchen Drup (bu ston rin chen grub) and translated a number of tantric works in the Kangyur and Tengyur as well as a set of sūtras from the Theravāda tradition.

*snying po bzang po*, Skt. *śobhanasāgara*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

*rnam par dag pa’i dmigs pa*, Skt. **viśuddhyālambana*, See Schmithausen 2014, p. 362, §306.5 and n. 1644.

*spyod yul*, Skt. *gocara*, Also translated here as “sphere of activity.” See .

## object of veneration
See “venerable one.”

## objectionable
*kha na ma tho ba dang bcas pa*, Skt. *sāvadya*, The term is applied to actions, describing those that are negative in the sense either of being naturally wrong or of transgressing a formal rule or commitment, and is often translated as wrongdoing, unwholesome, etc. In some passages in this text the “objectionable” or “censurable” quality of actions is extended to any that are tainted with dualistic notions.

## objective basis
The Tibetan can translate both a noun (ālambana) and a related verb (in which case the third person singular is ālambate, “[one] perceives or conceives [something] as having an objective basis”). This term is tied to the general idea that an act of sense perception or mental conception takes an object of some kind that forms the basis or support for its continuing perception or conception.

## Objective of the Noble
*’phags pa’i don*, Skt. *’phags pa’i don*, Mother of the buddha Bhāgīratha.

## Objectives Accomplished
*don grub*, Skt. *don grub*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Gaṇin.

## objects of consciousness
*gzugs kyi chos*, The objects of consciousness, namely, objects of sight up through mental objects.

## objects of meditative immersion
Best known by the equivalent Pali term kasiṇa or kasiṇāyatana, this term refers to a set of ten objects of meditative contemplation used to induce deep meditative stability (dhyāna), to the mental image born from that contemplation, and to the resultant meditative stability. The ten meditative objects are the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space; the colors blue, yellow, red, and white; and consciousness. In some lists, “consciousness” is replaced with “light.”

## oblation
*gtor ma*, Skt. *bali*, A food offering made to a deity or spirits; such an offering may be varied and elaborate, or may be a simple sacrificial cake.

## obscuration
*sgrib pa*, Skt. *āvaraṇa*, The obscurations to liberation and omniscience. They are generally categorized as two types: affective obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa), the arising of afflictive emotions, and cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa), those caused by misapprehension and incorrect understanding about the nature of reality.

## obscuration of karma
*las kyi sgrib pa*, Skt. *karmāvaraṇa*, An obscuration consisting of negative actions committed in the past that prevents progress on the path to awakening in the present.

## Obscurations
*sgrib pa*, Skt. *āvaraṇa*, factors which veil one's Buddha-nature. See also: [two obscurations](#two-obscurations), [four obscurations](#four-obscurations).

Traditional garments symbolizing spirituality and sacredness. In Buddhism, they are worn by monks to signify renunciation, simplicity, and detachment from material possessions. In Hinduism, they denote a pious demeanor and devotion, typically worn during pilgrimages.

It is also the birthplace of [Garab Dorje](#garab-dorje). The use of "Oḍḍiyāna" coupled with titles such as "Great One", "[Second Buddha](#second-buddha)", "Great Master", and so on invariably refers to [Padmasambhava](#padmasambhava-of-oḍḍiyāna).

*rgan zhugs*, Skt. *mahallaka*, this term refers to those who renounce the world late in life, generally after having had and raised children of their own. It is somewhat pejorative; it is telling, for instance, that such monastics are directly addressed as “old-timers” rather than as “venerable,” the customary address for ordained monks.

## omniscience
*thams cad mkhyen pa*, Skt. *sarvajñatā*, This refers to the gnosis of the Buddha, with which there is nothing he does not know. However, not to confuse “omniscience” with the theistic conception of an omniscient god, the “everything” here is specifically everything about the source of the predicament of worldly life and the way of transcendence of that world through liberation. Since “everything” is only an abstract term without any particular referent, once we are clear about the implications of infinity, it does not refer to any sort of ultimate totality, since a totality can only be relative, i.e., a totality within a particular frame of reference. Thus, as Dharmakīrti has remarked, “it is not a question of the Buddha’s knowing the number of fish in the ocean,” i.e., since there are infinity of fish in infinity of oceans in infinity of worlds and universes. The Buddha’s omniscience, rather, knows how to develop and liberate any fish in any ocean, as well as all other living beings.

## one destined for only one more rebirth

The term is often rendered “once-returner.” “Rebirth” refers to rebirth in cyclic existence; in the Great Vehicle context the term is sometimes transposed to the bodhisattva path to designate one whose next rebirth will be in the Tuṣita realm before becoming a buddha.

## one hundred sextillion
If the Abhidharma system is followed, this is a number calculated by multiplying a koṭi (bye ba), or ten million, by a niyuta (khrag khrig), or a hundred billion, and by a śatasahasra (brgya stong), or one hundred thousand, which all together equals ten to the 23rd power or a hundred sextillion. This term is often used to express a number so large as to be inconceivable.

*chos kyi rjes su ’brang ba*, Skt. *dharmānusārin*, Someone who follows his or her goal according to the teaching of the sūtras and so forth.

## one who follows the meaning
*don gyi rjes su ’brang ba*, Skt. *arthānusārin*, According to the Abhi­dharma­kośa­bhāṣya, both those who “follow out of conviction” and those who “follow due to the Dharma” are actually “following the meaning/goal.” On the other hand, the JAA seems to take this as a separate subdivision.

## one who has performed any of the acts with immediate results
The acts with immediate results are the five extremely negative actions that result, at the time of one’s death, in immediate rebirth in the hells without the experience of the intermediate state. They are killing an arhat, killing one’s mother, killing one’s father, creating a schism in the Saṅgha, and maliciously drawing blood from a tathāgata’s body.

## One Who Makes No Promises
*dam ’cha’ bar mi mdzad pa*, Skt. *dam ’cha’ bar mi mdzad pa*, Name of a buddha.

## One Who Satisfies the Kingdom with Rain from Dharma Clouds
*chos kyi sprin gyi char gyis ryal srid shin tu tshim pa*, Skt. *chos kyi sprin gyi char gyis ryal srid shin tu tshim pa*, A buddha.

## one who would no longer regress
*phyir mi ldog pa*, Skt. *avaivartika*, The stage on a bodhisattva’s path when there is no longer any chance of regressing to a preceding stage or state.

## One With Houses
*khyim ldan*, Skt. *khyim ldan*, A river.

## One with the Great Gaze of the Holder of the Jewel and the Lotus
*nor bu chen po pad+ma la lta ba*, Skt. *mahā­maṇi­padma­vilokita*, The name of an emperor. “The Jewel and the Lotus” (Maṇipadma) could in itself be treated as a proper name, as it happens to be the name of one of the lokeśvara emanations of Avalokiteśvara.

## One With the Lake
*mtsho ldan*, Skt. *mtsho ldan*, A river. Lit. “has a lake.” Possibly the Sarasvatī river, or one of the rivers connected to Lake Manasarovar, perhaps the Brahmaputra.

## one with wisdom
*ye shes ldan*, Skt. *jñānavatī*, One of the twelve retentions of the bodhisattvas.

## One-Braid
*gtsug phud gcig pa*, Skt. *gtsug phud gcig pa*, A vighna/vināyaka.

## One-Pointed Light
*rtse gcig ’od*, Skt. *rtse gcig ’od*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Praśāntagāmin (483 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## one-pointed mind
*yid rtse gcig*, Skt. *ekāgracitta*, The mind focused one-pointedly.

## One-Toothed One-Eyed Great Revatī
The name of one of the eighteen primary emanations of the goddess described in this text.

## One-Toothed One-Eyed Revatī
A grahī. This seems to be another name for the grahī otherwise called One-Toothed One-Eyed Great Revatī (nam gru chen mo so gcig mig gcig ma).

## only one birth remaining
*skye ba gcig gis thogs pa*, Skt. *eka­jāti­pratibaddha*, A term for a bodhisattva held back from buddhahood by only a single remaining lifetime, as exemplified by Maitreya.

## Śoṇottara
*sho no ta ra*, Skt. *śoṇottara*, A noble one who in a former life gave a ball of cow dung mixed with cowhage to a pratyekabuddha for his bath.

## oozing pustules
*mdzes*, Skt. *kuṣṭha*, symptom that may be evidence of an illness considered an impediment to ordination.

## oozing rashes
*khyi rngo*, Skt. *kacchu*, symptom that may be evidence of an illness considered an impediment to ordination. According to Monier-Williams, any cutaneous disease.

## śopagalikā
An unidentified ritual substance.

## open state
*bla gab med pa*, Literally “without cover.”

## opener of the gateways
*sgo rnam par ’byed pa*, A meditative stability.

## opening statement
A term for the opening statement or introduction to a text.

## opening under the earth
This term refers to the ability to locate and see points of access to buried treasures or any object that might be buried underground. In Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra, this process generally requires mastery of the collyrium siddhi—the application of concoctions of various substances around one’s eyes in order to gain supernatural abilities.

## opinion
*lta bar gyur pa*, Skt. *dṛṣṭi­kṛta*, Also translated here as “false view.”

## opponent
*phas kyi rgol ba*, Skt. *paravāda*, One who teaches a false doctrine.

## opportunity so hard to find
*dal ba rnyed dka’*, Skt. *kṣaṇadaurlabhya*, “Opportunity” in this phrase, found frequently in the commentarial literature, refers to the leisure and freedom to study and practice the Dharma characteristic of a human lifetime free of the eight inopportune states (q.v.); “so hard to find” is a reminder of the rarity of such a lifetime, seen both from a numerical comparison to other forms of existence and from the improbability that an individual might gather together the meritorious causes and conditions that give rise to it.

## oppositional factors
*gnyen po*, Skt. *pratipakṣa*, In this text, refers to reciprocally determined constructs deriving from dualistic thought that are transcended in wisdom.

## Oppressor
*rab gnon*, Skt. *rab gnon*, Oppressor (one who subjugates or treats harshly), also the name of a yakṣa.

## Oḍra
Oḍra is the ancient name of the region roughly equivalent with the modern Indian state of Oḍisha.

## oracle
*gsal bar ston pa*, Skt. *prasenā*, An oracular spirit that can be summoned into a reflective object or made to take possession of a human medium, typically a young child.

## Orange Light
*dmar ser ’od*, Skt. *dmar ser ’od*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Śūra (218 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## orchid tree
*kun nas ’du ba*, Skt. *kovidāra*, Bauhinia variegata, Phaneria variegata. In other sūtras kovidāra is translated as sa brtol.

## ordain
*bsnyen par rdzogs pa*, Skt. *upasaṃpadā*, the formal term for granting orders and confirming a candidate as a monk.

## ordinary neutral phenomena
*lung du ma bstan pa’i chos rnams*, As listed in , these are physical karma, verbal karma, and thinking-mind karma, the four great elements, the five faculties, the four formless absorptions, the aggregates, constituents, and sense fields, and maturation.

## ordinary people
*so so’i skye bo*, Skt. *pṛthagjana*, Anyone who has not entered the “Path of Seeing” (i.e., has no stable direct realization of selflessness) is an ordinary person as opposed to a noble one.

## ordinary person
*so so’i skye bo*, Skt. *pṛthagjana*, In the Buddhist taxonomy of persons, someone who has not reached any of the four stages of the path (stream enterer, once-returner, non-returner, or arhat) and is still bound by the ten fetters (saṃyojana) that bind one to saṃsāra and who is thus contrasted with those four stages.

## ordinary requirements
*’jig rten pa’i ’tsho ba’i yo byad*, Skt. *jīvitopakaraṇa*, Food, drink, beds and seats, and medicines for sicknesses, tools, gems, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, corals, silver, and gold‍. This is a list of requirements for sustaining oneself that differs from the requirements (yo byad, pariṣkāra) of an ordained person (robes, alms, beds and seats, and medicines for sicknesses). bod rgya tshig mdzod chen mo gives ’tshog chas as an old word for ’tsho ba’i yo byad.

## ordinary unwholesome phenomena
*’jig rten pa’i chos mi dge ba rnams*, As listed in , these comprise the ten unwholesome actions— killing, stealing, illicit sex because of lust, lying, backbiting, insulting, babbling nonsense, coveting, malice, and wrong view—and also anger, bearing a grudge, dissembling, nursing pent-up anger, violence, jealousy, envy, and pride.

## ordination stick
*tshul shing*, Skt. *śalākā*, A bamboo stick given to monks, listing their ordination name as a means of identification.

## organ for excreting is hidden in a sheath
*’doms kyi lba ba sbubs su nub*, Skt. *kośopagata­vasti­guhya*, Mvy

## Orgyen
Nephew of Gar Dampa Chödingpa, Orgyen or Orgyenpa was one of the main heads of his uncle’s monasteries Phulung Rinchen Ling and Choding, under whom they greatly flourished.

## Orgyen Tashi
The eighth Degé king, Orgyen Tashi (mid- to late seventeenth century) was the head of the house of Degé in its thirty-eighth generation.

## Orgyenpa (Rinchen Pal)
*o rgyan pa rin chen dpal* (1230-1309), a great [siddha](#siddha) of the [Drukpa Kagyu](#kagyupa) tradition, [disciple](#disciple) of [Gotsangpa](#gotsangpa-gonpo-dorje). He traveled widely, visiting [Oḍḍiyāna](#oḍḍiyāna), Bodhgaya and China. Among his [disciple](#disciple)s were [Karmapa](#karmapa) Rangjung Dorje, Kharchupa and Dawa Senge.

## orifices are without deterioration
*bu ga’i sgo rnams yongs su ma nyams pa*, Skt. *pari­pūrṇa­vyañjana­tā*, Fifty-fourth of the eighty minor marks.

## Origin
*kun ’byung*, Skt. *kun ’byung*, Origin (the point where something begins), also the name of a sage.

## Origin of Jewels
*rin chen ’byung*, Skt. *rin chen ’byung*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Precious Tārā. Likely a shortened name for the thus-gone one Glory of the Origin of Pure Jewels.

## origin of suffering
*kun ’byung ba*, Skt. *samudaya*, Second of the four truths of the noble ones.

## origin of the ten powers
*stobs bcu’i ’byung gnas su gyur pa*, A meditative stability.

## Ornament
*rgyan*, Skt. *rgyan*, Ornament (a decorative object or adornment), also the name of an attendant of the buddha Sucīrṇabuddhi.

## Ornament of the Mind
*yid kyi rgyan*, Skt. *yid kyi rgyan*, One of the twenty-seven realms of the Heaven Free from Strife.

## Ornamental Display of Courage
*spobs pa’i rgyan bkod pa*, Skt. *spobs pa’i rgyan bkod pa*, A bodhisattva in the buddhafield at the nadir called Appearing as Illumination.

## Ornamented by Pure Conduct
*tshangs par spyod pas brgyan pa*, Skt. *tshangs par spyod pas brgyan pa*, Name of the world system of the thus-gone one Glory of the Incense of Non-ignorance.

## Ornamented with Pure Eyes
*spyan dag pas brgyan*, The prophesied name of a thousand bodhisattvas in the Buddha’s retinue when they attain awakening in the future.

## Ornaments of the Buddhas
*sangs rgyas phal po che*, Skt. *buddhāvataṃsaka*, A collection of forty-five sūtras presented as a single, long sūtra, although many of its chapters are independent works.

## orris root
*in+d+ra hasta*, Skt. *indrahasta*, Bletilla hyacinthina, hyacinth orchid. See Ludvik 2007, p. 310. Or possibly Rhizoma iridis. The root of the iris flower, specifically the Indian iris (Iris pallida). The root is said to resemble an arm, while the leaves resemble swords, and therefore there is a folktale of its having originated from Indra cutting off a yakṣa’s arm. (Toh 557: dbang po’i lag)

## ostārakī
A female ostāraka.

## ostāraka
*gnon po*, Skt. *ostāraka*, An obscure Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit term. Sanskrit equivalent: avastāraka. Translated into Tibetan as “suppressor, one who presses down on someone.” Presumably from avastṛ (“to cover over, as with a blanket”).

## Otalā
*o ta la*, Skt. *otalā*, A region of ancient India, not far from Mathurā.

## Otalā Forest
*o ta la’i nags*, Skt. *o ta la’i nags*, A forest near Otalā.

## Otalāyana
*o ta la’i bu*, Skt. *otalāyana*, A brahmin.

## other-powered
*gzhan dbang*, Skt. *paratantra*, One of the three natures. Also rendered here as “dependent.”

## out of order
*snrel zhi*, Skt. *vyatyasta­samāpatti*, The 29th meditative stability in chapters 6 and 8.

## outcast
*gdol pa*, Skt. *caṇḍāla*, The lowest and most disparaged class of people within the caste system of ancient India, they fall outside of the caste system altogether due to their low rank in society.

## outcast bodhisattvas
*byang chub sems dpa’ gdol ba*, Skt. *bodhi­sattva­cāṇḍāla*, Bodhisattvas who are attached to disciplined practices and living in remote areas.

## outcaste
A member of a tribe or ethnic group that falls outside the four caste categories (varṇa) of the brahmanical caste system. In brahmanical law books this social group of untouchables, also known as caṇḍālas, is sometimes defined as being as the result of the transgressive union of a low-caste śūdra man with a brahmin woman, but in origin the term was probably the name of a specific indigenous tribe.

## outcasts
*gdol pa*, Skt. *caṇḍāla*, The lowest and most disparaged class of people within the caste system of ancient India, who fall outside of the caste system altogether due to their low rank in society.

## outer emptiness
*phyi stong pa nyid*, Skt. *bahirdhā­śūnyatā*, One of the fourteen emptinesses and eighteen emptinesses

## outer limits of society
*mtha’ ’khob*, Skt. *paryanta*, I.e., those living beyond the pale of civilization, out of reach of the sacred Dharma.

## outer patched robe
*sbyar ma*, Skt. *saṃghāṭī*, Name of the outer robe worn by fully ordained monks on formal occasions, including teachings and begging for alms, is fashioned of patches, their number indicative of the monastic order to which they belong‌. See, e.g., Zhang Yisun et al (1985): pp. 1594–95.

## outer robe
One of the three robes of a monk or one the five robes of a nun. In Tibetan the term chos gos (“dharma robe”) can also be used for all the robes.

## outflow
*zag pa*, Skt. *āsrava*, The metaphor explaining outflows (āsrava), rendered as “contaminated,” is a house with a faulty roof. But it does not simply mean that something from the outside, hatred or greed, drips in on the pristine mind of a person. Rather the drips come from within the person. They arise from unskillful mindsets that give rise to the afflictions, hence “outflows” rather than “inflows.”

## outflows
*zag pa*, Skt. *āsrava*, Literally, “to flow” or “to ooze.” Mental defilements or contaminations that “flow out” toward the objects of cyclic existence, binding us to them

## outflows dried up
*zag pa zad pa*, Skt. *kṣīṇāsrava*, See “outflows.”

## out-of-date
*rdzubs pa*, Skt. *khustaka*, a deprecatory term meaning “old” or “out-of-date.”

## Outshining Flower
*me tog zil gyis gnon pa*, Skt. *me tog zil gyis gnon pa*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Steady Pillar of Sandalwood.

## outside the common living
*tha dad du gnas pa*, Skt. *nānāsaṃvāsika*, Monastics are “outside the common living” of the saṅgha either (1) by dint of the deviant attitudes that they hold, or (2) because they are serving out a suspension imposed by the saṅgha. A monk on suspension must endure a loss of privileges, listed in The Book of Supplements (Toh 7a, F.277.b–278.a). The saṅgha can rescind this suspension and reinstate the monk to full status, unless the monk is intransigent and unrepentant, in which case he remains “outside the common living.”

## Overcoming Fears with Words of Renown
*grags pa’i sgras ’jigs pa bcom pa*, Skt. *grags pa’i sgras ’jigs pa bcom pa*, The name of a bodhisattva in the Buddha’s audience.

## Overcoming through Triumph in Battle
*g.yul las rnam par rgyal te rgal ba*, Skt. *g.yul las rnam par rgyal te rgal ba*, Name of the world system of the thus-gone one Guru of Many.

## Overflow
*rgyu mthun pa*, Skt. *rgyu mthun pa*, Overflow (a flowing over of excess liquid), also the name of a forest on Holder of Joy.

## Overjoyed
*rab tu spro ba*, Skt. *rab tu spro ba*, Overjoyed (extremely happy), also the name of an asura king of the fourth level, Immovable.

## Overpowering Splendor
*gzi brjid thul*, Skt. *gzi brjid thul*, Attendant of the buddha Arciskandha.

## Overpowering Wisdom
*ye shes zil gyis gnon pa*, Skt. *ye shes zil gyis gnon pa*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Harivaktra.

## Overpowering with the Light of an Array of the Reflections of Jewels
*rin chen gzugs bkod ’od gnon*, A buddha in the northern direction in the present.

## Overwhelming All with Precious Qualities
*kun tu yon tan rin po ches rnam par gnon pa*, Skt. *kun tu yon tan rin po ches rnam par gnon pa*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Endowed with Jewels.

## overwhelming of all beings
*sems can thams cad zil gyis gnon pa*, Skt. *sarva­sattvābhibhavano*, The thirty-fourth of the fifty-one meditative stabilities manifested to Sadāprarudita in chapter 73.

## Overwhelming with Golden Light
*gser snang bas rnam par gnon pa*, Skt. *gser snang bas rnam par gnon pa*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Guru of the Moon.

## oviparous birth
*sgo nga las skyes pa*, Skt. *aṇḍaja*, Second of the four modes of birth.

## Owner of the ground
*sa bdag*, Skt. *bhūmipati*, a spirit occupying a place.

## Oxus
Skt. *vakṣu*, A river in Gandhāra, today known as Amu Daria.

## Pūṣa
The name of a deity.

## Üpa Losal
Üpa Losal (thirteenth to fourteenth century) was a student of both Chomralpa and Jamgak Pakṣi, and he was an important scholar in the production of the first Kangyur and Tengyur at Narthang monastery.

## Üpa Sangyé Bum
*dbus pa sangs rgyas ’bum*, Skt. *dbus pa sangs rgyas ’bum*, A scholar of Narthang (1270–1355) also known as Üpa Losal (dbus pa blo gsal). He was a student of Chomden Rikpai Raltri (bcom ldan rig pa'i ral gri) and worked on the gathering of translations and compiling of the contents of the earliest Kangyurs. Lotsawa Chokden (q.v.) was one of his students.

## paṇa
*pa Na*, Skt. *paṇa*, According to Alexander Cunningham, one paṇa “was a handful of cowrie shells, usually reckoned as 80.” (See Cunningham 1996, p. 1.)

## Paṭaccara
The name of a people in northern India. In the Mahābhārata they are described as living around the Kuru region, from where they fought with the Pāṇḍavas against the Kauravas.

## paṭaha drum
Skt. *paṭaha*, A barrel drum that can be hung by a strap from the body and played sitting or standing by beating the upper surface, or both surfaces, with two curved drumsticks. There is also an identification of this term with a disk-shaped drum with the skin on one side only, similar to a tambourine, and also a drum like the mṛdaṅga with a thick middle and one end smaller than the other.

## paṇḍaka
*ma ning*, Skt. *paṇḍaka*, An imprecise, catchall term, difficult to translate. It designates people with various kinds of unclear gender status, including but not restricted to physical intersex conditions and hermaphrodites. It can, for example, also mean a eunuch, or from the Vinaya account of the expulsion of a paṇḍaka , a male who sought other males to have sex with him. See also the glossary entry in Miller (2018). It could also be applied to a transgender male, not necessarily a eunuch, such as the hijras. Hijras, men who dress as women, have been an established part of Indian society since ancient times and all-hijra communities still have a significant societal role. Hijra is a more recent term with a Hindustani-Urdu origin.

## paṇava
*mkhar rnga*, Skt. *paṇava*, Listed among Indian instruments as an hourglass drum, played in the hand, and the ancestor of the present day huḍukka, somewhat larger than the ḍamaru. See Saṅgītaśiromaṇi: A Medieval Handbook of Indian Music, edited by Emmie Te Nijenhuis, p. 549. However, Dutt describes it as a drum made of bell metal, which matches the Tibetan translation as “bronze drum,” but he may have been influenced by the Tibetan translation of chapter 30. In an earlier chapter paṇava is simply transcribed into Tibetan. An example of a bell metal drum would be the ceṇṇala, a small flat gong of bell metal that is hit with a stick and used to keep time in South Indian music. Other instruments mentioned are of the South Indian tradition.

## paṇava drum
A middle-sized hourglass drum that is struck with one hand while its pitch is modified with the other.

## Pabtong
*pab tong*, Skt. *pab tong*, The editor of this sūtra. No details of this person are known.

## Pañcacūḍa
Skt. *pañcacūḍa*, A nāga king.

## Pañcaśikha
*gtsug phu lnga pa*, Skt. *pañcaśikha*, A gandharva who was very prominent in early Buddhism and is featured on early stupa reliefs playing a lute and singing. He would come to Buddha Śākyamuni, who was not portrayed as omniscient, to inform him of what was occuring in the paradises. He also accompanies Indra on a visit to the Buddha and plays music to bring the Buddha out of his meditation. He performs the same role in the Mahāyāna sūtra The White Lotus of Compassion (Toh 112). He was portrayed as living on a five-peaked mountain, and appears to be the basis for Mañjuśrī, first known as Mañjughoṣa (Beautiful Voice) with Pañcaśikha still being one of Mañjuśrī’s alternate names. In this sūtra he is clearly distinct from Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.

## Pañcakesarī
*seng ge lnga*, Skt. *pañcakesari*, An ancient city, probably corresponding to the modern Panchakesari in Orissa.

## Pañcala
*pany+tsa la*, Skt. *pañcala*, One of the fifteen lands in ancient India at the time of the Buddha. This was at the western end of the Ganges basin, corresponding in the present time to an area in the western part of Uttar Pradesh.

## Pacana
The name of a king.

## Pañcaśīrṣa
*mgo lnga*, Skt. *pañcaśīrṣa*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Pañcarakṣā
*gzungs chen grwa lnga*, Skt. *pañcarakṣā*, The term used to describe both the scriptures and the deities of the “five protectress goddesses” popular in the Mahāyāna-Vajrayāna tradition. The five goddesses are Mahāpratisarā, Mahāsāhasrapramardanī, Mahāmāyūrī, Mahāśītavatī, and Mahāmantrānusāriṇī.

## Pacification of Flaws
*skyon zhi*, Skt. *skyon zhi*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Guṇārci (222 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Pacified and Tamed
*rab tu zhi dul*, Skt. *rab tu zhi dul*, Birthplace of the buddha Praśāntagātra.

## Pacifier of Disturbing Emotions
*nyong mongs pa zhi bar byed pa*, Skt. *nyong mongs pa zhi bar byed pa*, A buddha.

## Pacifier of Enemies
*dgra zhir gyur pa*, Skt. *dgra zhir gyur pa*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Dharmavikrāmin (633 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Pacifier of Existence
*srid pa zhi byed*, Skt. *srid pa zhi byed*, A sage; a former incarnation of the Buddha.

## Pacifier of the Māras
*bdud zhi byed pa*, Skt. *bdud zhi byed pa*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Praśānta.

## pacifying
*zhi ba*, Skt. *śāntika*, A ritual activity pacifying hostile and obstructive forces, as well as disease and ill omens; one of the four main categories of ritual activity.

## Pacifying Roar
*rab tu zhi ba’i nga ro*, Skt. *rab tu zhi ba’i nga ro*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Viśiṣṭa­svarāṅga.

## Pañcika
*lngas rtsen*, Skt. *pañcika*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK; also the name of a yakṣa.

## Pack Leader
*khyu mchog*, Skt. *khyu mchog*, The name of a yakṣa.

## Pañcālā
*lnga len*, Skt. *pañcālā*, A river queen.

## Pañcāla
The name of a region in the north of the Indian subcontinent, situated among the plains along the Ganges River to the east of the Kuru region, covering the central part of the present-day state of Uttar Pradesh.

## Pañcāla cloth
*pany+tsa li ka’i gos*, Skt. *pañcālikāvastra*, Fabric from the north Indian kingdom of Pañcāla.

## Pañcālagaṇḍa
*tshigs lnga ser po*, Skt. *pañcālagaṇḍa*, A yakṣa general in the intermediate directions.

## Padakrama
*rkang pa’i ’gros*, Skt. *padakrama*, One of the kings of Nepal.

## Padampa Sangye
*pha dam pa sangs rgyas* (11th-12th century), Indian [siddha](#siddha) who established the teachings of the Shijepa (*zhi byed pa*) school. Teacher of [Machik Labdrön](#machik-labdrön), to whom he transmitted the [Cho](#cho) teachings. He traveled to Tibet several times.

## Padavikṣepa
*rkang pa ’phen pa*, Skt. *padavikṣepa*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Padmā
*pad mo*, Skt. *padmā*, Name of a world system in the direction of the nadir, where the buddha Padmaśrī teaches the perfection of wisdom to bodhisattva great beings.

## Padma
the name by which [Padmasambhava](#padmasambhava-of-oḍḍiyāna) refers to himself. The name [means](#means) "lotus".

## Padma Thotreng
*padma thod phreng rtsal*, lit. [Padma](#padma) garlanded with skulls. One of the names of [Padmasambhava](#padmasambhava-of-oḍḍiyāna).

## Padma Yamāri
*pad+ma gshin rje’i gshed*, Skt. *padmayamāri*, “Lotus Yamāri.” A deity in the maṇḍala of Black Yamāri. Also known as Padmapāṇi and Padmavajra.

## Padma­bhadrābhirāma­netra­śrī
*pad+mo bzang mo mig yid du ’ong ba’i dpal gyi zla ba*, Skt. *padma­bhadrābhirāma­netra­śrī*, Refers to Padma­bhadrābhirāma­netra­śrī­candrā, a cakravartin’s princess in the distant past. Also called Samanta­jñānārci­padma­bhadrābhirāma­netra­śrī­candrā.

## Padma­bhadrābhirāma­netra­śrī­candrā
*pad+mo bzang mo mig yid du ’ong ba’i dpal gyi zla ba*, Skt. *padma­bhadrābhirāma­netra­śrī­candrā*, A cakravartin’s princess in the distant past. Also called Samanta­jñānārci­padma­bhadrābhirāma­netra­śrī­candrā and Padma­bhadrābhirāma­netra­śrī.

## Padmacāriṇī
*pad+ma spyod byed ma*, Skt. *padmacāriṇī*, One of the goddesses associated with Amoghapāśa.

## Padmadharā
*pad ma ’dzin pa*, Skt. *padmadhāra*, One of the names of Śrī Mahādevī.

## Padmadhara

*pad ma ka*, Skt. *pad ma ka*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

*pad ma’i tog*, Skt. *padmaketu*, A buddha.

*pad+ma’i lte*, Skt. *padmanābha*, One of the lokeśvaras.

*pad+ma’i spyan ma*, Skt. *padmanetrī*, One of the goddesses associated with Amoghapāśa.

## Padmapāṇi
*pad+ma’i phyag*, Skt. *padmapāṇi*, “One with the Lotus in His Hand” is one of the lokeśvara emanations of Avalokiteśvara and, possibly, also another name of Amoghapāśa as well as an epithet of Avalokiteśvara himself.

*pad+ma rab snang ma*, Skt. *padma­prabhāsinī*, One of the goddesses associated with Amoghapāśa.

## Padmaśrīgarbha
*pad ma dpal gyi snying po*, Skt. *padmaśrīgarbha*, The name of a young bodhisattva, who is one of the interlocutors of the Buddha in this text.

## Padma­śrī­garbha­saṃbhavā
*pad mo dpal gyi snying po ’byung ba*, Skt. *padma­śrī­garbha­saṃbhavā*, A queen in another world in the distant past.

A buddha in the buddha domain of Padmavatī whose name is attested in the Sanskrit manuscript of this sūtra.

*pad+ma ’byung ba*, Skt. *padmasambhava*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Padmasambhava of Oḍḍiyāna
*o rgyan [padma](#padma) 'byung gnas*, the Lotus-born Teacher from [Oḍḍiyāna](#oḍḍiyāna), often known as [Guru Rinpoche](#guru-rinpoche). During the reign of [King Trisong Detsen](#trisong-detsen), the great master subjugated the evil forces hostile to the propagation of Buddhism in Tibet, spread the Buddhist teaching of [Vajrayāna](#vajrayāna) in that country and hid innumerable [spiritual treasures](#spiritual-treasure) for the sake of future generations. He is venerated as the Second [Buddha](#buddha) whose coming was predicted by the first one, [Buddha](#buddha) [Śākyamuni](#śākyamuni), to give the special teachings of [Vajrayāna](#vajrayāna).

*pad+ma mdzes pa*, Skt. *padmasundarī*, This seems to be another name of Unfailing Lotus Noose-Goad as Pure as a Lotus.

## Paiśāca
Sometimes appearing as Paiśācī, this is considered one of the great canonical languages of Indian Buddhist texts although there are no extant examples of this language. The name literally means “language of the ghosts.” Its history is unclear, but it is often identified as an ancestor of the Indo-Aryan Dardic languages spoken in the Kashmir region.

## palash
*pa la sha*, Skt. *palāśa*, Butea frondosa or Butea monosperma. A tree that grows up to 15 meters tall and has bright red flowers. Other names include flame of the forest, riddle tree, Judas tree, parrot tree, bastard teak, dhak (in Hindi), palas (in Hindi), porasum (in Tamil), and khakda (in Gujarati). There is a tradition of combining its leaves together to make a plate for food. This is also known as kiṃśuka, which is translated in other sūtras as ne tso ci las grub pa.

## Palatial Mountain
*gzhal yas khang gi ri*, Skt. *gzhal yas khang gi ri*, A forest in Total Pleasure.

*gser ser skya*, Skt. *gser ser skya*, A nāga king.

## Palgi Lhünpo
*dpal gyi lhun po*, Skt. *dpal gyi lhun po*, One of the greatest Tibetan translators. He lived in the eighth to ninth century. See also .

## Palgyi Lhünpo
*dpal gyi lhun po*, apart from Butön’s inclusion of Palgyi Lhünpo in his list of translators, there does not appear to be much biographical information available on this ninth-century translator. In addition to his work on the [vinaya](#vinaya), Palgyi Lhünpo translated at least two [Mahāyāna](#mahāyāna) [sūtra](#sūtra)s (the Buddhapiṭakaduḥśīlanigraha and the Drumakinnararājaparipṛcchā), several chapters of [dhāraṇī](#dhāraṇī), and several works in verse included in the Tengyur. The colophons of his translations indicate that [Paltsek](#paltsek) revised some of his translations, including the Vinayavastu and the Bhikṣuṇī Vinayavibhaṅga, to either complete unfinished work or reflect newly adopted standards.

## Palgyi Lhunpo
A Tibetan translator during the imperial period.

## Palgyi Yang
*dpal gyi dbyangs*, More commonly known as Palyang (dpal dbyangs), and also as Ba Ratna (sba rat na), Ba Palyang (sba dpal dbyangs), Ba Trisik (sba khri gzigs), and Śrīghoṣa, he was a translator and the first of the group of seven Tibetans to be ordained and trained by Śāntarakṣita.

## Pāṭali
*dmar bu can*, Skt. *pāṭali*, A village which eventually became Pāṭaliputra, the capital of Magadha.

## Pāṭaliputra
*pa ta la’i bu*, Skt. *pāṭaliputra*, The capital of Magadha was moved to the city of Pāṭaliputra during the Mauryan expansion, after which it served as the capital of Aśoka’s empire. It is identified with the modern Indian city of Patna. In this chapter, Pāṭaliputra is the location of the bodhisattva dwelling place called the Golden Park of the Saṅgha.

## palm tree
The palmyra palm tree, native to South and Southeast Asia, which can grow to a height of nearly one hundred feet.

## Palāmaratna­vṛkṣa­ratna
*rin chen ljon shing ’bras bu dpag med rin po che*, Skt. *palāmaratna­vṛkṣa­ratna*, A southern buddha realm that Buddha Śākyamuni sees.

## Palmo (nun)
*dge slong ma dpal mo*, famous Indian nun who propagated the practice of Nyung-ne (one-day fast and vow of silence) and attained the [supreme accomplishment](#supreme-accomplishment) through the practice of [Avalokiteśvara](#avalokiteśvara).

## palms and soles are red

*phyag gi mthil mnyam pa*, Skt. *tūla­sadṛśa­sukumāra­pāṇi­tā*, Thirty-first of the eighty minor marks.

## palmyra
Borassus flabellifer.

## Palmyra Trees Reaching the Sky
*ta la nam mkha’ la nye ba*, Skt. *ta la nam mkha’ la nye ba*, Name of the world system of the thus-gone one Lamp of the Sky of Dharma. Likely the same as the world system Fully-Adorned Sky.

## Palpung
Palpung monastery is an important Karma Kagyü monastery in Degé founded by Situ Paṇchen, the eighth Tai Situ Chökyi Jungné, in 1727 on the site of a previous Drigung Kagyü monastery. The construction of its main temple and assembly hall was supported by the Degé king, Tenpa Tsering.

## Paltsek
*dpal brtsegs*, Paltsek, from the village of Kawa north of Lhasa, was one of Tibet’s preeminent translators. He was one of the first seven Tibetans to be ordained by [Śāntarakṣita](#śāntarakṣita) and is counted as one of [Guru Rinpoche](#guru-rinpoche)’s twenty-five close [disciple](#disciple)s. In a famous verse by Ngok Lotsawa, Paltsek is named with Chokro Luyi Gyaltsen and Zhang Nanam Yeshé as part of a group of translators whose skills were surpassed only by [Vairotṣana](#vairotṣana). He translated works from a wide variety of genres, including [sūtra](#sūtra), [śāstra](#śāstra), [vinaya](#vinaya), and [tantra](#tantra) and was an author himself (for a list of his translations and writings, see Martin, 2011). Paltsek was also one of the most important editors of the early period, one of nine translators installed by Trisong Deutsen to supervise the translation of the [Tripiṭaka](#tripiṭaka) and help catalogue translated works for the first two of three imperial catalogs (the ldan kar ma and bsam yas mchims phu ma catalogs, which were probably the initiative of Tride Songtsen; see Raine, 2010, 8).

## Paltsek Rakṣita
*dpal brtsegs rak+Shi ta*, Skt. *dpal brtsegs rak+Shi ta*, One of the greatest Tibetan translators, most commonly known as Kawa Paltsek. Kawa Paltsek lived in the eighth to ninth century. Translating numerous canonical texts, both sūtra and tantra, he became one of the most active translators of his time. He was one of the initial seven Tibetans to be ordained during the founding of the first Tibetan monastery of Samyé.

*dpal yul*, one of the six great monasteries of the [Nyingmapa](#nyingmapa) school.

## parasol
Skt. *chattra*, First of the eighty designs on the palms and soles of the Tathāgata. In general Indian iconography it is a symbol of protection and royalty. In Buddhism it symbolizes protection from the blazing heat of afflictions, desire, illness, and harmful forces, just as a physical parasol protects one from the blazing sun or the elements. It is also included in the eight auspicious emblems.

## parinirvāṇa
*yongs su mya ngan las ’das pa*, Skt. *parinirvāṇa*, Nirvāṇa, the state beyond sorrow, denotes the ultimate attainment of liberation, the permanent cessation of all suffering and the afflicted mental states that cause and perpetuate suffering, along with all misapprehension with regard to the nature of reality. As such, it is the antithesis of cyclic existence. Three types of nirvāṇa are identified: (1) the residual nirvāṇa where the person is still dependent on conditioned psycho-physical aggregates, (2) the non-residual nirvāṇa after an arhat or buddha has passed away, when the conditioned psycho-physical aggregates have ceased, and (3) the non-abiding nirvāṇa transcending the extremes of phenomenal existence and quiescence. Parinirvāṇa generally refers to the non-residual attainment.

*pa ri pe la*, Skt. *paripelava*, Cyperus rotundus.

## parivrājaka
*kun tu rgyu*, Skt. *parivrājaka*, “Wandering mendicant,” parivrājaka (Sanskrit, wanderer; Pāli, paribbājaka). Refers to a class of Indian religious mendicants holding a variety of beliefs who wandered in India from ancient times, including during the time of the Buddha. These peripatetic ascetics, who included women in their number, engaged with one another in debate on a range of topics. Some of their metaphysical views are presented in the early Buddhist discourses of the Pāli Canon.

## partial understanding of selflessness with respect to personal identity
*gang zag la bdag med par phyogs gcig shes pa*, Skt. *ekāntika­pugdala­nair­ātmya­jñāna*, Selflessness in this context‌ implies the lack of inherent existence in personal identity and also in physical and mental phenomena. Śrāvakas are said to expound the doctrine of selflessness only in terms of the absence of personal identity, while pratyekabuddhas additionally realize the emptiness of external phenomena, composed of atomic particles. However, unlike bodhisattvas they do not realize that the internal phenomena of consciousness too are without inherent existence.

## Parīttabṛhat
*chung che*, Skt. *parīttabṛhat*, Literally meaning “Small Great,” the name used in this text and in the Hundred Thousand for what is, in the Prajñāpāramitā literature, the fourteenth of the sixteen levels of the god realm of form that correspond to the four meditative concentrations. The Sanskrit equivalent is attested in the Sanskrit of the Hundred Thousand, while the name Anabhraka (q.v.) is used in the later Sanskrit manuscripts that correspond more closely to the eight-chapter Tengyur version of this text. In other genres, this is the tenth of twelve levels of the god realm of form that correspond to the four meditative concentrations.

## Parīttaśubha
*dge chung*, Skt. *parīttaśubha*, Lit. “Those Whose Virtue Is Circumscribed.” The seventh of the seventeen heavens of the form realm; also the name of the gods living there. In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and pure abodes‍, or Śuddhāvāsa‍, it is listed as the first of the three heavens that correspond to the third of the four concentrations.

## Parī­ttaśubha
*dge ba*, Skt. *parī­ttaśubha*, The lowest of the three paradises that are the third dhyāna paradises in the form realm.

The Sanskrit equivalent is attested in the Sanskrit of the Hundred Thousand, while the name Anabhraka (q.v.) is used in the later Sanskrit manuscripts that correspond more closely to the eight-chapter Tengyur version of this text. In other genres, this is the tenth of twelve levels of the god realm of form that correspond to the four meditative concentrations.

In the form realm, which is structured according to the four concentrations and pure abodes‍, or Śuddhāvāsa, it is listed as the first of the three heavens that correspond to the second of the four concentrations.

## Path and Result
The Path and Result is the highest teaching of the Sakya lineage of Tibetan Buddhism. It is rooted in the understanding that the path to awakening and the result of awakening itself are contained within one another. The teachings of the Path and Result are based on Virūpa’s Vajra Verses (rdo rje’i tshig rkang), whereas the practice is based on the Hevajra Tantra.

## Path Giver
*lam byin*, Skt. *lam byin*, A sage; a former incarnation of the Buddha.

## Path of accumulating
*tshogs lam*, Skt. *sambhāramārga*, the first of the [five paths](#five-paths) towards [total enlightenment](#total-enlightenment), according to the [Bodhisattva](#bodhisattva) [vehicle](#vehicle). On this [path](#path) one accumulates the causes which will make it possible to proceed towards [enlightenment](#enlightenment).

## path of cultivation
*sgom lam*, Skt. *bhāvanā­mārga*, Fourth of the five paths, preceded by the paths of provisions, connection, and insight, and followed by the path of no-more-learning.
