## prologue
*gleng gzhi*, Skt. *nidāna*, The introductory sections of a sūtra. Literally it can mean “cause.” One of the nine aspects of the Dharma according to this sūtra. More commonly there are said to be twelve that include these nine.

## prominent nose
*sna'i gzengs mtho ba*, Skt. *tuṅganāsa*, a prominent nose, i.e. with a high nasal root, was considered an attractive feature in ancient India. This may refer to an aquiline nose.

## Promotion
*sbyor ba la ’jug pa*, Skt. *yogāvaha*, Promotion (advancement to a higher position or rank), also the name of a realm in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

## prompt
*gleng ba*, Skt. *codanā*, During the rite of lifting restrictions, each monk extends an “invitation” or “lifts restrictions” (Tib. dgag dbye bya ba; Skt. pravāraṇam pravārayitum) to the other monks with whom he has passed the rains retreat. Other monks may then “prompt” (Tib. gleng ba; Skt. codanā) him with evidence of or well-grounded suspicion for an offense he has failed to confess. The semantic range of the Tib. verb gleng ba (Skt. codanā) in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya extends from gentle exhortation to reproof and compelling questioning. Hence it may be translated with “to prompt” or even “to accuse,” depending upon context. Kalyāṇamitra gives “should not prompt, that is, announce a fault,” and, “should not remind, that is, add assistance while [the confessant] is confessing”. See Kalyāṇamitra (F.319.a): gleng bar mi bya zhes bya ba ni nyes pa bsgrags pas so/ / dran par mi bya zhes bya ba ni bshags pa’i dus dang grogs brjod pas so. Here, the commentator emphasizes the verbal nature of the act without implying any of the rancor or contentiousness usually associated with the English verb “accuse.” Yijing, the translator of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya into Chinese, likewise renders the underlying Skt. codanā with yan 言 (Taishō 1044c17), a generic verb for “speak.” The commentator Śura explains that “when [a monk] is made to lift restrictions, [the monk] withdraws to an isolated place on the boundary and, having gathered his recollection and attentiveness, he should ‘prompt’ [the other monk’s memory] with the circumstances of what he has seen, heard, or suspected. If, when thus prompted with the circumstances, [the accused monk] is unable to recall, he should be reminded with the place, time, and circumstances.” Śura (vol. nu, F.76.a): des de la skabs ’byed du bcug ste dus dben pa’i mthar dran pa dang shes bzhin nye bar gzhag ste mthong ba ’am/ thos pa ’am/ dogs pa’i gzhi dang bcas bas gleng bar bya’o/ /de ltar gzhi dang bcas pas glengs pa na ma dran na yul dang/ dus dang/ gzhi gang nas ltung ba byung ba gleng ba pos ji ltar mthong ba ’am/ thos pa ’am/ dogs pa’i sgo nas dran par bya’o. See Dharmamitra (vol. yu, F.348.a–349.a) for comments on Guṇaprabha’s digest.

## Propagator of the Meaningful Name
*don yod ming sgrogs*, Skt. *don yod ming sgrogs*, A great bodhisattva.

## propensities for afflicted mental states that cause linking up
*bag chags kyi mtshams sbyor ba’i nyon mongs pa*, Skt. *vāsanānusaṃdhi­kleśa*, The mundane process of rebirth within saṃsāra, impelled by the propensities of past actions. See also The Precious Discourse on the Blessed One’s Extensive Wisdom That Leads to Infinite Certainty (Toh 99), , and .

## propensity
*bag la nyal ba*, Skt. *anuśaya*, The BHS anuśaya differs from its meaning in Sanskrit but is the same as the Pali anusaya. It can also mean “tendency” and “disposition,” and the meaning can be positive as well as negative.

## proper
*chos dang ldan pa*, Skt. *dhārmika*, The Sanskrit term dharma, from which dhārmika is derived, here denotes the “proper” or “customary” way of doing things. For example, Kalyāṇamitra explains that a “proper” recitation of The Prātimokṣa Sūtra involves reciting the correct text in the prescribed way on the appropriate days. See Kalyāṇamitra (F.315.b).

## Proper Adherence
*legs gnas*, Skt. *legs gnas*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Mahābala.

## proper production
*yang dag skyed pa*, Skt. *yang dag skyed pa*, The name of a karmic wind involved in the formation of an embryo in its twenty-first week.

## proper understanding
*so so yang dag par rig pa*, Skt. *pratisaṃvid*, Correct understanding of meaning, Dharma, language, and eloquence.

## proper way
*rigs pa*, Skt. *nyāya*, The Nibandhana explains nyāya as follows: “Nyāya refers to the dharma of nirvāṇa, for it has been said that āya means a path, and that an “eternal path” (nityam āyaḥ) is called nyāya.”

## prophecies
*lung du bstan pa’i sde*, Skt. *vyākaraṇa*, One of the twelve branches of Buddhist scriptures.

## prophecy
*lung bstan pa*, Skt. *vyākaraṇa*, In this text and many others, the formal statement by a buddha that a particular individual (or occasionally a group) will attain awakening as a named tathāgata, often in a named world system during a named future eon. The same term is also used (though not in this text) to refer to a category of scriptures in which such prophetic statements are made; more generally, it can mean simply a teaching or explanation.

## Prophesied Attainment
*lung bstan mchog thob*, A bodhisattva. (Toh 555: gong du lung bstan pa thob pa)

## prophetic declaration
*lung bstan pa*, Skt. *vyākaraṇa*, In the evolution of bodhisattvas, the formal prophecy or prophetic declaration made by a buddha that they will attain awakening at a specified future time is a key event frequently described in the sūtras and other narrative accounts. It is also the third of the twelve branches of the scriptures.

## prophetic declarations
*lung du bstan pa’i sde*, Skt. *vy­ākaraṇa*, Third of the twelve branches of the scriptures.

## Proponent of the View That All Phenomena Exist
*thams cad yod par smra ba*, Skt. *sarvāstivādin*, The name of a monk in the lineage of the buddha Mahāvyūha and the name of the order founded by that monk after Mahāvyūha entered parinirvāṇa.

## prose put into verse
*dbyangs bsnyad*, Skt. *geya*, The repetition of prose passages in verse form. Literally “that which is to be chanted.” One of the nine aspects of the Dharma according to this sūtra. More commonly there are said to be twelve that include these nine.

## Prostration
*phyag 'tshal ba*, gesture of reverence, in which the forehead, the two hands and the two knees touch the ground.

## Protected by Gods
*lhas bsrungs*, Skt. *lhas bsrungs*, Father of the buddha Maruttejas.

## Protected by the Buddha
*sangs rgyas skyabs*, Skt. *buddhapāla*, A Licchavī youth.

## Protected by the Dharma
*chos skyabs*, Skt. *dharmapāla*, A Licchavī youth.

## Protected by the Saṅgha
*dge ’dun skyabs*, Skt. *saṅghapāla*, A Licchavī youth.

## Protected by the Sky
*nam mkha’ skyabs*, Skt. *ākāśapāla*, A Licchavī youth.

## Protected by Vajras
*rdo rje skyabs*, Skt. *vajrapāla*, A Licchavī youth.

## Protecting Guardian
*rtas bsrungs*, Skt. *rtas bsrungs*, Name of a sage.

## protection circle
*srung ba’i ’khor lo*, Skt. *rakṣācakra*, In The Tantra of Black Yamāri, a visualized wheel, the spokes of which consist of sharp blades.

## protection cord
*skud pa*, Skt. *tantuka*, A cord that is incanted with a mantra and worn on the body to protect against attack from human and nonhuman beings.

## protection hand-mudrā
*mi ’jigs pa’i phyag rgya*, Skt. *abhayamudrā*, A hand mudrā that signifies granting protection and safety.

## Protection of the Worthy Ones
*dgra bcom bsrung*, Skt. *dgra bcom bsrung*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Siṃhagati.

## Protector
*skyob pa*, Skt. *skyob pa*, Protector (one who protects or guards), also the name of the father of the buddha Sūryānana.

## protector deity
This term denotes any protector deity, from those associated exclusively with a localized area to deities such as Mahākāla who are considered protectors of both localized areas, trans-local populations, and the Dharma itself.

## protector of all worlds
*’jig rten thams cad skyob pa*, A meditative stability.

## Protector of Excellence
*bzang skyong*, Skt. *bzang skyong*, A devaputra present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Protector of Glory
*dpal srung*, Skt. *dpal srung*, A buddha.

## Protector of Men
*mi skyob pa*, Skt. *mi skyob pa*, Name of a bodhisattva.

## protector of the world
*’jig rten skyong ba*, Skt. *lokapāla*, One category of Dharma protectors in Buddhism.

## Protector Sight
*mgon po mthong*, Skt. *mgon po mthong*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Guṇottama.

## Protectors
see [Dharma protectors](#dharma-protector).

## Protectors of the Three Families
*rigs gsum mgon po*, the [Bodhisattvas](#bodhisattva) [Mañjuśrī](#mañjuśrī), [Avalokiteśvara](#avalokiteśvara) and [Vajrapāṇi](#vajrapāṇi). The three families are respectively those of the body, speech and mind of the [Buddha](#buddha).

## protectors of the world
*’jig rten skyong ba*, Skt. *lokapāla*, A set of deities, each guarding a certain direction. Most commonly these are Indra (Śakra) for the east, Agni for the southeast, Yama for the south, Sūrya or Nirṛti for the southwest, Varuṇa for the west, Vāyu (Pavana) for the northwest, Kubera for the north, and Soma (Candra), Iśāni, or Pṛthivī for the northeast.

## Proud
*nga rgyal can*, Skt. *nga rgyal can*, Proud (feeling deep pleasure or self-esteem), also the name of a son of the buddha Puṇyahastin.

## provided with a supremely rich and fine complexion
Part of a repeat phrase found in this and other sūtras (gzugs bzang ba/ mdzes pa/ blta na sdug pa/ kha dog bzang po rgyas pa mchog dang ldan pa), probably more literally meaning having a fullness of excellent color over the entire body. The Mahāvyutpatti suggests this is to be read as a single feature.

## Provider of All Beings’ Satisfaction
*sems can thams cad tshim byed*, Skt. *sems can thams cad tshim byed*, Name of a bodhisattva.

## Provider of Carriage
*bzhon par mdzad*, Skt. *bzhon par mdzad*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Anupamarāṣṭra (266 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## provision
*tshogs*, Skt. *sambhāra*, This term denotes the two provisions of merit and wisdom that are gathered by bodhisattvas on the path to complete buddhahood. The fulfilment of the provision of merit (puṇyasambhāra, bsod nams kyi tshogs) and the provision of wisdom (jñānasambhāra, ye shes kyi tshogs) constitutes the fruition of the entire path according to the Great Vehicle, resulting in the maturation of the buddha body of form (rūpakāya)and the buddha body of reality (dharmakāya), respectively.

## provisional meaning
*drang ba’i don*, Skt. *neyārtha*, A statement that is context-specific or which which requires further explanation. Contrasted with “definitive meaning.”

## Provisions for the Path of Seeing
*mthong ba’i lam rgyags*, Skt. *mthong ba’i lam rgyags*, A holy site blessed by the presence of sages.

## provisions that are definitely authentic
*yang dag pa nyid du nges pa’i tshogs*, Skt. *samyak­tva­niyata­rāśi*, First of the three provisions.

## provisions that are definitely erroneous
*log pa nyid du nges pa’i tshogs*, Skt. *mithyā­tva­niyata­rāśi*, Second of the three provisions.

## provisions that are of indefinite provenance
*ma nges pa’i tshogs*, Skt. *a­ni­yata­rāśi*, Third of the three provisions.

## provoking illness
*nad slong*, Skt. *nad slong*, A type of worm (srin bu) that lives in and feeds on the body.

## proximate kleśa
*nye ba’i nyon mongs pa*, Skt. *upakleśa*, The subsidiary afflictive emotions that arise in dependence upon the six root afflictive emotions (attachment, hatred, pride, ignorance, doubt, and wrong view); they are (1) anger (krodha, khro ba), (2) enmity/malice (upanāha, ’khon ’dzin), (3) concealment (mrakṣa, ’chab pa), (4) outrage (pradāsa, ’tshig pa), (5) jealousy (īrṣyā, phrag dog), (6) miserliness (mātsarya, ser sna), (7) deceit (māyā, sgyu), (8) dishonesty (śāṭhya, g.yo), (9) haughtiness (mada, rgyags pa), (10) harmfulness (vihiṃsā, rnam par ’tshe ba), (11) shamelessness (āhrīkya, ngo tsha med pa), (12) non-consideration (anapatrāpya, khril med pa), (13) lack of faith (aśraddhya, ma dad pa), (14) laziness (kausīdya, le lo), (15) non-conscientiousness (pramāda, bag med pa), (16) forgetfulness (muṣitasmṛtitā, brjed nges), (17) non-introspection (asaṃprajanya, shes bzhin ma yin pa), (18) dullness (nimagna, bying ba), (19) agitation (auddhatya, rgod pa), and (20) distraction (vikṣepa, rnam g.yeng) (Rigzin 329, 129).

## Prāsaṅgika
*thal ’gyur ba*, Skt. *prāsaṅgika*, The sub-school of the Mādhyamika philosophical school founded by Buddha-Pālita and further developed by Candrakīrti.

## Pārāsara
*pha rol mtha’ med*, Skt. *pārāsara*, A yakṣa general.

## Prāṇītajñāna
*ye shes gya nom*, Skt. *prāṇītajñāna*, The 620th buddha in the first list, 619th in the second list, and 612th in the third list.

## Pārthiva
*sa bdag*, Skt. *pārthiva*, The 607th buddha in the first list, 606th in the second list, and 600th in the third list.

## prātihāra
*cho ’phrul gyi zla phyed*, Skt. *prātihāra*, A bright fortnight that is particularly auspicious; this term is used frequently, but the exact meaning is elusive.

## Prātimokṣa
*so sor thar pa*, lit. individual [liberation](#liberation). The vows of individual [liberation](#liberation) are the eight categories of vows taught in the [Vinaya](#vinaya), from the simple one day vow up to the complete vows of fully ordained monks. See [three vows](#three-vows).

## prātimokṣa vows
The vows and regulations that constitute the foundation of Buddhist discipline. The number and scope of the vows differ depending on one’s status (lay, novice monastic, or full monastic) and whether one is female or male.

## prudent
*yid bzhungs pa*, Skt. *medhāvin*, A term describing the quality of a being’s intellect.

## Pāruṣika
A garden in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the highest of the heavens. The garden is named, presumably, for the prevalence of Grewia asiatica, a berry bush known as phalsa.

## Pāruṣyaka
The name of one of the groves of the deities of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. In Praises to Śrīdevī Kālī , Pāruṣyaka is identified as a vast grove (tshal chen po) on the summit of Mount Sumeru.

## Pāruṣyaka grove
*rtsub ’gyur gyi tshal*, Skt. *pāruṣyaka*, “Rough Grove.” One of the four heavenly groves outside the city of Sudarśana on Mount Meru. It owes its name to the fact that anyone who enters it becomes rough and violent and when the gods go there before battle they become donned with armor and weapons according to their needs.

## Pūrvī
*shar phyogs*, Skt. *pūrvī*, A country in the east, possibly the same as Prācī.

## Pārśva
*pha rol phyin rta*, Skt. *pārśva*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Pūrva Aparā
*khrums stod*, Skt. *pūrva aparā*, A constellation in the north.

## Pūrvabhadrapadā
*khrums stod*, Skt. *pūrva­bhadra­padā*, The name of a lunar asterism. Its chief star is known as Alpha Pegasi in the occidental tradition.

## Pūrvabhādrapadā
“Former Auspicious Feet.” The asterism of the two main stars in the constellation Pegasus.

## Pūrvaka
*sngon du ’gro ba*, Skt. *pūrvaka*, A great bodhisattva.

## Pūrvaphalgunī
*gre*, Skt. *pūrvaphalgunī*, The name of a lunar asterism. Its chief star is known as Delta Leonis in the occidental tradition.

## Pūrvaphālgunī
*gre*, Skt. *pūrvaphālgunī*, A lunar mansion in the south.

## Pūrva­praṇidhi­nirmāṇa­candra
*sngon gyi smon lam gyi ’phrul pa’i zla ba*, Skt. *pūrva­praṇidhi­nirmāṇa­candra*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Pūrva­praṇidhāna­saṃcodana­svara
*sngon gyi smon lam yongs su bskul ba’i sgra*, Skt. *pūrva­praṇidhāna­saṃcodana­svara*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## Pūrṇāvara
*gang po ngan*, Skt. *pūrṇāvara*, Hearer present in the circle around Śākyamuni.

## Pārvatī
*ri*, Skt. *pārvatī*, A goddess; wife of Śiva in the Purāṇic traditions.

## Pūrvavideha
*lus ’phags po*, Skt. *pūrvavideha*, One of the four continents of the human world according to traditional Indian cosmology, it is situated to the east of Mount Sumeru.

## Pūrva­videha
*lus ’phags*, Skt. *pūrva­videha*, The eastern continent of the human world according to traditional Indian cosmology, characterized as “sublime in physique”

## Pūrvāṣādhā
The twentieth of the twenty-seven constellations, or nakṣatras, in Vedic astrology. Here it corresponds to the sixth month of the Tibetan calendar, when the moon is full in the constellation.

## Pūrvāṣāḍhā
“Former Unconquered One.” The asterism of the two main stars in the archer part of the constellation Sagittarius.

## Prāvārika
*dgag dbye can*, Skt. *prāvārika*, A mango forest.

## Pārāyaṇa
*pha rol ’gro byed*, Skt. *pārāyaṇa*, A lost verse text, which was possibly a Mūla­sarvāstivādin counterpart of the Pārāyanavagga of the Suttanipāta in the Pāli canon and included in the Kṣudraka­piṭaka of the Mūla­sarvāstivādins.

## Pāṃsupiśācī
*phyag dar khrod kyi sha za mo*, Skt. *pāṃsupiśācī*, One of the great piśācīs.

## psycho-physical aggregate
*phung po*, Skt. *skandha*, See “five psycho-physical aggregates.”

## psychophysical bond
*tshogs kyi mdud pa*, Skt. *kāyagrantha*, A set of four bonds that bind the psychophysical body (Skt. kāya, Tib. tshogs) to cyclic existence. See also

## Pīta
*ser po*, Skt. *pīta*, See “Supīta.”

## pūta
*srul po*, Skt. *pūta*, A class of spirits that seems to be identical with the pūtanas.

## Āpāta
Skt. *āpāta*, One of the grahas.

## Pātanī
*ltung byed ma*, Skt. *pātanī*, A deity personifying the true nature of the element of earth; a goddess invoked to cause downfall.

## Pūtanā
*srul mo*, Skt. *pūtanā*, One of the great mātṛs.

## pūtana
*srul po*, Skt. *pūtana*, A class of disease-causing spirits associated with cemeteries and dead bodies. The name probably derives from the Skt. pūta, “foul-smelling,” as reflected also in the Tib. srul po. The morbid condition caused by the spirit shares its name and comes in various forms, with symptoms such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, skin eruptions, and festering wounds, the latter possibly explaining the association with bad smells.

## Pṛthakśravas
“Distinct Renown,” one of the four kings who support the earth.

## Pṛthivī
*sa*, Skt. *pṛthivī*, The earth personified; also, one of the rāśis.

## Pṛthivīdevatā
*sa yi lha*, Skt. *pṛthivīdevatā*, The name of the earth deity.

## pṛthivī­dhātvaparyanta
*sa’i khams mu med pa*, Skt. *pṛthivī­dhātvaparyanta*, Lit. “limitless earth element.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Pṛthivīvajrā
*rdo rje sa*, Skt. *pṛthivīvajrā*, One of the goddesses in the maṇḍala of Vajrasattva.

## Pṛthurāṣṭra
*khams chen po*, Skt. *pṛthurāṣṭra*, A region in South India.

## Pṛthvī
*sa*, Skt. *pṛthvī*, One of the eight goddesses in the north, called upon to grant protection.

## Pātāla
*sa’i ’og*, Skt. *pātāla*, The underworlds, of which there are said to be seven, include the realms of the daityas and yakṣas. The lowest is the realm of the nāgas. They are said to be pleasant and free from distress and even more beautiful than the higher realms.

## pātragata
*snod du gyur pa*, Skt. *pātragata*, Lit. “become a vessel.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

## Pāṃśu
*rdul gyi ri*, Skt. *pāṃśuparvatāḥ*, Unidentified mountains.

## Pāṇḍu
*skya ba seng*, Skt. *pāṇḍu*, A legendary king before the time of the Buddha, whose story features in the Mahābhārata. He could not produce descendants due to a curse, so his two wives conceived five children with different gods, after invoking them through a special mantra. Their sons became known as the five Pāṇḍava brothers. It’s for this reason that this text states this family has confused their genealogy. See .

## Puṇḍarīkā
*pad ma dkar*, Skt. *puṇḍarīkā*, One of the eight goddesses in the west, called upon to grant protection.

## Puṇḍarīka
*pad+ma dkar po*, Skt. *puṇḍarīka*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Puṇḍavardhana
*’phral ris ’phel*, Skt. *puṇḍavardhana*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Puchungwa, (Geshe)
*phu chung ba*, one of the [Three Brothers](#three-brothers).

## Puṃgava
*skyes mchog*, Skt. *puṃgava*, The 555th buddha in the first list, 555th in the second list, and 548th in the third list.

## Pāṃśughoṣa
*rdul dbyangs*, Skt. *pāṃśughoṣa*, An ājīvika ascetic who asks King Puṇyabala, a previous life of the Buddha Śākyamuni, for his eyes and skin.

## Puṣkara
*shin tu rgyas pa*, Skt. *puṣkara*, A buddha in the past.

## Puṣkarasārin
“He Who Has the Essence of a Lotus.” A learned brahmin who lived in the district town of Utkaṭa upon its endowment by the king. In Pali sources, in which his name is Pokkharasāti, he is described as becoming a follower of the Buddha after regretfully sending his student Ambaṭṭha to him first (DN I 87ff.). Other students of his were Vāseṭṭha, who plays a key role in the Vāseṭṭha Sutta (Sn 115ff.), and Subha Todeyyaputta, who figures in the Subha Sutta (MN II 197ff.). In the Subha Sutta Pokkharasāti is said to belong to the Opamañña (Aupamanya) lineage of brahmins.

## pukṣayā
An unidentified ritual ingredient.

## Puṣkiriṇī
*rdzing*, Skt. *puṣkiriṇī*, One of the groves in the realm of Thirty-Three.

## Pukkasī
*puk+ka sI*, Skt. *pukkasī*, One of the female deities in the retinue of Hevajra.

## pukkasa
*g.yung po*, Skt. *pukkasa*, The name of a group of people positioned outside, and thus below, the primary caste hierarchies of Indic society

## Pāṁśula
*rdul ldan*, Skt. *pāṁśula*, The name of an ancient city ruled by King Diśāṃpati. Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana are said to have lived on the outskirts of this city during their former lifetimes as ascetics.

## Pulaha
*spu zing sel*, Skt. *pulaha*, A lord of beings.

## Pulasti
*pul sti*, Skt. *pulasti*, One of the sages (ṛṣi).

## Pulastya
*mdun du bdar*, Skt. *pulastya*, A lord of beings.

## Pulina
*ldan ba*, Skt. *pulina*, A south Indian king contemporary with Mahendra.

## Pulinda
The name of a people in the southern part of the Indian subcontinent.

## Pulindo
*pu lin do*, Skt. *pulindo*, A land to the north of Jambudvīpa.

## pulmonary consumption
*skem pa*, Skt. *śoṣa*, symptom that may be evidence of an illness considered an impediment to ordination.

## Pulverizing
*thal bar rlog*, Skt. *thal bar rlog*, Pulverizing (crushing into powder or dust), also the name of the buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Arthasiddhi (589 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## punala tree
An unidentified ritual ingredient.

## Punarnavā
*pu na rna ba*, Skt. *punarnavā*, The name of a nakṣatra.

## Punarvasū
*nab so*, Skt. *punarvasū*, The name of a lunar asterism. Its chief star is known as Beta Geminorum in the occidental tradition.

## Punarvasu
*nab so*, Skt. *punarvasu*, one of the notorious “group of six’ monks whose antics and heavy-handed interference prompted a great many of the [Buddha](#buddha)’s injunctions on conduct. Also known as Punarvasuka.

## Punarvasuka
*nab so*, Skt. *punarvasuka*, A nāga. See also .

## punitive act
*chad pa'i las*, Skt. *daṇḍakarman*, a generic name for [disciplinary act](#disciplinary-act)s imposed by the [saṅgha](#saṅgha).

## Pure Abode
*gnas gtsang ma’i ris*, Skt. *śuddha­nivāsa*, These realms and abodes denote the hierarchy of the gods who, in the manner of human beings and antigods, partake of the higher realms (svarga, mtho ris) of rebirth, but nonetheless remain trapped within cyclic existence. The gods altogether comprise (i) six god realms within the world system of desire, commencing with Catur­mahā­rāja­kāyika and Trayas­triṃśa, and concluding with Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇa­rata, and Para­nirmita­vaśa­vartin; (ii) the twelve Brahmā realms, extending from Brahmakāyika through Brahmapurohita, Mahā­brahmā, Parī­ttābha, A­pramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parītta­śubha, A­pramāṇa­śubha, Śubha­kṛtsna, An­abhraka, and Puṇya­prasava to Bṛhat­phala, which are attained corresponding to lesser, middling, and higher degrees of the four meditative concentrations; and (iii) the five Pure Abodes at the pinnacle of the world system of form, extending from Avṛha, through Atapa, Su­dṛśa, and Sudarśana to Akaniṣṭha. See also and . This hierarchy is conveniently illustrated in the form of a chart. See, for example, Dudjom Rinpoche (1991): 14–15.

## Pure Abodes
*gnas gtsang ma*, Skt. *śuddhāvāsa*, The five Pure Abodes are the highest heavens of the form realm and result from mastery of the fourth meditative absorption. They comprise the heavens of the Insentient Beings, Unlofty Heaven, Sorrowless Heaven, Heaven of Sublime Vision, Heaven of Great Vision, and Highest Heaven. The Pure Abodes are never destroyed during the cycles of the destruction and creation of the universe. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing the fourth meditative absorption.

## purity
*yongs su dag pa*, Skt. *pariśuddhi*, A monk’s “purity” is lost when he incurs an offense, but he can restore his purity by confessing and making amends appropriate to that class of offense. All monks on site must profess their purity before The Prātimokṣa Sūtra is recited during the restoration rite. If a monk cannot attend, he must profess his purity through a proxy, who conveys it to the saṅgha. See Kalyāṇamitra (F.318.a–b).

## puruṣa
*skyes bu*, Skt. *puruṣa*, A fundamental ontological principle of the non-Buddhist Sāṅkhya tradition, puruṣa is the basic mode of timeless awareness. When puruṣa comes into contact with prakṛti, the undifferentiated potentiality that contains all possible transformations of thought and matter, prakṛti begins a sequential unfolding of internal and external metaphysical principles, thereby creating the known world. Puruṣa remains as the eternal, passive witness to this creation, until such time as puruṣa withdraws from prakṛti, thereby ending the process of creation and manifestation.

## Puṇya

## Puṣya
*rgyal ba*, Skt. *puṣya*, One of the twenty-eight asterisms or constellations that the sun passes through during the course of a year, which are “lunar mansions” in the plane of the sky. It is composed of the three star systems: Gamma Cancri, Delta Cancri, and Theta Cancri. In the Western zodiac it is equivalent to the very end of Cancer and nearly half of Leo—in other words, the end of July and the first part of August.

## Puṇyabala
*bsod nams kyi stobs*, Skt. *puṇyabala*, The name means “Power of Merit”; he is a leading character in a number of the Buddha’s past life stories. In The Exemplary Tale of Puṇyabala, the Buddha tells of his past life as Prince Puṇyabala, whose compassionate acts of generosity demonstrated that merit is the most prized possession of human beings.

## Puṇya­pradīpa­dhvaja
*bsod nams sgron ma’i rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *puṇya­pradīpa­dhvaja*, A buddha in the distant past.

*bsod nams sgron ma’i rgyal po*, Skt. *puṇya­pradīpa­rāja*, The 848th buddha in the first list, 847th in the second list, and 837th in the third list.

## Puṇya­pradīpa­saṃpatketu­prabhā
*bsod nams sgron ma phun sum tshogs pa kun nas dpal gyi ’od*, Skt. *puṇya­pradīpa­saṃpatketu­prabhā*, A bodhimaṇḍa goddess in a world in the eastern direction in a past kalpa, a previous life of the night goddess Praśanta­ruta­sāgara­vatī.

## Puṇya­pradīpa­saṃpatsamanta­ketu­prabhā
*bsod nams sgron ma phun sum tshogs pa kun nas dpal gyi ’od*, Skt. *puṇya­pradīpa­saṃpatsamanta­ketu­prabhā*, A bodhi-tree goddess, a past life of Praśanta­ruta­sāgara­vatī.

## Puṇyaprasava
*bsod nams ’phel*, Skt. *puṇyaprasava*, Literally meaning “Increasing Merit,” the more usual name for what is, in the Prajñāpāramitā literature, the fifteenth of the sixteen levels of the god realm of form that correspond to the four meditative concentrations, and in this text and in the Hundred Thousand is instead rendered Apramāṇabṛhat (q.v.). Puṇyaprasava is used in the later Sanskrit manuscripts that correspond more closely to the eight-chapter Tengyur version of this text. In other genres, it is the eleventh of twelve levels corresponding to the four meditative concentrations.

## Puṇya­prasava
*bsod nams ’phel ba*, Skt. *puṇya­prasava*, In the Sarvāstivada tradition, the second highest of the three paradises that correspond to the fourth dhyāna in the form realm.

## Puṇyapriya
*bsod nams dgyes*, Skt. *puṇyapriya*, The 917th buddha in the first list, 916th in the second list, and 907th in the third list.

## Puñyaraśmi
*bsod nams ’od zer*, Skt. *puñyaraśmi*, One of the Buddha’s former rebirths.

## Puṇyaraśmi
*bsod nams ’od zer*, Skt. *puṇyaraśmi*, The 602nd buddha in the first list, 601st in the second list, and 595th in the third list.

*bsod nams dpal gyi snying po*, Skt. *puṇya­śrī­garbha*, A bodhisattva mahāsattva.

## Puṇyarāśi
*bsod nams phung po*, Skt. *puṇyarāśi*, The 569th buddha in the first list, 569th in the second list, and 562nd in the third list.

*bsod nams ri rab*, Skt. *puṇya­sumeru*, A buddha in the distant past.

## Puṅyālaṃkāra
*bsod nams brgyan*, Skt. *puṅyālaṃkāra*, One of Māra’s sons who developed faith in Prince Siddhārtha and tried to dissuade Māra from attacking him on the evening of his awakening.

*bsod nams ’phags*, Skt. *puṇyodgata*, An ancient king.

## Pāyila
*btung ’dzin*, Skt. *pāyila*, One of the twelve great yakṣa generals who protect and serve those who bear, read, recite, copy, or commission a copy of the Bhaiṣajya­guru­vaiḍūrya­prabha­rāja­sūtra.

## Qualities

## qualities of buddhahood
*sangs rgyas kyi chos*, Skt. *buddhadharma*, The specific qualities of a buddha; may sometimes be used as a general term, and sometimes referring to sets such as the ten strengths, the four fearlessnesses, the four correct discriminations, the eighteen unique qualities of buddhahood, and so forth; or, more specifically, to another set of eighteen: the ten strengths; the four fearlessnesses; mindfulness of body, speech, and mind; and great compassion. Alternatively, in the context of this sūtra, see Chapter Six.

## qualities of stability and skill
*brtan mkhas kyi yon tan*, to [accept charge of](#accept-charge-of) monk [apprentice](#apprentice)s and monk journeymen, a monk must himself be both [stable](#stable), meaning he has been ordained at least five or ten years without incurring an offense, and knowledgeable, meaning he has at least one of the twenty-one sets of five qualities described in “The Chapter on Going Forth.”

## qualities that are conducive to awakening
List of thirty-seven mental factors the cultivation of which is said to lead to the achievement of awakening (bodhi), including the four applications of mindfulness, the four foundations for superhuman power, the four right efforts, the five powers, the five spiritual faculties, the eightfold path, and the seven constitutive factors of awakening.

*bye ba khrag khrig brgya stong phrag*, Skt. *koṭi­nayuta­śata­sahasra*, Quintillion (a million million million) is here derived from the classical meaning of nayuta as “a million.” The Tibetan gives nayuta a value of a hundred thousand million, so that the entire number would mean a hundred thousand quintillion.

## Śrī
*dpal*, Skt. *śrī*, The great goddess Śrī, better known as Lakṣmī, who promises to aid those who recite this sūtra and to ensure its preservation so that beings will have good fortune. She dwells in a palace in the paradise of Alakāvati.

## ūrṇā
*mdzod spus*, Skt. *ūrṇā*, A circle of hair located between the eyebrows. It is considered an auspicious mark and is included in some lists of the thirty-two major marks of a great being. In images it is often depicted as a gem between the eyebrows.

*snang ba mtha’ yas dpal*, Skt. *śrī amitābha*, A buddha.

## ūrṇā hair
*mdzod spu*, Skt. *ūrṇākośa*, One of the thirty-two signs of a great being, it is a coiled white hair between the eyebrows. Literally, the Sanskrit ūrṇā means “wool hair,” and kośa means “treasure.”

## Śrī Mahādevī
*dpal lha mo chen mo*, Skt. *śrī mahādevī*, “Glorious Great Goddess.” This is also a widespread name in Hindu contexts; it is, for example, an epithet of Śiva’s consort, but this name could refer to a number of different figures.

## Śrī Siṃha
*dpal gyi seng ge* (4th century), the third human teacher in the lineage of transmission of the [Great Perfection](#great-perfection) teachings, [disciple](#disciple) of [Mañjuśrīmitra](#mañjuśrīmitra).

## Ra Gelong Chörap
The great editor and translator Ra Gelong Chörap was active during the eleventh century and is one of the translators of Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra.

## ūrṇa hair

*sgyu rtsal shes kyi bu ring du ’phur*, Skt. *āḷāra kālāma*, A Sāṃkhya teacher with whom Siddhārtha studied.

## Ra Lotsāwa Dorjé Drak
Ra Lotsāwa Dorjé Drakpa (rwa lo tsā ba rdo rje grags pa, c. 1016–1128) was an important translator and lineage holder of the Vajrabhairava teachings. He received his main tantric training (Vajrabhairava and Vajravārāhī) in Nepal under the master Bharo Chakdum (bha ro phyag rdum).
