## Sovereign Goddess of the Desire Realm
*’dod khams dbang phyug ma*, An epithet for Śrīdevī Mahākālī. According to The Tantra of the Flaming Ḍākinī (Toh 842), Śrīdevī Mahākālī prays that in her next life she may meet the Buddha and become the sovereign goddess of the desire realm. When this becomes reality, she becomes known as “Sovereign Goddess of the Desire Realm‍.”

## Sovereign Goddess of the Desire Realm‍
*’dod pa’i khams kyi dbang phyug ma*, An epithet for Devī Mahākālī. According to The Tantra of the Flaming Ḍākinī (Toh 842), Śrīdevī Mahākālī prays that in her next life she may meet the Buddha and become the sovereign goddess of the desire realm. When this becomes reality, she becomes known as “Sovereign Goddess of the Desire Realm‍.”

## Sovereign King of All Flowers’ Fragrance
*me tog thams cad kyi dri’i dbang phyug rgyal po*, Skt. *me tog thams cad kyi dri’i dbang phyug rgyal po*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Moon-like.

## Sovereign King of Brahmā
*tshangs pa’i dbang phyug rgyal po*, Skt. *tshangs pa’i dbang phyug rgyal po*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Pristine Pearl Lattice.

## Sovereign King of Incense
*spos kyi dbang phyug rgyal po*, Skt. *spos kyi dbang phyug rgyal po*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Lord of Movement.

## Sovereign King of Nāgas
*klu’i dbang phyug rgyal po*, Skt. *klu’i dbang phyug rgyal po*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Endowed with Honey.

## Sovereign Light Display
*’od bkod pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *’od bkod pa’i rgyal po*, A tathāgata in the northwestern buddhafield Free of Darkness.

## Sovereign of Powerful Reverberating Sound
*sgra bsrags pa’i stobs kyi rgyal po*, Skt. *sgra bsrags pa’i stobs kyi rgyal po*, A bodhisattva in the western buddhafield Illuminated.

## Sovereign of Supreme Reverberating Sound
*sgra bsgrags mchog gi rgyal po*, Skt. *sgra bsgrags mchog gi rgyal po*, A tathāgata of the buddhafield, at the zenith, called Adorned by Ornaments.

## Sovereign of the Magical Display of All Phenomena
*chos thams cad rnam par ’phrul pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *chos thams cad rnam par ’phrul pa’i rgyal po*, A bodhisattva.

## sovereign power
*byin gyi rlabs*, Skt. *adhiṣṭhāna*, This term is usually translated into English with “blessings.” However, as explained in Edgerton 1953, p. 15; Eckel 1994, pp. 90–93; Gómez 2011, pp. 539 and 541; and Fiordalis 2012, pp. 104 and 118, adhiṣṭhāna conveys the notions of control (of one’s environment as a result of meditative absorption), authority, or protection (see Abhidharmakośa VII.51, cf. La Vallée Poussin 1925, p. 119ff.). Adhiṣṭhāna is also used to convey the idea of transformation through exerting one’s control over objects, people, and places. The term “sovereign power” seems to cover all these shades of meaning as well as the various usages of the Sanskrit term, for example satyādhiṣṭhāna “the sovereign power of truth” and adhiṣṭhānādhiṣṭita “empowered by the sovereign power (of the Tathāgata).”

## sovereign ritual
*cho ga zhib mo’i rgyal po*, Skt. *kalparāja*, Literally “king of rites,” the term can refer to an actual ritual or a ritual text, such as the AP.

## Sovereign Who Emanates All Phenomena
*chos thams cad rnam par ’phrul pa’i rgyal po*, Skt. *chos thams cad rnam par ’phrul pa’i rgyal po*, A bodhisattva in the buddhafield, at the zenith, called Adorned by Ornaments.

## sowing discord
*dbye ba*, Skt. *vidveṣaṇa*, A ritual activity for causing division between two or more individuals and to sow dissent.

## Space Crest
*nam mkha’i tog*, Skt. *nam mkha’i tog*, A buddha.

## space dwellers
*nam mkha’ la gnas pa*, Skt. *nam mkha’ la gnas pa*, A class of asuras.

## space vajra
In Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra, this term signifies that the realization of emptiness is accompanied by the arising of profound bliss.

## space-like
*nam mkha’ lta bu*, Skt. *gaganakalpo*, The twenty-sixth of the fifty-one meditative stabilities manifested to Sadāprarudita in chapter 73.

## space-like and without attachment, hence free and without blemish
*nam mkha’ ltar chags pa myed pas rnam par grol zhing gos pa myed pa*, Skt. *ākāśāsaṅgha­vimukti­nirupalepa*, A meditative stability.

## Space-like Splendor
*nam mkha’i dpal*, Skt. *nam mkha’i dpal*, A bodhisattva.

## spaces between the worlds
*’jig rten gyi bar*, Skt. *lokāntarika*, According to abhidharma cosmology, when different world systems form, they drift near each other, but remain divided by the spaces (small according to some descriptions, immense according to others) between the massive rings of stone that surround each of them. These spaces are completely dark, unreached by any light from the suns of the worlds they lie between. Often classified as one kind of hell, these frigid and desolate places are populated by beings brought there by very negative karma. They cling to the cliffs, climbing around in darkness searching for sustenance. When they encounter fellow sufferers, they fight and try to push each other off, and tumble into the icy waters below.

## Spaces between worlds
*’jig rten gyi bar*, Skt. *lokāntarikā*, The places between adjacent world systems, outside their defining ring of mountains, that are said to be miserable and in utter darkness as the suns and moons of the world systems can shed no light there. They are nevertheless said to be inhabited by numerous beings and are sometimes counted among the hell realms.

## Spacious Mind
*yangs pa’i blo*, Skt. *yangs pa’i blo*, A bodhisattva.

## Spacious Palanquin Houses
*khyogs kyi khang bu yangs pa*, Skt. *khyogs kyi khang bu yangs pa*, A park in Moving in the Stream.

## Sparkling with Brilliant Jewels
*nor bu’i cha shas rnams kyis rnam par bkra ba*, Skt. *nor bu’i cha shas rnams kyis rnam par bkra ba*, A mountain in Total Pleasure.

## Sparks and Parasites
*me’i phye ma srin bu*, Skt. *asthicūrṇakṛmi*, One of sixteen realms that surround the Howling Hell.

## sparrow mouth
*bye’u kha*, Skt. *bye’u kha*, A type of worm (srin bu) that lives in and feeds on the body.

## Spatial Intellect Completely Pure
*nam mkha’i blo gros rnam par dag pa*, Skt. *ākāśaviśuddhiprajña*, A deva.

## speak first
*gsong por gsung ba*, Skt. *pūrvābhi­lāpin*, Thirty-eighth of the eighty minor marks.

## speak with confidence
See also “eloquence and confidence.”

## Speaker
*gsung mdzad*, Skt. *gsung mdzad*, Speaker (one who speaks), also the name of a buddha.

## Speaker of Gentle Words
*ngag ’jam brjod pa’i tshig can*, Skt. *ngag ’jam brjod pa’i tshig can*, Mother of the buddha Saṃtoṣaṇa.

## Speaker with Beautiful Voice
*dbyangs snyan sgrogs par mdzad pa*, Skt. *dbyangs snyan sgrogs par mdzad pa*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Subāhu (100 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## speaking falsehoods
See “lying.”

## Spear Holder
An epithet for Śiva.

## Special Action
*spyod pa khyad par can*, Skt. *spyod pa khyad par can*, A great bodhisattva.

## special days
*cho ’phrul gyi phyogs*, Skt. *prātihāryapakṣa*, A sacred day; an ancient festival, not now kept. A special period of religious observance. Pali pāṭihāriyapakkha.

## special demeanor
*khyad par gyi spyod pa*, a monk who has received a [punitive act](#punitive-act), a [probation](#probation) and [penance](#penance), must accept a [probation](#probation) that involves rejecting the honors accorded to observant monks and adopting a position of deference.

## Special Drink
*lhag pa thung ba*, Skt. *lhag pa thung ba*, A forest on Flocking Peacocks.

## Special Gift
*khyad par byin*, Skt. *khyad par byin*, A great bodhisattva.

## special insight
*lhag mthong*, Skt. *vipaśyanā*, One of the basic forms of Buddhist meditation, aimed at developing insight into the nature of reality. Often presented as part of a pair of meditation techniques, the other being “tranquility.”

## Special Intelligence of Excellent Concern and Attention
*legs par bsam pa sems pa khyad par blo gros*, Skt. *legs par bsam pa sems pa khyad par blo gros*, A great bodhisattva.

## Special Joy
*lhag par dga’ ba*, Skt. *lhag par dga’ ba*, A realm of the ever-infatuated gods.

## Special Knowledge
*lhag shes*, Skt. *lhag shes*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Niyatabuddhi.

## Special Mind
*khyad par sems*, Skt. *khyad par sems*, Attendant of the buddha Janendra.

## special modes of knowledge
Four types of knowledge that are particularly oriented toward teaching the Dharma: knowledge of things, meanings, etymologies, and inspired eloquence.

## special qualities
*chos*, Skt. *dharma*, The polysemous word chos (usually a translation of dharma) is used here in the sense of “qualities,” as when someone or something is said to possess particularly efficacious, good, or beneficial qualities. It also can mean “virtue” in the nonreligious and nonmoral sense.

## specialists in the lists
*ma mo ’dzin pa*, Skt. *mātṛkādhara*, The ancient specialists in what later evolved to be the ābhidharmikas.

## speck of dirt on a cow
A large-size dust particle, seven of which are equal to the size of a louse egg.

## speck of dirt on a hare
A small-size dust particle, seven of which make up one speck of dirt on a sheep.

## speck of dirt on a sheep
A medium-size dust particle, seven of which make up one speck of dirt on a cow.

## Speech Conqueror
*smra ba ’joms byed*, Skt. *smra ba ’joms byed*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Dharmākara.

## speech is pervasive, in conformity with their assembly, but it does not extend outside their assembly
*gsung ni ’khor dang ’thun par khyab par mdzad kyi ’khor gyi phyi rol du gsung mi ’gro*, Skt. *vāg anu­kūla­varti­parṣado bahir na nir­gacchati*, Sixty-eighth of the eighty minor marks.

## speech is sweet and fully perfected
*gsung snyan cing rnam pa thams cad yongs su rdzogs pa*, Skt. *madhura­cārumañju­svara­tā*, Forty-sixth of the eighty minor marks.

## Speech Strewing
*lab ’thor ma*, Skt. *lab ’thor ma*, One of the eight nāga ladies.

## speech that is pleasant, gentle, and comforting
*snyan cing ’jam pa dang nyams su bde ba’i gsung dang ldan pa*, Skt. *madhura­cāru­mañju­svara*, Fifty-second of the eighty minor signs.

## spell
*rig sngags*, Skt. *vidyā*, A type of incantation or spell used to accomplish a ritual goal. This can be associated with either ordinary attainments or those whose goal is awakening.

## Sphere Endowed with Diverse Music
*sil snyan rnam pa sna tshogs kyi sgra dang ldan pa*, Skt. *sil snyan rnam pa sna tshogs kyi sgra dang ldan pa*, A forest in Engaging in Clarification.

## Sphere of Absolute Nothingness
*ci yang med pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *ākiṃ­canyāyatana*, One of the three lower formless realms among the four formless realms, so termed because in its preparatory phase absolute nothingness is the object of meditation.

## sphere of activity
*spyod yul*, Skt. *gocara*, Also translated here as “object of experience.”

## sphere of boundless space
*nam mkha’ mtha’ yas skye mched*, Skt. *ākāśānantyāyatana*, Alt. “the activity field infinite as boundless space” (Rangjung Yeshe Dictionary). Here the Blessed One begins an enumeration of the four formless realm states.

## Sphere of Infinite Consciousness
*rnam shes mtha’ yas skye mched*, Skt. *vi­jñānānantyāyatana*, One of the three lower formless realms among the four formless realms, so termed because in its preparatory phase infinite consciousness is the object of meditation.

## sphere of infinite space
*nam mkha’ mtha’ yas skye mched*, Skt. *ākāśānantyāyatana*, The first of the four states of imperturbability. In the formless realm (Skt. ārūpyadhātu), no bodies or materiality of any kind exist, only mind; rebirth there is the result of accomplishing four formless meditative absorptions (Skt. ārūpya­samāpatti; five absorptions, i.e., if one includes the stage of Skt. saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha or nirodhasamāpatti).

## sphere of infinity of consciousness
*rnam shes mtha’ yas skye mched*, Skt. *vijñānānantyāyatana*, One of the four attainments of the formless states. Also a class of gods in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). In this realm, there is no body, only mind; it is the result of accomplishing the formless meditative absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti).

## sphere of infinity of space
*nam mkha’ mtha’ yas skye mched*, Skt. *ākāśānantyāyatana*, One of the four attainments of the formless states. Also a class of devas in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). In this realm there is no body in this world, only mind; it is the result of accomplishing the formless meditative absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti).

## sphere of mastery
*zil gyis gnon pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *abhibhvāyatana*, The ability to disassociate oneself from external appearances based on attainment in concentration.

## sphere of neither mind nor no-mind
*sems med pa dang sems med pa ma yin pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *naiva­saṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*, The fourth of the four states of imperturbability or formless meditative absorptions or attainments (Skt. ārūpya­samāpatti), which leads to rebirth in the formless realm (Skt. ārūpyadhātu) as a deva without form.

## sphere of neither perception nor absence of perception
*’du shes med ’du shes med min gyi skye mched*, Skt. *naiva­saṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*, The fourth meditative state pertaining to the formless realm.

## Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception
*’du shes med ’du shes med min skye mched*, Skt. *naiva­saṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*, The highest of the four heavens of the formless realm, so termed because conceptions there are weak but not entirely absent. Also called “the peak of existence.”

## sphere of neither perception nor nonperception
*’du shes med ’du shes med min skye mched*, Skt. *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*, One of the four attainments of the formless states and the highest class of devas in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu); also called Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra).

## sphere of nothing whatsoever
*ci yang med pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *ākiñcanyāyatana*, Name of the third of the four formless realms and of the third formless concentration, so termed because in its preparatory phase absolute nothingness is the object of meditation.

## sphere of nothing-at-all
*cung zad med pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *a­kiñ­canyāyatana*, The third formless meditative absorption and its resultant formless realm of existence.

## sphere of nothingness
*ci yang med pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *ākiñcanyāyatana*, The third of the four attainments of the formless states. Also a class of devas in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu); there is no body in this world, only mind. Rebirth there results from accomplishing the formless meditative absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti).

## sphere of phenomena
*chos kyi dbyings*, Skt. *dharmadhātu*, Things as they truly are, with nothing imputed to them through dualistic thinking. The term is rendered elsewhere in this translation as “dharmadhātu.”

## sphere of reality
*chos kyi dbyings*, Skt. *dharmadhātu*, The element, or nature, of ultimate reality.

## sphere of sound
An expression found in this sūtra that refers to the expanse or reach of the sound of a realized one’s voice.

## Sphere of the Infinity of Consciousness
*rnam shes mtha’ yas skye mched*, Skt. *vijñānānantyāyatana*, Second of the four heavens of the formless realm. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing one of the formless meditative absorptions.

## Sphere of the Infinity of Space
*nam mkha’ mtha’ yas skye mched*, Skt. *ākāśānaṃtyāyatana*, First of the four heavens of the formless realm. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing one of the formless meditative absorptions.

## sphere of totality
*zad par gyi skye mched*, Skt. *kṛtsnāyatana*, The ability to transform the four elements based on attainment in concentration.

## spheres of mastery
*zil gyis gnon pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *abhibhvāyatana*, This refers to the miraculous perceptual transformation that ensues when one (1) regards lesser external forms, (2) regards greater external forms, (3) regards blue external forms, (4) regards yellow external forms, (5) regards red external forms, (6) regards white external forms, (7) abides in the sphere of infinite space, or (8) abides in the sphere of infinite consciousness.

## spheres of totality
*zad par gyi skye mched*, Skt. *kṛtsnāyatana*, The ten spheres of totality comprise the total meditative immersion into (1) the earth element, (2) the water element, (3) the fire element, (4) the wind element, (5) the space element, (6) blueness, (7) yellowness, (8) redness, (9) whiteness, and (10) consciousness.

## Sphoṭanī
*’gems ma*, Skt. *sphoṭanī*, A great rākṣasī.

## Sphoṭana
*rgyas byed*, Skt. *sphoṭana*, A nāga king.

## Sphāraśīrṣa
*mgo bo che*, Skt. *sphāraśīrṣa*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## spicy
*tsha*, Skt. *kaṭuka*, One of the eight supreme flavors. Also, one of the six tastes of the Āyurveda and Tibetan medical traditions.

## spider lily
*man dzu Sha ka*, Skt. *mañjūṣaka*, Lycoris albiflora. These flowers are both white and red and are said to also grow in the deva realms.

## spiked ginger lily
*gol la*, Skt. *śatī*, Hedychium spicatum.

## spikenard
*na la da*, Skt. *nalada*, Identified as Nardostachys jatamansi, or Indian spikenard, a plant recognized for its medicinal properties in the Atharvaveda and Suśrutasaṃhitā. The Sanskrit epic poem called Naiṣadhacarita identifies this plant as the root of Andropogon muricatus. A number of classical Sanskrit lexicographers identify this plant as the blossom of Hibiscus rosa sinensis.

## sūpāśimbī
A type of tree.

## spirit
*byung po*, Skt. *bhūta*, A broad class of demonic, possessing beings of which there are numerous subdivisions outlined in Āyurvedic literature and Śaiva tantras, such as the Netratantra and Kriyākallotara, that preserve material from the now-lost genre of bhūtatantra that discusses the symptomology, pathology, and treatment of demonic possession.

## spirit of enlightenment
*byang chub kyi sems*, Skt. *bodhicitta*, “Spirit” is preferred to “mind” because the mind of enlightenment should rather be the mind of the Buddha, and to “thought” because a “thought of enlightenment” can easily be produced without the initiation of any sort of new resolve or awareness. “Will” also serves very well here.

## spiritual attainment
*dngos grub*, Skt. *siddhi*, The mundane and transcendent abilities that are conferred through the perfection of yogic practices.

## spiritual benefactor
*dge ba’i bshes gnyen*, Skt. *kalyāṇamitra*, A Mahāyāna teacher is termed “friend,” or “benefactor,” which indicates that a bodhisattva-career depends on one’s own effort and that all a teacher can do is inspire, exemplify, and point the way.

## Spiritual companions
*chos grogs*, students of the same teacher, or with whom one has received teaching. It is considered vital to have harmonious relations with such people, particularly in the [Vajrayāna](#vajrayāna).

## spiritual family
*rigs*, Skt. *gotra*, Literally, the class, caste or lineage. In this context, it is the basic disposition or propensity of an individual that determines which kind of vehicle (śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, or bodhisattva) they will follow and therefore which kind of awakening they will obtain. tathāgata­garbha), i.e., in the sense that all beings are constituted with the disposition to fully awaken as a buddha.-->

## Spiritual friend
*dge ba'i gshes gnyen*, Skt. *kalyāṇamitra*, a synonym for spiritual teacher.

## spiritual guide
*dge ba’i bshes gnyen*, Skt. *kalyāṇamitra*, A teacher who can contribute to an individual’s progress on the spiritual path to awakening and act wholeheartedly for the welfare of students.

## spiritual insight
*chos kyi mig pa*, Skt. *dharmacakṣus*, Literally “Dharma eye,” this term refers to different, advanced modes of insight into the nature of reality.

## spiritual level
*sa*, Skt. *bhūmi*, Refers to stages of spiritual progress according to different spiritual paths or vehicles. See “ten spiritual levels.”

## spiritual life
*tshangs par spyod pa*, Skt. *brahmacārya*, Lit. “brahma conduct.” A term that in some contexts refers specifically to chastity or complete celibacy. It can also be used to refer in general to a spiritual life as a devout person or a renunciant.

## spiritual mentor
*dge ba’i bshes gnyen*, Skt. *kalyāṇamitra*, A spiritual teacher who can contribute to an individual’s progress on the spiritual path to enlightenment and act wholeheartedly for the welfare of students.

## Spiritual Teacher of Pleasant Voice
*snyan pa’i bshes gnyen*, Skt. *snyan pa’i bshes gnyen*, A buddha.

## Spiritual treasure
*gter ma*, teachings, with statues and other objects, that were hidden by [Padmasambhava](#padmasambhava-of-oḍḍiyāna), [Yeshe Tsogyal](#yeshe-tsogyal) and others in earth, rocks, lakes and trees, or even in more subtle locations such as space or mind for the sake of future generations, and then rediscovered in miraculous ways by incarnations of [Padmasambhava's](#padmasambhava-of-oḍḍiyāna) [disciple](#disciple)s, the [treasure discoverer](#treasure-discoverer)s.

## spirituous liquor
*’bru’i chang*, Usually a drink that has been fermented or distilled from grains.

## spite
*’tshig pa*, Skt. *pradāśa*, One of twenty or twenty-four so-called secondary mental defilements/afflictions (upakleśa), the basis of which seems to be feelings of jealousy and anger. Edgerton translates pradāsa as “envious rivalry” (BSHD, s.v. “pradāsa”). In Pāli commentaries it is defined as “yugaggāha [imperiousness], grasping after preëminence for oneself over others, […] primarily, concealment of the good qualities of others, jealous disparagement, nasty disposition, ill-will” (BHSD, s.v. “mrakṣa”).

## spṛkkā
*’bu gsug*, Skt. *spṛkkā*, Tib. is unrecorded in Negi. Skt. spṛkkā might possibly be Trigonella corniculata (McHugh, 2008, p 180, n30).

## Splashing Swan Wings
*ngang pas’i gshog pas bcom pa*, Skt. *ngang pas’i gshog pas bcom pa*, A pond on Equal Peaks.

## Splendid
*gzi brjid dang ldan pa*, Skt. *gzi brjid dang ldan pa*, Splendid (magnificent, grand, or brilliant), also the name of a ruler of the Heaven Free from Strife.

## Splendid Acumen
*spobs pa’i gzi brjid*, Skt. *spobs pa’i gzi brjid*, Son of the buddha Udgata.

## Splendid Adornment
*rab tu brgyan pa’i gzi brjid*, Skt. *rab tu brgyan pa’i gzi brjid*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Siṃhacandra.

## Splendid Aggregation Adorned with Precious Flowers
*rin po che’i me tog gis rab tu brgyan pa’i gzi brjid phung po*, Skt. *rin po che’i me tog gis rab tu brgyan pa’i gzi brjid phung po*, Mother of the buddha Puṣpa.

## Splendid Armor Bearer
*shin tu go cha bgos pa’i dpal*, Skt. *shin tu go cha bgos pa’i dpal*, A buddha.

## Splendid Array
*gzi byin bkod pa*, Skt. *gzi byin bkod pa*, Birthplace of the buddha Mokṣatejas.

## Splendid Array of Infinite Light
*snang ba mtha’ yas pa’i gzi brjid bkod pa*, Skt. *snang ba mtha’ yas pa’i gzi brjid bkod pa*, Birthplace of the buddha Ābhāsaraśmi.

## Splendid Beauty
*gzi brjid mdzes pa*, Skt. *gzi brjid mdzes pa*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Ṛṣīndra (759 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Splendid Brightness
*gzi brjid mdangs*, Skt. *gzi brjid mdangs*, Attendant of the buddha Devaruta.

## Splendid Creation
*gzi brjid sprul*, Skt. *gzi brjid sprul*, Birthplace of the buddha Candra.

## Splendid Crest
*tog gi gzi brjid*, Skt. *tog gi gzi brjid*, Attendant of the buddha Varuṇa.

## Splendid Delight
*gzi brjid sdug*, Skt. *gzi brjid sdug*, Birthplace of the buddha Tejorāśi.

## Splendid Display of the Body of All the Buddhas
*sangs rgyas thams cad kyi sku kun tu ston pa’i dpal*, Skt. *sangs rgyas thams cad kyi sku kun tu ston pa’i dpal*, A buddha.

## Splendid Display of the Body of Buddhas Beyond Observation
*dmigs pa mtha’ yas pa’i sangs rgyas kyi sku kun tu ston pa’i dpal*, Skt. *dmigs pa mtha’ yas pa’i sangs rgyas kyi sku kun tu ston pa’i dpal*, A buddha.

## Splendid Enjoyment
*dga’ byed gzi brjid*, Skt. *dga’ byed gzi brjid*, Mother of the buddha Gaṇiprabha.

## Splendid Excellence
*gzi brjid bzang po*, Skt. *gzi brjid bzang po*, Father of the buddha Mahādarśana.

## Splendid Fame
*gzi brjid grags pa*, Skt. *gzi brjid grags pa*, Son of the buddha Puṇyābha.

## Splendid Flashes of Highly Superior Illumination

## Splitting Open Like a Blue Lotus Hell
*ud pal ltar gas pa*, Skt. *utpala*, Sixth of the eight cold hells of Buddhist cosmology. The extreme cold of this hell turns the skin of its inhabitants blue until they crack apart in five or six pieces. Also rendered here as “Blue Lotus Hell.”

## Splitting Open Like a Great Lotus Hell
*pad ma ltar gas pa chen po*, Skt. *mahā­padma*, Eighth (and heaviest) of the eight cold hells of Buddhist cosmology. The extreme cold of this hell turns the skin of its denizens blue, red, and then extremely red until they crack apart in a hundred or more pieces. Also rendered here as “Great Lotus Hell.”

## Splitting Open Like a Lotus Hell
*pad ma ltar gas pa*, Skt. *padma*, Seventh of the eight cold hells of Buddhist cosmology. The extreme cold of this hell turns the skin of its denizens blue and then red until they crack apart in ten or more pieces. Also rendered here as “Lotus Hell.”

## stage
Eight or ten levels or stages through which the bodhisatva traverses on the journey to complete awakening.

## stage of devoted conduct
*mos pas spyod pa’i sa*, Skt. *adhimukti­caryā­bhūmi*, The level of devoted conduct is said to comprise the first two of the five paths, those of accumulation and preparation, which lead up to the path of seeing. This level is also presented as the second of seven spiritual levels in the Bodhisattva­bhūmi, which follows the initial level of the spiritual potential (gotrabhūmi).

## stage of engagement through aspiration
*mos pa spyod pa’i sa*, Skt. *adhimukticaryābhūmiḥ*, Mahāvyutpatti 897.

## stage of neither thought nor no thought
*’du shes med ’du shes med min skye mched pa*, Skt. *naiva­saṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*, The highest of the four divine attainments (absorptions) of the formless realm.

## stage of no impediment
*mi lcog med pa*, Skt. *mi lcog med pa*, The preparatory stage for the first concentration.

## stages of the strengths
*dbang po rnams kyi rim pa*, Skt. *indriyavaimātratā*, The development of various levels of capacities or capabilities as one progresses on the path.

## star jasmine
*kun da*, Skt. *kunda*, Trachelospermum jasminoides. It has its name because of its starlike white blossoms. In India it is used in speech as an example of whiteness, i.e., “as white as star jasmine.” Also called downy jasmine, Chinese jasmine, Chinese ivy, and trader’s compass.

*skar ma lta bu*, Skt. *skar ma lta bu*, An eon following the eon called Great Renown, during which time eighty thousand ministers of the universal monarch Vast Mind (a previous incarnation of the buddha Dīpaṅkara) will awaken to buddhahood.

## starving spirit
*yi dags*, Skt. *preta*, One of the five or six classes of sentient beings, considered to be the karmic fruition of past miserliness. In Sanskrit, literally “the departed”; they are analagous to the ancestral spirits of Vedic tradition, the pitṛs, who starve without the offerings of descendants. They live in the realm of Yama, the Lord of Death. They are particularly known to suffer from great hunger and thirst and the inability to acquire sustenance.

## Sātatagiri
*g.yung drung ri*, Skt. *sātatagiri*, Name of a yakṣa.

## state
*skye mched*, Skt. *āyatana*, This term has various meanings according to context. Here in this sūtra it is used to refer to the four meditative states associated with the formless realm: (1) infinite space, (2) infinite consciousness, (3) nothingness, and (4) neither perception nor nonperception. In the context of epistemology, it is one way of describing experience and the world in terms of twelve sense sources, which can be divided into inner and outer sense sources, namely: (1–2) eye and form, (3–4) ear and sound, (5–6) nose and odor, (7–8) tongue and taste, (9–10) body and touch, (11–12) mind and mental phenomena. In the context of the twelve links of dependent origination, only six sense sources are mentioned, and they are the inner sense sources (identical to the six faculties) of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

## state in which all dharmas are just so
*chos thams cad kyi de bzhin nyid*, Skt. *sarva­dharmānāṃ tathatā*, Also rendered as the “suchness of all dharmas.”

## state of all-knowing
*thams cad mkhyen pa nyid*, Skt. *sarvajñatva*, The state of knowing all possible and actual states of affairs of the past, present, and future (i.e., total omniscience) or knowing all that is most soteriologically relevant, the basic nature of reality (i.e., essential omniscience).

## state of arhatship
*dgra bcom pa nyid*, Skt. *arhattva*, The level of attainment of an arhat, one who is worthy of worship (pūjām arhati), or one who has conquered the enemies, the mental afflictions, and has reached liberation from the cycle of rebirth and suffering. The fourth and highest of the four fruits attainable by hearers (śrāvakas).

## state of infinite consciousness
*rnam shes mtha’ yas skye mched*, Skt. *vijñānānantyāyatana*, The second level of the four levels of the formless realm and its meditation, when everything is perceived as consciousness.

## state of infinite space
*nam mkha’ mtha’ yas skye mched*, Skt. *ākāśānantyāyatana*, The first of the four levels of the formless realm and its meditation, when all appears to be space.

## state of neither perception nor nonperception
*du shes med ’du shes med min skye mched*, Skt. *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*, The “highest” of the four formless realms, which have no location other than where the meditator passed away.

## state of nirvāṇa
Seemingly conceived of as either the state or nature of being or that of a being. One of a number of applications of the term dhātu, which can have the sense of an element or constituent part of the world and of the person. It can also be used in the sense of “the true state of things” (dharmadhātu) and “the sphere of the worlds” (lokadhātu).

## state of nothingness
*ci yang med pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *ākiñcanyāyatana*, The third of the four levels of the formless realm and its meditation, when there is the perception of nothingness.

## state of subjugation
*zil gyis gnon pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *abhi­bhavāyatana*, State when the power of meditation is more powerful than any perception, which therefore cannot disturb it.

## state of totality
*zad par gyi skye mched*, Skt. *kṛtsnāyatana*, State of meditation in which one can transform whatever is perceived.

## state of utter joy
In Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra, this phrase describes the state that arises when the vital winds of the left and right channels are suppressed.

## statement
*brjod pa*, Skt. *pra­vyāhāra*, Also translated here as “description.”

## statements made for a purpose
*ched du brjod pa*, Skt. *udāna*, Fifth of the twelve branches of the scriptures. See also .

## states of existence
*srid pa*, The five states of existence refer to the five destinies of birth as a god, as a human, as an animal, as a preta (or “hungry ghost”), and in the hells.

## states of meditative attainment
*snyoms par ’jug pa*, Skt. *samāpatti*, One of several common terms that are used to describe meditative states. The four states of meditative attainment refer here to the states of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither perception nor absence of perception.

## states of misery
A collective name for the realms of animals, anguished spirits (pretas), and denizens of the hells.

## sātatikā
*rtag pa las byung ba’i rims*, Skt. *sātatikā*, A class of spirits causing a lasting disease.

## station
*skye mched*, Skt. *āyatana*, Here station refers to sucessive stages of formless absorption, namely: station of endless space, station of endless consciousness, station of nothing-at-all, and station of neither perception nor nonperception. In other contexts in this sūtra, āyatana refers to the twelve sense fields; see “sense field.”

## station of complete suffusion
*mtha’ dag gi skye mched*, Skt. *kṛtsnāyatana*, See “ten stations of complete suffusion.”

## station of endless consciousness
*rnam shes mtha’ yas skye mched*, Skt. *vijñānānantyāyatana*, Second of the four formless realms. The term also refers to the class of gods that dwell there, and the name of the second of the four formless absorptions. The other three realms are the station of endless space, the station of nothing-at-all, and the station of neither perception nor nonperception.

## station of endless space
*nam mkha’ mtha’ yas skye mched*, Skt. *ākāśānantyāyatana*, First of the four formless realms. The term also refers to the class of gods that dwell there and the name of the first of the four formless absorptions. The other three realms are the station of endless consciousness, the station of nothing-at-all, and the station of neither perception nor nonperception.

## station of mastery
*zil gyis gnon pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *abhibhvāyatana*, See “eight stations of mastery.”

## station of neither perception nor nonperception
*’du shes med ’du shes med min skye mched*, Skt. *naiva­saṃjñā­nāsaṃjñāyatana*, The highest of the four formless realms. The term also refers to the class of gods that dwell there and the name of the fourth of the four formless absorptions. The other three realms are the station of endless space, the station of endless consciousness, and the station of nothing-at-all.

## station of nothing-at-all
*ci yang med pa’i skye mched*, Skt. *ākiṃcityāyatana*, Third of the four formless realms. The term also refers to the class of gods that dwell there and the third of the four formless absorptions. The other three realms are the station of endless space, the station of endless consciousness, and the station of neither perception nor nonperception.

## station of the endless-space absorption
*nam mkha’ mtha’ yas skye mched kyi snyoms par ’jug pa*, Skt. *nam mkha’ mtha’ yas skye mched kyi snyoms par ’jug pa*, See “station of endless space.”

## station of the neither perception nor nonperception absorption
*’du shes med ’du shes med min skye mched kyi snyoms par ’jug pa*, Skt. *’du shes med ’du shes med min skye mched kyi snyoms par ’jug pa*, See “station of neither perception nor nonperception.”

## station of the nothing-at-all absorption
*ci yang med pa’i skye mched kyi snyoms par ’jug pa*, Skt. *ci yang med pa’i skye mched kyi snyoms par ’jug pa*, See “station of nothing-at-all.”

## stations of complete immersion
*zad par gyi skye mched*, Skt. *kṛtsnāyatana*, See “ten stations of complete immersion.”

## Stavakarṇin
*rgya skegs kyi rna rgyan can*, Skt. *stavakarṇin*, Another name of Bhavatrāta, a half brother of Pūrṇa from Sūrpāraka.

## Sātavāhana
*sa la yi ni bzhon pa*, Skt. *sātavāhana*, A dynasty in south India whose rule ended in the third century ce.

## Stavārha
*bstod ’os*, Skt. *stavārha*, A self-awakened one in the future.

*gzhi ji bzhin pa*, Skt. *yathā­saṃstarika*, Eleventh of the twelve ascetic practices.

*tsho ba brtan pa*, Skt. *dhruvabhikṣā*, “To establish steady alms,” i.e. to establish an endowment, thereby ensuring that monks have good food and drink. Also rendered “steady alms living” (Tib. mthun pa’i mchod sbyin brtan po; Skt. dhruvabhikṣā).

## steady alms living
*mthun pa’i mchod sbyin brtan po*, Skt. *dhruvabhikṣā*, “To establish steady alms,” i.e. to establish an endowment, thereby ensuring that monks have good food and drink.

*ri mnyam*, Skt. *sātāgiri*, A yakṣa general in the intermediate directions; a yakṣa who is a “Dharma brother” of Vaiśravaṇa.

*bde ba’i ri nyid*, Skt. *sātāgirista*, A yakṣa king. (Toh 555: bde ba’i ri)

*ka ba*, Skt. *sthalā*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

*ka ba*, Skt. *sthala*, A yakṣa general.

## sthavira
*gnas brtan*, Skt. *sthavira*, Literally “elder,” a respectful term for a senior monk or nun (seniority being defined by the number of years since full ordination); also the name of the sixteen arhats who are said to preserve the Teaching (Dharma) until the arrival of the future Buddha Maitreya.

## Sthavira Cave
*gnas brtan gyi phug*, Skt. *gnas brtan gyi phug*, A dwelling place of bodhisattvas located in the region called Increasing Joy.

*gnas brtan pa’i tshigs su bcad pa*, Skt. *sthaviragāthā*, A lost verse text possibly included in the Kṣudraka­piṭaka of the Mūla­sarvāstivādins.

*gnas brtan ma’i tshigs su bcad pa*, Skt. *sthavirīgāthā*, A lost verse text possibly included in the Kṣudraka­piṭaka of the Mūla­sarvāstivādins.

*brtan pa*, Skt. *sthirā*, A capital city in South India.

## Sthiramati
*blo gros brtan pa*, Skt. *sthiramati*, (c. fourth century). One of the important masters of the Vijñānavāda school, he wrote important commentaries on the works of Vasubandhu and Āryāsaṅga.

A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra whose name means something like “Steady Stepper.”

*blo gnas pa*, Skt. *sthitabuddhi*, The 157th buddha in the first list, 156th in the second list, and 156th in the third list.

*blo gros brtan pas byin*, Skt. *sthita­buddhi­datta*, A buddha in the past.

## Sthita­buddhi­rūpa
*blo gnas rang bzhin*, Skt. *sthita­buddhi­rūpa*, The 852nd buddha in the first list, 851st in the second list, and 841st in the third list.

*spos gnas*, Skt. *sthitagandha*, The 667th buddha in the first list, 666th in the second list, and 658th in the third list.

*grogs brtan*, Skt. *sthitamitra*, The 421st buddha in the first list, 420th in the second list, and 414th in the third list.

*sems med par gnas pa*, Skt. *sthitaniścitta*, Lit. “firm without mind.” Name of a meditative stabilization.

*gnas pa bsdus pa*, Skt. *sthitisamāsa*, Text by Sahajavajra (Toh 2227).

*thang la spyod*, Skt. *sthālabhuja*, The second of the five young brahmin attendants of the brahmin Samudrareṇu. The Buddha Ratnagarbha prophesies that he will be the Buddha Sukhendriyamati, the 1,001st of the 1,005 buddhas in the Bhadraka eon.

*mgo bo che*, Skt. *sthūlaśira*, A great ṛṣi.

*bang mdzod stug po can gyi tshal*, Skt. *bang mdzod stug po can gyi tshal*, A forest near Sthūlakoṣṭhaka, a village in the country of Kuru.

*tshon mo dga’ mo*, Skt. *sthūlanandā*, A certain nun who is tricked in The Hundred Deeds by the Band of Six. She resided at the nunnery Royal Garden.

## Sthālisugandha
*snod dri zhim*, Skt. *sthālisugandha*, The name of Prince Kuśa disguised as a cook.

## sthūlātyaya offense
*ltung ba sbom po*, Skt. *sthūlātyaya*, The third gravest type of offense for a monk or nun, which requires confession in the presence of another monk or nun. Attempting one of the two gravest offenses, pārājika and saṅghāvaśeṣa, constitutes this category. For instance, if a monk attempts to kill a person and does not succeed, his offense is categorised as sthūlātyaya.

## Sthāmaprāpta
*mthu ni thob pa*, Skt. *sthāmaprāpta*, The 214th buddha in the first list, 213th in the second list, and 213th in the third list.

*mthu yi dpal*, Skt. *sthāmaśrī*, The 370th buddha in the first list, 369th in the second list, and 364th in the third list.

*gnas kyi mu khyud*, Skt. *sthānanemin*, One of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin.

## Sthāvarā
*brtan ma*, Skt. *sthāvarā*, The earth goddess who was present at the eve of Siddhārtha’s awakening.

## Sthāṇvīśvara
*gnas na dbang phyug*, Skt. *sthāṇvīśvara*, An ancient city corresponding to the modern Thaneswar in Haryana, India.

## Āstika
*yod pa pa*, Skt. *āstika*, One of the sages (ṛṣi).

## stilling
*zhi gnas*, Skt. *śamatha*, One of the basic forms of Buddhist meditation, which focuses on calming the mind. Often presented as part of a pair of meditation techniques, the other technique being “higher insight.”

## stinginess
*ser sna*, Skt. *matsara*, The mental state of stinginess, matsara is sometimes translated as “miserliness” or “avarice.” It is classified as one of the twenty subsidiary afflictions (upakleśa).

## stingy
*ser sna*, Skt. *mātsarya*, One of twenty or twenty-four so-called secondary mental defilements or afflictions.

## stinkvine
*ba dra li*, Skt. *bhadrālī*, Paederia foetida.

## Stirrer of the Ocean of Existence
*srid pa’i rgya mtsho ’khrugs byed*, Skt. *srid pa’i rgya mtsho ’khrugs byed*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Mahāraśmi.

## Sūtkhalin
*mud ka li*, Skt. *sūtkhalin*, One of the sixteen gods guarding the seat of awakening.

## Stomach
*gsus pa nyid*, Skt. *gsus pa nyid*, Stomach (the digestive organ of the abdomen), also the name of an area in Kuru.

## Stopper
*te ma bu ka*, Skt. *te ma bu ka*, Stopper (something that plugs or blocks an opening), also the name of a ṛṣi present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

*rtogs pa’i don la gnas pa ’dor ba ldog par byed pa*, Skt. *rtogs pa’i don la gnas pa ’dor ba ldog par byed pa*, Mother of the buddha Sthitagandha.

## Storehouse of the Domain of the Sacred Dharma
*dam pa’i chos kyi dkyil ’khor gyi mdzod*, Skt. *dam pa’i chos kyi dkyil ’khor gyi mdzod*, A minister of the Dharma king Great Diligent Nāga.

## stores of merit and wisdom
*bsod nams dang ye shes kyi tshogs*, Skt. *puṇya­jñāna­saṃbhāra*, The two great stores to be accumulated by bodhisattvas: the store of merit, arising from their practice of the first three transcendences, and the store of wisdom, arising from their practice of the last two transcendences. All deeds of bodhisattvas contribute to their accumulation of these two stores, which ultimately culminate in the two bodies of the Buddha, the body of form and the ultimate body.

## storied mansion
*khang pa brtsegs pa*, Skt. *kūṭāgāra*, A distinctive Indian assembly hall or temple with one ground-floor room and a high ornamental roof, sometimes a barrel shape with apses but more usually a tapering roof, tower, or spire. It contains at least one additional upper room within the structure. The term kūṭāgāra literally means “upper chamber” and is short for kūṭāgāraśālā (“hall with an upper chamber”).

## stories of former births
*skyes pa’i rabs kyi sde*, Skt. *jātaka*, One of the twelve branches of Buddhist scriptures.

## stotra
*bstod pa*, Skt. *stotra*, Hymn of praise.

## Stūpa
*mchod rten*, lit. support of offering, symbolic representation of the [Buddha](#buddha)'s mind. The most typical Buddhist monument, which often has a wide square base, a rounded mid-section, and a tall conical upper [section](#section) topped by a sun and moon. Stūpas frequently contain the relics of enlightened beings. They vary in size from tiny clay models to the vast stūpas at Borobodur in Indonesia and Bodha in Nepal.

## Stūpa Chariot
*mchod rten shing rta*, Skt. *mchod rten shing rta*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Jñānasāgara.

## Stūpa Endowed with Gathering
*tshogs ldan mchod rten*, Skt. *tshogs ldan mchod rten*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Brahmaketu.

*brtul zhugs mchod rten*, Skt. *brtul zhugs mchod rten*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Dṛḍhadharma.

*’jigs pa med pa’i mchod rten*, Skt. *’jigs pa med pa’i mchod rten*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Vigatabhaya.

*mchod rten dga’*, Skt. *mchod rten dga’*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Kṛtāntadarśin.

*yon tan mchod rten*, Skt. *yon tan mchod rten*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Puṣpa­dama­sthita.

*phyogs kyi mchod rten*, Skt. *phyogs kyi mchod rten*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Yaśodatta.

*rgyal ba’i mchod rten*, Skt. *rgyal ba’i mchod rten*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Rāhu­sūrya­garbha.

*ye shes mchod rten*, Skt. *ye shes mchod rten*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Prāmodyarāja (69 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

*yon tan mchod rten*, Skt. *yon tan mchod rten*, Mother of the buddha Puṣpaprabha.

*rin chen snang bas rnam par gnon pa’i mchod rten*, Skt. *rin chen snang bas rnam par gnon pa’i mchod rten*, Name of the thus-gone one of the world system Future Hearers.

*mchod rten mchod*, Skt. *mchod rten mchod*, Birthplace of the buddha Brahmaruta.

*mchod rten dpal chen ma*, Skt. *stūpamahāśriyā*, “Great Splendor of Reliquaries,” one of the mantra deities.

## Sūtra
*mdo*, a concise text spoken by the [Buddha](#buddha); one of the Three [Piṭakas](#piṭaka). See [Tripiṭaka](#tripiṭaka). See also: Wikipedia's [List of suttas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_suttas), Access to Insight's [Index of Suttas](https://www.accesstoinsight.org/index-sutta.html), and 84,000's reading room with [The Kangyur and The Tengyur](https://read.84000.co/section/lobby.html).

*bstan bcos*, a commentary on the [Buddha's](#buddha) teachings.

## Sūtra of the Parable of the Axe
*ste’u lta bu’i mdo*, Skt. *ste’u lta bu’i mdo*, A sūtra in the section of the aggregates in the Saṃyuktāgama, which corresponds to SĀc 263, SN 22.101, etc.

## sūtra section
*mdo sde*, Skt. *sūtra*, One of the twelve branches of Buddhist scriptures, usually referring to a discourse by the Buddha. When not referring to the words of the Buddha, the term refers to any concise doctrinal statement.

## Sūtracunaka

## stream enterer

This is the first of the four (or eight) stages of the realization of the supermundane path (and fruit) leading to awakening or liberation.

## strengths
*stobs*, Skt. *bala*, The strengths are enumerated as five or ten. As five, they are a stronger form of the five powers: faith, mindfulness, diligence, samādhi, and wisdom. As ten, they are the strenths of knowing what is proper and improper, knowing the maturation of karma, knowing the variety of beings’ aspirations, knowing the variety of their inclinations, knowing the variety of their capacities, knowing everywhere each path leads, knowing the dhyānas, liberations, samāpattis, samādhis and so forth, being able to recall previous states of being, and knowing the details of death and rebirth.

## Study
*thos pa*, lit. listening. Traditionally, listening to the teachings was the main way of learning in Tibet. Before studying from a text, it is important to receive the aural transmission by actually hearing the teacher's words. The term "study" should therefore be understood as rather more than simply reading a text.

## Subhūti
One of the Buddha Śākyamuni’s principal pupils and a close relative of the Buddha’s famous patron Anāthapiṇḍada. According to the Pali tradition, Subhūti is considered foremost among the Buddha’s disciples for dwelling peacefully in isolated places (Pali: dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ) and being a worthy recipient of gifts (Pali: araṇa­vihārīnaṃ aggo). He is said to have become an arhat through meditative concentration on loving-kindness (Skt. maitrīdhyāna, Pali: mettajhāna). On his alms rounds, Subhūti would cultivate loving-kindness for every household he visited, and thereby he bestowed the conditions for the highest possible merit for his donors. In the Mahāyāna tradition, he is particularly known to be one of the primary interlocutors in the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras and is sometimes referred to as the foremost among the Buddha’s disciples for understanding emptiness, although as we see by his verse given in The Prophecy for Bhadra the Illusionist he still retains his association with gift giving and generosity. Pali: Subhūti

## subsidiary affliction
*nye ba’i nyon mongs*, Skt. *upakleśa*, The secondary afflictive emotions that arise in dependence upon the six root afflictions (attachment, hatred, pride, ignorance, doubt, and wrong view); they are (1) anger (krodha, khro ba), (2) resentment (upanāha, ’khon ’dzin), (3) concealment [of faults] (mrakṣa, ’chab pa), (4) irritation (pradāśa, ’tshig pa), (5) jealousy (īrśyā, phrag dog), (6) avarice (matsara, ser sna), (7) craftiness (māyā, sgyu), (8) fickleness (śāṭhya, g.yo), (9) pompousness (mada, rgyags pa), (10) harmfulness (vihiṃsā, rnam par ’tshe ba), (11) shamelessness (āhrīkya, ngo tsha med pa), (12) non-embarrassment (anapatrāpya, khrel med pa), (13) lack of faith (aśraddhya, ma dad pa), (14) laziness (kausīdya, le lo), (15) carelessness (pramāda, bag med pa), (16) forgetfulness (muṣitasmṛtitā, brjed ngas), (17) inattentiveness (asaṃprajanya, shes bzhin ma yin pa), (18) dullness (nimagna, bying ba), (19) agitation (auddhatya, rgod pa), and (20) distraction (vikṣepa, rnam g.yeng).

## subsidiary afflictions
*nye ba’i nyon mongs*, Skt. *upakleśa*, These are various mental afflictions that negatively impact the mind, such as rage, resentment, envy, miserliness, laziness, distraction, etc.

## subsidiary afflictive emotions
*nye ba’i nyon mongs*, Skt. *upakleśa*, The secondary afflictive emotions that arise in dependence upon the six root afflictive emotions (attachment, hatred, pride, ignorance, doubt, and wrong view); they are (1) anger (krodha, khro ba), (2) enmity/malice (upanāha, ’khon ’dzin), (3) concealment (mrakśa, ’chab pa), (4) outrage (pradāsa, ’tshig pa), (5) jealousy (īrśya, phrag dog), (6) miserliness (matsarya, ser sna), (7) deceit ( māyā , sgyu), (8) dishonesty (śāṭhya, g.yo), (9) haughtiness (mada, rgyags pa), (10) harmfulness (vihiṃsa, rnam par ’tshe ba), (11) shamelessness (āhrīkya, ngo tsha med pa), (12) non-consideration (anapatrāpya, khril med pa), (13) lack of faith (aśraddhya, ma dad pa), (14) laziness (kausīdya, le lo), (15) non-conscientiousness (pramāda, bag med pa), (16) forgetfulness (muśitasmṛtitā, brjed nges), (17) non-introspection (asaṃprajanya, shes bzhin ma yin pa), (18) dullness (nigmagṇa, bying ba), (19) agitation (auddhatya, rgod pa), and (20) distraction (vikṣepa, rnam g.yeng) (Rigzin 329, 129).

## subtle knowledge
*shes pa phra ba*, Skt. *sūkṣmajñāna*, The various aspects of the knowledge that engages in subtlety of conduct, etc., include the knowledge that engages with subtle transmigration at the time of death, the knowledge that engages with subtle processes of rebirth, and the knowledge that engages with subtle buddha activities—emanation, renunciation, consummate enlightenment, turning the wheel of the Dharma, consecrating the lifespan, passing into final nirvāṇa, and so forth. See also .

## subtle wisdom

## suffer hardship
*nyon mongs nas sdug*, Skt. *nyon mongs nas sdug*, See also “distress.”

## suffering
*sdug bsngal ba*, Skt. *duḥkha*, The first of the four truths of the noble ones. The term “suffering” includes all essentially unsatisfactory experiences of life in cyclic existence, whether physical or mental. These comprise (1) the suffering of suffering, i.e., the physical sensations and mental experiences that are self-evident as suffering and toward which spontaneous feelings of aversion arise; (2) the suffering of change, i.e., all experiences that are normally recognized as pleasant and desirable, but which are nonetheless suffering in that persistent indulgence in these always results in changing attitudes of dissatisfaction and boredom; and (3) the suffering of the pervasive conditioning underlying the round of birth, aging, and death.

## Sumeru
*ri rab*, Skt. *sumeru*, According to ancient Buddhist cosmology, Sumeru is the great mountain forming the axis of the universe. At its summit lies Sudarśana, home of Śakra and his thirty-two gods, and on its flanks live the asuras. The mount has four sides facing the cardinal directions, each of which is made of a different precious stone. Surrounding it are several mountain ranges and the great ocean where the four great island continents lie: in the south, Jambudvīpa (our world); in the west, Godānīya; in the north, Uttarakuru; in the east, Pūrvavideha. Above it are the abodes of the gods of the realm of desire. Often also referred to as Mount Meru.

## summaries

## summary
*sdom*, Skt. *uddāna*, The content of The Chapters on Monastic Discipline is condensed into metered lists called “summaries” (Tib. sdom; Skt. uddāna) or “verse summaries” (Tib. sdom gyi tshigs su bcad pa; Skt. uddānagāthā). Each chapter has a “global summary,” composed of several topics, which form the basis of subsequent “summaries.” Very occasionally, specific elements of a chapter will be recapitulated in “intervening summaries” (Tib. bar sdom; Skt. antaroddāna).

## Sundarī
*mdzes ma*, Skt. *sundarī*, This refers to the beautiful wandering female mendicant Sundarī, who in one of the stories of the life of the Buddha is enlisted by some heretics, jealous of the Buddha’s fame, to tempt the Buddha to have sex with her and thus destroy his reputation as a virtuous sage. She pretends to do so, and the heretics, believing her story, then hire some drunkards to murder her and bury her body under a pile of flowers near the Buddha’s monastery in order to make the public believe that the Buddha has ravished and killed her. As the rumour spreads, the citizenry is at first outraged but are then led to reconsider the story told by the Buddha’s monks, who pass on their master’s advice to avoid unsubstantiated hearsay and rumors. The truth eventually comes to light when King Prasenajit sends his secret service to investigate the matter, and the true perpetrators are brought to justice. This story is found in the Sundarīsutta, Udāna 4.8.

*nyi ma’i snying po*, Skt. *ādityagarbha*, The name for this jewel, “essence of the sun” in both the Sanskrit and Tibetan, appears to be a synonym for sūryakānta (“sunstone”). ## super-knowledge
*mngon par shes pa*, Skt. *abhijñā*, A type of extrasensory perception gained through spiritual practice, in the Buddhist presentation consisting of a list of five types: (1) miraculous abilities, (2) divine eye, (3) divine ear, (4) knowledge of others’ minds, and (5) recollection of past lives.

## superknowledge
Supernormal knowledge or psychic abilities acquired as a byproduct of meditative concentration (dhyāna). These are typically classified in a set of five or six: (1) clairvoyance (divyacakṣus, “the divine eye”), (2) clairaudience (divyaśrotra, “the divine ear”), (3) knowledge of the minds of others (paracittājñāna), (4) remembrance of past lives (pūrvanivāsānu­smṛti), (5) the ability to perform magical display (ṛddhividhi), and (6) the knowledge of the destruction of all mental defilements (āsravakṣaya). The first five are considered mundane or worldly and can be attained to some extent by non-Buddhist yogis as well as Buddhist arhats and bodhisattvas. The sixth is considered to be supramundane and can be attained only by Buddhist yogis.

## Superknowledge Gift

## superknowledges
*mngon par shes pa*, Skt. *abhijñā*, Special powers of which five, acquired through the meditative contemplations (dhyāna), are considered mundane (laukika) and can be attained to some extent by outsider yogis as well as Buddhist arhats and bodhisattvas; and a sixth—being acquired through a bodhisattva’s realization, or by buddhas alone according to some accounts—is supramundane (lokottara). The first five are: divine eye or vision (divyacakṣu), divine hearing (divyaśrotra), knowledge of others’ minds (paracittajñāna), knowledge of former (and future) lives (pūrva­[para]­nivāsānu­smṛti­jñāna), and knowledge of magical operations (ṛddhi­vidhi­jñāna). The sixth, supramundane one is knowledge of the exhaustion of defilements (āsravakṣaya­jñāna).

## Supernatural knowledge
*mngon par shes pa*, Skt. *abhijñā*, There are five supernatural faculties resulting from meditative concentration: divine sight, divine hearing, knowing others’ minds, recollecting past lives, and the ability to perform miracles.

## supernatural power
*rdzu ’phrul*, Skt. *ṛddhi*, The supernatural powers of a śrāvaka correspond to the first abhijnā: “Being one he becomes many, being many he becomes one; he becomes visible, invisible; goes through walls, ramparts and mountains without being impeded, just as through air; he immerses himself in the earth and emerges from it as if in water; he goes on water without breaking through it, as if on [solid] earth; he travels through the air crosslegged like a winged bird; he takes in his hands and touches the moon and the sun, those two wonderful, mighty beings, and with his body he extends his power as far as the Brahma world” (Lamotte 2003: 20). The great supernatural powers (mahāṛddhi) of bodhisattvas are: “causing trembling, blazing, illuminating, rendering invisible, transforming, coming and going across obstacles, reducing or enlarging worlds, inserting any matter into one’s own body, assuming the aspects of those one frequents, appearing and disappearing, submitting everyone to one’s will, dominating the supernormal power of others, giving intellectual clarity to those who lack it, giving mindfulness, bestowing happiness, and finally, emitting beneficial rays.” (Lamotte 2003: 30).

## supernormal faculties
Derived from a verb that has the sense of direct knowing, this term refers to a number of types of extraordinary knowledge and powers, grouped as five or six. When stated to be five, they include the first five of the list that follows: (1) various superhuman powers (ṛddhi); (2) the ability to know others’ minds; (3) extraordinary powers of hearing, or the divine ear; (4) extraordinary powers of sight, or the divine eye; (5) the ability to remember one’s past lives, and (6) the knowledge that the defilements have been destroyed and it is one’s last lifetime. When the fifth is not specified, then oftentimes the sixth or all six types are implied. The last three of the list are the same as the three types of knowledge (vidyā), and are tantamount to the description of the awakening experience in some presentations.

## supernormal knowledge
*mngon par shes pa*, Skt. *abhi­jñā*, The six modes of supernormal cognition or ability, namely, clairvoyance, clairaudience, knowledge of the minds of others, remembrance of past lives, the ability to perform miracles, and the knowledge of the destruction of all mental defilements. The first five are considered mundane or worldly and can be attained to some extent by non-Buddhist yogis as well as Buddhist arhats and bodhisattvas. The sixth is considered to be supramundane and can be attained only by Buddhist yogis.

## supernormal powers
*mngon shes*, Skt. *abhijñā*, Divine eye, divine ear, knowledge of others’ minds, recollection of past lives, and miracles.

## super-sensory cognition
*mngon par shes pa*, Skt. *abhijñā*, A type of extrasensory perception gained through spiritual practice. In the Buddhist presentation, this consists of five types: (1) miraculous abilities, (2) divine eye, (3) divine ear, (4) knowledge of others’ minds, and (5) recollection of past lives.

## supplements to the Vedas
*rig byed kyi yan lag*, Skt. *vedāṅga*, The name of a group of auxiliary works that supplement the Vedas, usually numerated as six different works on the six subjects of 1. śikṣa (pronunciation and phonetics); 2. chandas (meter); 3. vyākaraṇa (grammar and linguistic analysis); 4. nirukta (explanation of difficult terms); 5. jyotiṣa (astronomy); and 6. kalpa (ceremony) (Monier-Williams 1016.3).

## supplies of merit and knowledge
The two main kinds of supplies or provisions that a bodhisattva accumulates and stores, which then provide the fuel for the pursuit of the goal of the path. Sometimes translated as “accumulation” or “equipment” and also “provisions.”

## supply
*tshogs*, Skt. *saṃbhāra*, Usually of two kinds, the supply of merit and the supply of knowledge, but also more generally the supplies or provisions that a bodhisattva accumulates and stores, which then provide the fuel for the pursuit of the goal of the path. This sūtra provides a long list of such supplies, which are mainly qualities or virtues the bodhisattva develops.

## support
*gnas*, Skt. *niśraya*, A “support” is the preceptor (Tib. mkhan po; Skt. upādhyāya) of a new renunciant or ordained person, who is called the preceptor’s “ward” (Tib. lhan gcig gnas pa; Skt. sārdhaṃvihārin). For at least five years after ordination, monastics newly admitted to the saṅgha must live with or near a monastic mentor or “support.” If a new monk or nun wishes to travel while their mentor does not (or vice versa), the monk or nun must take a new support from among the saṅgha elders at their final destination. The new support is known as the “support instructor” (Tib. gnas kyi slob dpon; Skt. niśrayācārya) while the new monk or nun is known as their “apprentice” (Tib. nye gnas pa; Skt. antevāsika). See The Chapter on Going Forth (Toh 1, ch. 1, 1.628–1.678).

## supramundane knowledge
*mngon shes*, Skt. *abhijñā*, Nāropa gives the following five supramundane knowledges: divine eye (Tib. lha’i mig), divine ear (Tib. lha’i rna ba), knowing the minds of others (Tib. gzhan gyi sems shes pa), recollecting the past lives of oneself and others (Tib. rang dang gzhan gyi sngon gyi gnas rjes su dran pa), and the miraculous power of being able to walk in the sky (Tib. nam mkha’ la ’gro ba’i rdzu ’phrul).

## supramundane phenomena
*’jig rten las ’das pa’i chos*, Skt. *lokottara­dharma*, Supramundane phenomena include the following: the four applications of mindfulness, the four correct exertions, the four supports for miraculous ability, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven branches of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the three gateways to liberation, faculties that will enable knowledge of all that is unknown,--> the faculty of coming to understand what one has not yet understood, faculties that acquire the knowledge of all phenomena,--> the faculty of fully understanding, faculties endowed with the knowledge of all phenomena,--> the faculty of knowing one has fully understood, the meditative stability with an initial mental application and with a sustained mental application, the meditative stability without an initial mental application but with just a sustained mental application, the meditative stability without an initial mental application and without a sustained mental application, the eighteen emptinesses (starting from the emptiness of internal phenomena and ending with the emptiness of an essential nature of nonentities), the ten powers of the tathāgatas, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of exact knowledge, great loving kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas.

## supreme truth
*bden pa mchog*, Skt. *paramasatya*, An unusual feature of the Bhava­saṅkrānti­sūtra is that it presents a third “supreme truth” in contrast to the usual doctrinal presentation of the two truths (the relative truth and the ultimate truth). In doing so, the Bhava­saṅkrānti­sūtra does not propose a third ontological category but demonstrates in its final verse that both the relative and ultimate truths are conceptual categories and therefore provisional to understanding the ultimate nature of reality. The conception of ultimate truth should not be misunderstood, like a finger pointing to the moon, but to arrive at its actual understanding one must transcend any dualistic notion or designation altogether. See .

*lha mdzes*, Skt. *surasundara*, A nāga king.

## Surata
*bzang dga’*, Skt. *surata*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Suratapriyā
Skt. *suratapriyā*, ‟Fond of Sex,” one of the six kinnara queens

## Surathī
*shing rta bzang*, Skt. *surathī*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Suratna
*rin chen bzang po*, Skt. *suratna*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Suravatī
*chang ldan ma*, Skt. *suravatī*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Surādevī
*stong lha mo*, Skt. *surādevī*, One of the eight goddesses in the north, called upon to grant protection.

## Surendra
*su ren+t+ra bo d+hi*, Skt. *surendrabodhi*, Surendrabodhi came to Tibet during reign of King Ralpachen (ral pa can, r. 815–38 ce). He is listed as the translator of forty-three texts and was one of the small group of paṇḍitas responsible for the Mahāvyutpatti Sanskrit–Tibetan dictionary.

## Surendrabodhi
*su ren dra bo dhi*, Skt. *surendrabodhi*, One of the Indian teachers invited to Tibet at the time of the emperor Ralpachen (early ninth century). He was one of the great Indian pandits who assisted the Tibetan translators such as Yeshé Dé with the translation of Buddhist texts from Sanskrit.

## Surendrābhā
*lha dbang ’od*, Skt. *surendrābhā*, The kalyāṇamitra of chapter 45, a goddess of the Trāyastriṃśa paradise.

## Sureśvaraprabha
*lha’i dbang phyug ’od*, Skt. *sureśvaraprabha*, A king in the distant past. (Toh 555: lha’i dbang phyug gi ’od)

## Sureśvara­prabha
*lha’i dbang phyug ’od*, Skt. *sureśvaraprabha*, A king in the distant past. (Toh 555: lha’i dbang phyug gi ’od)

## Surāntaka
*lha mthar byed*, Skt. *surāntaka*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Surūpā
*gzugs bzang ba*, Skt. *surūpā*, One of the names of Śrī Mahādevī.

## Surūpa
*gzugs bzang*, Skt. *surūpa*, The 594th buddha in the first list, 593rd in the second list, and 587th in the third list.

## surpassing all phenomena
*chos thams cad las shin du ’phags pa*, Skt. *sarva­dharmodgata*, The 6th meditative stability in chapters 6 and 8.

## Surūpavyūha
*gzugs mdzes bkod pa*, Skt. *surūpavyūha*, “Beautiful Array.” One of the bodhisattvas in the entourage of the Buddha Śākyamuni when he taught the girl Vimalaśraddhā.

## Surāṣṭra
*yul ’khor bzang*, Skt. *surāṣṭra*, The 841st buddha in the first list, 840th in the second list, and 830th in the third list.

## Surrounded by Nyaronya
*nya ro hi ’khor ba*, Skt. *nya ro hi ’khor ba*, A river on Saṅkāśa.

## surrounding wall
A term that can refer to a fence, an enclosure, a rampart, or the wall surrounding a courtyard or building.

## Surārthā
*lha don*, Skt. *surārthā*, One of the nakṣatras.

## Suruci
*legs smon*, Skt. *suruci*, A self-awakened one.

## Suśruta
Skt. *suśruta*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Suśrutasaṃhitā
Skt. *suśrutasaṃhitā*, An ancient Indian Āyurvedic work.

## surveying the crown pinnacle
*spyi gtsug rnam par lta ba*, Skt. *avalokita­mūrdha*, The 8th meditative stability in chapters 6 and 8.

## Suryagarbha

## Suryatejas

## Susaṃbhava

## Susaṃbhava­vyūha
*legs byung rnam brgyan*, Skt. *susaṃbhava­vyūha*, A buddha in the distant past. BHS verse: Susaṃbhava­viyūha .

## Susaṃgṛhita
A buddha in the distant past, a future life of the weaver Sūtracunaka.

## Susaṃhata
Skt. *susaṃhata*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Susambhavābha
*’byung med ’od*, Skt. *susambhavābha*, One of the tathāgatas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Susaṃprasthita

## Susaṃ­prasthita
*legs par yang dag zhugs*, Skt. *susaṃ­prasthita*, A great bodhisattva.

## Su­saṃ­prasthita
*shin tu yang dag zhugs*, Skt. *su­saṃ­prasthita*, Name of a bodhisattva.

## Susaṃ­prasthita­rāja
*shin tu yang dag zhugs kyi rgyal po*, Skt. *susaṃ­prasthita­rāja*, A buddha.

## Susaṃ­vṛttas­kandha
*dpung mgo shin tu zlum ba*, Skt. *susaṃ­vṛttas­kandha*, A buddha.

## Susena
*sde bzangs*, Skt. *susena*, A minister, brother of Sena.

## Susiddha
*grub pa bzang po*, Skt. *susiddha*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Susīmā
*mtshams bzang ma*, Skt. *susīmā*, A great rākṣasī.

## Susīma
*mtshams bzangs*, Skt. *susīma*, The name of a god from the realm of Tuṣita and the main interlocutor of Mañjuśrī’s Teaching. In the Kangyur, Susīma appears as a minor interlocutor in several other sūtras; his other most notable appearance is as an interlocutor in conversation with Māra in The Chapter on Mañjuśrī’s Magical Display, Toh 97, 1.68–1.78. He also appears in some Pali sources; see Buddhist Dictionary of Pali Proper Names, Susīma (4–5).

## Susmita
Skt. *susmita*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Susoma
*zla bzang*, Skt. *susoma*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Susārthavaha
*ded dpon bzang po*, Skt. *susārthavaha*, A bodhisattva great being present in the audience of this sūtra.

## Susārthavāha
*ded dpon dam pa*, Skt. *susārthavāha*, Name of a bodhisattva. His name is rendered “Sārthavāha” in the Twenty-Five Thousand.

## Sustained by Fruition
*’bras bus nye bar ’tsho ba*, Skt. *’bras bus nye bar ’tsho ba*, A realm inhabited by garland-bearer gods.

## Sustained by the Finest Tastes
*ro brgya mchog gis bsten pa*, Skt. *ro brgya mchog gis bsten pa*, A grove in Unmixed.

## Sustained calm
*zhi gnas*, Skt. *śamatha*, the basis of all [concentration](#concentration)s. "The distraction of the mind by other objects having been calmed (*zhi*), the mind stays (*gnas*) without wavering in [concentration](#concentration)." DICT.

## sustained mental application
*rnam par dpyod pa*, Skt. *vicāra*, See

## Sustainer
*gso byed*, Skt. *gso byed*, Sustainer (one who supports or maintains), also the name of an attendant of the buddha Vaidyarāja.

## Sustaining the Saṅgha
*dge ’dun skyong*, A Licchavī youth. (Toh 555: dge ’dun skyabs)

## Sustaining through Form and Adhering to the Nature of All People
*gzugs kyis ’tsho ba skye bo thams cad ky ngo bo’i rjes su ’jug pa*, Skt. *gzugs kyis ’tsho ba skye bo thams cad ky ngo bo’i rjes su ’jug pa*, A former life of the Buddha, who was a very good-looking person.

## sustenances
*zas*, Skt. *āhāra*, See “four kinds of sustenance.”

## Susthali
*sus tha li*, Skt. *susthali*, A land to the north of Jambudvīpa.

## Susthita
*legs gnas*, Skt. *susthita*, The 546th buddha in the first list, 546th in the second list, and 539th in the third list.

## Susthitamati
*blo gros rab gnas*, Skt. *susthitamati*, Lit. “Stable Intellect.” A god living in the buddhafield of the tathāgata Samantakusuma.

## Susudhī
Skt. *susudhī*, The unfaithful wife of the king of Benares.

## Suṃsumāragiri
The name of the capital of the country of the Bhaggas (Skt. Bhargas), a small tribal oligarchy belonging to the Vṛji confederacy and situated between Vaiśālī and Śrāvastī (cf. Witzel 2003, p. 55). The Pali word susumāra literally means “child killing.” See also in the translation.

## Susvarā
*skad snyan ma*, Skt. *susvarā*, One of the great yakṣiṇīs.

## Susvara
*dbyangs snyan*, Skt. *susvara*, The 631st buddha in the first list, 630th in the second list, and 623rd in the third list.

## Suśītala
*shin tu bsil ba*, Skt. *suśītala*, The 906th buddha in the first list, 905th in the second list, and 896th in the third list.

## Sutanu
*lus mdzes*, Skt. *sutanu*, A lord of beings.

## Sutasoma
*zla ba’i bu*, Skt. *sutasoma*, One of the Buddha’s former rebirths.

## Suteja
*gzi brjid bzang po*, Skt. *(not in the skt. source of the mmk)*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK. This name, which occurs only in the Tibetan translation of the MMK, may represent a case of scribal dyslexia in which the last two syllables of the extant Skt. name Sujeta have been reversed.

## Sutejas
*gzi brjid mdzes*, Skt. *sutejas*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Sutejomaṇḍala­rati­śrī
*gzi brjid kyi dkyil ’khor bzang pos dga’ ba’i dpal*, Skt. *sutejomaṇḍala­rati­śrī*, The forest goddess of Lumbinī and the kalyāṇamitra of chapter 42.

## Sutāpa
*gdung ba bzang po*, Skt. *sutāpa*, One of the kings of the piśācas.

## Sutārā
*sgrol ma bzang po*, Skt. *sutārā*, One of the vidyārājñīs dwelling with Śākyamuni in the realm of the Pure Abode.

## Sutīrtha
*stegs bzang po*, Skt. *sutīrtha*, The 735th buddha in the first list, 734th in the second list, and 724th in the third list.

## sutta
The Pali equivalent of Sanskrit sūtra.

## Suśubha
*rab tu bzang po*, Skt. *suśubha*, One of the disciples of the Buddha.

## Suśuddha
*dag pa*, Skt. *suśuddha*, One of the five celestial bodhisattvas associated with Mañjuśrī.

## suṣumnā
*yid bzang*, Skt. *suṣumnā*, The middle channel above the navel.

## Suutthitā
*legs par langs*, Skt. *suutthitā*, One of the eight goddesses in the south, called upon to grant protection.

## Suvṛṣa
*khyu mchog bzang po*, Skt. *suvṛṣa*, One of the kings of Nepal.

## Suvajra
*rdo rje bzang po*, Skt. *suvajra*, A bodhisattva mahāsattva.

## Suvakṣa
*mthon ka bzang po*, Skt. *suvakṣa*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Suvaktra
*zhal bzangs*, Skt. *suvaktra*, The 791st buddha in the first list, 790th in the second list, and 780th in the third list.

## Suvarṇa
*gser*, Skt. *suvarṇa*, A pore on Avalokiteśvara’s body.

## Suvarṇa­bhadra­vimala­vasucitra­tejolalita­garbha
*gser bzang zhing dri ma med pa’i dbyig gis spras pa’i gzi brjid mdzes pa’i snying po*, Skt. *suvarṇa­bhadra­vimala­vasucitra­tejolalita­garbha*, A bodhisattva mahāsattva.

## Suvarṇabhujendra
*gser gyi lag pa’i dbang po*, Skt. *suvarṇabhujendra*, A king in the distant past.

## Suvarṇa­bhujendra
*gser gyi lag pa’i dbang po*, Skt. *suvarṇa­bhujendra*, A king in the distant past.

## Suvarṇacūḍa
*gtsug gi gser*, Skt. *suvarṇacūḍa*, The 609th buddha in the first list, 608th in the second list, and 602nd in the third list.

## Suvarṇadhvaja
*dam pa gser gyi rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *suvarṇadhvaja*, “Golden Banner.” The palace of the goddess Śrī, also known as Lakṣmī.

## Suvarṇadvīpa
*gser gling*, Skt. *suvarṇadvīpa*, home of King [Suvarṇapati](#suvarṇapati) who figures in a prophecy made by [Śāriputra](#śāriputra) and [Maudgalyāyana](#maudgalyāyana)’s teacher [Sañjayin](#sañjayin-the-teacher) that convinces them of their teacher’s prescience, which in turn gives them conviction to seek out the [Buddha](#buddha) as [Sañjayin](#sañjayin-the-teacher) advised they should.

## Suvarṇadvīpa (Lord of)
*gser gling pa*, a Buddhist master, Dharmakīrti, who lived in Sumatra in the 10th century. [Atīśa](#atīśa) considered him as the most important of the teachers from whom he received the teachings on bodhicitta.

## Suvarṇaśṛṅga
*gser gyi rtse mo*, Skt. *suvarṇaśṛṅga*, A mountain king.

## Su­varṇa­garbha
*gser gyi snying po*, Skt. *su­varṇa­garbha*, A great bodhisattva.

## Suvarṇajaṭa
*ral pa gser 'dra*, Skt. *suvarṇajaṭa*, a young [brahmin](#brahmin) from [Suvarṇadvīpa](#suvarṇadvīpa) who brings news to [Śāriputra](#śāriputra) and [Maudgalyāyana](#maudgalyāyana) that confirms their teacher [Sañjayin](#sañjayin-the-teacher)’s prophecy and sparks their search for the [Buddha](#buddha).

## Suvarṇa­jambudhvajakāñca­nābha
*’dzam bu’i gser gyi rgyal mtshan gyi ’od*, Skt. *suvarṇajambudhvajakāñcanābha*, A buddha in the distant future who is Rūpyaketu, the son of Ruciraketu, in the time of Śākyamuni. (Toh 555: gser dang rin po che’i ri bo’i rgyal po )

## Suvarṇa­jambu­dhvaja­kāñcanābha
*gser ’dzam bu’i gser gyi rgyal mtshan gyi ’od*, Skt. *suvarṇa­jambu­dhvaja­kāñcanābha*, A buddha in the distant future who is Rūpyaketu, the son of Ruciraketu, in the time of Śākyamuni. (Toh 555: Suvarṇa­ratnākaracchatra­kūṭa; gser dang rin po che’i ri bo’i rgyal po)

## Suvarṇakeśa
Skt. *suvarṇakeśa*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Suvarṇapati
*gser bdag*, Skt. *suvarṇapati*, a king of [Suvarṇadvīpa](#suvarṇadvīpa) who figures in a prophecy made by the teacher [Sañjayin](#sañjayin-the-teacher) that convinces [Śāriputra](#śāriputra) and [Maudgalyāyana](#maudgalyāyana) of his prescience. This in turn gives them conviction to seek out the [Buddha](#buddha) as [Sañjayin](#sañjayin-the-teacher) advised they should.

## Suvarṇaprabhā
*gser du snang ba*, Skt. *suvarṇaprabhā*, A world realm in the distant future. (Toh 555: gser ’od)

## Suvarṇaprabha
*gser ’od*, Skt. *suvarṇaprabha*, The name of the buddha who Rūpyaprabha is predicted to become.

## Suvarṇa­prabha
*gser ’od*, Skt. *suvarṇaprabha*, A bodhisattva.

## Suvarṇa­prabhagarbha
*gser du snang ba’i snying po*, Skt. *suvarṇaprabhagarbha*, A tathāgata.

## Suvarṇa­prabhā­garbha
*gser du snang ba’i snying po*, Skt. *suvarṇa­prabhā­garbha*, A tathāgata.

## Suvarṇaprabhāsā
A nāga queen of the nāga king Kālika, whose name is attested in the Sanskrit manuscript of this sūtra as well as the Lalitavistara.

## Suvarṇa­prabhāsā
*dam pa gser ’od*, Skt. *suvarṇa­prabhāsā*, The chief queen of Kālika, the nāga king.

## Suvarṇa­prabhāsottama
*gser ’od dam pa*, Skt. *suvarṇa­prabhāsottama*, A bodhisattva with the same name as the title of the sūtra. (Toh 555: gser gyi ’od)

## Suvarṇaprastha

## Suvarṇapārśva
*gser logs*, Skt. *suvarṇapārśva*, A mountain king.

## Suvarṇapuṣpa
*gser gyi me tog*, Skt. *suvarṇapuṣpa*, Lit. “The One Who Had the Golden Flowers.” Future name of the nun Gaṅgadevī when she becomes a bodhisattva in the buddhafield of Akṣobhya, and also when she becomes a buddha, during the eon called Tārakopama.

## Suvarṇa­puṣpa­jvalaraśmi­ketu
*gser gyi me tog ’bar ba’i ’od zer gyi tog*, Skt. *suvarṇapuṣpajvalaraśmiketu*, A tathāgata. (Toh 555: gser gyi me tog ’od zer rgyal mtshan)

## Suvarṇa­puṣpa­jvala­raśmi­ketu
*gser gyi me tog ’bar ba’i ’od zer gyi tog*, Skt. *suvarṇa­puṣpa­jvala­raśmi­ketu*, A tathāgata. (Toh 555: Suvarṇa­puṣpa­raśmi­dhvaja; gser gyi me tog ’od zer rgyal mtshan)

## Suvarṇa­puṣpābha­maṇḍala
*’od kyi dkyil ’khor gser gyi me tog*, Skt. *suvarṇa­puṣpābha­maṇḍala*, A park in another world in the distant past. The name as given in the prose. In verse it is called Svarṇa­puṣpa­prabhava.

## Suvarṇa­ratnākaracchatra­kūṭa
*gser rin chen ’byung gnas gdugs brtsegs*, Skt. *suvarṇa­ratnākaracchatra­kūṭa*, A buddha in the distant future who is the bodhisattva Ruciraketu in the time of Śākyamuni. (Suvarṇa­ratnākaracchatra­kūṭa; Toh Degé 556: gser ri rin chen ‘byung gnas gdugs brtegs, Suvarṇaparvataratnākarachattrakūṭa; Toh 555: gser gdugs rin po che brtsegs pa )

## Suvarṇaskandhin
*gser gyi phung po*, Skt. *suvarṇa­skandhin*, A buddha.

## Suvarṇottama
*gser mchog*, Skt. *suvarṇottama*, The 664th buddha in the first list, 663rd in the second list, and 655th in the third list.

## Suvarṇottama­prabhā­śrī
*gser mchog ’od dpal*, Skt. *suvarṇottama­prabhā­śrī*, The name of a bodhisattva. “Glorious Golden Light.”

*gser mchog snang ba*, Skt. *suvarṇottamaprabhāsā*, One of King Bimbisāra’s daughters.

*su be lang gi nags*, Skt. *su be lang gi nags*, A forest on Great Slope.

## Suvāha
A king.

*shin tu rnam par phye ba*, Skt. *suvibhakta*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Suviśākha
A wealthy brahmin in the city Gone to Bliss during the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, father of the girl Receiver of Goodness. See note 25.

## Suvikrāmin
*rnam par gnon pa bzang po*, Skt. *suvikrāmin*, A head merchant’s son in Dhanyākara.

## Suvikrānta

## Suvikrāntavikrāmin
*mthu dam pas rnam par gnon pa*, Skt. *suvikrānta­vikrāmin*, Name of a bodhisattva.

## Suvikrānta­vikrāmin
*rab kyi rtsal gyis rnam par gnon pa*, Skt. *suvikrānta­vikrāmin*, Lit. “Pressing with Utmost Skill.”

## Suvi­krānta­vikrāmin
*rab kyi rtsal gyis rnam par gnon pa*, Skt. *suvi­krānta­vikrāmin*, A great bodhisattva.

## Su­vikrānta­vikrāmin
*rab kyi rtsal gyis rnam par gnon pa*, Skt. *su­vikrānta­vikrāmin*, A bodhisattva great being present in the audience of this sūtra.

## Suviśālābha
