*rtsod rnyog mi bzad yang dag ’khrug*, Skt. *tīvrakaluṣa­saṃkṣobhana*, The name of a future eon in which the bodhisattva Saṃrocana will become the Buddha Acintyarocana.

## twelve ascetic practices
*sbyangs pa’i yon tan gnyis bcu*, Skt. *dvādaśa­dhūta­guṇa*, The twelve ascetic practices as set out in this text comprise (1) staying in isolation (āraṇyaka, dgon pa ba), (2) begging for alms (paiṇḍapātika, bsod snyoms pa), (3) wearing cast-off clothes (pāṃśukūlika, phyag dar khrod pa), (4) restricting eating after midday (khalu paścād bhaktika, zas phyis mi len pa), (5) eating the daily meal in a single sitting (ekāsanika, stan gcig pa), (6) accepting just whatever alms have been obtained (prasthapiṇḍika, ci thob pa’i bsod snyoms len pa), (7) frequenting charnel grounds (śmāśānika, dur khrod pa), (8) sitting in exposed places (ābhyavakāśika, bla gab med pa), (9) sitting under trees (vṛkṣamūlika, shing drung pa), (10) sitting upright even during sleep (naiṣadyika, cog pu pa), (11) staying wherever one happens to be (yathā­saṃstarika, gzhi ji bzhin pa), and (12) owning only three robes (traicīvarika, chos gos gsum pa). They are listed in the text at . The list varies slightly between texts in both order and content, and the set of twelve in the Mahāvyutpatti (127–39) is close but not identical; lists in some texts comprise thirteen items.

## twelve ascetic virtues
*sbyangs pa’i yon tan bcu gnyis*, Skt. *dvādaśa­dhūta­guṇa*, The twelve ascetic virtues comprise wearing clothing from a dust heap, owning only three robes, wearing felt or woolen clothes, begging for food, eating one’s meal at a single sitting, restricting the quantity of food, staying in solitude, sitting under trees, sitting in exposed places, sitting in charnel grounds, sitting even during sleep, and staying wherever one happens to be. For the Sanskrit and Tibetan terms, see Mahā­vyutpatti 127–39; also Dudjom Rinpoche (1991), vol. 2: 169.

## twelve aspects of the excellent wheel of the Dharma
*chos kyi ’khor lo shin tu gya nom pa rnam pa bcu gnyis*, See “twelve forms of the teaching.”

## twelve austerities
*sbyangs pa’i yon tan bcu gnyis*, Skt. *dvādaśadhūta­guṇa*, Twelve ascetic practices that renunciants may choose to engage in, they are wearing clothing from a dust heap, owning only three robes, wearing felt or woolen clothes, begging for food, eating one’s meal in a single sitting, restricting the quantity of food, staying in solitude, sitting under trees, sitting in exposed places, sitting in charnel grounds, sitting even during sleep, and staying wherever one happens to be.

## twelve Brahmā realms
*tshangs pa’i ’jig rten bcu gnyis*, Skt. *dvādaśa­brahma­loka*, See notes and .

## twelve branches of excellent speech
*gsung rab yan lag bcu nyis*, Skt. *dvādaśāṅga­pravacana*, The “twelve branches of excellent speech” or the “twelve categories of the Buddha’s teachings” are discourses (Tib. mdo’i sde, Skt. sūtra), verse narrations (Tib. dbyangs kyis bsnyad pa’i sde, Skt. geya), prophecies (Tib. lung du bstan pa’i sde, Skt. vyākaraṇa), poetic verses (Tib. tshigs su bcad pa’i sde, Skt. gāthā), aphorisms (Tib. ched du brjod pa’i sde, Skt. udāna), ethical narrations (Tib. gleng gzhi brjod pa’i sde, Skt. nidāna), narrative discourses (Tib. rtogs pa brjod pa’i sde, Skt. avadāna), parables (Tib. de lta bu byung ba’i sde, Skt. itivṛttaka), past-life stories (Tib. skye pa’i rabs kyi sde, Skt. jātaka), extensive sayings (Tib. shin tu rgyas pa’i sde, Skt. vaipulya), marvels (Tib. rmad du byung ba’i chos kyi sde, Skt. abidhutadharma), and resolutions (Tib. gtan la bab par bstan pa’i sde, Skt. upadeśa).

## twelve branches of the scriptures
*gsung rab yan lag bcu nyis*, Skt. *dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*, The twelve branches of the scriptures or “twelve branches of excellent speech” are discourses (Tib. mdo’i sde, Skt. sūtra), sayings in prose and verse (Tib. dbyangs kyis bsnyad pa, Skt. geya), prophetic declarations (Tib. lung du bstan pa, Skt. vyākaraṇa), verses (Tib. tshigs su bcad pa, Skt. gāthā), statements made for a purpose (Tib. ched du brjod pa, Skt. udāna), introductions (Tib. gleng gzhi brjod pa, Skt. nidāna), narratives (Tib. rtogs pa brjod pa, Skt. avadāna), accounts (Tib. de lta bu byung ba, Skt. itivṛttaka), tales of past lives (Tib. skyes pa’i rabs kyi sde, Skt. jātaka), marvelous events (Tib. rmad du byung ba’i chos kyi sde, Skt. adbhūtadharma), and established instructions (Tib. gtan la bab par bstan pa, Skt. upadeśa), and most extensive teachings (Tib. shin tu rgyas pa, Skt. vaipulya).

## Twelve categories of teaching in the piṭakas
*sde snod bcu gnyis*, lit. twelve [piṭaka](#piṭaka)s, also called the Twelve Branches of Excellent Speech (*gsung rab yan lag bcu gnyis*). The twelve types of teaching given by the [Buddha](#buddha) correspond to twelve types of text: condensed (*mdo sde*, Skt. *sūtra*), melodious (*dbyangs bsnyan*, *geya*), prophetic (*lung bstan*, *vyākaraṇa*), verse (*tshigs bcad*, *gāthā*), spoken with a purpose (*ched brjod*, *udāna*), conversatory (*gleng gzhi*, *nidāna* - questions, talks, etc.), concerning his past lives (*skyes rab*, *jātaka*), marvelous (*rmad byung*, *adbhutadharma*), establishing a truth (*gtan babs*, *upadeśa*), biographical or "expressing realization" (*rtogs brjod*, *avadāna*), historical (*de ltar byung*, *itivrittaka*), and very detailed (*shin tu rgyas pa*, *vaipulya*).

## twelve entrances
*skye mched bcu gnyis*, Skt. *dvādaśāyatana*, Twelve collections of similar dharmas under which all compounded and uncompounded dharmas may be included: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and their objects—visible forms, sounds, smells, flavors, tangibles, and dharmas.

## twelve essential qualities
*yon tan gyi snying po bcu gnyis*, Skt. *yon tan gyi snying po bcu gnyis*, Twelve qualities of the perfect buddha realm in which a thus-gone one attains awakening.

## twelve forms of the teaching
*gsung rab yan lag bcu gnyis*, Skt. *dvādaśāṅgapravacana*, The “twelve branches of excellent speech” or the “twelve categories of the Buddha’s teachings” are discourses (Tib. mdo’i sde, Skt. sūtra), verse narrations (Tib. dbyangs kyis bsnyad pa’i sde, Skt. geya), prophecies (Tib. lung du bstan pa’i sde, Skt. vyākaraṇa), poetic verses (Tib. tshigs su bcad pa’i sde, Skt. gāthā), aphorisms (Tib. ched du brjod pa’i sde, Skt. udāna), ethical narrations (Tib. gleng gzhi brjod pa’i sde, Skt. nidāna), narrative discourses (Tib. rtogs pa brjod pa’i sde, Skt. avadāna), parables (Tib. de lta bu byung ba’i sde, Skt. itivṛttaka), past-life stories (Tib. skye pa’i rabs kyi sde, Skt. jātaka), extensive sayings (Tib. shin tu rgyas pa’i sde, Skt. vaipulya), marvels (Tib. rmad du byung ba’i chos kyi sde, Skt. abidhutadharma), and resolutions (Tib. gtan la bab par bstan pa’i sde, Skt. upadeśa).

## twelve great yakṣa generals
This group of yakṣas mentioned in The Dhāraṇī of Vaiḍūryaprabha. This most likely refers to the unique group of twelve yakṣa generals who pledge themselves in service of the Thus-Gone One Bhaiṣajya­guru in The Detailed Account of the Previous Aspirations of the Blessed Bhaṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabha (Toh 504).

## twelve limbs of existence
*srid pa’i yan lag bcu gnyis*, Skt. *dvādaśa bhavāṅgāni*, Twelve successive parts in which to subdivide the longest possible process of dependent arising for one sentient being: ignorance, formations, consciousness, name and form, six entrances, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, old age, and death.

## twelve links of becoming
*srid pa’i yan lag bcu gnyis*, Skt. *srid pa’i yan lag bcu gnyis*, See “twelve links of dependent arising.”

## twelve links of conditioned existence
*srid pa’i yan lag bcu gnyis*, Skt. *dvādaśabhavāṅga*, The twelve links of dependent arising: ignorance, formations, consciousness, name and form, six entrances, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, old age, and death.

## twelve links of dependent arising
*rten cing ’brel bar ’byung ba yan lag bcu gnyis pa*, Skt. *dvādaśāṅga­pratītya­samutpāda*, The twelve causal links that perpetuate life in saṃsāra, starting with ignorance and ending with death.

## twelve links of dependent origination
*rten ’brel gyi yan lag bcu gnyis*, Skt. *dvā­daśāṅga­pratītya­samutpāda*, The principle of dependent origination asserts that nothing exists independently of other factors, the reason for this being that things and events come into existence only by dependence on the aggregation of multiple causes and conditions. In general, the processes of cyclic existence, through which the external world and the sentient beings within it revolve in a continuous cycle of suffering, propelled by the propensities of past actions and their interaction with afflicted mental states, originate dependent on the sequential unfolding of twelve links, commencing from fundamental ignorance and ending with birth, aging, and death (see –). It is only through deliberate reversal of these twelve links that one can succeed in bringing the whole cycle to an end. See .

## Twelve Mountains
*ri bcu gnyis la nges par gnas pa*, Skt. *ri bcu gnyis la nges par gnas pa*, An island in the vicinity of Jambudvīpa.

## Twelve qualities of full training
*sbyangs pa'i yon tan bcu gnyis*, Skt. *dvādaśadhūtaguṇa*, twelve [ascetic](#ascetic) practices of [śrāvakas](#śrāvaka) and [pratyekabuddhas](#pratyekabuddha), such as eating only once a day, living in solitude, possessing only the three monastic garments, etc.

## twelve sense fields
*skye mched bcu gnyis*, Skt. *dvādaśāyatana*, The twelve fields or sense sources consist of (a) the six sense organs or inner sense fields (Tib. nang gi skye mched drug, Skt. ṣaḍādhyātmikāyatana)—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and (b) their respective six objects or outer sense fields (Tib. phyi’i skye mched drug, Skt. ṣaḍbāhyāyatana): sights, sounds, odors, tastes, tangible objects, and mental phenomena. They are sometimes collectively called “the six sense sources,” meaning the six pairs of inner and outer sense fields.

## Twelve Vajra Laughs
*rdo rje gad mo bcu gnyis*, a teaching of the [Great Perfection](#great-perfection).

## twelve wheels of the Dharma
*chos kyi ’khor lo rnam pa bcu gnyis*, Skt. *dharmacakra*, The classification of all aspects of Buddha’s teachings into twelve types: sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, avadāna, itivṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, adbhutadharma, and upadeśa (see individual terms). Respectively, the sūtras, literally “threads,” does not mean entire texts as in the general meaning of sūtra but the prose passages within texts; the geyas are the verse versions of preceding prose passages; the vyākaraṇas are prophecies; the gāthās are stand-alone verses; the udānas are teachings not given in response to a request; the nidānas are the introductory sections; the avadānas are accounts of the previous lives of individuals who were alive at the time of the Buddha; the itivṛttakas are biographies of buddhas and bodhisattvas in the past; the jātakas are the Buddha’s accounts of his own previous lifetimes; the vaipulyas are teachings that expand upon a certain subject; the adbhutadharmas are descriptions of miracles; and the upadeśas are explanations of terms and categories.

## twenty high peaks of the mountain of views concerning the transitory collection
*’jig tshogs la lta ba’i ri’i rtse mo mthon po nyi shu*, Skt. *’jig tshogs la lta ba’i ri’i rtse mo mthon po nyi shu*, “The body is not the self nor does the self have a body; / The self is not based on the body [n]or body on self. / Know that these four relations apply to all skandhas; / So these are considered the twenty views of self.” (Goldfield 387).

## twenty higher aspirations
*lhag pa’i bsam pa nyi shu*, Skt. *vimśatyadhi­citta*, These twenty higher aspirations (vimśatyadhi­citta, lhag pa’i bsam pa nyi shu) are enumerated and explained in the Śata­sāhasrikā­prajñā­pāramitā­bṛhaṭṭīkā (Toh 3807, Degé Tengyur vol. 91, F.39.a et seq.). They comprise (1) the supreme aspiration of higher faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha (sangs rgyas dang chos dang dge ’dun la lhag par dad cing sems pa mchog gi bsam pa); (2) the aspiration of the higher attitude to ethical discipline that adopts the vows of the bodhisattvas’ ethical discipline (byang chub sems dpa’i tshul khrims kyi sdom pa yang dag par blang ba la lhag par sems pa’i tshul khrims kyi bsam pa); (3) the aspiration of the higher attitude to perfection in order to achieve the perfections of generosity, tolerance, perseverance, meditative concentration, and wisdom (sbyin pa dang bzod pa dang brtson ’grus dang bsam gtan dang shes rab yang dag par grub par bya ba’i phyir lhag par sems pa’i pha rol tu phyin pa’i bsam pa); (4) the aspiration of the genuine higher attitude concerning the nonself of phenomena and individual persons, ultimate reality, and the profound real nature of phenomena (chos dang gang zag la bdag med pa dang don dam pa dang chos kyi de bzhin nyid zab mo la lhag par sems pa yang dag pa’i don gyi bsam pa); (5) the unchanging and steadfast aspiration that one-pointedly establishes the certainty of complete enlightenment (yang dag par rdzogs pa’i byang chub tu sems rtse gcig tu nges par gyur cing mi ’gyur ba brtan pa’i bsam pa); (6) the impure aspiration of the higher attitude to the level of engagement through belief (mos pas spyod pa’i sa la lhag pa’i bsam pa ma dag pa’i bsam pa); (7) the pure higher aspiration concerning the levels from the first to the eighth (sa dang po nas sa brgyad pa’i bar gyi lhag pa’i bsam pa dag pa); (8) the utterly pure higher aspiration concerning the ninth and concluding [tenth] levels (mthar phyin pa’i sa ste sa dgu pa dang bcu pa’i lhag pa’i bsam pa shin tu dag pa); (9) the higher aspiration concerning the inconceivable might of the extrasensory powers of the buddhas and bodhisattvas (sangs rgyas dang byang chub sems dpa’ rnams kyi mngon par shes pa bsam gyis mi khyab pa’i mthu la lhag par bsam pa); (10) the beneficial aspiration that introduces beings to the practice of virtuous action (sems can rnams dge ba byed du ’jug pa phan pa’i bsam pa); (11) the aspiration that is undeceiving concerning the teacher and the object of generosity (bla ma dang sbyin gnas la mi slu ba’i bsam pa); (12) the aspiration to bring about happiness when bodhisattvas associate with conduct in conformity with the Dharma (byang chub sems dpa’ chos mthun par spyod pa dang / ’grogs na bde bar bya ba’i bsam pa); (13) the aspiration to overpower the minds of those overwhelmed by the afflicted mental states, the subsidiary afflicted mental states, and all the deeds of Māra (nyon mongs pa dang / nye ba’i nyon mongs pa dang bdud kyi las thams cad zil gyis mnan pa dag gi sems kyi dbang du gyur par bya ba’i bsam pa); (14) the aspiration of the view concerning the defects in all formative predispositions (’du byed thams cad la skyon du lta ba’i bsam pa); (15) the aspiration of the view concerning the advantages in the attainment of nirvāṇa (mya ngan las ’das pa la phan yon du lta ba’i bsam pa); (16) the aspiration to constantly cultivate the factors conducive to enlightenment (byang chub kyi phyogs kyi chos rnams rtag tu bsgom pa bya ba’i bsam pa); (17) the aspiration to stay in isolation until one attains conformity with cultivation of those very factors conducive to enlightenment (byang chub kyi phyogs kyi chos de dag nyid bsgom pa dang mthun pa’i bar du dben pa la gnas pa’i bsam pa); (18) the aspiration that disregards mundane materialism, acquisition, and fame (’jig rten gyi zang zing dang / rnyed pa dang bkur sti la mi lta ba’i bsam pa); (19) the aspiration to realize the Great Vehicle, abandoning the Lesser Vehicle (theg pa chung ngu spangs te theg pa chen po rtogs par bya ba’i bsam pa); and (20) the aspiration to accomplish all the aims of all beings (sems can thams cad kyi don thams cad bya ba’i bsam pa).

## Twenty One Genyen
*dge bsnyen nyer gcip*, a group of spirits who were subdued by [Padmasambhava](#padmasambhava-of-oḍḍiyāna) and became the [protectors](#protectors) of the [Dharma](#dharma).

## twenty surpassing aspirations
*lhag pa’i bsam pa nyi shu*, Skt. *viṃśati adhyāśaya*, Bṭ1 na, 39a3–b3 lists the following: (1–3) faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha (the finest aspiration); (4) for morality (moral aspiration); (5–9) aspiration for the perfections (surpassing aspiration for the other five perfections); (10–13) aspiration for the profound selflessness of persons and dharmas, the ultimate, and the reality of dharmas (aspiration for the real dharmas); (14–15) a single-pointed mind and clairvoyance (inconceivable aspiration); (16) aspiration to establish beings in the wholesome; (17–18) the pure aspiration of the ninth and tenth levels; and (19–20) aspiration for the inconceivable force of a buddha’s clairvoyance, etc.

## twenty-eight great yakṣa generals
*gnod sbyin gyi sde dpon chen po nyi shu rtsa brgyad*, Skt. *gnod sbyin gyi sde dpon chen po nyi shu rtsa brgyad*, Seven sets of four yakṣa generals dwelling in the four cardinal directions, the sky, the earth, and the intermediate directions.

## Twenty-five disciples
*rje 'bang nyer lnga*, the greatest Tibetan [disciple](#disciple)s of [Padmasambhava](#padmasambhava-of-oḍḍiyāna). All of them attained the [supreme accomplishment](#supreme-accomplishment). The most famous were [King Trisong Detsen](#trisong-detsen), [Yeshe Tsogyal](#yeshe-tsogyal), and [Vairotṣana](#vairotṣana). Many of the great masters of Tibetan Buddhism are [emanation](#emanation)s of the twenty-five disciples.

## twenty-four sacred places
*yul nyi shu rtsa bzhi*, A common list of sites important for Tantric Buddhism that are typically mentioned only by name. For a more detailed description see the Cakrasaṃvara History (bde mchog chos ’byung) of Butön Rinchen Drup (1290–1364).

## twenty-two faculties
*dbang po gnyis shu rtsa gnyis*, Skt. *dvāviṃśatīndriya*, Listed here as the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the thought faculty, the male faculty, the female faculty, the life faculty, the suffering faculty, the pleasure faculty, the mental well-being faculty, the mental anguish faculty, the neutrality faculty, the faith faculty, the heroism faculty, the mindfulness faculty, the samādhi faculty, the wisdom faculty, the “I will completely know what I don’t yet know” faculty, the complete-knowledge faculty, and the “I have completely known” faculty.

## twice-born
A term used to refer to brahmins (sometimes also kṣatriyas and vaiśyas) on account of having undergone upanayana, the initiation rite in which one receives the sacred thread and is “born” a second time as a fully initiated member of the brahmin caste.

## Twice-Marked Crest Bearer
*mtshan gnyis gtsug gtor can*, Skt. *mtshan gnyis gtsug gtor can*, A buddha.

## Twice-Marked Light
*mtshan gnyis ’od*, Skt. *mtshan gnyis ’od*, A great bodhisattva.

## twister
*’khyil bar byed pa*, Skt. *’khyil bar byed pa*, The name of a karmic wind involved in the formation of an embryo in its seventh week.

## Two accumulations
*tshogs gnyis*, Skt. *saṃbhāradvaya*, the accumulation of [merit](#merit) (*bsod nams*, Skt. *puṇya*) and that of [wisdom](#wisdom) (*ye shes*, *jñāna*).

## two day fevers
*nyin gnyis pa*, Skt. *dvaitīyaka*, symptom that may be evidence of an illness considered an impediment to ordination.

## two extremes
*mtha’ gnyis*, Skt. *antadvaya*, The two views of (1) eternalism (śāśvatānta), the belief in a permanent, causeless creator and/or the belief in an independent, permanent, singular self; and (2) nihilism (ucchedānta), the belief that things ultimately do not exist and/or the denial of the law of cause and effect or of past and future lives.

## two extremes of eternalism and nihilism
*rtag pa dang chad pa’i mtha’ gnyis*, Skt. *śāśvatānta ucchedānta*, The two extreme views to be avoided when seeking an insight into emptiness.

## two factors
The obscurations of afflictive emotions (nyon mongs pa’i sgrib pa) and the obscurations of meditative attainment (snyoms par ’jug pa’i sgrib pa).

## two gates
*sgo gnyis*, Skt. *dvayamukhatā*, The gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī.

## two modes of awareness
*rig pa gnyis*, Skt. *dvi­vidyā*, The two modes of awareness are intrinsic and extraneous. In this context‌, the former may indicate the awareness of one’s own mind and the latter the awareness of the minds of others.

## Two obscurations
*sgrib gnyis*, the [obscurations of negative emotions](#obscurations-of-negative-emotions) and [conceptual obscurations](#concept-obscurations). See also [obscurations](#obscurations) and [four obscurations](#four-obscurations).

## two pacification seed syllables
*zhi ba’i yig ’bru gnyis pa*, A phrase describing a mantra syllable in the “selection of mantra syllables” (Tib. sngags btu ba; Skt. mantroddhāra) instructions in The Tantra of Great Gaṇapati.

## Two Supreme Ones
*mchog gnyis*, Guṇaprabha (*yon tan 'od*) and Śākyaprabha (sha kya 'od).

## Two truths
*bden pa gnyis*, the [absolute](#absolute-truth) and [relative truths](#relative-truth).

## twofold act and motion
*gsol ba dang gnyis las*, Skt. *jñāptidvitīyakarman*, A formal act of the saṅgha that requires an initial motion followed by the statement of the proposed act. Such an act is needed to grant the vows of full ordination to a nun, among other occasions.

## Twofold goal
*don gnyis*, one's own goal, benefit or welfare (*rang don*) and that of others (*gzhan don*). Often understood in the ultimate sense of the goal for oneself being achieved by the realization of [emptiness](#emptiness), the [dharmakāya](#dharmakāya), and the goal for others by compassion manifesting as the [rūpakāya](#rūpakāya).

## twofold liberation
Being liberated by means of wisdom, (prajñā, shes rab) and the meditative concentration (dhyāna, bsam gtan).

## Twofold purity
*dag pa gnyis*, original purity (*rang bzhin ye dag*), which is the [Buddha nature](#buddha-nature) in all beings, and purity from all adventitious stains (*blo bur phral dag*). Only a [Buddha](#buddha) has this second purity as well.

## Two-Minded Wish
*yid gnyis ’dod*, Skt. *yid gnyis ’dod*, Mother of the buddha Maticintin.

## Tāṇḍyāyanīya
The name of a family lineage.

## uṣṇīṣa
*gtsug tor*, Skt. *uṣṇīṣa*, One of the thirty-two signs of a great being. In its simplest form it is a pointed shape to the head (like a turban), or more elaborately it is a dome-shaped extension on the crown of the head, or even an invisible extension of infinite height. The term may can be used to refer to a class of deities such as the uṣṇiṣarājas or uṣṇīṣa­tathāgatas.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from a Breeze
*ser bu ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *ser bu ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of eight uṣṇīṣa buddhas mentioned in this text that do not appear elsewhere in the canon.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from Beginningless and Endless Emptiness
*thog ma dang tha ma med pa stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *thog ma dang tha ma med pa stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of sixteen uṣṇīṣa buddhas named after the sixteen emptinesses.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from Inner Emptiness
*nang stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *nang stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of sixteen uṣṇīṣa buddhas named after the sixteen emptinesses.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from Nutritious Food
*ro bcud kyi snying po ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *ro bcud kyi snying po ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of eight uṣṇīṣa buddhas mentioned in this text that do not appear elsewhere in the canon.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from Outer and Inner Emptiness
*phyi nang stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *phyi nang stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of sixteen uṣṇīṣa buddhas named after the sixteen emptinesses.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from Outer Emptiness
*phyi stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *phyi stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of sixteen uṣṇīṣa buddhas named after the sixteen emptinesses.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from the Boundless Essence
*snying po dpag med ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *snying po dpag med ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of eight uṣṇīṣa buddhas mentioned in this text that do not appear elsewhere in the canon.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from the Emptiness of All Phenomena
*chos thams cad stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *chos thams cad stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of sixteen uṣṇīṣa buddhas named after the sixteen emptinesses.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from the Emptiness of Compounded Phenomena
*’dus byas stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *’dus byas stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of sixteen uṣṇīṣa buddhas named after the sixteen emptinesses.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from the Emptiness of Emptiness
*stong pa nyid stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *stong pa nyid stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of sixteen uṣṇīṣa buddhas named after the sixteen emptinesses.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from the Emptiness of Nonentities
*dngos po med pa stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *dngos po med pa stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of sixteen uṣṇīṣa buddhas named after the sixteen emptinesses.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from the Emptiness of Nonrejection
*dor ba med pa stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, Skt. *dor ba med pa stong pa nyid ’byung ba’i gtsug tor*, One among a list of sixteen uṣṇīṣa buddhas named after the sixteen emptinesses.

## Uṣṇīṣa Arisen from the Emptiness of Own-Characteristics

According to The Root Manual of the Rites of Mañjuśrī, they are Cakravartyuṣṇīṣa, Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa, Sitātapatra, Jayoṣṇīṣa, Kamaloṣṇīṣa, Vijayoṣṇīṣa, Tejorāśi, and Unnatoṣṇīṣa. There are, however, different sets with other names included.

## Śuddhāvāsa
*gnas gtsang ma*, Skt. *śuddhāvāsa*, Lit. “Those in the Pure Abodes.” The five Pure Abodes are the highest heavens of the form realm and result from mastery of the fourth meditative absorption. They comprise the heavens of Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha. The Pure Abodes, or Śuddhāvāsa, are never destroyed during the cycles of the destruction and creation of the universe. Rebirth there is the karmic result of accomplishing the fourth concentration.

## Śuddhāvāsa gods
*gnas gtsang ma’i ris kyi lha*, Skt. *śuddhāvāsa­kāyika*, The gods who live in Śuddhāvāsa heavens, the five “pure abodes” that form the highest realms that constitute the realm of subtle form (rūpadhātu) and which comprise the fourth of the meditative concentrations (dhyāna).

## udumbara flower
In Buddhist texts, the udumbara flower is a symbol for extremely rare occurrences, since it is said to bloom once every three thousand years. It is often identified as the cluster fig (Ficus glomerata).

## ultimate
*don dam pa*, Skt. *paramārtha*, “Ultimate” is preferable to the usual “absolute” because it carries fewer connotations than “absolute”—which, however, when understood logically, is also correct. It is contrasted with “superficial” (vyavahāra) or “relative” (samvṛtti) to give the two types, or “levels.,” of truth. It is synonymous with ultimate reality, the uncompounded, voidness, reality, limit of reality, absolute, nirvāṇa, ultimate liberation, infinity, permanence, eternity, independence, etc. It also has the soteriological sense of “sacred” as opposed to “profane” as is conveyed by its literal rendering “supreme” (parama) “object” (artha).

## ultimate goal
See “summit of existence.”

*don gyi yon tan*, Skt. *don gyi yon tan*, Father of the buddha Suviniścitārtha.

## ultimate reality
The quality or condition of things as they really are, which cannot be conveyed in conceptual, dualistic terms.

## ultimate realm
*chos kyi dbyings*, Skt. *dharmadhātu*, This compound is actually metaphorical in sense, with (at least) two interpretations possible because of ambiguities in the word dhātu. Dhātu as in the expression kāmadhātu (desire-realm), may mean “realm”; or it may mean “element,” as in the eighteen elements (see entry), where it is explained as analogous to a mineral such as copper. Thus the realm of the Dharma is the dharmakāyā, the pure source and sphere of the Dharma. And the element of the Dharma is like a mine from which the verbal Dharma, the buddha-qualities, and the wisdoms of the arhats and bodhisattvas are culled. This is metaphorical, as Vimalakīrti would remind us, because the Dharma, the ultimate, is ultimately not a particular place; it is immanent in all places, being the actuality and ultimate condition of all things and being relatively no one thing except, like voidness, the supremely beneficent of concepts.

## ultimate state of existence
See “summit of existence.”

## ultimate truth
*don dam*, Skt. *paramārtha*, Paramārtha­satya literally means “the highest-object truth,” because it is what is realized by wisdom (prajñā) as the highest form of mind. It refers to the absolute understanding of phenomena and reality as it is perceived by a mind that is purified of all delusion, in contrast to the relative truth that is perceived by ordinary unenlightened beings.

## ultimate within the domain of truth
*chos kyi dbyings kyis klas pa*, Skt. *dharmadhātuparamaḥ*, Mahāvyutpatti 6429.

## ultimately real
*yongs su grub pa*, Skt. *pariniṣpanna*, The direct perception of the nature of the mind and its objects. An alternative translation is “the absolute.” One of the three natures that are central to the philosophy of the Yogācāra tradition.

## Uluvillikā
*skra lcang lo rgyas*, Skt. *uluvillikā*, One of the ten girls who attended upon Prince Siddhārtha while he was practicing austerities.

## Umā
*dka’ zlog*, Skt. *umā*, A goddess who is the wife of Mahādeva (Śiva). The name Umā is often synonymous with the two goddesses Durgā and Pārvatī. The Tibetan rendering of her name is also at times used as a translation of the name Durgā, a fact that highlights the close relationship between these two goddesses.

## Uṣmā
*tsha ba ma*, Skt. *uṣmā*, One of the subtle channels in the body.

## Umadevī
*lha mo u ma de ba*, Skt. *lha mo u ma de ba*, To help the devas win a battle against the asuras, Vajrapāṇi manifested the goddess Umadevī. Together with the god Mahādeva, she has two children: the girl Red Cāmuṇḍī and the boy Yāma Mahākāla.

*gnod mdzes rdo rje*, Skt. *śumbhavajraka*, Another name of Vajrapāṭāla.

## Umādevī
*lha mo u ma*, Skt. *umādevī*, Umādevī is also known as Pārvatī. The name is of obscure origin, but can mean “splendor,” “tranquility,” or “light.” She is the consort of Śiva, also known as Maheśvara, and believed to be the rebirth of Sīta, his previous consort.

## Umeśvara
*u ma’i dbang phyug*, Skt. *umeśvara*, The name that Avalokiteśvara prophecies the goddess Umādevī will have on attainment of Buddhahood.

## Umāpati
*dka’ thub zlog pa’i bdag po*, Skt. *umāpati*, A form of Śiva, so-named for being the spouse of Umā.

## Umāriṣṭa

## unable to be turned back
A description of a bodhisattva who has reached a particular stage along the path to becoming a buddha at which the bodhisattva is certain of doing so. Different Buddhist works place this stage at different points along the path. According to some works, it is a highly advanced stage that is connected with having received a prediction of future buddhahood. Modern scholars have also sometimes connected it to the acceptance of the fact that things do not arise, but it is also connected with other attainments.

## Unaffected
*tshugs pa med*, Skt. *tshugs pa med*, Unaffected (not changed or influenced), also the one foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Guṇākara.

## Unaltered
*ma bcos pa*, Skt. *naisargika*, left in its original state, without manipulations or fabrications.

*gzhal du med pa*, Skt. *amāpya*, This term in some contexts may refer to a large number equivalent to ten to the power of 57.

## unatonable
*lhag ma med pa*, Skt. *nirvaśeṣa*, Defeats (Tib. phas pham pa; Skt. pārājika) are unatonable offenses and result in “being denied the common living” (Tib. gnas pa ma yin pa; Skt. asaṃvāsa) with the saṅgha, meaning that one can no longer participate in the saṅgha’s official acts or partake of its resources and offerings. The other four types of offense, such as saṅgha remnant (Tib. dge ’dun lhag ma; Skt. saṃghāvaśeṣa) are atonable, meaning that one may be reinstated to full status in the community once one has properly made amends and served any penance or probation required. Note that Yijing translates 他勝 as “defeat” (Skt. pārājika) rather than “unatonable” (Taishō 1446, 1047b18).

## unchaste conduct
The opposite of “pure conduct,” which, in the context of Buddhist monasticism, normally indicates celibacy. Here the context indicates that “unchaste conduct” stands in for the more common formulation of the third basic precept as “sexual misconduct.”

The uncommon phenomena from the perspective of ordinary persons are listed at .

## unconditioned
*’dus ma byas*, Skt. *asaṃskṛta*, When referring to phenomena or constituents of experience, asaṃskṛta usually means “unconditioned.” But it can also mean “unrefined,” “unadorned,” “unpolished.” It seems that the text is here playing on the multivalence of the term in combination with the multivalence of the term “dharma.”

## unconditioned phenomena
*’dus ma byas*, Skt. *asaṃskṛta*, Unconditioned phenomena are defined in as those which are nonarising, nondwelling, and nonperishing, while the Ten Thousand () adds nontransformation with respect to all things, the cessation of desire, the cessation of hatred, the cessation of delusion, the abiding of phenomena in the real nature, reality, the realm of phenomena, maturity with respect to all things, the real nature, the unmistaken real nature, the one and only real nature, and the finality of existence. Although the Prajñā­pāramitā analysis ultimately places all phenomena in this category, that analysis derives its force by contrasting with the way in which the various Abhidharma traditions classify the unconditioned, principally including nirvāṇa and in some cases space and certain kinds of cessation. See also .

*zag pa ma mchis pa’i chos*, Skt. *anāsrava­dharma*, Uncontaminated phenomena, as described in , include the four applications of mindfulness, the four correct exertions, the four supports for miraculous ability, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven branches of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the four truths of the noble ones, the eight aspects of liberation, the nine serial steps of meditative absorption, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, all the gateways of the meditative stabilities and the dhāraṇīs, the ten powers of the tathāgatas, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of exact knowledge, great loving kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas. See also .

## Unexcelled Heaven
*’og min*, Skt. *akaniṣṭha*, The eighth and highest level of the realm of form (rūpadhātu); it is only accessible as the result of specific states of concentration. According to some texts this is where non-returners (anāgāmin) dwell in their last lives. In other texts it is the realm of the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) and is a buddhafield associated with the buddha Vairocana that is accessible only to bodhisattvas on the tenth level.

## unfortunate
*mi khom pa*, Skt. *akṣaṇa*, The Sanskrit has its origins in the vocabulary of dice gambling, but in Buddhism refers to rebirths, human or otherwise, in which one will be unable to practice the Dharma. The Tibetan (also found as mi khoms pa) is based on the opposite of khom, khoms meaning leisure, opportunity, freedom. There is a list of eight unfortunate rebirths: as hell beings, pretas, animals, or long-living deities; in lands without the Dharma; with defective faculties; holding wrong views; and in a world where a buddha has not appeared.

## unfortunate rebirth destinies
*ngan song*, Skt. *apāya*, Usually Tibetan ngan song [gsum] is an expression for the three lower realms of rebirth according to Buddhist cosmology: animals, ghosts, and hell beings. Here, however, the asuras are counted among lower rebirths too.

## unfortunate rebirth-destiny
Literally “misery” or “misfortune,” a collective name for the three lower realms of existence, i.e., the realms of animals, ghosts, and hell beings. Occurs often in a formula together with its synonym apāya and its near synonyms “the lower worlds” and “hell” (Pali niraya/naraka; Tib. sems can dmyal ba).

## unfortunate state
*ngan ’gro*, Skt. *durgati*, Rebirth in one of the three lower states of existence, namely, the hell realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm.

## unfortunate states
*mi khom*, Skt. *akṣaṇa*, See “eight unfortunate states.”

## unfounded pride
*mngon pa’i nga rgyal*, Skt. *abhimāna*, A conceited, false sense of attainment. On a more subtle level, it can also refer to dualistic concepts about emptiness or ultimate reality. One of seven types of pride related to the spiritual path.

## unfree states
*mi khom pa*, Skt. *akṣaṇa*, Literally, “without leisure.” This refers to being born in a state in which one will not have the opportunity to meet with a buddha or their teachings. Eight situations are typically listed: (1) being born in a hell realm, (2) as an animal, (3) as a hungry ghost, (4) as a long-life god, (5) in a borderland or non-Buddhist country, (6) having wrong views, (7) as someone with impaired faculties who is unable to understand the teachings, or (8) in a time or place where no buddha has come.

## unfree states of existence
*mi khom pa*, Skt. *akṣaṇa*, See “eight unfree states.”

## unique attributes
*ma ’dres pa’i chos*, Skt. *āveṇikadharmā*, Special qualities unique to buddhas and thus unshared by any others, they are often presented in a list of eighteen.

## unique attributes of a buddha
Special features of a buddha’s behavior, realization, activity, and knowledge that are not shared by other beings. They are generally listed as eighteen: (1) he never makes a mistake, (2) he is never boisterous, (3) he never forgets, (4) his concentration never falters, (5) he has no notion of distinctness, (6) his equanimity is not due to lack of consideration, (7) his motivation never falters, (8) his endeavor never fails, (9) his mindfulness never falters, (10) he never abandons his concentration, (11) his wisdom (prajñā) never decreases, (12) his liberation never fails, (13) all his physical actions are preceded and followed by knowledge (jñāna), (14) all his verbal actions are preceded and followed by knowledge, (15) all his mental actions are preceded and followed by knowledge, (16) his knowledge and vision perceive the past without attachment or hindrance, (17) his knowledge and vision perceive the future without attachment or hindrance, and (18) his knowledge and vision perceive the present without attachment or hindrance.

## unique buddha qualities
*sangs rgyas kyi chos ma ’dres pa*, Skt. *āveṇikā­buddha­dharma*, Eighteen qualities that are exclusively possessed by a buddha. These are listed in the as follows: The tathāgata does not possess (1) confusion, (2) noisiness, (3) forgetfulness, (4) loss of meditative equipoise, (5) cognition of distinctness, or (6) nonanalytical equanimity. A buddha totally lacks (7) degeneration of zeal, (8) degeneration of vigor, (9) degeneration of mindfulness, (10) degeneration of absorption, (11) degeneration of insight, (12) degeneration of complete liberation, and (13) degeneration of seeing the wisdom of complete liberation. (14) A tathāgata’s every action of body is preceded by wisdom and followed through with wisdom; (15) every action of speech is preceded by wisdom and followed through with wisdom; (16) a buddha’s every action of mind is preceded by wisdom and followed through with wisdom; and (17) a tathāgata engages in seeing the past through wisdom that is unattached and unobstructed and (18) engages in seeing the present through wisdom that is unattached and unobstructed.

## unique qualities
*ma ’dres pa’i chos*, Skt. *āveṇikadharma*, Eighteen special features of a buddha’s behavior, realization, activity, and wisdom that are not shared by other beings. They are as follows: (1) he never makes a mistake, (2) he is never boisterous, (3) he never forgets, (4) his concentration never falters, (5) he has no notion of distinctness, (6) his equanimity is not due to lack of consideration, (7) his motivation never falters, (8) his endeavor never fails, (9) his mindfulness never falters, (10) he never abandons his concentration, (11) his insight never decreases, (12) his liberation never fails, (13) all his physical actions are preceded and followed by wisdom (jñāna), (14) all his verbal actions are preceded and followed by wisdom, (15) all his mental actions are preceded and followed by wisdom, (16) his wisdom and vision perceive the past without any attachment or hindrance, (17) his wisdom and vision perceive the future without any attachment or hindrance, and (18) his wisdom and vision perceive the present without any attachment or hindrance.

## unique qualities of a buddha
*sangs rgyas kyi chos ma ’dres pa*, Skt. *āveṇika­buddha­dharma*, They are as follows: (1) he never makes a mistake; (2) he is never boisterous; (3) he never forgets; (4) his concentration never falters; (5) he has no notion of distinctness; (6) his equanimity is not due to lack of consideration; (7) his motivation never falters; (8) his endeavor never fails; (9) his mindfulness never falters; (10) he never abandons his concentration; (11) his wisdom (prajñā) never decreases; (12) his liberation never fails; (13) all his physical actions are preceded and followed by wisdom (ye shes); (14) all his verbal actions are preceded and followed by wisdom (ye shes); (15) all his mental actions are preceded and followed by wisdom (ye shes); (16) his wisdom (ye shes) and vision perceive the past without any attachment or hindrance; (17) his wisdom (ye shes) and vision perceive the future without any attachment or hindrance; and (18) his wisdom and vision perceive the present without any attachment or hindrance.

## unique qualities of buddhahood
*sangs rgyas rnams kyi ma ’dras chos*, Skt. *āveṇikabuddhadharma*, Eighteen qualities that are exclusively possessed by a buddha. These are listed in the Dharma­saṃgraha as follows: The tathāgata does not possess (1) confusion; (2) noisiness; (3) forgetfulness; (4) loss of meditative equipoise; (5) cognition of distinctness; or (6) nonanalytical equanimity. A buddha totally lacks (7) degeneration of motivation; (8) degeneration of perseverance; (9) degeneration of mindfulness; (10) degeneration of samādhi; (11) degeneration of prajñā; (12) degeneration of complete liberation; and (13) degeneration of seeing the wisdom of complete liberation. (14) A tathāgata’s every action of body is preceded by wisdom and followed through with wisdom; (15) every action of speech is preceded by wisdom and followed through with wisdom; (16) a buddha’s every action of mind is preceded by wisdom and followed through with wisdom. (17) A tathāgata engages in seeing the past through wisdom that is unattached and unobstructed and (18) engages in seeing the present through wisdom that is unattached and unobstructed.

## unnatural death
*dus ma yin pa’i ’chi ba*, Skt. *akālamaraṇa*, This term literally means an “untimely death.” In both Buddhist and non-Buddhist South Asian literature, human beings are said to be allotted a certain lifespan, and that lifespan is a function of the age in which they live. In the current age, the full human lifespan is said to be one hundred years. Thus any death that occurs before one has lived out an entire one hundred years is technically considered an “untimely death.” The list of various “untimely deaths” in Buddhist literature generally includes tragic and unnatural ways of dying such as drowning, contracting a sudden illness, being burned to death, etc.

## Unseen Pinnacle
*spyi gtsug bltar mi mthong ba*, Skt. *an­ava­lokita­mūrdha*, Name of the seventh meditative stability. See also Pinnacle of their crown cannot be seen.

## Unshakable
*mi g.yo ba*, Skt. *acalā*, Unshakable (firmly fixed; not able to be shaken), also the name of the eighth ground of the bodhisattvas.

## Unshakable Array
*bkod pa mi ’khrugs pa*, Skt. *bkod pa mi ’khrugs pa*, Birthplace of the buddha Vimalaprabha.

## Unshakable Fame
*’khrug med grags*, Skt. *’khrug med grags*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Jñānavara.

## Unshakable Power
*mthu rtsal mi g.yo ba*, Skt. *mthu rtsal mi g.yo ba*, Father of the buddha Devaraśmi.

## Unshakable Powerful Qualities
*yon tan mthu rtsal mi g.yo ba*, Skt. *yon tan mthu rtsal mi g.yo ba*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Laḍitavyūha.

## Unshakeable
*mi ’gul bar byas pa*, Skt. *mi ’gul bar byas pa*, Unshakeable (firm; not able to be shaken), also the name of a world in the distant past in a story the Buddha tells.

## Unstained by Attacks
*phas rgol dri ma med pa*, Skt. *phas rgol dri ma med pa*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Vajrasena.

## Unstained by the Realm of Māras
*bdud yul mi gos*, Skt. *bdud yul mi gos*, A bodhisattva.

## Unstoppable Melodious Roar
*thogs pa med pa’i dbyangs kyi nga ro*, Skt. *thogs pa med pa’i dbyangs kyi nga ro*, A buddha.

## Unsubdued by Others
*gzhan gis mi thub*, Skt. *gzhan gis mi thub*, Name of a buddha realm in the east where the buddha Exceedingly Widely Renowned Glory resides.

## Unsullied
*rnyog pa med*, Skt. *rnyog pa med*, Unsullied (not stained or made impure), also the one foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Sūryaprabha.

## Unsullied Aim
*rnyog pa med don*, Skt. *rnyog pa med don*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Guṇāgradhārin (140 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Unsullied Mind
*rnyog pa med pa’i blo*, Skt. *rnyog pa med pa’i blo*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Mahāraśmi.

## Unsullied Objective
*rnyog pa med don*, Skt. *rnyog pa med don*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Sarvatejas (614 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Unsupported
*gnas med*, Skt. *gnas med*, Unsupported (not held up or backed), also the son of the buddha Gagana.

## Unsupported Conduct
*spyod pa mi gnas pa*, Skt. *spyod pa mi gnas pa*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Praśāntagātra.

## Unsurpassable
*bla med*, Skt. *bla med*, Unsurpassable (not able to be exceeded), also the son of the buddha Rāhudeva.

## unsurpassable, completely perfect enlightenment
*bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa’i byang chub*, Skt. *anuttara­samyak­saṃbodhi*, An enlightenment that is authentically complete.

## unsurpassable good
*grub pa dang bde ba*, Skt. *yogakṣema*, See Edgerton 1953, p. 448,1–2; Tillemans 1997, p. 157ff. Lamotte translates this term with ‘…de sécurité suprême’; see Lamotte 1935, p. 175.

## Unsurpassable Intention
*bla na med par sems pa*, Skt. *bla na med par sems pa*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Druma.

## Unsurpassable Light Rays
*bla na med pa’i ’od zer*, Skt. *bla na med pa’i ’od zer*, A buddha.

## Unsurpassable Splendor
*gong na med pa’i gzi brjid*, Skt. *gong na med pa’i gzi brjid*, A great bodhisattva.

## unsurpassable, truly complete awakening
The full, unlimited, and completely perfect awakening to which followers of the Mahāyāna aspire.

## Unsurpassed
*mi che ba*, Skt. *avṛha*, Unsurpassed (not exceeded by any other), also the name of one of the five pure abodes.

## unsurpassed and perfect awakening
*bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa’i byang chub*, Skt. *anuttara­samyak­saṃbodhi*, The awakening of the buddhas, so-named to distinguish it from the limited realizations of lesser beings such as arhats, solitary buddhas, and the like.

## unsurpassed, complete, perfect awakening
*bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa’i byang chub*, Skt. *anuttarasamyak­saṃbodhi*, The fully awakened state of a buddha.

## unsurpassed, completely perfect awakening
*bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa’i byang chub*, Skt. *anuttara­samyak­saṃbodhi*, The awakening of a buddha, which is superior to all other forms of awakening. According to the Mahāyāna, in anuttara­samyak­saṃbodhi, both of the two kinds of obscuration, the afflictive obscuration (Skt. kleśāvaraṇa) and the obscurations to omniscience (Skt. jñeyāvaraṇa), have been completely overcome.

## Unsurpassed Concentration
*bsam gtan bla ma*, Skt. *bsam gtan bla ma*, A monk.

## Unsurpassed Diligence
*brtson ’grus gong na med*, Skt. *brtson ’grus gong na med*, A bodhisattva in the retinue of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Unsurpassed Knowledge
*shes rab bla ma*, Skt. *shes rab bla ma*, A bodhisattva.

## unsurpassed leader of those to be trained
Skt. *anuttara­puruṣa­damya­sārathi*, An epithet of a buddha. Here it is the seventh epithet through which the Buddha Śākyamuni is to be recollected when experiencing fear, trepidation, or terror. In some enumerations of the epithets, “unsurpassed” (anuttaraḥ, bla na med pa), instead of being a qualifier of “leader …” is counted as an independent epithet of its own, increasing the number of epithets to nine.

## unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening
*bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa’i byang chub*, Skt. *anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*, The complete awakening of a buddha, as opposed to the attainments of arhats and pratyekabuddhas.

## Unsurpassed Standard
Name of the tathāgata from whom the Buddha received The Dhāraṇī of Dhvajāgrakeyūrā in a past life as a bodhisattva.

## unsurpassed, supreme welfare
*g.yung drung gi mthar thug pa grub pa dang bde ba*, Skt. *g.yung drung gi mthar thug pa grub pa dang bde ba*, In this text, being “established … in the unsurpassed, supreme welfare of nirvāṇa” appears as a synonym for the attainment of arhatship.

## Unsurpassed Wisdom
*ye shes bla ma*, Skt. *ye shes bla ma*, A monk and a past buddha.

## Unswerving Power
*mthu rtsal g.yo med*, Skt. *mthu rtsal g.yo med*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Guṇaskandha.

## Untainted (action)
*zag med*, Skt. *anāsrava*, done without concepts of subject, object, and action.

## untangled hair
*dbu skra ma ’dzings pa*, Skt. *asaṃlulitakeśa*, Seventy-seventh of the eighty minor signs.

## untenable
*gnas ma yin*, Skt. *asthāna*, This terms refers to all that is unreasonable and cannot be expected to occur. Among the ten powers of a Buddha, the first is knowing what is tenable and untenable (Skt. sthānāsthāna, Tib. gnas dang gnas ma yin), i.e., the natural laws that govern the world in which we live.

## untimely death
*dus ma yin pa’i ’chi ba*, Skt. *akālamaraṇa*, See “unnatural death.”

## Untiring
*sgyid mi lug pa*, Skt. *sgyid mi lug pa*, Untiring (not becoming tired; persistent), also the name of an attendant of the buddha Nārāyaṇa.

## Untiring Diligence
*brtson ’grus skyo med*, Skt. *brtson ’grus skyo med*, A great bodhisattva.

## Untiring Intellect
*ngoms pa med pa’i blo*, Skt. *ngoms pa med pa’i blo*, Attendant of the buddha Vratatapas.

## Untiring Mind
*yid mi skyo*, Skt. *yid mi skyo*, Attendant of the buddha Brahmagāmin.

## untouchable
A general term for anyone occupying a social standing that is entirely outside of the brahmanical system of laws and customs governing caste and the stages of life (varṇāśrama­dharma).

## Untouched Sunrise
*nyi ma shar bar gyur bas mi reg pa*, Skt. *nyi ma shar bar gyur bas mi reg pa*, A river on Saṅkāśa.

## Untruthful One
*bden mi ldan*, Skt. *bden mi ldan*, Name of a rākṣasī and Dharma protector.

## unvanquished
*mi pham pa*, Skt. *ajaya*, The 44th meditative stability in chapters 6 and 8.

## Unwavering
*mi g.yo ba*, Unwavering (steady and resolute; not faltering), also King Ajātaśatru when he becomes a bodhisattva in the future.

## Unwavering Attention
*mi g.yo ba yid la byed*, A bodhisattva in Mañjuśrī’s retinue.

## Unwavering Gait
*bgrod pa ma nyams pa*, Skt. *bgrod pa ma nyams pa*, A certain buddha who lived before the time of Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Unwavering Gaze
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra.

## Unwavering Mind
*g.yo ba med pa’i blo*, Skt. *g.yo ba med pa’i blo*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Anihata.

## Unwavering Power
*mthu rtsal mi g.yo ba*, Skt. *mthu rtsal mi g.yo ba*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Arthamati.

## Unwavering Yogic Discipline
*brtul zhugs mi g.yo ba*, Skt. *brtul zhugs mi g.yo ba*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Vigatabhaya.

## unwholesome dharmas
*mi dge ba’i chos rnams*, Skt. *akalyānadharma*, See “ten unwholesome actions.”

## Unwinking Gaze
*mig mi ’dzums*, Skt. *mig mi ’dzums*, A bodhisattva.

## Upāṃśa
*nye ba’i cha shas*, Skt. *upāṃśa*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upaśamavat
*nye bar zhi ba mnga’ ba*, Skt. *upaśamavat*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Upabindu
*nye ba’i thigs pa*, Skt. *upabindu*, A nāga king.

## Upacitaskandha
*phung po bstsags pa*, Skt. *upacitaskandha*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Upacāru
*nye mdzes*, Skt. *upacāru*, A lay brother living in Nādikā.

## Upadardara
*u pa da ra da ra*, Skt. *upadardara*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## upadeśa
*gtan phab*, Skt. *upadeśa*, As one of the twelve aspects of the Dharma, it means the explanation of details in the teachings and is synonymous with Abhidharma. See also “twelve wheels of the Dharma.”

## Upadhanika
*nye ba’i nor can*, Skt. *upadhanika*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upadharma
*nye ba’i chos*, Skt. *upadharma*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## upadrava
*gnod pa*, Skt. *upadrava*, A category of celestial beings who can be responsible for large-scale calamities such as famine, plague, and so forth.

## Upadravya
*nye rdzas*, Skt. *upadravya*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upadruma
*nye ba’i ljon pa*, Skt. *upadruma*, One of the kinnara kings.

## Upadukura
*nye ba’i dbus*, Skt. *upadukura*, One of the kings of the nāgas.

## Upadundubhi
*nye ba’i rnga bo che*, Skt. *upadundubhi*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## upagraha
*nye ba’i gza’ rgyad*, Skt. *upagraha*, A class of beings related to grahas.

## Upagupta
*nye srung*, Skt. *upagupta*, Fifth in the apostolic succession that carried on the Buddha’s teachings after his parinirvāṇa.

## Upaharita
*nye ba’i ljang sngon*, Skt. *upaharita*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upaḍimbhaka
*nye ba’i byis pa*, Skt. *upaḍimbhaka*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upajaṭā
*nye ba’i ral pa ma*, Skt. *upajaṭā*, One of the female śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upakambala
*nye ba’i la ba*, Skt. *upakambala*, One of the kings of the nāgas.

## Upakara
*phan byed*, Skt. *upakara*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upakeśinī
*nye ba’i skra can ma*, Skt. *upakeśinī*, One of the vidyās attending upon Mañjuśrī.

## Upakṣepa
*nye bar ’phen pa*, Skt. *upakṣepa*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Upaketu
*nye ba’i tog*, Skt. *upaketu*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upakāśika
*nye ba’i ka shi can*, Skt. *upakāśika*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upakāla
*nye ba’i dus*, Skt. *upakāla*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upakālaka
*nye gnag po*, Skt. *upakālaka*, A yakṣa general.

## Upakāragati
*phan ldan gshegs*, Skt. *upakāragati*, The 847th buddha in the first list, 846th in the second list, and 836th in the third list.

## Upakumbha
*nye ba’i bum pa*, Skt. *upakumbha*, One of the rāśis.

## Upakurukulla
*nye ba’i ku ru ku la*, Skt. *upakurukulla*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upamadā
*nye rgyags ma*, Skt. *upamadā*, A great piśācī.

## Upanaḍa
*nye ba’i ’dam bu*, Skt. *upanaḍa*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Upanala
*nye bar mi zhum pa*, Skt. *upanala*, A nāga king.

## Upananda
*nye dga'*, Skt. *upananda*, one of the notorious "group of six" monks whose antics and heavy-handed interference prompted a great many of the [Buddha](#buddha)'s injunctions on conduct.

## Upananda (the minister)
*nye dga’ bo*, Skt. *upananda*, Along with Nanda, one of King Mahā­deva’s two chief ministers in the city of Mithilā. Not to be confused with “Upananda,” the nāga; or with Upananda, the monk.

## Upananda (the monk)
*nye dga’ bo*, Skt. *upananda*, A member of the Śākya clan and monk of the Buddha’s order, he often appears in the vinaya texts, as here, to exemplify certain wrong behaviors. Not to be confused with Upananda, one of King Mahā­deva’s ministers; or with Upananda, the nāga.

## Upananda (the nāga)
*nye dga’ bo*, Skt. *upananda*, The name of a certain nāga. Not to be confused with “Upananda,” one of King Mahā­deva’s ministers; or with Upananda, the monk.

## Upanandana
*nye dga’*, Skt. *upanandana*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upanandika
*nye ba’i dga’ ldan*, Skt. *upanandika*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upanandinī
*nye ba’i dga’ byed ma*, Skt. *upanandinī*, One of the great yakṣiṇīs.

## upanayana ceremony
The initiation rite by which a boy of the higher castes becomes a full member of his caste. It involves having all his hair shaven except for a tuft on the crown of the head (śikhā) and receiving the sacred thread (upavīta) and the appropriate mantra.

## Upanemi
*nye ba’i mu khyud*, Skt. *upanemi*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upaśāntā
*nye bar zhi ba*, Skt. *upaśāntā*, Name of a world system in the western direction, where the buddha Ratnārcis teaches the perfection of wisdom to bodhisattva great beings.

## Upaśānta
*nye bar zhi ba*, Skt. *upaśānta*, ”Peaceful.” A world system in the western direction, where the buddha Ratnārcis now dwells.

## Upaśāntamati
*blo gros nye bar zhi ba*, Skt. *upaśāntamati*, A western buddha realm that the Buddha Śākyamuni sees.

## Upapañcaka
*nye lnga po*, Skt. *upapañcaka*, A yakṣa who is a “Dharma brother” of Vaiśravaṇa.

## Upapañcika
*nye ba’i lngas rtsen*, Skt. *upapañcika*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upaphala
*nye ba’i ’bras bu*, Skt. *upaphala*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upapīlu
*nye ba’i pI lu*, Skt. *upapīlu*, One of the kings of the piśācas.

## Upapūrṇa
*nye ba’i gang ba*, Skt. *upapūrṇa*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Uparaja
*nye ba’i rdul*, Skt. *uparaja*, One of the rāśis.

## Upareṇu
*nye ba’i rdul*, Skt. *upareṇu*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upariṣṭa
*nye ba’i ’dod pa*, Skt. *upariṣṭa*, One of the eight chief pratyeka­buddhas.

## Upasanat
*nye ba’i kun bged*, Skt. *upasanat*, One of the grahas.

## Upasena
*nye sde*, Skt. *upasena*, a monk of one year whose premature taking of a ward prompted the [Buddha](#buddha) to decree that only those who had been monks for ten years could allow going forth, grant ordination, [accept charge of](#accept-charge-of) [novice](#novice)s, give [refuge](#refuge), and [live independently](#live-independently).

## Upasāgara
*nye ba’i rgya mtsho*, Skt. *upasāgara*, One of the kings of the nāgas.

## Upasiṃha
*nye ba’i seng ge*, Skt. *upasiṃha*, A yakṣa general in the south.

## Upasita
*nye dkar*, Skt. *upasita*, A mountain king.

## Uṣāpati
*mtshams kyi bdag*, Skt. *uṣāpati*, A deity in Vajrānaṅga’s maṇḍala.

## Upatiṣya
*nye rgyal*, Skt. *upatiṣya*, [Śāriputra](#śāriputra)'s grandfather named him Upatiṣya, "[Tiṣya](#tiṣya)'s Heir," to honor [Śāriputra](#śāriputra)'s father [Tiṣya](#tiṣya).

## Upavarṇaka
*nye ba’i snyan pa*, Skt. *upavarṇaka*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upavartana
*nye bar gnas*, Skt. *upavartana*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## upavasatha
*bsnyen gnas*, Skt. *upavasatha*, A fast or related observance undertaken during the full or new phase of the moon. The Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit term poṣadha was derived from the classical Sanskrit term upavasatha and translated into Tibetan both as gso sbyong and as bsnyen gnas, i.e. the monastic restoration rite and the eightfold observance both lay and monastic Buddhists may do on the upavasatha.

## Upavṛṣṭi
*nye ba’i char ’bebs*, Skt. *upavṛṣṭi*, One of the grahas.

## Upavīrā
Skt. *upavīrā*, One of the female śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upayāyika
*nye ba’i ’char ba*, Skt. *upayāyika*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## upādhyāya
*mkhan po*, Skt. *upādhyāya*, In India, a person’s particular preceptor within the monastic tradition, guiding that person for the taking of full vows and the maintenance of conduct and practice. The Tibetan translation mkhan po has also come to mean “a learned scholar,” the equivalent of a paṇḍita, but that is not the intended meaning in the sūtras.

## upādānaskandha
*nye bar len pa’i phung po*, Skt. *upādānaskandha*, The “skandhas of appropriation” or “appropriated skandhas,” this refers to the five skandhas as the bases upon which a nonexistent self is mistakenly projected. That is, they are the basis of “appropriation” (Skt. upādāna) insofar as all grasping arises on the basis of the skandhas.

## Upekṣaka
*btang snyoms pa*, Skt. *upekṣaka*, One of the kinnara kings.

## Upendra
*nye dbang*, Skt. *upendra*, Considered the “younger brother” of Indra, the name Upendra appears as an epithet of Viṣṇu or Kṛṣṇa in Sanskrit epic and purāṇic literature.

## Upeta
Skt. *upeta*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Upāgata
*nye bar ’ongs*, Skt. *upāgata*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## upholder of the Vinaya
*’dul ba ’dzin pa*, Skt. *vinayadhāra*, A term used to designate someone who is a master of Buddhist monastic discipline.

## upholders of enumerations
The title of a specialist in the Buddhist canon who focuses on upholding the lists of enumerations of key Buddhist tenets.

## Upāli
*nye [bar](#bar) 'khor*, Skt. *upāli*, a great upholder of monastic discipline, who recited the [vinaya](#vinaya) at the First Council following the [Buddha](#buddha)'s passing.

## Uplifted by Dharma
*chos ’phags*, Skt. *chos ’phags*, One of the eight yakṣa generals.

## Upālin
*nye ba ’khor*, Skt. *upālin*, A disciple of the Buddha.

## upoṣadha
*gso sbyong*, Skt. *upoṣadha*, The eight vows kept by laypeople on the four sacred days of the month: the full-, new-, and half-moon days.

## Upodāyika
*nye ba’i ’char ba*, Skt. *upodāyika*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## upper arm
*dpung pa*, Skt. *dpung pa*, A type of worm (srin bu) that lives in and feeds on the body.

## upper robe
*bla gos*, Skt. *uttarāsaṅga*, one of a Buddhist monk's [three robes](#three-robes).

## upper room
*khang pa brtsegs pa*, Skt. *kūṭāgāra*, an acceptable form of shelter for a monk, as identified in the [Four Supports](#four-supports) [section](#section) of the ordination ritual. Also, terraced cottage, tower, pavilion, penthouse, etc.

## Upāriṣṭa
*ldang ba*, Skt. *upāriṣṭa*, One of the pratyeka­buddhas in the maṇḍala of Mañjuśrī (it is not clear if upāriṣṭa here is a variant spelling of upariṣṭa, i.e. one of the eight chief pratyeka­buddhas).

## upright dweller
*tsog pu ba*, Skt. *naiṣadyika*, A monk who never lies down to sleep.

## upright posture
*sku shin tu drang por ’khrungs pa*, Skt. *ṛju­kāyodbhava­tā*, Eighteenth of the thirty-two major marks.

## upāsaka
*dge bsnyan*, Skt. *upāsaka*, An unordained male practitioner who observes the five precepts not to kill, lie, steal, be intoxicated, or commit sexual misconduct.

## upside down
*khas spub*, Skt. *khas spub*, A type of worm (srin bu) that lives in and feeds on the body.

## upāsikā
*dge bsnyan ma*, Skt. *upāsikā*, An unordained female practitioner who observes the five precepts not to kill, lie, steal, be intoxicated, or commit sexual misconduct.

## upward mover
*gyen du rgyu*, Skt. *gyen du rgyu*, A class of nonhuman beings associated with disease and misfortune.

## Upward Ocean
*rgya mtsho gyen du ’gro ba*, Skt. *rgya mtsho gyen du ’gro ba*, A mountain on Videha.

## uśīra
*rtswa u shi ra*, Skt. *uśīra*, Andropogon muricatus (a species of grass).

## Uṣṭra
*rnga bong*, Skt. *uṣṭra*, A sage with a human body and the face of a donkey and expert in astrology, he was a past life of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## urad bean
Vigna mungo, also known as black gram.

## Uragā
*brang gis ’gro*, Skt. *uragā*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## uraga
Snake, serpent, or reptile. Literally, ones that “crawl on the belly,” sometimes an epithet of nāgas.

## uraga sandalwood
*tsan dan sbrul gyi snying po*, Skt. *uraga­sāra­candana*, One kind of Indian sandalwood (Santalum album) said to be “blue” on the inside. The name “essence of snakes” is said to come from snakes being particularly attracted to those trees.

## uragasāra
*sbrul gyi snying po*, Skt. *uragasāra*, One kind of Indian sandalwood (Santalum album) said to be “blue” on the inside. The name “essence of snakes” is said to come from snakes being particularly attracted to those trees.

## uragasāra sandalwood
*tsan dan sbrul gyi snying po*, Skt. *uragasāra*, A variety of sandalwood. The name means “snake essence” because snakes were said to live in the forests of those trees because they were attracted to their scent.

## Uragādhipa
*brang ’gro’i bdag po nag po*, Skt. *uragādhipa*, A nāga king.

## uraria plant
Uraria lagopodioides, the flower of which resembles a “hairy tail” or lāṅgūla.

## urethral fistula
*mtshan par rdol ba*, Skt. *bhagaṃdara, bhasmaka*, symptom that may be evidence of an illness considered an impediment to ordination.

## urinary retention
*chus bgags pa*, Skt. *mūtrarodha*, symptom that may be evidence of an illness considered an impediment to ordination.

## Urubilvā
*lteng rgyas*, Skt. *urubilvā*, Known in Pali as Uruvela, Urubilvā is another name for Gayā. The Buddha inspired a group of one thousand dreadlocked ascetics to join his order of monks and ordained them there. Also spelled Uruvilvā.

## Urubilvā Kāśyapa
*lteng rgyas ’od srung*, Skt. *urubilvā kāśyapa*, One of the monks attending this teaching in Śrāvastī, at Jeta’s Grove.

## Uru­bilvā­kāśyapa
*lteng rgyas ’od srung gi bu*, Skt. *uru­bilvā­kāśyapa*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Urumuṇḍa
*ri bo rtse mthon*, Skt. *urumuṇḍa*, A mountain.

## Uruvela-Kalpa
*lteng rgyas ltar*, Skt. *uruvela­kalpa*, One of the places the Buddha traveled to.

## Uruvilvā
*lteng rgyas*, Skt. *urubilvā, uruvilvā*, known in Pali as Uruvela, Uruvilvā is another name for Gayā. The [Buddha](#buddha) inspired a group of one thousand dreadlocked [ascetic](#ascetic)s to join his order of monks and ordained them there. Also spelled Urubilvā.

## Uruvilvā Kāśyapa
*lteng rgyas ’od srung*, Skt. *uruvilvā kāśyapa*, An arrogant brahmin who challenged the Buddha but was humbled and developed faith in the Buddha’s teaching.

## Uruvilva Kāśyapa
*lteng rgyas ’od srung*, Skt. *uruvilva kāśyapa*, Close Śravaka disciple of the Buddha.

## Uruvilvakāśyapa
*lteng rgyas ’od srung*, Skt. *uruvilvakāśyapa*, The brother of Gayākāśyapa and Nadīkāśyapa. A practitioner of fire offering at Uruvilva (Bodhgaya), he and his five hundred students were converted to becoming bhikṣus of the Buddha. He and his brothers and their students were the third group to become followers of the Buddha after his enlightenment.

## Uruvilva­kāśyapa
*ltang rgyas ’od srung*, Skt. *uruvilva­kāśyapa*, The brother of Gayākāśyapa and Nadīkāśyapa. A practitioner of fire offering at Uruvilva (Bodhgayā), he and his five hundred pupils were converted to becoming bhikṣus of the Buddha. He and his brothers and their students were the third group to become followers of the Buddha after his enlightenment. (Urubilvakāśyapa; steng rgyas ’od srung; lteng rgyas ’od srung; lting rgyas ’od srung)

## Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa
*lteng rgyas ’od srung*, Skt. *uruvilvā-kāśyapa*, A disciple of the Buddha.

## Uruvilvākāśyapa
*lteng rgyas ’od srung*, Skt. *uruvilvākāśyapa*, A great śrāvaka disciple of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Uruvilvā­Kāśyapa
*lteng rgyas ’od srung*, Skt. *uruvilvā­kāśyapa*, A monk (bhikṣu) and disciple of the Buddha.

## Uru­vilvā­kāśyapa
*ltang rgyas ’od srung*, Skt. *uru­vilvā­kāśyapa*, The brother of Gayākāśyapa and Nadīkāśyapa. A practitioner of fire offering at Uruvilvā (Bodhgaya), he and his five hundred pupils were converted to becoming bhikṣus of the Buddha. He and his brothers and their pupils were the third group to become followers of the Buddha after his enlightenment.

## Urvaśī
*brang na gnas pa ma*, Skt. *urvaśī*, An apsaras/goddess.

## used for any rite
Various permutations of this phrase frequently appear in tantric Buddhist literature to describe the potency and versatility of particular mantras or any other ritual component. In these contexts the term las (Skt. karman) should be understood as the equivalent of the English terms “rite,” “ritual,” or “ritual action.”

## useful
*gces spras byed pa*, Skt. *bahukara*, See Edgerton 1953, p. 398.

## User of Evil
*bdud bsten*, Skt. *bdud bsten*, Name of a bodhisattva in a story Buddha tells.

## user of the grass mat
*cog bu pa*, Skt. *naiṣadyika*, A spiritual practitioner who adheres to the practice of residing on a straw mat.

## Utkaṭā
*shas che ba*, Skt. *utkaṭā*, A village.

## Utkaṭa
“Abounding.” The name of a district town in the region of Kośala, situated by the Himalayan foothills that lie to the north of the city of Śrāvastī. It was given as an endowment to the brahmin Puṣkarasārin by the king of Kośala.

## Utkṛṣṭakṣepa
*tshol bar ’phen pa*, Skt. *utkṛṣṭakṣepa*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Utkhalī
*u khu li*, Skt. *utkhalī*, One of the four goddesses who attended and kept guard over Prince Siddhārtha while he was in the womb of his mother.

## Utkhalin
*ud ka li*, Skt. *utkhalin*, One of the sixteen gods guarding the seat of awakening.

## Utmost Joy
A pond in one of the parks of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

## Utpalā
*ud pa la*, Skt. *utpalā*, A lady.

## Utpalī
*ut+pa la*, Skt. *utpalī*, It is not clear who this goddess is.

## Utpala
*ud pal*, Skt. *utpala*, The 941st buddha in the first list, 940th in the second list, and 931st in the third list.

## Utpala Colors
*ud pa la’i mdog*, Skt. *ud pa la’i mdog*, A realm of the ever-infatuated gods.

## Utpala Eye
*ud pal pad mig*, Skt. *ud pal pad mig*, Mother of the buddha Hitaiṣin.

## utpala flower
Nymphaea caerulea. The “blue lotus” is actually a lily, so it is also known as the blue water lily.

## Utpala Fragrance
*ud pal dri*, Skt. *ud pal dri*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Saṃtoṣaṇa (642 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Utpala Garland
*ud pa la phreng*, Skt. *ud pa la phreng*, Mother of the buddha Padma.

## Utpala Gift
*ud pa la sbyin*, Skt. *ud pa la sbyin*, A merchant in Jambudvīpa, later to be reborn as Auspicious Time.

## Utpala Petals
*ud pal ’dab*, Skt. *ud pal ’dab*, Birthplace of the buddha Kṛtārthadarśin.

## Utpalabhūti
*ut pa la*, Skt. *utpalabhūti*, A perfume-seller head merchant and the kalyāṇamitra of chapter 24.

## Utpalacandra
*ud pa la zla ba*, Skt. *utpalacandra*, A bodhisattva who praises the brahmin Samudrareṇu but is not mentioned elsewhere in the sūtra.

## Utpalahasta
*lag na ud pa la*, Skt. *utpalahasta*, A bodhisattva who praises the brahmin Samudrareṇu but is not mentioned elsewhere in the Kangyur.

## Utpalaka
*ud pal*, Skt. *utpalaka*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Utpalanetra
*ud pal mig*, Skt. *utpalanetra*, One of the Buddha’s former rebirths.

## Utpalaparṇā
*ut+pa la’i ’dab ma*, Skt. *utpalaparṇā*, One of the female śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Utpalaśrī
*ud pa la’i dpal*, Skt. *utpalaśrī*, A great bodhisattva.

## Utpala­śrī­garbha
Skt. *utpala­śrī­garbha*, A bodhisattva mahāsattva.

## Utpalasaṃtīraṇa
*ud pa la yang dag rtog*, Skt. *utpala­saṃtīraṇa*, The name of the eon in which the Buddha Ratnagarbha’s eighty brothers will become buddhas in the realm named Baliṣṭhā.

## Utpalavaktra
*ud pa la’i gdong*, Skt. *utpalavaktra*, “With a Face Like a Water Lily,” the name of a legendary king.

## Utpalavarṇā
*ut+pa la’i kha dog ma*, Skt. *utpalavarṇā*, Arhat nun slain by Devadatta following his botched attempt to assassinate the Buddha.

## Utpalākara
*ud pa la ’byung ba*, Skt. *utpalākara*, The name of an eon.

## Utraka
*u tra ka*, Skt. *u tra ka*, The King of Rauraka.

## utsāraka
*g.yengs byed*, Skt. *utsāraka*, A class of malevolent spirits.

## Uttama
*mchog*, Skt. *uttama*, The 579th buddha in the first list, 579th in the second list, and 572nd in the third list.

## Uttamadeva
*lha mchog*, Skt. *uttamadeva*, The 606th buddha in the first list, 605th in the second list, and 599th in the third list.

## Uttapta­muni­jñāneśvara
*thub chen ye shes ’bar ba’i dbang phyug*, Skt. *uttaptamuni­jñāneśvara*, One of the hundred names prophesied by the Buddha Ratnagarbha for 2,500 buddhas, presumably the name of twenty-five of those buddhas.

## Uttaptaśrī
*dpal shin tu ’bar ba*, Skt. *uttaptaśrī*, The name of a kalpa in the distant past.

## Uttaptavīrya
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra whose name is attested in the Rāṣṭrapāla­pari­pṛcchā, but apparently the translation of the Lalitavistara has Dīptavīrya for the same translation.

## Uttarā
*gong ma*, Skt. *uttarā*, One of Sujātā’s servants.

## Uttara
*bla ma*, Skt. *uttara*, a young [brahmin](#brahmin) whose awakening as [Śākyamuni](#śākyamuni) was foretold by the [Buddha](#buddha) [Kāśyapa](#kāśyapa).

## Uttara Aparā
*khrums smad*, Skt. *uttara aparā*, A constellation in the north.

## Uttarabhadrapadā
*khrums smad*, Skt. *uttara­bhadra­padā*, The name of a lunar asterism. Its chief star is known as Gamma Pegasi in the occidental tradition.

## Uttarabhādrapadā
“Latter Auspicious Feet.” The asterism of the stars in the latter part of the constellation Pegasus.

## Uttaradatta
*bla mas bon pa*, Skt. *uttaradatta*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Uttaraka
*bla ma*, Skt. *uttaraka*, A nāga king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Uttarakuru
*byang gi sgra mi snyan*, Skt. *uttarakuru*, The northern continent of the human world according to traditional Indian cosmology, literally meaning “northern unpleasant sound.”

## Uttaramati
A bodhisattva in the audience of this sūtra, whose name is attested in Saddharma­puṇḍarīka and elsewhere.

## Uttara­mati
*blo gros rgya chen*, Skt. *uttara­mati*, Name of a bodhisattva.

## Uttaramatin
*blo gros dam pa*, Skt. *uttaramatin*, A bodhisattva great being present in the audience of this sūtra.

## Uttaramānuṣa
*mi’i bla ma*, Skt. *uttaramānuṣa*, A nāga king.

## Uttaraphalgunī
The twelfth of the twenty-seven constellations, or nakṣatras, in Vedic astrology. Here it corresponds to the second month of the Tibetan calendar.

## Uttaraphālgunī
*dbo*, Skt. *uttaraphālgunī*, A lunar mansion in the south.

## Uttarāṣāḍhā
“Latter Unconquered One.” The asterism of the two main stars in the bow part of the constellation Sagittarius.

## Uttarāṅkura
The name of an island located north of Varika.

## Utter Excellence
*shin tu bzang po*, Skt. *shin tu bzang po*, Foremost in terms of insight among the followers of the buddha Vairocana.

## Utter Joy
The name of the first ground (sa, bhūmi) that one attains after completing the path of accumulation (tshogs lam, sambhāramārga) and the path of application (sbyor lam, prayogamārga), and that one enters through path of seeing (mthong lam, darśanamārga) the ultimate.

## Utter Purity
*rab tu gtsang ba*, Skt. *rab tu gtsang ba*, A mountain range in the Heaven Free from Strife.

## Utter Vastness
*shin tu yangs pa*, Skt. *shin tu yangs pa*, A pool in Swan Forest.

## utterly chaste in their habitual conduct
*kun spyod pa shin du gtsang ba*, Skt. *śucisamācāra*, Fortieth of the eighty minor signs.

## Utterly Delightful to Behold
*mthong na kun dga’ ba*, Skt. *mthong na kun dga’ ba*, (1) A lotus pond in Living by Rājanina (mthong na kun dga’ ba). (2) A mountain on Vast Garlands of Bliss (kun nas mthong na dga’ ba).

## utterly devoid of delimitation
*yongs su gcod pa*, Skt. *niratiśaya*, The 85th meditative stability in chapters 6 and 8.

## Utterly Disciplined
*shin tu dul ldan*, Skt. *shin tu dul ldan*, A kingdom where the buddha named Voice Proclaiming the Cloud of Dharma dwelled.

## Utterly Dreadful
*kun du mi dga’ ba*, Skt. *nirānanda*, One of sixteen realms that surround the Reviving Hell.

## Utterly Fearless
*shin tu ’jigs med*, Skt. *shin tu ’jigs med*, Attendant of the buddha Candra.

## Utterly Glorious
*rab tu dpal ldan*, Skt. *rab tu dpal ldan*, Name of a sage.

## Utterly Hidden
*kun nas sbas pa*, Skt. *kun nas sbas pa*, A great bodhisattva.

## Utterly Illuminating Crown
*kun tu rnam par snang byed cod pan*, Skt. *kun tu rnam par snang byed cod pan*, A bodhisattva.

## Utterly Lofty
*rab tu mtho ba*, Skt. *rab tu mtho ba*, One of the twenty-seven realms in the Heaven Free from Strife.

## utterly perfect minor marks
*dpe byad shin du rdzogs pa*, Skt. *paripūrṇa­vyañjana*, Twenty-fourth of the eighty minor marks.

## utterly perfect minor signs
*dpe byad shin du rdzogs pa*, Skt. *paripūrṇa­vyañjana*, Twenty-fourth of the eighty minor signs.

## Utterly Pure Mind
*shin tu rnam par dag pa’i blo*, Skt. *shin tu rnam par dag pa’i blo*, Father of the buddha Bodhana.

## Utterly Scrutinized Conduct
*shin tu brtags spyod*, Skt. *shin tu brtags spyod*, Name of a brahmin, a former incarnation of the Buddha while he was a practicing bodhisattva.

## Utterly Stable Conduct
*spyod pa rab tu brtan pa*, Skt. *spyod pa rab tu brtan pa*, King and sage; a former incarnation of the Buddha.

## Utterly Tamed
*rab tu dul ba*, Skt. *rab tu dul ba*, A goddess present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## Utterly True
*shin tu bden pa*, Skt. *shin tu bden pa*, Attendant of the buddha Mahāsthāman.

## Utterly Unborn
*shin tu ma skyes pa*, Skt. *shin tu ma skyes pa*, A forest on Forest Garlands.

## utterly youthful body
*sku shin du gzhon pa*, Skt. *sukumāragātra*, Twenty-seventh of the eighty minor signs.

## Uttāpana­rāja­mati
*sbyong ba’i rgyal po*, Skt. *uttāpana­rāja­mati*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Uttīrṇaśoka
*mya ngan rgal*, Skt. *uttīrṇaśoka*, The 936th buddha in the first list, 935th in the second list, and 926th in the third list.

## Uttīrṇapaṅka
*dam brgal*, Skt. *uttīrṇapaṅka*, The 689th buddha in the first list, 688th in the second list, and 679th in the third list.

## Uttārāṣāḍhā
*chu smad*, Skt. *(not in the skt. source of the mmk)*, The name of a nakṣatra. One of the two Āṣāḍhās.

## Uttrāsanī
*dngangs byed ma*, Skt. *uttrāsanī*, A great rākṣasī.

## uḍumbara
In Buddhist texts, the uḍumbara flower is a symbol for extremely rare occurrences, since it is said to bloom once every three thousand years.

## Vīṇā
an Indian musical instrument, with strings that are plucked.

## Vīṇā configuration
An astronomical configuration in which all planets are situated in seven separate lunar asterisms.

## Vaṃśā
*gling bu ma*, Skt. *vaṃśā*, One of the goddesses in the maṇḍala of Vajrasattva.

## vīṇa
