*tsher ma med pa*, Skt. *tsher ma med pa*, Birthplace of the buddha Vimalakīrti.

## without uncomposed minds
*thugs mnyam par ma bzhag pa myi mnga’*, Skt. *nāsty asamāhitacitta*, Fourth or fifth (depending on the list) of the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas.

## Without Womb
*mngal med*, Skt. *mngal med*, A buddha.

## Wönpo Tö
A place in Tibet.

## woman craver
*bud med la sred pa*, Skt. *bud med la sred pa*, A class of vidyādharas.

## Wondrous
*rmad du byung ba*, Skt. *rmad du byung ba*, Wondrous (marvelous, inspiring wonder), also the name of the birthplace of the buddha Arhadyaśas.

## wondrous display of extraordinary power
An expression used to refer to a display of extraordinary power (ṛddhi) that elicits wonder in an audience. In Buddhist literature, one of three types of wonders or miracles (prātihārya), the others being “reading others’ minds” and “teaching the Dharma.”

## Wondrous Light
*rmad du byung ba’i ’od*, Skt. *rmad du byung ba’i ’od*, Birthplace of the buddha Prajñādatta.

## Wondrous Stūpa
*mchod rten rmad du byung*, Skt. *mchod rten rmad du byung*, Birthplace of the buddha Merudhvaja.

## wondrous transformation with superhuman powers
The term used generally to describe the performance of a wondrous display, but which often has the narrower sense of changing one thing into something else by means of superhuman powers.

## wood apple
Limonia acidissima. The wood apple tree, also known as the elephant apple.

## wood face
A type of worm (srin bu) that lives in and feeds on the body.

## wooden hut
*spang leb khang*, Skt. *phalacchadana*, an acceptable form of shelter for a monk, as identified in the [Four Supports](#four-supports) [section](#section) of the ordination ritual.

## wool
*be'u ras*, Skt. *prāvāra*, an acceptable form of cloth for a monk, as identified in the [Four Supports](#four-supports) [section](#section) of the ordination ritual.

## woolen cloth
*bal gos*, Skt. *aurṇakavāsa*, an acceptable form of cloth for a monk, as identified in the [Four Supports](#four-supports) [section](#section) of the ordination ritual.

## Word Leader
*tshig gi kha lo sgyur*, Skt. *tshig gi kha lo sgyur*, Foremost in terms of miraculous abilities among the followers of the buddha Sucīrṇabuddhi.

## word of the Buddha
*sangs rgyas kyi bka’*, Skt. *buddhavacana*, A term used to denote the teachings of the Buddha, which in the case of this sūtra can be anything that the Buddha taught or any statement that precisely accords with what the Buddha taught.

## words for interpreting
*nges tshig*, Skt. *nirukti­pada*, One of ten different kinds of verbal phrase or statement (Skt. pada) mentioned in this text.

## words for interpreting the language of gods
*lha tshig nges tshig*, Skt. *deva­nirukti­pada*, One of ten different kinds of verbal phrase or statement (Skt. pada) mentioned in this text.

## words for interpreting universally understood language
*kun la ’jug pa’i tshig nges tshig*, Skt. *sarva­praveśa­nirukti­pada*, One of ten different kinds of verbal phrase or statement (Skt. pada) mentioned in this text.

## words of reprimand
*zhe gcod pa*, Skt. *pāruṣya*, Sixth of the ten nonvirtuous actions. Also rendered as “verbal abuse” or “harsh words.”

## words of truth
*bden pa’i tshig*, Skt. *satyavacana*, True words, the formal statement of which can have a wondrous effect that confirms the truth of the statement.

## words with distinct syllables
*yi ge dbye tshig*, Skt. *akṣarabhedapada*, One of ten different kinds of verbal phrase or statement (Skt. pada) mentioned in this text.

## worked to harm the king
*rgyal po la gnod pa'i las byed pa*, Skt. *\*rājāpathya*, one of the classes of people barred from joining the renunciate order.

## world
*’jig rten*, Skt. *loka*, In this translation, the term “world” is generally used as a translation for both loka (“world”) and lokadhātu (which could also be rendered “galaxy” or “universe,” or more literally, a “container of worlds”), except in the case of the phrases “cosmos of a billion worlds” (tri­sāha­sramahāsāhasra­lokadhātu), “galaxy of a thousand worlds” and “galaxy of a hundred thousand worlds,” since the English word “world” is flexible and can refer to both the earth and the universe more generally.

## World Endowed with All Qualities
*chu klung gang ga’i bye ma snyed ’das pa na ’jig rten gyi khams yon tan kun dang ldan pa*, Skt. *chu klung gang ga’i bye ma snyed ’das pa na ’jig rten gyi khams yon tan kun dang ldan pa*, A buddha realm.

## world guardian
*’jig rten skyong*, Skt. *lokapāla*, A class of guardian deities. Sometimes used to refer to the Four Great Kings (see “Four World Guardians”).

## world guardians
*’jig rten gyi mgon po*, Skt. *lokapāla*, These are a set of deities, each guarding a certain direction. Most commonly these are Indra (Śakra) for the east, Agni for the southeast, Yama for the south, Sūrya or Nirṛti for the southwest, Varuṇa for the west, Vāyu (Pavana) for the northwest, Kubera for the north, and Soma (Candra) or Iśāni or Pṛthivī for the northeast.

## World Holder
*’gro ba ’dzin*, Skt. *’gro ba ’dzin*, Mother of the buddha Surabhigandha.

## World Illuminator
*’jig rten gsal mdzad*, Skt. *’jig rten gsal mdzad*, Name of a future buddha.

## world of Brahmā
*tshangs pa’i ’jig rten*, Skt. *brahmāloka*, The heaven of Brahmā, usually located just above the desire realm (kāmadhātu) as one of the first levels of the form realm (rūpadhātu) and equated with the state that one achieves in the first meditative absorption (dhyāna).

## world of Death
*gshin gyi ’jig rten*, Skt. *yamaloka*, The Vedic afterlife presided over by the lord of death, Yama, and inhabited by the ancestors (pitṛ). See also .

## World of Highest Delight
*’jig rten bla ma dgyes*, Skt. *’jig rten bla ma dgyes*, Birthplace of the buddha Siṃhagati.

## World of Joy
*’jig rten mngon par dga’*, Skt. *’jig rten mngon par dga’*, Birthplace of the buddha Priyaṅgama.

## World of Joyous Qualities
*’jig rten yon tan dga’*, Skt. *’jig rten yon tan dga’*, Birthplace of the buddha Yaśaḥkīrti.

## world of Patient Endurance
*’jig rten gyi khams mi mjed*, Skt. *sahālokadhātu*, The human world of Patient Endurance, according to traditional Indian cosmology, comprising four continents.

## world of “patient endurance”
*mi mjed ’jig rten gyi khams*, Skt. *sahā­loka­dhātu*, The human world of “patient endurance,” according to traditional Indian cosmology, comprising four continents. See also .

## World of the Lord of Death
*gshin rje’i ’jig rten du ’dzin pa*, Skt. *yamaloka*, This is a synonym for the realm of the pretas, or hungry ghosts.

## world of Yama
*gshin rje’i ’jig rten*, Skt. *yamaloka*, The land of the dead ruled over by Yama, the Lord of Death. While the dominion of Yama is often said to include the hells, too, in this and other texts “the world of Yama” mostly figures in mentions of the three lower realms and can be taken as referring to the realm of anguished spirits (preta), where beings generally suffer from deprivation, hunger, and thirst as the ripening of harmful actions driven by miserly attachment and stinginess. In a few passages, however (in chapters 32 and 46), the anguished spirits are explicitly mentioned as well as the beings of the world of Yama, and it is not clear what the distinction may be.

## world protector
*’jig rten skyong ba*, Skt. *lokapāla*, A collective term for deities committed to protecting Buddhism. Often, but not always, refers to the Four Guardian Kings of the four directions.

## world protectors
*’jig rten skyong ba*, Skt. *lokapāla*, Also known as the four great kings (mahārāja), Vaiśravaṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, and Virūpākṣa are pledged to protect practitioners of the Dharma.

## world realm
*’jig rten gyi khams*, Skt. *lokadhātu*, This can refer to one world with its orbiting sun and moon, and also to groups of these worlds in multiples of thousands, in particular a world relam of a thousand million worlds, which is said to be circular, with its circumference twice as long as its diameter.

## world system
*’jig rten gyi khams*, Skt. *lokadhātu*, This can refer to one world with its orbiting sun and moon, and also to groups of these worlds in multiples of thousands, in particular a world realm of a thousand million worlds, which is said to be circular, with its circumference twice as long as its diameter.

## Worldly concentrations
[concentration](#concentration)s leading not to [enlightenment](#enlightenment) but only to rebirth in god [realm](#realm)s. See [four concentrations](#four-concentrations).

## worldly concerns
*’jig rten pa’i chos*, Skt. *lokadharma*, These are often listed as eight in number, as in the commentary: gain and no gain, happiness and suffering, praise and criticism, fame and lack of fame.

## worldly dharmas
*’jig rten gyi chos*, Skt. *loka­dharma*, See “eight worldly dharmas.”

## worldly protector
*’jig rten skyong ba*, Skt. *’jig rten skyong ba*, A class of guardian deities, usually presiding over the quarters of the world.

## worldly science
The term lokāyata specifically refers to the ancient Indian materialist school of thought that investigated the world purely on the basis of direct perception, without recourse to religious conceptions.

## world-protecting gods
Typically references the Four Great Kings of the four directions, namely Vaiśravaṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, and Virūpākṣa, whose mission is to report on the activities of mankind to the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and who have pledged to protect the practitioners of the Dharma. Each world has its own world protectors.

## World’s Superior
*’jig rten bla ma*, An epithet for the Buddha.

## world-system
*’jig rten gyi khams*, Skt. *lokadhātu*, Refers to any world or group of worlds illumined by one sun and moon, its own Mount Meru, continents, etc.

## worm
*srin bu*, Skt. *kṛmi*, When refering to the human body, these are creatures that inhabit it and may either harm or contribute to its health. Note that this term can also mean insects and worms in general.

## worn out by the road

## worn out by women

## Worshiped in All Lands
*yul phyogs kun mchod*, Skt. *yul phyogs kun mchod*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Jñānapriya (55 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Worshiper
*mchod sbyin ma*, Skt. *mchod sbyin ma*, Worshiper (one who worships or venerates), also the name of the mother of the buddha Vigatabhaya.

## worthy
*dgra bcom pa*, Skt. *arhat*, One who has attained liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra and abides within the final peace of nirvāṇa. The final attainment according to the śrāvaka path of liberation. Also used as an epithet of the Buddha.

## Worthy Flower of Precious Splendor
*dgra bcom me tog rin chen gzi brjid*, Skt. *dgra bcom me tog rin chen gzi brjid*, Mother of the buddha Kuśalapradīpa.

## worthy of admiration
*khyu mchog gi gnas su zhal gyis ’che ba*, Skt. *udārārṣabha*, An epithet of a buddha. Literally “superb bull” in Skt.

## worthy of beholding
*lta bar ’os pa dag*, Skt. *sam­anta­prāsādika­tā*, Twentieth of the eighty minor marks.

## Worthy of Looking
*blta bar ’os*, Skt. *blta bar ’os*, Mother of the buddha Roca.

## worthy of offerings
*sbyin gnas*, Skt. *dakṣiṇīya*, In general, a term for a fitting object of generosity who can be considered a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra). Typically refers to monks or ascetics.

## Worthy of Offerings litany
*yon rabs*, Skt. *dakṣiṇādeśanā*, A litany chanted by the monastic saṅgha as a way of giving thanks and recognizing the merit generated by a donation or alms. cf. ’dul ba’i mdo, D 261, F.80.b.

## Worthy of Worship
*mchod par ’os*, Skt. *mchod par ’os*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Brahmagāmin (661 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## worthy one
In this sūtra, used only as an epithet of the buddhas, and traditionally used as an epithet for someone who has achieved awakening and thereby is worthy (arh). The Tibetan translation derives from one of the traditional Buddhist etymologies of the term, and could be translated “one who has destroyed (hata) one’s enemies” (ari), the enemies here referring to the afflictions of lust, hatred, ignorance, and so forth.

## worthy recipient of offerings
A person considered worthy of veneration with material offerings. In the context of Tibetan Buddhist history, this is the term often translated as “priest” when paired with the term “patron” (Tib. sbyin bdag/ yon bdag, Skt. dānapati) in the compound phrase “priest-patron relationship.”

## worthy recipients of offerings
*sbyin pa’i gnas*, Skt. *dakṣiṇīya*, In general, a term for a pure monk or ascetic (or the saṅgha as a whole) who can be considered as a field of merit (Skt. puṇyakṣetra) due to his or her (innate) ability to karmically reciprocate acts of generosity and kindness toward him or her.

## Worthy Relinquishment
*dgra bcom spong*, Skt. *dgra bcom spong*, Birthplace of the buddha Vratasthita.

## worthy repository
*snod du gyur pa*, Skt. *pātragata*, A meditative stability.

## Worthy Wish
*dgra bcom ’dod*, Skt. *dgra bcom ’dod*, Attendant of the buddha Praśāntagāmin.

## Wrapped in Every Possible Pain
*sdug bsngal kun dkris*, Skt. *sarvaduḥkhāvarta*, One of sixteen realms that surround the Hell of Ultimate Torment.

## wrath
A general term for the features and behaviors that invoke fear and danger. The term is also used in this text to refer to the body of rites otherwise known as abhicāra (mngon spyod), which include rites for aggressively overcoming adversarial influences, both human and nonhuman.

## Wrathful
*drag shul can*, Skt. *drag shul can*, Wrathful (full of anger, fierce), also the name of an attendant of the buddha Subāhu.

## Wrathful Black True Mother
*ma cig khros ma nag mo*, Skt. *Krodhakālī*, lit. the one mother wrathful and black. A manifestation of Samantabhadrī
in wrathful [saṃbhogakāya](#saṃbhogakāya) form, an aspect of Vajravārāhī (*rdo rje phag mo).

## Wrathful Lotus
*pad+ma khros pa*, An epithet for the deity Hayagrīva.

## Wrathful Lotus Lord
*pad+ma khros pa’i bdag*, An epithet for the deity Hayagrīva.

## Wrathful Master
*’jigs byed bla ma*, Skt. *’jigs byed bla ma*, A king.

## wrathful one
*khro bo*, Skt. *krodha*, This term is used in some of the Kriyātantra rites for the goddess Mārīcī to describe the party performing any of the rites aimed at harming a target or enemy.

## write the name
*a mu ka bri*, A command that appears in the Mahākāla mantra. Half of this command is in Sanskrit and half is in Tibetan. The Sanskrit term amuka (Tib. che ge mo) means “such and such a person or thing.”

## wrong course of action
There are four wrong courses of action, as motivated by lust (chanda), hatred (dveṣa), delusion (moha), and fear (bhaya).

## wrong livelihood
*log pa’i ’tsho ba*, Skt. *mithyājīva*, —

## Wrong view
*log lta*, Skt. *mithyādṛṣṭi*, AT: false belief, particularly a [view](#view) that will lead one to courses of action that bring more suffering.

## wrong view of annihilation
*chad par lta ba*, Skt. *ucchedadṛṣṭi*, The view that causes (and thus actions) do not have effects, and that the self is the same as one (or all) of the psycho-physical aggregates (Skt. skandhas) and that it is destroyed at death; often mentioned together with “wrong view of eternalism.” Also often translated as “nihilism.”

## wrong view of eternalism
*rtag par lta ba*, Skt. *sāśvatadṛṣṭi*, The wrong view or belief that the self exists in or as one or all of the psycho-physical aggregates (skandhas) or independent from them and that it lives on unchanged and eternally after death; mentioned together with “wrong view of annihilation” (ucchedadṛṣṭi).

## wrong view of nihilism
*med par lta ba*, Skt. *nāstikadṛṣṭi*, For Buddhists, someone who does not believe in karma, the law of cause and effect or the moral retribution of actions.

## wrong view that actions are without consequence
*bya ba’i mi rigs par lta ba*, Skt. *akriyādṛṣṭi*, Literally “the view or theory of nonaction,” which defines a view that is ascribed to the teacher Pūraṇa Kassapa in the Sāmaññaphalasutta (DN I,53), who propounded that actions, whether good or evil, have no consequences whatsoever or, more precisely, that one’s soul or true self (and thus salvation or liberation) remains ever unaffected by good or bad actions.

## wrong views
*log par lta ba*, Skt. *mithyā­dṛṣṭi*, Tenth of the ten non-virtuous actions.

## wrong way of making a living
*log par ’tsho ba*, Skt. *mithyājīva*, The opposite of the fifth limb of the eightfold path of the noble ones (Skt. āryāṣṭāṅgikamārga).

## wrongly conceive
*mngon par zhen*, Skt. *abhiniviśanti*, See Edgerton 1953, p. 53. The term has various shades of meaning such as “to be attached to,” “to adhere to,” “to wrongly conceive,” “to hold fast to,” and “to believe in” with a negative connotation.

## Xuanzang
A great seventh-century Chinese scholar of Buddhism, Xuanzang journeyed overland from China to India on a pilgrimage to the holy places of the Buddha’s life. He returned to China in 645 ce, bringing with him 657 Sanskrit manuscripts, of which this was one. With the support of the Tang Emperor Taizong, he established a large translation bureau in Chang’an (modern Xi’an) and spent the next nineteen years until his death translating them into Chinese.

## Yaśā
*rab grags ma*, Skt. *yaśā*, One of the names of Śrī Mahādevī.

## Yaśa
One of six wicked mendicants in the distant past, during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin.

## Yaśaḥparvata

## Yaśaḥprabha
*grags pa’i ’od*, Skt. *yaśaḥprabha*, Name of a tathāgata.

*grags ’od*, Skt. *yaśaḥprabhāsa*, Name of a tathāgata.

## Yaśas
*grags pa*, Skt. *yaśas*, the son of a wealthy merchant in [Vārāṇasī](#vārāṇasī). After the five excellent [disciple](#disciple)s, Yaśas was the next to [go forth](#go-forth) and receive ordination. He was followed in short order by [Pūrṇa](#pūrṇa), [Vimala](#vimala), [Gavāmpati](#gavāmpati), and [Subāhu](#subāhu), all five together being referred to as the "five excellent companions."

## Yaśaskāma
*grags ’dod*, Skt. *yaśaskāma*, The name means “Desirer of Fame,” and he was so called because of his inferior motivation at that time. This is the bodhisattva in the distant past who would eventually become Maitreya.

## Yaśasvin
*grags ldan*, Skt. *yaśasvin*, The father of King Loka.

## Yaśasvinī
*grags chen ma*, Skt. *yaśasvinī*, A mantra goddess, one of the great dūtīs.

## Yaśaḥ­śuddhodita
*grags pa dag pas byung ba*, Skt. *yaśaḥ­śuddhodita*, One of the future buddhas of this kalpa.

## Yaśavatī
*grags ldan ma*, Skt. *yaśavatī*, One of the great dūtīs attending upon Lord Vajrapāṇi. The name is rendered elsewhere in this translation as “Yaśovatī.”

## Yadhvaja
*gro ba’i rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *yadhvaja*, One of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin.

## Yadu
*ya de ba*, Skt. *yādava*, See .

## Yaṅgarvatī
*yang gar ba ti*, Skt. *yaṅgarvatī*, Name of the world system of the thus-gone one Delivered through Powerful Diligence.

## Yagyal Phel
The fourth Degé king, Yagyal Phel (b. late fifteenth century; d. late sixteenth century) was the head of the house of Degé in its thirty-fourth generation. He had three sons, Künga Rinchen, who would become the fifth Degé king, Namkha, and Dorjé Lhundrup. For more on his life see his entry at The Treasury of Lives.

## Yaśika
*grags ldan*, Skt. *yaśika*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Yajñasvara
*mchod sbyin nga ro*, Skt. *yajñasvara*, The 767th buddha in the first list, 766th in the second list, and 756th in the third list.

## Yajur Veda
*mchod sbyin gyi rig byed*, Skt. *yajurveda*, Along with the Ṛg Veda, Sāma Veda, and Atharva Veda, one of the four Vedas, the most ancient Sanskrit religious literature of India.

## Yajurveda
*mchod sbyin*, Skt. *yajurveda*, Along with the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda, one of the four Vedas, the most ancient Sanskrit religious literature of India. It is primarily comprised of instructions and arrangements for Vedic rites.

## Yajurveda branch
The category of priests in the brahmanical tradition who specialize in the ritual prose formulas of the Yajurveda.

## Yakṣī
*gnod sbyin mo*, Skt. *yakṣī*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## yak face
*’bri gdong*, Skt. *’bri gdong*, The name of a karmic wind involved in the formation of an embryo in its seventeenth week.

## Yakṣa
*gnod sbyin*, a class of spirits.

## yakṣa daughter
*gnod sbyin gyi bu mo*, A young female yakṣa, a class of potentially harmful nonhuman beings.

## yakṣa general
*gnod sbyin gyi sde dpon chen po*, Skt. *yakṣasenāpati*, Leaders of armies of yakṣas.

## yakṣa graha
*gnod sbyin gyi gdon*, Skt. *yakṣa graha*, A class of beings said to dwell in the north, under the jurisdiction of the great king Vaiśravaṇa.

## Yakṣakumārī
*gzhon nu ma*, Skt. *yakṣakumārī*, One of the seven yakṣiṇīs.

## yakṣiṇī
*gnod sbyin mo*, Skt. *yakṣiṇī*, A female yakṣa, a class of nonhuman beings who inhabit forests, mountainous areas, and other natural spaces, or serve as guardians of villages and towns, and may be propitiated for health, wealth, protection, and other boons, or controlled through magic. According to tradition, their homeland is in the north, where they live under the jurisdiction of the Great King Vaiśravaṇa. Several members of this class have been deified as gods of wealth (these include the aforementioned Vaiśravaṇa) or as bodhisattva generals of yakṣa armies. They have entered the Buddhist pantheon in a variety of forms, including, in tantric Buddhism, those of wrathful deities.

## yak-tail fan
*rnga yab*, Skt. *cāmara*, The bushy tail of the yak used as a whisk for repelling flying insects. It is one of the insignia of royalty.

## Yama
*gshin rje*, the [Lord of Death](#lord-of-death).

## Yama Dharmarāja
Literally “Dharma-king.” An epithet of Yama, the Lord of Death, who judges the dead and rules over the hells. He was converted and bound by oath to Vajrabhairava as the special protector of the Vajrabhairavatantras.

## Yamadūtī
*gshin rje’i pho nya mo*, Skt. *yamadūtī*, A great rākṣasī.

## Yamakaśāla Grove
*shing sA la zung gi tshal*, Skt. *yamakaśālavana*, The grove of śāla trees outside Kuśinagara where the Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa.

## Yamakasāla Grove
*sA la zung gi nags*, Skt. *yamakasāla­kavana*, Another name of the Sāla Grove.

## Yamarāja
Another name for Yama, the lord of death.

## Yama’s realm
*gshin rje’i ’jig rten*, Skt. *yamaloka*, The land of the dead ruled over by the Lord of Death. In Buddhism it refers to the preta realm, where beings generally suffer from hunger and thirst, which in traditional Brahmanism is the fate of those departed without descendants to make ancestral offerings.

## Yama’s Sister
*gshin rje’i lcam mo*, An epithet for Śrīdevī Mahākālī. According to The Tantra of the Flaming Ḍākinī (Toh 842), Śrīdevī Mahākālī was originally born as a divine girl called Red Cāmuṇḍī. Her father was Mahādeva, her mother was Umadevī, and her brother at that time was called Yama Mahākāla. Hence, she is “Yama’s Sister.”

## Yama’s Slayer
*gshin rje mthar byed pa*, Skt. *yamaghna*, An epithet of Yamāri.

## Yama’s staff
An implement held by Mahākāla in Mahākāla’s Sovereign Tantra. Yama is the lord of death, who judges the dead and rules over the hells.

## Yama’s world
*gshin rje’i ’jig rten*, Skt. *yamaloka*, The world of the dead, another term for the realm of anguished spirits.

## Yama­varuṇa­kubera­vāsava­śrī
*gshin rje dang chu lha dang ku be ra dang brgya byin la sogs pa’i dpal*, Skt. *yama­varuṇa­kubera­vāsava­śrī*, One of the names of Śrī Mahādevī.

## Yamāna
*nges ’tsho*, Skt. *yamāna*, One of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin.

## Yamāntaka
*gshin rje bshed*, wrathful form of [Mañjuśrī](#mañjuśrī).

## Yamāri
*gshin rje’i gshed*, Skt. *yamāri*, “Yama’s enemy,” also known as Yamāntaka, “Yama’s Killer” is a wrathful form of Mañjuśrī who, in red and black forms, is a prominent deity in both the Indian and Tibetan Buddhist tantric traditions. The term yamāri is also applied to other deities in Yamāntaka's maṇḍala, specifically to the manifestations of Yamāri associated with the afflictive emotions.

## Yamāri Dveṣavajra
*zhe sdang rdo rje gshin rje’i gshed*, Skt. *dveṣavajra­yamāri*, “Yamāri Vajra Hatred,” a deity in the maṇḍala of Black Yamāri. Also known as Dveṣa Yamāri.

## Yamāri Mohavajra
*gti mug rdo rje gshin rje’i gshed*, Skt. *moha­vajrāyamāri*, “Yamāri Vajra Ignorance, a deity in the maṇḍala of Black Yamāri. Also known as Mohavajra and Moha Yamāri.

## Yamāri Piśunavajra
*phra ma rdo rje gshin rje’i gshed*, Skt. *piśuna­vajrayamāri*, “Yamāri Vajra Miserliness,” a deity in the maṇḍala of Black Yamāri. Also known as Piśunavajra and Piśuna Yamāri.

## Yamāri Rāgavajra
*’dod chags rdo rje gshin rje’i gshed*, Skt. *rāgavajra­yamāri*, “Yamāri Vajra Desire,” a deity in the maṇḍala of Black Yamāri. Also known as Rāgavajra and Rāga Yamāri.

## Yamāri Īrṣyāvajra
*phrag dog rdo rje gshin rje’i gshed*, Skt. *īṛṣyāvajra­yamāri*, “Yamāri Vajra Jealousy,” a deity in the maṇḍala of Black Yamāri. Also known as Īrṣyāvajra and Yamāri Īrṣyāvajra.

## yamāri vajra
*gshin rje’i gshed po rdo rje*, Skt. *yamārivajra*, The name of a meditative absorption.

## Yamunā
*ya mu nA*, Skt. *yamunā*, A river in Jambudvīpa, still called by the same name today.

## Āṇḍāyana
One of the sublineages connected with the Vāsiṣṭha lineage of the brahmanical tradition.

## yantra
*’khrul ’khor*, Skt. *yantra*, A diagram used for a variety of ritual purposes. In The Tantra of Black Yamāri, the primary yantra consists of two concentric circles with varying numbers of cells in which mantra syllables and/or the name of the rite’s target are written. The term can also refer more broadly to a tool or device.

## Yaśodā
*grags sbyin ma*, Skt. *yaśodā*, One of the female śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Yaśoda
*grags sbyin*, Skt. *yaśoda*, One of the śrāvakas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Yaśodatta
*grags pa byin*, Skt. *yaśodatta*, The 593rd buddha in the first list, 592nd in the second list, and 586th in the third list.

## Yaśodeva
*grags sbyin*, Skt. *yaśodeva*, One of the monks attending this teaching in Śrāvastī, at Jeta’s Grove.

## Yaśodgata
*grags pas ’phags pa*, Skt. *yaśodgata*, A bodhisattva present in Śrāvastī.

## Yaśodharā
*grags ’dzin*, Skt. *yaśodharā*, The wife of Prince Siddhartha and mother of his son Rāhula. She took up an ascetic lifestyle after his departure from the palace, and later, when women were finally allowed to go forth, became a nun under Mahāprajāpatī. She attained the level of arhat and was declared foremost among nuns possessing the superknowledges.

## Yaśodhara
*grags ’chang*, Skt. *yaśodhara*, A buddha.

## Yaśomati
*blo gros pa*, Skt. *yaśomati*, The 107th buddha in the first list, 107th in the second list, and 108th in the third list.

## Yaśomitra
*grags pa’i bshes gnyen*, Skt. *yaśomitra*, The 333rd buddha in the first list, 332nd in the second list, and 327th in the third list.

## Yaśonandin
*snyan pa dang dga’ can*, Skt. *yaśonandin*, Divided into two names in the Tibetan but appears as one name in the Sanskrit and Chinese. The name that the Buddha Ratnagarbha prophesies will be that of one of his eighty brothers (the fortieth) when he becomes a buddha.

## Yaśoratna
*rin chen grags pa*, Skt. *yaśoratna*, The 438th buddha in the first list, 437th in the second list, and 431st in the third list.

## Yaśottara
*grags mchog*, Skt. *yaśottara*, In chapter 29 the name of the eighth buddha in a list that begins with Kanaka­muni. In the Mahāvastu there is a list of past buddhas in which Yaśottara appears between Tiṣya and Puṣya.

## Yaśovat
*grags ldan*, Skt. *yaśovat*, One of the bodhisattvas attending the delivery of the MMK.

## Yaśovatī
*grags ldan ma*, Skt. *yaśovatī*, “Renowned.” The title of this text containing multiple dhāraṇīs. This name may refer to a goddess, to the dhāraṇī itself, or to both. See .

## yard
*sab mos bskor ba*, Skt. *vātadattikā, vāṭadattikā*, an acceptable form of shelter for a monk, as identified in the [Four Supports](#four-supports) [section](#section) of the ordination ritual.

## Yarlung Lotsāwa Drakpa Gyaltsen
*yar klungs lo tsA ba grags pa rgyal mtshan*, Skt. *yar klungs lo tsA ba grags pa rgyal mtshan*, The translator of a number of tantras in the Kangyur and commentarial works in the Tengyur, active in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries (1242–1346), probably at Sakya.

## Yarlung Valley
*yar lung*, A valley in South Tibet.

## Yasyana
*yas sya na*, Skt. *yasyana*, One of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin.

## Āyatī
*’byung bar byed*, Skt. *āyatī*, A yakṣa general.

## āyatana
*skye mched*, Skt. *āyatana*, This term has variousPlease replace with standard def, as in 555. meanings according to context, Within the phases of dependent origination it means the sensory faculties only: the six sensory faculties of the eyes, nose, ear, tongue, body, and mind, which form in the womb and will eventually have contact with the external six bases of sensory perception: form, smell, sound, taste, touch, and phenomena. All these together are called the twelve āyatanas, or bases of sensory perception. Also this term is used to refer to the four meditative states associated with the formless realm: 1) infinite space, 2) infinite consciousness, 3) nothingness, and 4) neither perception nor non-perception.

## Yatrava
*sdom brtson ’khor*, Skt. *yatrava*, One of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin.

## Yavana
As a Sanskritization of the Middle Indic yona, the term referred to the Hellenistic “Ionians” who had settled in the Bactrian region and in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent after the conquest of Alexander the Great. In later times it came to refer to anyone coming from the Iranian plateau, including Arab Muslims. The Tibetan rendering reflects an understanding of the Sanskrit yavana as etymologically derived from yava (“barley”).

## Yavanadvīpa
*nas kyi gling*, Skt. *yavanadvīpa*, Literally “The Barley Islands,” this refers to the land of the Greeks, whose empire at one time extended along the northern coasts of the Persian gulf as far as India.

## yawning lion
*seng ge rnam par bsgyings pa*, Skt. *siṃha­vijṛmbhita*, The 28th meditative stability in chapters 6 and 8, and a meditative stability on its own. According to the Long Commentary on the Hundred Thousand Lines (Toh 3807, F.53.a), it refers to a tathāgata’s power to overcome or even preempt all opposition by sheer power and magnificence.

## yearners
*zhen byed*, Skt. *zhen byed*, Parasites that are said to live on the sides of women’s necks and heads.

## Yearning
*rab tu gdung ba*, Skt. *rab tu gdung ba*, Yearning (intense longing or desire), also the name of the father of the buddha Vaśavartirāja.

## years
*lo khyud ’khor*, Skt. *saṃvatsara*, Lit. “yearly cycle.”

## Yellow Acala
*mi g.yo ba ser po*, Skt. *pītācala*, Acala corresponding to Buddha Ratnasambhava in the south of the maṇḍala.

## Yellow Honey-Color
*ser po sbrang rtsi’i mdog*, Skt. *ser po sbrang rtsi’i mdog*, A rākṣasa king present in the assembly of the Buddha Śākyamuni.

## yellow myrobalan
Terminalia chebula. One of the three myrobalan fruits.

## yellow orpiment
A substance used in the performance of tantric rituals as a kind of ink for writing down mantras or as an additive for a number of ritual preparations.

## yellow sandalwood
*dus dang mthun pa’i tsan dan*, Skt. *kālānusāri­candana*, Sanskrit dictionaries also define the word as “gum benzoin” (not to be confused with the unrelated chemical, benzoin) and the Shisham or Indian Rosewood tree (Dalbergia sissoo). However, in this sūtra this is evidently referring to a kind of sandalwood (Santalum album). The name, which means “following time,” refers to the long-lasting scent of the wood. In other texts kālānusāri­candana is translated as dus kyi rjes su ’brang ba.

## Yellow scroll
*shog ser*, piece of paper (not necessarily yellow) on which the texts of [spiritual treasures](#spiritual-treasure) are written.

## yellow-berried nightshade
*sman bri ha ti*, Skt. *bṛhatī*, Solanum xanthocarpum.

## Yellow-Robed
*ser mo*, Skt. *ser mo*, A Hindu goddess, unidentified. McCombs (p. 128) suggests that the Sanskrit name for this goddess might be Pītā or Vāruṇī.

## Yerpa
*yer pa*, Skt. *yer pa*, A site in Tibet near Lhasa, originally a place of retreat, with many caves and small temples.

## Yeshé Dé
*ye shes sde*, Skt. *ye shes sde*, Yeshé Dé (late eighth to early ninth century) was the most prolific translator of sūtras into Tibetan. Altogether he is credited with the translation of more than one hundred sixty sūtra translations and more than one hundred additional translations, mostly on tantric topics. In spite of Yeshé Dé’s great importance for the propagation of Buddhism in Tibet during the imperial era, only a few biographical details about this figure are known. Later sources describe him as a student of the Indian teacher Padmasambhava, and he is also credited with teaching both sūtra and tantra widely to students of his own.

## Yeshé Nyingpo
*ye shes snying po*, Skt. *ye shes snying po*, The sūtra’s Tibetan translator.

## Yeshé Wangpo
Full name Ba Yeshé Wangpo (dba’ ye shes dbang po), he was a Tibetan monk and translator active in the eighth century and a disciple of Śāntarakṣita.

## Yeshe Tsogyal
*ye shes mtsho rgyal*, [Padmasambhava's](#padmasambhava-of-oḍḍiyāna) mystic [consort](#consort) and greatest [disciple](#disciple). She served him perfectly, and helped him to propagate his teachings, in particular concealing [spiritual treasures](#spiritual-treasure) to be rediscovered later for the sake of future [disciple](#disciple)s.

## Yāṣṭi
Skt. *yāṣṭi*, One of the grahas.

## Yidam
*yi dam*, Skt. *devatā*, *iṣṭadevatā*, a [deity](#deity) representing [enlightenment](#enlightenment), in a male or female, peaceful or wrathful form corresponding to one's individual nature. The yidam is the source of [accomplishment](#accomplishment)s. See [three roots](#three-roots).

## Yielding All Fruits
*’bras bu kun phyed*, Skt. *’bras bu kun phyed*, A park in Sustained by Fruition.

## Yielding as Wished
*bsams bzhin ster*, Skt. *bsams bzhin ster*, Birthplace of the buddha Samṛddha.

## Yielding to Pressure and Bouncing Back
*mnan na nem la bteg na ’phar ba*, Skt. *mnan na nem la bteg na ’phar ba*, A forest on Tamer of Deer Enemies.

## Yijing
Skt. *A seventh-century Chinese Buddhist monk, who studied in Nālandā*, A seventh-century Chinese Buddhist monk, who studied in Nālandā monastery in India and translated many texts including the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya.

## Yāmā
*yA ma*, Skt. *yāmā*, A great rākṣasī.

## Yāma
*’thab bral*, Skt. *yāma*, Lit. “The Discharged.” The third of the six heavens of the realm of desire; also the name of the gods living there. The Tibetan translation ’thab bral, “free from strife or combat,” derives from the idea that these devas, because they live in an aerial abode above Sumeru, do not have to engage in combat with the asuras who dwell on the slopes of the mountain.

## Śyāma
*ljang gu*, Skt. *śyāma*, A brahmin youth who was the Buddha in a former life.

## Yāma class
*’thab bral*, Skt. *yāma*, A class of devas of the realm of sensuous desire (kāmadhātu). The Tibetan translation ’thab bral (“free of conflict/without combat”) derives from the idea that these gods, because they live in an aerial abode above Mount Sumeru, do not have to engage in combat with the asuras who dwell on the slopes of the mountain.

## Yāma Heaven
The third of the six heavens of the realm of desire; also the name of the gods living there. The Tibetan translation ’thab bral, “free from strife or combat,” derives from the idea that these devas, because they live in an aerial abode above Sumeru, do not have to engage in combat with the asuras who dwell on the slopes of the mountain.

## Yāma Mahākāla
*gshin rje ma hA kA la*, Skt. *gshin rje ma hA kA la*, The divine brother of Red Cāmuṇḍī. His parents are the goddess Umadevī and the god Mahādeva.

## yāmaka
*gshin rje*, Skt. *yāmaka*, A class of supernatural beings.

## Śyāmaka
A brahmin in this sūtra; the Sanskrit name is attested as names of a king and a muni in the Bodhisattvāvadāna­kalpalatā and the Rāṣṭrapāla­pari­pṛcchā, respectively.

## yāmas
See also “Yāma Heaven”.

## Śyāmākajātaka
*dkar sham gyi skyes pa’i rabs*, Skt. *śyāmākajātaka*, See Kudo 2004, pp. 250–51, n. 23, for parallel versions and further readings for this sūtra.

## Śyāmāvatī
One of King Udayana’s wives.

## Yāmyā
*gshin rje mo*, Skt. *yāmyā*, One of the great mātṛs.

## yāna
*theg pa*, Skt. *yāna*, A “way of going,” which primarily means a path or a way. It can also mean a conveyance or carriage; this definition is represented in commentarial literature by the Tibetan translation as “carrier,” and therefore it is also translated into English as “vehicle.”

## Yodhana
*’thab pa*, Skt. *yodhana*, One of the kings of the rākṣasas.

## Yodheya
*g.yul ’gyed ldan pa*, Skt. *yodheya*, A geographical location in this sūtra.

## Yogī or Yoginī
*rnal 'byor pa* or *rnal 'byor ma*, someone who practices [yoga](#yoga), a spiritual practitioner.

## Yoga
*rnal 'byor*, practice, lit. a method for uniting (*'byor*) with the [natural state](#natural-state) (*rnal ma*).

## Yogapratiṣṭha
*rnam ’byor ’gro*, Skt. *yogapratiṣṭha*, One of the rāśis.

## yogācāra
*rnal ’byor spyod pa*, Skt. *yogācāra*, A “practitioner of yoga” meaning one dedicated to meditation practice. It can be synonymous with yogin. This is not reference to the Yogācāra school of thought that developed within the Mahāyāna.

## Yogeśvara
*rnal ’byor dbang phyug*, Skt. *yogeśvara*, One of the sages (ṛṣi).

## yogic conduct
*brtul zhugs*, Skt. *vrata*, A prescribed mode of behavior, typically time-delimited, that is observed in connection with specific rites and practices.

## Yogic Discipline
*brtul zhugs*, Skt. *brtul zhugs*, Attendant of the buddha Brahmaghoṣa.

## Yogic Discipline of Liberation
*thar pa’i brtul zhugs*, Skt. *thar pa’i brtul zhugs*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Avraṇa (811 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## Yogic Discipline of Wisdom
*ye shes brtul zhugs*, Skt. *ye shes brtul zhugs*, Buddha in the presence of whom the buddha Anihata (433 according to the third enumeration) first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

## yogic practice
*rnal ’byor*, Skt. *yoga*, A term which is generally used to refer to a wide range of spiritual practices. It literally means to be merged with or “yoked to,” in the sense of being fully immersed in one’s respective discipline. The Tibetan specifies “union with the natural state.”

## yogin
*rnal ’byor pa*, Skt. *yogin*, “The one who is united,” a succesful practitioner who has attained realization. The Tibetan means “one who is united with the genuine nature.”

## yoginī
Depending on the context, this term can signify a class of potentially harmful female beings, goddesses associated with various astrological conjunctions, female yoga practitioners (both human and nonhuman), the awakened consorts of male tantric deities, and the awakened female leaders of tantric maṇḍalas.

## Yoginītantra
*rnal ’byor ma’i rgyud*, Skt. *yoginī­tantra*, The last development of Buddhist tantra in India, focused upon the figure of the yoginī and the meditative manipulation of the subtle energetic anatomy of the physical body. Typified by the He­vajra­tantra, Cakrasaṃvaratantra, and the Mahā­māyā­tantra.

## yojana
*dpag tshad*, Skt. *yojana*, A common measure of distance in ancient India. It refers to the distance that an ox cart can traverse in one day, that is, in one “harnessing” (yojana), i.e., before unyoking the oxen. Each region seems to have had its own estimate of this distance. In the eastern region of Magadha, a yojana consisted of four krośas, thus equalling about 4.5 miles or 7.4 kilometers. In Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośa (III 88), on the other hand, a yojana is defined as consisting of eight krośas, which indicates that in the northwestern region of Gandhāra it referred to a distance twice as long as in Magadha.

## yojanas
The longest unit of distance in classical India. The lack of a uniform standard for the smaller units means that there is no precise equivalent, especially as its theoretical length tended to increase over time. Therefore it can mean between four and ten miles.

## yoke
*gnya’ shing*, Skt. *yuga*, The yoke, a wooden bar placed across an animal’s shoulders when ploughing, was commonly used as a measure of length, equal to four cubits.

## Yongzheng
The third emperor from the Manchu Qing dynasty to rule over China, Yongzheng was born in 1678 and ruled from 1722 until his death in 1735. King Tenpa Tsering submitted to him in 1728.

## young brahmin
*ma na ba*, Skt. *māṇava*, This renders the vocative Tibetan ma na ba, which is an approximate phonetic rendition of Sanskrit māṇava “lad, boy, youth; young brahmin” (cf. Apte, s.v. māṇava). When not in the vocative in direct speech, we have translated it as “brahmin youth.”

## young god
*lha’i bu*, Skt. *devaputra*, Generic term for a class of long-lived celestial beings.

## Your Majesty
*lha*, *(deva)*, The term *deva*, meaning “god,” was often used as an honorific term of address for divine beings and royalty.

## Youth of Latticed Light
*dra ba can gyi ’od gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *dra ba can gyi ’od gzhon nur gyur pa*, A bodhisattva.

## Youth Who Renounces All
*bdog pa thams cad yongs su gtong ba gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *sarva­tyāga­kumāra­bhūta*, A bodhisattva.

## Youth Who Turns the Dharma Wheel Upon Generating the Mind of Awakening
*sems bskyed ma thag tu chos kyi ’khor lo bskor ba gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *sems bskyed ma thag tu chos kyi ’khor lo bskor ba gzhon nur gyur pa*, A bodhisattva.

## Youthful Candraprabha
*zla ’od gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *candraprabha*, A bodhisattva.

## Youthful Clearer
*rnam par sel ba gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *rnam par sel ba gzhon nur gyur pa*, A bodhisattva.

## Youthful Glorious Essence
*dpal gyi snying po gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *śrī­garbha­kumāra­bhūta*, A bodhisattva.

## Youthful Jewel-Holder
*lag na rin chen gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *lag na rin chen gzhon nur gyur pa*, A bodhisattva.

## Youthful Lion
*seng ge gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *seng ge gzhon nur gyur pa*, A bodhisattva.

## Youthful Mañjuśrī
*’jam dpal gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *mañjuśrī­kumāra­bhūta*, Mañjuśrī who takes the form of a youth, an epithet by which the well-known bodhisattva is often referred. He is considered to be the embodiment of the transcendent perfection of insight and is portrayed wielding a sword in his right hand that cuts through delusion and a volume of the Prajñā­pāramitā­sūtra in his left that contains teachings on transcendent insight.

## Youthful Moonbeam
*zla ba’i ’od zer gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *candrāṃśu­kumāra­bhūta*, A bodhisattva.

## Youthful Moonlight
*zla ’od gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *candra­prabha­kumāra­bhūta*, A bodhisattva.

## youthful one
*gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *kumārabhūta*, The term, depending on context, can refer either to bodhisattvas who remain celibate, or to bodhisattvas at the advanced level of “crown prince” who are awaiting the final stages to buddhahood that include regency and consecration. See also “level of a crown prince.”

## youthful ones
*gzhon nur gyur pa*, An epithet for bodhisattvas.

## Youthful Ornament
*rgyan bkod pa gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *rgyan bkod pa gzhon nur gyur pa*, A bodhisattva.

## Youthful Precious Seal-Holder
*lag na phyag rgya rin chen gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *lag na phyag rgya rin chen gzhon nur gyur pa*, A bodhisattva.

## Youthful Sky-Treasury
*nam mkha’ mdzod gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *nam mkha’ mdzod gzhon nur gyur pa*, A bodhisattva.

## Youthful Splendorous Viśākha
*sa ga gzhon nu dpal*, A senior disciple of the Buddha.

## Youthful Supreme Intelligence
*mchog gi blo gros gzhon nur gyur pa*, Skt. *mchog gi blo gros gzhon nur gyur pa*, A bodhisattva.

## Yārmatha
*yar ma tha*, Skt. *yārmatha*, One of the thousand sons of King Araṇemin.

## Yātrā
*’gro ma*, Skt. *yātrā*, One of the great dūtīs attending upon Lord Vajrapāṇi.

## Yātu
Skt. *yātu*, A legendary king before the time of the Buddha.

## Yuddhajaya
*g.yul las rnam par rgyal ba*, Skt. *yuddhajaya*, A bodhisattva.

## Yudhiṣṭhira
*g.yul ngor brtan pa*, Skt. *yudhiṣṭhira*, One of the five Pāṇḍava brothers. Son of the god Dharma.

## yuga
A period of time, ranging from several years to an eon.

## Yugandhara
*gnya’ shing ’dzin*, Skt. *yugaṃdhara*, The innermost of the seven golden mountain ranges that encircle Sumeru, in the center of the disk of the world. It is presented differently in other systems; for example, it is sometimes the fourth of these mountains.

## Yugānta
*dus kyi mtha’*, Skt. *yugānta*, One of the grahas.

## Yugāntakara
*dus mthar byed*, Skt. *yugāntakara*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Yugāntārka
*dus kyi mtha’i nyi ma*, Skt. *yugāntārka*, A vidyārāja from the personal retinue of Vajrapāṇi.

## Āyurveda
*tshe’i rig byed*, Skt. *āyurveda*, The classical system of Indian medicine. (Toh 555: shes pa)

## Āyustejas
*’brug sgra*, Skt. *āyustejas*, A buddha in the past.

## Zalmo range
The Zalmogang is counted among the six mountain ranges of eastern Tibet. It covers areas such as Palyul, Degé, Denma, Nyarong, and Sershul.

## Zangkyong
*bzang skyong*, Skt. *bzang skyong*, Tibetan translator of the ninth century.

## Zhalu
The name of a monastery and a myriarchy in the Tsang region of Central Tibet. Zhalu is among the oldest monasteries in Tibet, with some structures dating to the first half of the eleventh century ce. The monastery was affiliated with the Kadampa school and had close ties with the Sakya school during parts of the Yuan period. The famous scholar and Tibetan Buddhist canon redactor Butön Rinchen Drup (bu ston rin chen grub, 1290–1364) became abbot of Zhalu in 1320, which marks the beginning of a new lineage called bu lugs tshul (“Tradition of Butön”) or zhwa lu pa (“Those of Zhalu”).

## Zhang Yeshe Dé
*zhang ye shes sde*, One of the most important Tibetan translators and chief editors of the early translation period (late eighth and early ninth century), responsible for a large number of canonical translations and author of several Tengyur texts.

## Zhi Qian
A famous translator into Chinese active in the first half of the third century.

## Zu Gador
*gzu dga’ rdor*, Skt. *gzu dga’ rdor*, Zu Gawé Dorjé (gzu dga’ ba’i rdo rje) was a Tibetan translator active in the second half of the eleventh century.

## Zu Gawé Dorjé
*gzu dga’ rdor*, Skt. *gzu dga’ rdor*, A Tibetan translator active in the second half of the eleventh century.

## Zu Gawé Dorje
*gzu dga’ ba’i rdo rje*, Skt. *gzu dga’ ba’i rdo rje*, A Tibetan translator active in the second half of the eleventh century.
